docs.title: Control Systems Standards
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from .claude/rules/control-systems.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in .claude/rules/.

⚠️ Mandatory for every signal path that moves hardware or estimates physical state.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
• CLAUDE.md
  • code-standards.md — general code standards
  • matlab-code-standards.md — MATLAB/Simulink specifics
  • project-config.json
  • skills/foc-motor-control

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This rule applies to any change under:

Source/ROS2_Control_System/ · Source/ROS2_Flight_Controller/ · Source/ROS2_JetOwl_Bridge/ Source/ROS2_Lidar_SLAM/ · Source/ROS2_Mission_Planner/ · Microcontroller/ · MATLAB/ Gazebo/ROS2_Hexacopter_Control/ · Gazebo/ROS2_Hexacopter_Gazebo/ · Gazebo/ROS2_Mcu_Emulator/

…and to any node elsewhere that consumes a sensor topic and publishes a command (geometry_msgs/Twist, PWM, servo, thrust, steering, gimbal).

docs.title: 1. The required signal chain
docs.text:
No actuator command may be derived directly from a raw sensor reading. Every path is built from these stages, and each stage is justified in the code and in the package README:

 ┌────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌───────────┐   ┌────────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌───────┐
 │ Sensor │──▶│ Filter  │──▶│ Estimator │──▶│ Controller │──▶│ Actuator │──▶│ Plant │
 └────────┘   └─────────┘   └───────────┘   └────────────┘   └──────────┘   └───┬───┘
      ▲         anti-alias     KF/EKF/UKF      PID / LQR /       saturation      │
      │         outlier        observer        MPC / FOC /       rate limit      │
      │         rejection      fusion          SMC / MRAC        deadzone        │
      └──────────────────────── feedback (measured state) ───────────────────────┘

Closed loop is the default. Open loop is permitted only when the controlled quantity is physically unobservable with the installed sensor set. Then the code must state why, bound the resulting error, and add a watchdog/timeout that drives the actuator to a safe state.

docs.title: 2.1 Sensor interface
docs.text:
Document, in the node's header comment and its parameter YAML:

  • Measurement model y[k] = h(x[k]) + v[k], with units in SI and the frame (base_link, imu_link, …).
  • Noise characterisation — variance R from datasheet or bench measurement. For IMUs, report the Allan-variance parameters (angle/velocity random walk N, bias instability B) and derive σ² = N²·f_s.
  • Sample rate f_s, latency and jitter, measured — not assumed.
  • Fault modes — dropout, saturation, NaN, stale timestamp — and the defined behaviour for each.

docs.title: 2.2 Filtering (mandatory before any estimator)
docs.text:
• Anti-aliasing: the sampled signal must satisfy Nyquist, f_s > 2·f_max; in practice design for f_s ≥ 10·f_bandwidth. If the analogue path cannot guarantee it, state the aliasing risk.
  • Low-pass: state the continuous prototype and the discretisation. First-order:
H(s) = ω_c / (s + ω_c)          ω_c = 2π f_c
Tustin (bilinear, ω_c pre-warped):  y[k] = (1-α)·y[k-1] + α·x[k],  α = (2π f_c T_s)/(1 + 2π f_c T_s)
Record f_c, the resulting phase lag φ(ω) = -arctan(ω/ω_c) at the loop crossover, and confirm the lag is inside the phase-margin budget of §4. - Outlier rejection: median or Hampel filter for spiky sensors (LiDAR, ToF, current sense); state the window length and the rejection threshold in σ. - Notch for known mechanical/propeller resonances: give the centre frequency and its source. - A moving average is a filter with a known response — y[k] = (1/N)Σx[k-i], |H(ω)| = |sin(NωT_s/2) / (N sin(ωT_s/2))|, group delay (N-1)T_s/2. Use it only with those numbers written down.

docs.title: 2.3 State estimation
docs.text:
Raw filtered measurements are not state. Fuse them:

Plant Estimator Linear, Gaussian Kalman filter Mildly nonlinear, differentiable EKF (Jacobians F, H derived in comments) Strongly nonlinear UKF (state α, β, κ) or particle filter Attitude from IMU only Complementary filter with derived crossover, or Madgwick/Mahony Unmeasured states, deterministic Luenberger observer / high-gain observer Unknown constant disturbance Disturbance observer (DOB) or integral action

Required in the code:

Predict:  x̂[k|k-1] = f(x̂[k-1|k-1], u[k-1])
          P[k|k-1]  = F·P[k-1|k-1]·Fᵀ + Q
Update:   K[k]      = P[k|k-1]·Hᵀ·(H·P[k|k-1]·Hᵀ + R)⁻¹
          x̂[k|k]    = x̂[k|k-1] + K[k]·(y[k] - h(x̂[k|k-1]))
          P[k|k]    = (I - K[k]·H)·P[k|k-1]        # use Joseph form when numerically marginal
  • Observability must be checked, not assumed: rank of O = [H; HF; …; HF^(n-1)] equals n, or the unobservable subspace is named and left uncontrolled.
  • Q and R come from physical noise densities, not from trial and error. If a term is tuned, say which one and against what data.
  • Consistency test required: NIS (normalised innovation squared) inside its χ² bounds over a recorded run. Store the plot or the numbers with the package.

docs.title: 2.4 Controller
docs.text:
Pick by plant and constraints — PID is a default, not the only answer:

Situation Controller SISO, benign dynamics, no hard constraints PID (with the terms of §2.4.1) MIMO, known linear model, quadratic cost LQR / LQG, gains from the Riccati solution Hard state/input constraints, preview available MPC (QP each step, horizon N, terminal cost/set stated) BLDC/PMSM torque and speed FOC — see foc-motor-control Matched uncertainty, robustness first Sliding mode (surface s, reaching law, chattering mitigation) Unknown/slowly varying parameters MRAC / adaptive, with the Lyapunov-derived update law Cascaded rigid-body dynamics (attitude→rate) Backstepping or nested loops with ≥5× bandwidth separation Known trajectory, invertible model Feedforward + feedback (2-DOF)

docs.title: 2.4.1 If it is a PID, it is a complete PID
docs.text:
Parallel form:  u(t) = Kp·e(t) + Ki∫e(τ)dτ + Kd·de(t)/dt
Realisable D:   D(s) = Kd·s / (1 + s·Kd/(Kp·N)),   N ∈ [8, 20]     # derivative filtering
Discrete (Ts):  integral by trapezoid, derivative by filtered backward difference
Anti-windup:    back-calculation  I[k] += Ki·Ts·e[k] + Tt⁻¹·(u_sat - u)·Ts,  Tt ≈ √(Ti·Td)
Bumpless:       hold I on mode switch; derivative on measurement, not on error (no setpoint kick)
Gains must come from a method that can be named: Ziegler–Nichols (as a starting point only), pole placement against an identified model, IMC/lambda tuning, or LQR-equivalent. Record the identified plant model G(s) and the resulting margins.

docs.title: 2.4.2 Discretisation and timing
docs.text:
• State T_s, and show T_s ≤ 1/(10·f_bw) … 1/(20·f_bw) for the closed-loop bandwidth f_bw.
  • Name the discretisation (ZOH, Tustin, Tustin with pre-warp) and keep it consistent between the MATLAB design and the C/Python implementation.
  • Account for computational and transport delay τ: it costs phase Δφ = -ω·τ. ROS 2 topic hops, DDS latency and serial links all count. Budget them in §4.

docs.title: 2.5 Actuator interface
docs.text:
• Saturation u_sat = clamp(u, u_min, u_max) — always, and fed back to anti-windup.
  • Rate limiting where the hardware has a slew limit; state it in units/s.
  • Deadzone / friction compensation for gimbals and drivetrains, with the measured deadband.
  • Mapping to hardware (PWM duty, SVPWM, servo µs) documented with its calibration.
  • Failsafe: on estimator divergence, stale feedback or watchdog timeout, command the defined safe output (zero torque, hover, brake) — never the last value silently.

docs.title: 2.6 Feedback closure
docs.text: The measured (not commanded) state returns to the controller. Log at minimum: setpoint, measurement, estimate, error, each controller term, the pre- and post-saturation command, and the loop timestamp. Without those logs a controller cannot be reviewed.

docs.title: 3. What is not acceptable
docs.text:
• Magic constants — speed = error * 0.37 — with no model, units or derivation.
  • Gains "tuned until it looked stable" with no margin or step-response evidence.
  • Feeding raw IMU/LiDAR/encoder data straight into a controller.
  • A derivative term on a noisy signal with no filter and no N.
  • An integrator with no anti-windup on a saturating actuator.
  • An estimator whose Q/R were chosen to make a plot look smooth.
  • Copying a control law from a blog or an LLM answer without the source and the derivation.
  • Open loop where a sensor exists that closes the loop.

docs.title: 4. Stability and performance evidence
docs.text:
Every controller change ships with:

  1. Plant model — first-principles or identified (tfest/ssest/step or PRBS response), with the validation fit reported.
  2. Margins — gain margin ≥ 6 dB, phase margin ≥ 45° (≥ 30° for inner current loops), computed including filter lag and transport delay. For discrete designs, all closed-loop poles |z| < 1.
  3. Time-domain spec — rise time, overshoot (typically ≤ 10–20 %), settling time, steady-state error, disturbance rejection. State the target before tuning.
  4. Nonlinear systems — a Lyapunov function V > 0, V̇ ≤ 0, or an explicitly stated region/assumption where the linearisation holds.
  5. Robustness — behaviour under ±20 % parameter error (mass, inertia, Kt, R, L) and sensor dropout.

Verification order (never skip ahead): MATLAB/Simulink model → software-in-the-loop (ROS 2 sim) → hardware-in-the-loop → bench with current limits → vehicle. Bench and HIL results belong in the PR.

docs.title: 5. Documentation template
docs.text:
Every controller/estimator header carries this block, after the SPDX header:

%  CONTROL DESIGN
%    Plant model   : G(s) = K/(τs+1)·e^(-Ls),  K=1.8 rad/s/V, τ=0.12 s, L=8 ms
%                    (identified from step response, Data/ident/motor_step_2026-09-12.csv, fit 94 %)
%    Sensor        : AS5048A encoder, 14-bit, f_s = 1 kHz, σ = 0.02 deg
%    Filter        : 2nd-order Butterworth LPF, f_c = 80 Hz, Tustin @ T_s = 1 ms, lag 14° @ 20 Hz
%    Estimator     : Kalman, states [θ, ω, b], Q = diag(...), R = 4e-4, NIS within 95 % bounds
%    Controller    : PI with back-calculation anti-windup, Kp = 2.4, Ki = 18, Tt = 0.05
%                    Designed by pole placement for ζ = 0.8, ω_n = 25 rad/s
%    Actuator      : PWM 20 kHz, u ∈ [-12, 12] V, slew 400 V/s, deadband ±0.35 V compensated
%    Loop          : closed, feedback = estimated θ; watchdog 50 ms → coast
%    Margins       : GM = 11 dB, PM = 58° @ 21 rad/s (incl. 8 ms delay)
%    Verification  : MATLAB/sim/motor_pi_test.slx, HIL log Data/hil/2026-09-14_motor.bag
%    Reference     : Åström & Hägglund, "Advanced PID Control", ch. 3

docs.title: 6. Approved references
docs.text:
Cite one of these (or a peer-reviewed paper / manufacturer application note) rather than an unattributed source:

  • K. J. Åström, R. M. Murray — Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers
  • K. J. Åström, T. Hägglund — Advanced PID Control
  • G. F. Franklin, J. D. Powell, A. Emami-Naeini — Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems
  • G. F. Franklin, J. D. Powell, M. Workman — Digital Control of Dynamic Systems
  • K. Ogata — Modern Control Engineering / Discrete-Time Control Systems
  • D. Simon — Optimal State Estimation: Kalman, H∞, and Nonlinear Approaches
  • Y. Bar-Shalom, X.-R. Li, T. Kirubarajan — Estimation with Applications to Tracking and Navigation
  • J. B. Rawlings, D. Q. Mayne, M. M. Diehl — Model Predictive Control: Theory, Computation, and Design
  • H. K. Khalil — Nonlinear Systems
  • M. Krstić, I. Kanellakopoulos, P. Kokotović — Nonlinear and Adaptive Control Design
  • D. W. Novotny, T. A. Lipo — Vector Control and Dynamics of AC Drives (FOC)
  • W. Leonhard — Control of Electrical Drives
  • P. D. Groves — Principles of GNSS, Inertial, and Multisensor Integrated Navigation Systems
  • S. Thrun, W. Burgard, D. Fox — Probabilistic Robotics
  • TI/ST/Microchip motor-control application notes (cite the document number)

docs.title: 7. Review checklist
docs.text:
• Signal chain complete: sensor → filter → estimator → controller → actuator → feedback
  • Sensor noise, sample rate, latency and units documented
  • Filter type, cutoff, discretisation and phase lag stated
  • Estimator chosen with justification; observability checked; Q/R traceable to physics
  • Estimator consistency (NIS/NEES) demonstrated on recorded data
  • Controller choice justified against the plant and its constraints
  • PID (if used) has derivative filtering, anti-windup and bumpless transfer
  • T_s stated and consistent with the closed-loop bandwidth; delays budgeted
  • Saturation, rate limit and failsafe implemented
  • Gain/phase margins or discrete pole locations reported, delays included
  • Simulation → SIL → HIL evidence attached to the PR
  • Reference cited for the control law
  • All loop signals logged for review

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: Every component follows Semantic Versioning: MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, PATCH for fixes. Package versions live in package.xml / setup.py and are quoted in the package README (for example ros2_control_system 0.6.0).

docs.title: Changelogs
docs.text:
Changelog Content <component>/CHANGELOG.md the component's own history (packages, CUDA/, DeepLearning/, Server_OTA/, …) .github/CHANGELOG.md repository-level summary of each merged change Docs/CHANGELOG.md the documentation site Changelog user-facing summary on this site

Entries follow the project template: What's New, Performance Improvements with numbers, Breaking Changes with old/new/migration, Known Limitations and Issues Addressed. Internal refactoring, test-only changes and formatting are not listed.

docs.title: Artefacts
docs.text:
Artefact How it is produced Where it goes Container images Docker/scripts/build_all.sh --push --tag vX.Y.Z registry 192.168.10.1:5000 Cluster deployment Helm/scripts/deploy.sh --set global.imageTag=vX.Y.Z --test k3s cluster Flight firmware make ota-upload VERSION=X.Y.Z (JetOwl_FlightControl) → jetowl_fc_vX.Y.Z.fw Server_OTA Camera firmware make ota-upload VERSION=X.Y.Z (JetOwl_Vision) → jetowl_vision_vX.Y.Z.fw Server_OTA Documentation push to master TNG-Blue/Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL-Docs (GitHub Pages)

Server_OTA validates every .fw package (header, SHA-256 and file name) on upload and never overwrites a published version.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. All quality gates green on master; firmware CI green in both firmware repositories.
  2. Component versions bumped and changelogs updated.
  3. Submodule pointers updated, and the submodule documentation snapshots regenerated with python3 Scripts/mkdocs_hooks/snapshot_submodules.py.
  4. Images built and pushed with the release tag; helm test passes on the cluster.
  5. Firmware packages uploaded; OTA confirmed on a bench unit before the fleet.
  6. A GitHub release created from the tag, linking the changelog entries.

docs.title: Example Unit Test
docs.text:
import pytest


class TestMyComponent:
    """Tests for MyComponent."""

    def test_initialization(self):
        """Test component initialization."""
        component = MyComponent()
        assert component is not None

    @pytest.mark.ros
    def test_ros_node(self):
        """Test ROS2 node functionality."""
        # Tests requiring ROS2 runtime
        pass

    @pytest.fixture
    def sample_data(self):
        """Provide sample data for tests."""
        return {"key": "value"}

    def test_with_fixture(self, sample_data):
        """Test using fixture."""
        assert sample_data["key"] == "value"

docs.title: Parameterized Tests
docs.text:
@pytest.mark.parametrize("input_value,expected", [
    (0, 0),
    (1, 1),
    (2, 4),
])
def test_square(input_value, expected):
    """Test square function."""
    assert input_value ** 2 == expected

docs.title: Test Markers
docs.text:
The following pytest markers are available:

  • @pytest.mark.ros - Tests requiring ROS2 packages or runtime

docs.title: Fixtures

Shared fixtures are defined in conftest.py. Common fixtures include:

  • Test data providers
  • Mock objects

Tests are automatically run in the CI/CD pipeline on:

pytest --cov=Source --cov-report=html
open htmlcov/index.html

docs.title: ROS2 Jazzy Compatibility
docs.text:
This testing framework is compatible with ROS2 Jazzy (Jalisco). Key considerations:

  • Use pytest-ros for ROS2-specific testing utilities
  • Initialize ROS2 context in fixtures when needed
  • Clean up ROS2 nodes properly in teardown
  • Use ROS2 launch testing for integration tests

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Test Isolation: Each test should be independent
  2. Clear Assertions: Use descriptive assertion messages
  3. Fast Tests: Keep unit tests fast (< 1 second each)
  4. Mock External Dependencies: Use mocks for external services
  5. Test Edge Cases: Include boundary conditions and error cases
  6. Documentation: Document complex test scenarios
  7. Consistent Style: Follow project coding standards (PEP 8)

docs.title: Tests Not Discovered
docs.text:
• Ensure test files start with test_
  • Ensure test functions start with test_
  • Check pytest.ini configuration

docs.title: ROS2 Tests Failing
docs.text:
• Verify ROS2 environment is sourced
  • Check ROS2 dependencies are installed
  • Ensure ROS2 nodes are properly initialized/cleaned up

docs.title: Import Errors
docs.text:
• Verify package is installed or PYTHONPATH is set
  • Check for circular dependencies
  • Ensure init.py files exist

docs.text: Tests assert derived properties — identities, invariants, consistency bounds, stability margins — rather than recorded outputs. They are organised by the verification order: analysis and unit tests first, then software-in-the-loop, then hardware.

docs.title: DNN Jetbot NanoOWL
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from DeepLearning/README.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in DeepLearning/.

CUDA-native object detection and tracking for Isaac ROS Jetbot — with a training-free path: mark an object once, detect only that object.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A complete object-detection perception pipeline built on the NVIDIA stack, with no OpenCV dependency anywhere in the image path. Camera capture, colour conversion, denoising, resizing, inference, decoding and suppression all run on the GPU; the frame never leaves device memory between the sensor and the detection result.

It is a pipeline, not a detection script. The chain is

camera → conditioning filter → detector → state estimator → tracks

and every stage is a documented closed-form result, derived in docs/MATH.md and asserted by the unit tests.

The chain stops at the estimate. This module produces perception output — stable ids, smoothed boxes, velocities, covariances — and does not command actuators. Any control law built on top lives outside it.

There are two ways to get detections into that chain:

Path Needs Recognises Setup Trained detector an ONNX/TensorRT model the categories it was trained on train or download a model Exemplar matching nothing the specific instance you marked draw one box

They compose: run a class-agnostic detector for proposals, then keep only what you marked.

docs.title: Why the stages are what they are
docs.text:
A detector is a noisy, intermittent sensor: boxes jitter frame to frame, objects are missed, and identities are not preserved. Wiring one straight to a motor controller feeds that noise into the actuators. So this module puts the classical chain in between:

Stage Role Method Guarantee Colour conversion Sensor decoding ITU-R BT.601/709 inverse matrix Exact inverse of the standard Temporal filter Noise conditioning Steady-state scalar Kalman Gain solves the scalar Riccati equation Letterbox + normalise Geometric conditioning Similarity transform + bilinear Aspect-preserving; interpolant is a convex combination Detector Measurement CNN + DFL decode + NMS Mask sweep provably equals greedy NMS Tracker State estimation Kalman (constant velocity), Joseph form Minimum-variance; covariance stays SPD for any gain Association Identity Hungarian algorithm Globally minimum-cost assignment

Nothing here is a heuristic with a tuned constant where a derivation was available. The temporal filter's gain comes from the sensor's noise variances, and the association gate is a calibrated χ² test with a stated false-rejection rate rather than a tuned pixel threshold.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
cd DeepLearning
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j$(nproc)
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

# Runs with no camera and no model: synthetic GPU frames + analytic ground truth
./build/04_detect_and_track 120

#include <dnn_jetbot_nanoowl.h>
using namespace cjn::dnn;

auto camera = create_camera_source(CameraConfig{});   // Argus → V4L2 → synthetic
camera->open();

Detector detector(DetectorConfig{});
detector.load_engine("model.engine");

MultiObjectTracker tracker;

GpuFrame frame;
std::vector<Detection> detections;
while (camera->acquire(&frame)) {
    detector.detect(frame, &detections);          // CUDA pre/post + TensorRT
    const auto& tracks = tracker.update(detections, dt);   // Kalman + Hungarian
    // tracks: stable id, smoothed box, velocity, covariance
    camera->release(frame);
}

docs.title: Learn by example — no training
docs.text:
Mark a region once. From then on, that object is detected and nothing else is.

ExemplarMatcher matcher;

// Once: the box comes from a mouse drag, a tap, or wherever you like.
matcher.learn(rgb, w, h, pitch, drawn_box, "my mug", stream);

// From then on, either filter a detector's proposals...
matcher.filter(rgb, w, h, pitch, &detections, stream);
// ...or search the frame with no model at all:
matcher.search(rgb, w, h, pitch, &found, stream);

matcher.memory().save("objects.dnnx");   // remembers across runs

No dataset, no labels, no gradient step, no weights. The region is reduced to a descriptor by closed-form transforms of the pixels, and stored as a prototype.

docs.title: What it is built from
docs.text:
Half Captures Invariant to Fooled by Hue-saturation histogram colour distribution rotation, deformation, exposure same-coloured distractors HOG (oriented gradients) local shape and texture illumination, contrast same-shaped distractors

Their blind spots are different, so the default is both, concatenated with weights \(\sqrt{w}\) and \(\sqrt{1-w}\) — which keeps the result on the unit sphere and makes the similarity decompose exactly as w·s_colour + (1−w)·s_hog. The tests demonstrate the complementarity directly: each half alone is fooled by one distractor, and neither is fooled by both.

docs.title: Every decision is an inequality, not a tuned constant
docs.text:
• The prototype is optimal. For exemplars on the unit sphere, the normalised mean is the direction maximising total similarity to all of them (Cauchy-Schwarz — Theorem 10.2). The test verifies it against 500 random competing directions.
  • The gate carries an error bound. On learning, background regions of the same frame are sampled and the threshold set to μ_bg + z·σ_bg. By Cantelli's inequality the false-accept rate is at most 1/(1+z²) — 5.9% at the default z = 4 — and that bound holds whatever the similarity distribution turns out to be, which matters because it is nowhere near Gaussian.
  • Ambiguity is rejected, not guessed. The winner must beat the runner-up by a margin; two objects that explain a region equally well make the choice a coin flip.
  • Showing a second view refines the prototype by an exact incremental mean, with no stored history. In practice two or three views matter far more than any threshold tuning.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text: It recognises the instance you marked, not its category. Marking one red mug teaches it that mug — not mugs. Category generalisation is what training buys; this is deliberately the other trade: instant, on the spot, for one object.

docs.title: Camera input, in CUDA
docs.text:
Backend Transport Copies to GPU Availability Argus libargus → EGLStream → CUDA zero Jetson CSI, JetPack V4L2 ioctl + mmap → pinned → DMA one any Linux, USB/UVC Synthetic generated by a CUDA kernel none always

The Argus path is the native Jetson route: the hardware ISP publishes into an EGLStream and CUDA consumes device pointers to NVMM memory. The V4L2 path has one unavoidable copy — a UVC device DMAs into kernel buffers CUDA cannot import — staged through page-locked memory so it overlaps with compute. The synthetic backend renders frames on the GPU with an analytically known object trajectory, which is what lets the whole pipeline be validated against ground truth with no hardware attached.

Formats handled by CUDA kernels: NV12, YUV420, YUYV, RGBA8, RGB8, GRAY8 — BT.601 and BT.709, limited and full range.

docs.title: Neural network: three backends, one interface
docs.text:
Backend What it optimises Speed Use it when TensorRT the whole network, ahead of time fastest the graph is fixed — deployment cuDNN each layer, at runtime fast the graph must stay malleable Native CUDA nothing — it is the reference slowest neither library is available

All three sit behind the same Detector, and all three are checked against the deliberately naive CPU implementations in src/reference_ops.cpp.

docs.title: TensorRT — compile the network
docs.text:
TrtBuildConfig config;
config.precision = TrtPrecision::FP16;        // Ampere tensor cores
config.timing_cache_path = "timing.cache";    // minutes -> seconds on a rebuild

TrtEngine engine;
engine.build_from_onnx("yolov8n.onnx", config);
engine.save_engine("yolov8n.engine");         // skip the build next time

TensorRT benchmarks candidate tactics on the actual GPU and fuses across layer boundaries — something neither of the other backends can do. build_from_onnx also takes an optimisation profile for dynamic input shapes, and reports what it actually enabled through build_log() (a requested precision the device cannot run fast is reported, not silently dropped). INT8 needs Q/DQ nodes in the ONNX: this module ships no calibrator, and says so rather than pretending.

docs.title: cuDNN — accelerate the layers
docs.text:
network->set_backend(ComputeBackend::CUDNN);  // or AUTO, the default
detector.set_network(std::move(network));
std::cout << network->backend_summary();      // per-layer: backend, algorithm, workspace

cuDNN carries hand-tuned kernels for every NVIDIA architecture, including the Ampere tensor-core paths a portable hand-written GEMM cannot reach. The layer asks cuDNN for the fastest algorithm whose scratch fits a budget (64 MiB by default — on a Jetson that memory is the host's too), and falls back to the native kernels when cuDNN cannot serve the geometry rather than failing. ReLU and sigmoid are fused into the convolution call; SiLU, hard-swish and leaky ReLU have no cuDNN mode, so those run as one extra element-wise pass.

ComputeBackend::AUTO picks cuDNN when the build and the device provide it, and the native path otherwise — so the same binary runs on a Jetson, a desktop without cuDNN, and in CI.

docs.title: Native CUDA — the fallback that is also the specification
docs.text:
Convolution lowered to im2col plus a tiled shared-memory GEMM with bias and activation fused into the epilogue; depthwise convolution runs direct; plus max-pool, nearest upsample, channel concat and residual add.

Batch norm is folded into the preceding convolution by an exact algebraic identity (§6.5), so the folded network computes the same values one kernel cheaper. Weights load from a flat .dnnw archive; tools/export_weights.py converts a PyTorch state_dict.

docs.title: A note on TF32
docs.text: cuDNN uses Ampere's TF32 tensor cores for FP32 convolutions by default. TF32 keeps FP32's exponent but truncates the mantissa to 10 bits, so agreement with the CPU reference is ~1e-3 relative rather than ~1e-6 — far below the 8-bit quantisation of the sensor upstream, and several times faster. Set CudnnConvOptions::allow_tf32 = false when bit-comparing against the reference; 05_backend_benchmark --strict does exactly that.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Four suites, 8,306 assertions, all runnable without a GPU:

test_math_core   5,891 checks   colour round-trips, HSV illumination invariance,
                                bilinear exactness, Riccati solution,
                                DFL shift-invariance, Kalman consistency over
                                400 cycles, pinhole projection round trip,
                                prototype optimality, Cantelli's bound
test_tracking    2,151 checks   Hungarian vs brute force (200 matrices),
                                NMS sweep vs greedy (300 cases), ID stability
                                through crossings, coasting through gaps
test_layers        158 checks   hand-computed convolutions, dilation, depthwise,
                                batch-norm folding equivalence, pooling,
                                backend selection and fallback, TensorRT config
test_exemplar      106 checks   descriptor invariance to exposure and position,
                                colour/shape discrimination and complementarity,
                                prototype refinement, memory persistence,
                                end-to-end learn-once-then-recognise

The tests assert analytic properties — identities, invariants, conservation laws, closed-form values — not recorded outputs. Because the CUDA kernels call the same math_core.h functions on the device that the tests call on the host, passing them validates the code that actually runs on the GPU.

docs.title: Scope and limitations
docs.text:
Stated plainly, so nothing here is mistaken for more than it is:

  • The Argus backend is not exercised by CI. This repository's CI has no Jetson, so the zero-copy CSI path is compiled but not run there. Validate it on the device with 01_camera_cuda_capture argus.
  • No model weights are shipped. Bring a TensorRT engine or a .dnnw archive; the examples fall back to synthetic data so the pipeline still runs.
  • The native CUDA backend is not competitive with TensorRT or cuDNN on real backbones, by design. It exists for inspectability and portability.
  • The cuDNN and TensorRT paths compile against real headers but are not run in CI, which has no GPU. Both compile warning-free against cuDNN 9.26 and TensorRT 10.7; validate throughput on the device with 05_backend_benchmark.
  • No INT8 calibrator is provided. INT8 requires an ONNX carrying Q/DQ nodes.
  • The Orin Nano Super has no DLA cores, so there is no DLA offload option here; that is a property of the hardware, not an omission.
  • No motor control or control feedback. The pipeline ends at the state estimate by design; there is no controller and no actuator interface. A previous revision carried an image-based visual-servo stage — it was removed as out of scope and remains recoverable from git history (commit 91406bf).
  • Range is a monocular estimate (§9.2) from apparent box height, so it needs the physical height of the object class and degrades as the box shrinks. It is reported as data; nothing in the module acts on it.
  • Exemplar matching is instance-level, not category-level. See above; this is the trade the method makes, not a defect to be fixed by tuning.
  • Dark and desaturated objects discriminate less well by colour, because pixels with no usable hue all pool into one achromatic bin. Measured, not assumed — see docs/MATH.md §10.6. Lower color_weight for such objects.
  • Sliding-window search is exhaustive, so its cost grows with the frame area and the number of scales. Filtering a detector's proposals is far cheaper when a detector is available.
  • Tracking runs on the CPU deliberately: for tens of tracks a kernel launch costs more than the whole update. See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.
  • Resize is aspect-preserving only. An anisotropic stretch is not a similarity transform and would break the inverse box mapping.
