docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from DeepLearning/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in DeepLearning/docs/.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
The module is a perception pipeline. Each stage has a defined role in the chain from sensor to state estimate, and the chain stops there: this module produces perception output and does not command actuators.

┌───────────────┐   NV12/YUYV (device ptr, zero copy on Argus)
│  CSI / USB    │
│  camera       │──────────────┐
└───────────────┘              ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────┐
   SENSOR           │ colour conversion   │  CUDA, §2
   CONDITIONING     │ temporal filter     │  CUDA, §4
                    │ letterbox+normalise │  CUDA, §3
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │ NCHW tensor
                    ┌──────────▼──────────┐
   MEASUREMENT      │ CNN inference       │  TensorRT / cuDNN / CUDA, §6
                    │ decode + NMS        │  CUDA, §5
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │
                               │   ── or, with no model at all ──
                               │   ┌─────────────────────────┐
                               │   │ exemplar matching, §10  │  CUDA
                               │   │ mark once -> find again │
                               │   └────────────┬────────────┘
                               │                │
                               ▼◄───────────────┘
                               │ detections (noisy, intermittent)
                    ┌──────────▼──────────┐
   STATE            │ Kalman filter       │  §8
   ESTIMATION       │ Hungarian assoc.    │  §8
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
                    tracks: stable id, smoothed box,
                    velocity, explicit covariance

Section numbers refer to MATH.md.

docs.title: Why each stage exists
docs.text:
Sensor conditioning. The camera delivers YCbCr, not RGB, and its output carries read and shot noise. Colour conversion is a fixed affine map from the sensor's standard; the temporal filter is a steady-state scalar Kalman filter whose gain is derived from the noise variances rather than tuned, with a robust gate so it does not smear moving objects.

Measurement. The detector converts the conditioned image into box measurements. It is a sensor, not an estimator: its output jitters frame to frame, misses objects, and carries no identity.

State estimation. Any consumer that acts on raw detections inherits that measurement noise. The Kalman filter provides a minimum-variance estimate with an explicit covariance, keeps predicting through missed frames, and — with optimal assignment — maintains identity through crossings. This is the module's output: a track carries a stable id, a smoothed box, a velocity and the uncertainty of each.

docs.title: What this module does not do
docs.text:
There is no controller and no actuator interface here. The estimate is handed to whatever consumes it — a ROS 2 node, a logger, an application — and any control law built on top lives outside this module. Consequences worth stating:

  • Nothing in the pipeline depends on a robot being present, so every stage is testable offline against the synthetic camera's ground truth.
  • The tracker's dt comes from the caller, not from a control loop's period, so the module imposes no rate.
  • depth_from_bbox_height (§9.2) reports a monocular range estimate as data. It is not used to close any loop.

docs.title: Module layout
docs.text:
DeepLearning/
├── include/dnn_jetbot_nanoowl/
│   ├── math_core.h       Header-only, host+device: every formula in the pipeline
│   ├── common.h          Types, errors, timing, device queries
│   ├── cudnn_ops.h       Backend selection + cuDNN conv/pool (pimpl, no cuDNN types)
│   ├── descriptor.h      Training-free region descriptors (colour histogram, HOG)
│   ├── exemplar.h        One-shot memory: learn a region, recognise it later
│   ├── tensor.h          RAII device/pinned buffers, NCHW tensors, streams
│   ├── camera.h          ICameraSource + Argus / V4L2 / synthetic backends
│   ├── preprocess.h      Colour conversion, denoise, letterbox, normalise
│   ├── layers.h          Conv2d, MaxPool2d, Upsample, concat, add
│   ├── network.h         Weight archive + DAG runner
│   ├── trt_engine.h      TensorRT backend (optional)
│   ├── detector.h        Decode + NMS + end-to-end detector
│   ├── nms.h             Host-side suppression sweep (header-only, testable)
│   └── tracker.h         Kalman tracking + Hungarian assignment
├── kernels/
│   ├── image_kernels.cu      Colour conversion, denoise, letterbox, synthetic
│   ├── nn_kernels.cu         im2col, tiled GEMM, depthwise, pool, upsample
│   ├── detection_kernels.cu  Anchors, DFL decode + gate, NMS mask
│   └── descriptor_kernels.cu Colour histogram, HOG, similarity, window proposals
├── src/                  Host implementations (cudnn_ops.cpp guarded by DNN_WITH_CUDNN)
├── examples/             Four runnable programs, synthetic camera by default
├── tests/                Three suites, all runnable without a GPU
├── tools/export_weights.py   PyTorch state_dict -> .dnnw
└── docs/                 MATH.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, INSTALLATION.md

docs.title: One implementation of every formula
docs.text: math_core.h is annotated __host__ __device__ and includes no CUDA headers. CUDA kernels call it on the device; the unit tests call the same functions on the host. There is no second copy to drift out of sync, and a test that passes has validated the code that actually runs on the GPU.

docs.title: No OpenCV anywhere in the image path
docs.text:
Step Implementation Capture libargus + EGLStream (CSI) or V4L2 ioctl (USB) YUV → RGB CUDA kernel, image_kernels.cu Denoise CUDA kernel Resize CUDA kernel, bilinear Normalise + NCHW fused into the resize kernel Image output (examples) PPM writer, 15-byte header + raw bytes

The CSI path never copies: the ISP publishes into an EGLStream and CUDA consumes device pointers to NVMM memory. The V4L2 path has one unavoidable copy — a UVC device DMAs into kernel buffers CUDA cannot import — staged through pinned memory so it overlaps with compute.

docs.title: Two ways to produce detections
docs.text:
trained detector                     exemplar matching
  ----------------                     -----------------
  needs an ONNX/TensorRT model         needs nothing
  recognises trained categories        recognises the marked instance
  setup: train or download             setup: draw one box
  cost: one forward pass               cost: one descriptor per candidate

            \                                 /
             \        they compose:          /
              +--> class-agnostic proposals from the detector,
                   filtered down to what was marked

ExemplarMatcher::filter is the composed path and the cheap one: the detector supplies a handful of proposals and each is described and matched. ExemplarMatcher::search is the standalone path: multi-scale sliding windows over the whole frame, which needs no model but costs proportionally to frame area times scale count.

Both run the same descriptor kernels, with one CUDA block per candidate region — the block resamples the region, accumulates its histogram in shared memory and normalises it before writing one row. That mapping is what makes a thousand-window search a single launch.

docs.title: Three inference backends
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │              Detector                    │
                    └───────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                 ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐
                 ▼                                     ▼
        ┌─────────────────┐                  ┌──────────────────┐
        │   TrtEngine     │                  │     Network      │
        │   (TensorRT)    │                  │   (DAG runner)   │
        └─────────────────┘                  └────────┬─────────┘
         whole-network,                    per layer  │
         ahead-of-time:              ┌────────────────┴───────────────┐
         cross-layer fusion,         ▼                                ▼
         measured tactics,   ┌───────────────┐              ┌──────────────────┐
         FP16 / INT8         │    cuDNN      │─ can't serve→│  native  kernels │
                             │ (per-layer)   │   fall back  │  (im2col + GEMM) │
                             └───────────────┘              └──────────────────┘

TensorRT compiles the whole network ahead of time. It fuses across layer boundaries, selects tactics by benchmarking them on the actual GPU, and reaches the Ampere tensor cores through FP16 and INT8. Fastest, but the graph is frozen at build time and the engine is tied to one GPU architecture and TensorRT version.

cuDNN accelerates individual layers of a graph this module still executes itself. It carries hand-tuned kernels for every NVIDIA architecture, so it beats a portable hand-written GEMM substantially, while the graph stays malleable at runtime. Algorithm choice is a heuristic query by default (cudnnGetConvolutionForwardAlgorithm_v7, no startup cost) with real benchmarking available through CudnnConvOptions::benchmark.

Native CUDA kernels are the fallback and, together with the CPU references in reference_ops.cpp, the specification the other two are checked against.

Selection is per layer and resolved at the first forward pass, because whether cuDNN can serve a layer depends on the input shape and the workspace budget. A graph can legitimately run partly on each backend; Network::backend_summary() reports what actually ran, with the cuDNN algorithm name and workspace size per layer.

The fallback chain is deliberate: ComputeBackend::AUTO takes cuDNN when the build and the device provide it; a layer cuDNN cannot serve — an unsupported geometry, or no algorithm within the budget — silently uses the native kernels rather than failing. Asking for ComputeBackend::CUDNN explicitly where it is unavailable throws and names the CMake flag, because that is a configuration mistake rather than a runtime condition.

docs.title: Fusion, and where it stops
docs.text:
Layer pattern TensorRT cuDNN Native conv + bias fused fused fused (GEMM epilogue) conv + bias + ReLU/sigmoid fused fused (cudnnConvolutionBiasActivationForward) fused conv + bias + SiLU/hard-swish/leaky fused conv+bias fused, activation separate fused conv + BN folded at load (§6.5) folded at load folded at load across layer boundaries yes no no

cuDNN has no SiLU, hard-swish or leaky-ReLU activation mode, so for those this module applies its own element-wise kernel over the output cuDNN just wrote — one extra bandwidth-bound pass, still far cheaper than the unfused alternative. That gap is the main reason TensorRT wins on real SiLU-heavy backbones.

docs.title: Numerical consequences
docs.text: cuDNN uses TF32 on Ampere by default for FP32 convolutions: FP32's exponent with a 10-bit mantissa. Agreement with the CPU reference is therefore ~1e-3 relative, not ~1e-6. That is well below the 8-bit quantisation of the sensor feeding the pipeline, so it is the right default — but it is a real difference, so CudnnConvOptions::allow_tf32 turns it off and 05_backend_benchmark --strict compares in true FP32. TensorRT's FP16 makes a comparable trade for a larger speed-up, and is likewise opt-out through TrtPrecision::FP32.

docs.title: Tracking runs on the CPU, deliberately
docs.text: The Kalman filter operates on 8×8 matrices and the assignment problem is sequential. At the tens-of-tracks scale this module targets, a kernel launch (~5 µs) costs more than the entire update (~2 µs for 100 tracks). Moving it to the GPU would be slower and harder to verify. The GPU is used where the work is genuinely parallel: per-pixel conversion, convolution, per-anchor decoding, and the \(N^2\) overlap matrix.

docs.title: Aspect-preserving resize only
docs.text: An anisotropic stretch is not a similarity transform: a box in network coordinates would no longer map back to the source by a single scale, and every shape prior the detector learned is distorted by a ratio that varies with the camera's resolution. The module therefore letterboxes and does not offer a stretch mode.

docs.title: Exemplar matching earns its thresholds
docs.text:
Everything about the exemplar path could have been a tuned constant, and none of it is:

Decision Basis The prototype Normalised mean maximises total similarity (Cauchy-Schwarz) Refining a prototype Exact incremental mean, no stored history Similarity measure Cosine on the unit sphere; for histograms, the Bhattacharyya coefficient via the Hellinger map Acceptance threshold μ_bg + z·σ_bg, calibrated per class against background regions False-accept rate Bounded by 1/(1+z²) — Cantelli, distribution-free Ambiguity Rejected when the margin to the runner-up is too small

The calibration is per class and per learning frame, so an object marked in a cluttered scene gets a stricter gate than one marked against a blank wall — automatically, because that is what the background statistics say.

docs.title: Failure is explicit
docs.text: Backends that are not compiled in throw NotAvailableError with the CMake flag that would enable them. A Cholesky factorisation that fails returns false rather than propagating NaNs. A Kalman update that cannot be applied leaves the previous valid state untouched. The candidate counter deliberately overruns its buffer so an overflow is visible rather than silent.

docs.title: Integration with the rest of the repository
docs.text:
Module Relationship CUDA/ Sibling GPU library; its PID/MPC controllers are a possible downstream consumer, not a dependency Source/Isaac_ROS-Object_Detection/ ROS 2 packaging of detection; this module is the CUDA-native alternative Source/ROS2_Control_System/ A possible downstream consumer of the tracks Train_Pytorch/ Produces the checkpoints tools/export_weights.py converts

To publish results into ROS 2, wrap Detector and MultiObjectTracker in a node and publish vision_msgs/Detection2DArray, carrying the track id in Detection2D::id and the filter's covariance alongside each box.

docs.title: Performance notes
docs.text:
Measure before tuning. The examples report per-stage latency; Network::summary prints per-layer MAC counts for a roofline estimate. On an Orin Nano Super (sm_87, 1024 CUDA cores, ~102 GB/s):

  • Colour conversion and letterbox are bandwidth bound — they touch every pixel once and do a handful of FLOPs each. Their floor is set by DRAM.
  • Convolution is compute bound once lowered to GEMM, which is why the tiled kernel matters: the 16×16 tile cuts global traffic by 16×.
  • Decoding is branch-divergent but sparse — the score gate means well under 1% of anchors do the expensive DFL work.
  • TensorRT will beat both other paths substantially on real backbones, and cuDNN will beat the native kernels. Use the native path for debugging and portability, cuDNN when the graph must change at runtime, TensorRT for deployment. 05_backend_benchmark measures the first two side by side on the actual device and checks both against the CPU reference — a faster backend is only useful if it computes the same thing.
  • A cuDNN handle costs tens of milliseconds to create and is shared process-wide through CudnnContext::instance(). It is not thread-safe across stream changes: use one context per inference thread, or serialise access.
  • Exemplar search cost is frames x scales x positions descriptor evaluations. The window count is computed exactly on the host before launching, so the budget is knowable in advance; ExemplarMatcher::last_window_count reports what was actually examined and last_search_overflowed says when the cap was hit rather than silently truncating.
  • TensorRT's first build takes minutes because tactic selection is measured. Set TrtBuildConfig::timing_cache_path and the next build takes seconds; save_engine removes the build from the deployment path entirely.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from DeepLearning/docs/INSTALLATION.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in DeepLearning/docs/.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Component Minimum Notes CMake 3.20 CUDA as a first-class language CUDA Toolkit 11.4 12.6 on JetPack 6.2 C++ compiler GCC 9 / Clang 10 C++17 cuDNN 8.5 Optional; 9.x on JetPack 6 TensorRT 8.5 Optional; 10.x on JetPack 6 nvonnxparser matching TensorRT Optional; needed only to compile ONNX in-process libargus + EGL JetPack Optional; CSI capture Linux kernel headers any Optional; V4L2 capture

The target is the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super (Ampere, sm_87, JetPack 6.2+). The module also builds on a desktop GPU — set -DJETSON_ORIN_NANO=OFF to compile for the local architecture.

Nothing here depends on OpenCV.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
cd DeepLearning
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j$(nproc)
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Effect JETSON_ORIN_NANO ON Compile for sm_87; OFF uses native ENABLE_TENSORRT ON TensorRT backend, if the headers are found ENABLE_CUDNN ON cuDNN layer backend, if the headers are found ENABLE_ARGUS ON Jetson CSI capture, if libargus is found ENABLE_V4L2 ON USB/UVC capture, if linux/videodev2.h exists BUILD_TESTS ON Unit tests BUILD_EXAMPLES ON Example programs

Every optional backend degrades gracefully: when it is not found, CMake says so and the corresponding class throws NotAvailableError naming the flag that would enable it. The synthetic camera is always available, so the pipeline runs on any machine with a CUDA device.

The configure summary states exactly what was found:

-- cuDNN: /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libcudnn.so (v9.3)
-- TensorRT: /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libnvinfer.so
-- TensorRT ONNX parser: /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libnvonnxparser.so
...
-- cuDNN backend:      TRUE
-- TensorRT backend:   TRUE
-- TensorRT ONNX:      TRUE

If cuDNN sits outside the standard paths, point CMake at it:

cmake -B build -DCUDNN_ROOT=/path/to/cudnn -DTENSORRT_ROOT=/path/to/TensorRT

On JetPack both are already installed under /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu and are found without hints.

docs.title: Desktop build without a Jetson
docs.text:
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DJETSON_ORIN_NANO=OFF -DENABLE_ARGUS=OFF
cmake --build build -j$(nproc)
./build/04_detect_and_track 120

docs.title: Tests without a GPU
docs.text:
math_core.h is header-only and CUDA-free, so the numerical core can be validated on any machine — useful in CI:

g++ -std=c++17 -I include tests/test_math_core.cpp -o test_math_core && ./test_math_core

docs.title: 1. Export to ONNX
docs.text:
From a PyTorch checkpoint (Ultralytics shown; any exporter works):

yolo export model=yolov8n.pt format=onnx opset=13 imgsz=640

docs.title: 2a. Build the engine from C++ (no trtexec needed)
docs.text:
When nvonnxparser is present the module compiles the ONNX itself:

TrtBuildConfig config;
config.precision = TrtPrecision::FP16;
config.workspace_bytes = 1024ull * 1024 * 1024;
config.timing_cache_path = "yolov8n.timing";   // reuse tactic measurements

TrtEngine engine;
engine.build_from_onnx("yolov8n.onnx", config);
std::cout << engine.build_log();               // what was actually enabled
engine.save_engine("yolov8n.engine");

build_log() reports the precisions that were genuinely enabled: a requested precision the GPU cannot run fast is reported rather than silently dropped.

For a dynamic input shape, supply an optimisation profile:

config.min_shape = Shape(1, 3, 320, 320);
config.opt_shape = Shape(1, 3, 640, 640);   // TensorRT optimises for this one
config.max_shape = Shape(1, 3, 960, 960);

docs.title: 2b. Build a TensorRT engine on the target device with trtexec
docs.text:
An engine is compiled for one GPU architecture and TensorRT version. It is not portable — build it on the Jetson that will run it:

/usr/src/tensorrt/bin/trtexec \
    --onnx=yolov8n.onnx \
    --saveEngine=yolov8n.engine \
    --fp16 \
    --memPoolSize=workspace:2048

FP16 roughly halves latency on Ampere with negligible accuracy loss for detection. For INT8 add --int8 --calib=<cache> and a calibration set.

The Orin Nano Super has no DLA cores (unlike AGX Orin and Xavier), so there is no DLA offload to configure here.

docs.title: 3. Run
docs.text: ./build/03_detection_postprocess yolov8n.engine

docs.title: Using exemplar matching (no model needed)
docs.text:
./build/06_learn_by_example 60 objects.dnnx

The first run learns from a marked region and saves the memory; later runs load it and skip learning. In an application the box comes from the user:

ExemplarMatcher matcher;                        // defaults: colour + HOG
const int id = matcher.learn(rgb, w, h, pitch, drawn_box, "mug", stream);

// Show it again from another angle to widen the prototype.
matcher.add_example(id, rgb, w, h, pitch, second_box, stream);

matcher.search(rgb, w, h, pitch, &found, stream);

Tuning, in the order that actually helps:

  1. Add a second and third view of the object with add_example. This matters far more than any threshold.
  2. Adjust color_weight for what the object is: lower it for dark or desaturated objects, raise it for brightly coloured ones with little structure.
  3. Adjust background_z for the false-accept rate you can live with: the bound is 1/(1+z²), so 3 gives 10%, 4 gives 5.9%, 5 gives 3.8%.
  4. Widen search_scales if the object's apparent size varies a lot, and tighten search_stride if it is being missed between windows — both cost linearly in search time.

docs.title: Choosing a layer backend for the native path
docs.text:
auto network = std::make_unique<Network>();
// ... build the graph ...
network->set_backend(ComputeBackend::AUTO);    // cuDNN if usable, else native
detector.set_network(std::move(network));

// After the first forward pass:
std::cout << network->backend_summary();
//  0  backbone.0  cudnn   IMPLICIT_PRECOMP_GEMM  128 KiB
//  1  backbone.1  cudnn   WINOGRAD_NONFUSED      2048 KiB
//  2  pool1       native
//  cudnn: 2 layers, native: 1 layers

Tuning the cuDNN path:

CudnnConvOptions options;
options.max_workspace_bytes = 256u * 1024u * 1024u;  // allow bigger algorithms
options.benchmark = true;      // measure instead of using cuDNN's heuristic
options.allow_tf32 = false;    // strict FP32, for reference comparisons
conv.set_cudnn_options(options);

Raising the workspace budget lets cuDNN consider algorithms it would otherwise skip (Winograd and FFT variants want the most). On an 8 GB Orin Nano that memory is shared with the host, hence the conservative 64 MiB default.

docs.title: Using the native CUDA backend instead
docs.text:
Convert the checkpoint to the module's weight archive and build the graph with Network:

python3 tools/export_weights.py yolov8n.pt yolov8n.dnnw
python3 tools/export_weights.py yolov8n.pt --list     # inspect tensor names

See network.h for the naming convention the loader expects and tools/export_weights.py --rename for mapping a checkpoint onto it.

docs.title: Configuring the detector for your model
docs.text:
DetectorConfig must match the model's head, or decoding will produce nonsense:

DetectorConfig config;
config.net_width  = 640;
config.net_height = 640;
config.num_classes = 80;
config.reg_max = 16;                       // DFL bins; 16 in the YOLOv8 family
config.strides = {8, 16, 32};              // must match the head's levels
config.layout = HeadLayout::DFL_CHANNELS_FIRST;
config.apply_sigmoid = true;               // false if the export already applied it

Check the ONNX output shape against [1, 4*reg_max + num_classes, anchor_count]. A mismatch in reg_max or strides shifts every decoded box.

docs.title: CSI (Argus)
docs.text:
ls /dev/video*                       # the sensor should enumerate
systemctl status nvargus-daemon      # must be running
./build/01_camera_cuda_capture argus 30

docs.title: USB / UVC (V4L2)
docs.text:
v4l2-ctl --list-devices
v4l2-ctl -d /dev/video0 --list-formats-ext    # confirm YUYV or NV12 support
./build/01_camera_cuda_capture v4l2 30

Set CameraConfig::device_path for a node other than /dev/video0.

docs.title: No camera
docs.text:
./build/01_camera_cuda_capture synthetic 30

The synthetic backend generates frames on the GPU with an analytically known object trajectory, which is what makes end-to-end validation possible without hardware.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix cannot deserialise ... engine The engine was built for another GPU or TensorRT version. Rebuild it on the target with trtexec. argus: no camera provider nvargus-daemon is not running: sudo systemctl restart nvargus-daemon. VIDIOC_S_FMT failed The device does not support the requested format or size. Check v4l2-ctl --list-formats-ext. A learned object is never found The window scales may not cover its apparent size — check search_scales against how much the object's size varies — or the gate may be too strict. Inspect ExemplarClass::threshold and the background statistics it came from. Everything matches the learned object The gate is too loose because the learning frame's background was featureless (σ_bg ≈ 0), so the floor applies. Raise min_similarity, or learn against a more representative background. Two different objects are confused Add more views of each with add_example, raise min_margin, or shift color_weight towards whichever half actually separates them. the region is featureless on learn The marked region has neither colour nor gradient — a patch of blank sky or wall. There is nothing to remember; mark something with structure. Track ids keep changing The detector is missing frames faster than max_age allows, or the χ² gate is too tight for the object's speed. Raise max_age, or the process noise sigma_pos. Boxes offset or scaled wrongly strides or reg_max do not match the model's head, or apply_sigmoid is set wrongly. Detections are all background score_threshold too low for an unsigmoided head, or apply_sigmoid inverted. out of memory on a Jetson GPU and CPU share DRAM. Lower the input size, the batch, or the TensorRT workspace. cuDNN reported unavailable despite being installed CudnnContext::available() also requires a usable CUDA device — it creates a handle to find out. Check nvidia-smi / tegrastats first. A layer silently runs on the native path cuDNN found no algorithm within max_workspace_bytes, or the geometry is unsupported. Raise the budget and check Network::backend_summary(). cuDNN results differ from the CPU reference by ~1e-3 That is TF32 on Ampere, working as intended. Set CudnnConvOptions::allow_tf32 = false to compare in true FP32. build_from_onnx throws "ONNX parser" nvonnxparser was not found at configure time. Install it, or build the engine with trtexec and use load. The TensorRT build takes minutes Tactic selection is measured, not predicted. Set TrtBuildConfig::timing_cache_path, and save_engine so it happens once.

docs.title: Mathematical Foundations
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from DeepLearning/docs/MATH.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in DeepLearning/docs/.

Every numerical step in this module is a documented, closed-form result. This file gives the derivations; the code references them by equation number, and tests/test_math_core.cpp asserts the properties claimed here rather than recorded outputs.

Section Topic Code Tests §1 Activations math_core.h §1 test_activations §2 Colour conversion math_core.h §2 test_color_conversion §3 Letterbox & bilinear resampling math_core.h §3 test_letterbox, test_bilinear §4 Temporal denoising math_core.h §4 test_temporal_filter §5 Detection decoding & NMS math_core.h §5 test_detection_geometry, test_nms §6 Convolution & batch-norm folding math_core.h §6 test_layers.cpp §7 Cholesky factorisation math_core.h §7 test_linear_algebra §8 Kalman filtering & association math_core.h §8 test_kalman, test_assignment §9 Camera geometry math_core.h §9 test_camera_geometry §10 Exemplar matching (training-free) math_core.h §10 test_exemplar_math, test_exemplar.cpp

The signal chain follows the estimation-engineering convention throughout:

sensor → conditioning filter → measurement → state estimator → estimate

Concretely: camera (§2) → temporal filter (§4) → detector (§5, §6) → Kalman estimator (§8) → tracks with an explicit covariance.

The chain stops at the estimate. This module produces perception output; it does not command actuators, and nothing here closes a loop through the scene.

docs.title: 1. Activations
docs.text:
(1.1) Logistic sigmoid.

\[\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\]

Evaluated as \(e^{x}/(1+e^{x})\) for \(x<0\). The two forms are equal in exact arithmetic (multiply numerator and denominator by \(e^{x}\)), but the naive form overflows for large \(|x|\) while the branched form never evaluates \(e^{|x|}\).

(1.2)–(1.5) ReLU, leaky ReLU, SiLU, hard-swish.

\[\mathrm{relu}(x)=\max(0,x),\qquad \mathrm{lrelu}(x)=\begin{cases}x & x>0\\ \alpha x & x\le 0\end{cases}\] \[\mathrm{silu}(x)=x\,\sigma(x),\qquad \mathrm{hswish}(x)=x\,\frac{\mathrm{clamp}(x+3,0,6)}{6}\]

SiLU (Elfwing et al., Neural Networks 107, 2018) is the activation of the YOLOv8-family backbones this module targets.

Proposition 1.1. \(\sup_x |\mathrm{hswish}(x)-\mathrm{silu}(x)| = 3/(1+e^{3}) \approx 0.14228\), attained at \(x=\pm 3\).

Proof. For \(x\le-3\), \(\mathrm{hswish}=0\) and the difference is \(|x|\sigma(x)\), which decreases monotonically to 0 as \(x\to-\infty\) and equals \(3\sigma(-3)\) at \(x=-3\). For \(x\ge 3\), \(\mathrm{hswish}=x\) and the difference is \(x(1-\sigma(x)) = x\sigma(-x)\), again maximal at the endpoint with value \(3\sigma(-3)=3/(1+e^{3})\). On \([-3,3]\) both functions are smooth and the difference stays below that value. ∎

The test computes the supremum numerically and checks it against the closed form — a claim that fails if either activation is mis-implemented.

docs.title: 2. Colour Conversion
docs.text:
The camera delivers YCbCr (NV12 from the Jetson ISP, YUYV from UVC); the network needs RGB. The conversion is the exact inverse of the standard's forward matrix.

(2.1) BT.601 luma. \(Y = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B\) (SDTV, \(K_r=0.299\), \(K_b=0.114\)).

(2.2) BT.709 luma. \(Y = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B\) (HDTV).

Forward transform. With \(K_g = 1-K_r-K_b\):

\[Y = K_r R + K_g G + K_b B,\qquad C_b = 128 + \frac{B-Y}{2(1-K_b)},\qquad C_r = 128 + \frac{R-Y}{2(1-K_r)}\]

(2.3) Inverse. Solving for \((R,G,B)\):

\[R = Y + 2(1-K_r)(C_r-128)$$ $$B = Y + 2(1-K_b)(C_b-128)$$ $$G = Y - \frac{2K_b(1-K_b)}{K_g}(C_b-128) - \frac{2K_r(1-K_r)}{K_g}(C_r-128)\]

Derivation of the green channel. From \(Y = K_rR + K_gG + K_bB\), \(G = (Y - K_rR - K_bB)/K_g\). Substituting the expressions for \(R\) and \(B\):

\[G = \frac{Y - K_r\!\left[Y + 2(1-K_r)\Delta_r\right] - K_b\!\left[Y + 2(1-K_b)\Delta_b\right]}{K_g}\]

with \(\Delta_r = C_r-128\), \(\Delta_b = C_b-128\). The \(Y\) terms collect to \(Y(1-K_r-K_b)/K_g = Y\), leaving the stated coefficients. ∎

Studio swing. Broadcast standards restrict luma to \([16,235]\) and chroma to \([16,240]\). Rescaling to full range multiplies luma by \(255/219 = 1.164383\) after subtracting the offset 16, and chroma by \(255/224 = 1.138393\). Every limited-range coefficient in the code is its full-range counterpart times \(255/224\).

The tests verify invertibility directly: forward-transform a set of RGB triples with the standard's definition, apply the implemented inverse, and require the original values back to within 0.02 code values.

docs.title: 3. Geometric Resampling
docs.text:
(3.1) Letterbox transform. To fit a \(W_s \times H_s\) source into a \(W_d \times H_d\) network input without distortion:

\[s = \min\!\left(\frac{W_d}{W_s}, \frac{H_d}{H_s}\right),\qquad p_x = \frac{W_d - sW_s}{2},\qquad p_y = \frac{H_d - sH_s}{2}\] \[u_d = s\,u_s + p_x,\qquad v_d = s\,v_s + p_y\]

A single scale on both axes is what preserves aspect ratio, and therefore the shape statistics the detector was trained on. The minimum guarantees \(sW_s \le W_d\) and \(sH_s \le H_d\), so the content fits; the halved remainder centres it. This module offers no anisotropic stretch: it is not a similarity transform, so a box in network coordinates would not map back by one scale.

(3.2) Inverse, half-pixel convention.

\[u_s = \frac{(u_d + 0.5) - p_x}{s} - 0.5\]

Pixel \(i\) covers \([i, i+1)\) with centre \(i+0.5\). Mapping centre to centre gives the \(\pm 0.5\) terms. Omitting them shifts the sampling grid by half a destination pixel — at 640×640 from 1920×1080 that is a systematic 1.5-source-pixel bias on every box edge.

(3.3) Bilinear interpolation. With \(x_0=\lfloor u\rfloor\), \(w_x = u - x_0\) (similarly for \(v\)):

\[I(u,v) = (1-w_x)(1-w_y)I_{00} + w_x(1-w_y)I_{10} + (1-w_x)w_y I_{01} + w_x w_y I_{11}\]

Lemma 3.1. The four weights are non-negative and sum to 1, so \(I(u,v)\) is a convex combination of the taps and cannot leave \([\min I_{ij}, \max I_{ij}]\).

Proof. \(w_x,w_y\in[0,1)\) makes each product non-negative, and the sum factorises as \(\left[(1-w_x)+w_x\right]\left[(1-w_y)+w_y\right] = 1\). ∎

Bilinear interpolation is also exact for any function of the form \(a + bx + cy + dxy\); the test checks this by reconstructing \(3x+5y+7\) at non-integer coordinates.

(3.4) Normalisation. \(\hat{x} = (x/255 - \mu)/\sigma\) per channel.

docs.title: 4. Temporal Denoising
docs.text:
Sensor noise is independent frame to frame; the scene is not. That asymmetry is what a temporal filter exploits — and the correct filter constant follows from the noise statistics rather than from tuning.

Model. Per pixel, a random walk observed in noise:

\[x_k = x_{k-1} + w_k,\quad w_k\sim N(0,q),\qquad z_k = x_k + v_k,\quad v_k\sim N(0,r)\]

(4.1)–(4.3) Scalar Kalman recursion.

\[P_k^- = P_{k-1} + q,\qquad \alpha_k = \frac{P_k^-}{P_k^- + r},\qquad P_k = (1-\alpha_k)P_k^-\]

(4.4) Steady-state gain. At steady state \(P_k = P_{k-1} = P\), so

\[P = \frac{(P+q)r}{P+q+r}\]

the scalar discrete algebraic Riccati equation. Writing \(M = P+q\) and \(\alpha = M/(M+r)\): from \(P = M(1-\alpha)\) and \(P = M-q\) we get \(M\alpha = q\), i.e. \(M = q/\alpha\); combined with \(M = \alpha r/(1-\alpha)\) this gives

\[r\alpha^2 + q\alpha - q = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \alpha = \frac{-\lambda + \sqrt{\lambda^2 + 4\lambda}}{2},\qquad \lambda = q/r\]

taking the positive root. The test asserts \(r\alpha^2 + q\alpha - q = 0\) directly.

(4.5) The filter. \(\hat{x}_k = \hat{x}_{k-1} + \alpha(z_k - \hat{x}_{k-1})\) — an exponential moving average whose constant is derived, not guessed. A noisier sensor (larger \(r\)) lowers \(\alpha\); a more agitated scene (larger \(q\)) raises it.

(4.6) Robust variant. A moving object violates the constant-scene hypothesis, and a plain EMA smears it. Attenuating the gain when the innovation is large relative to the sensor noise:

\[\alpha_{\text{eff}} = \alpha\exp\!\left(-\frac{\nu^2}{2k^2r}\right),\qquad \nu = z_k - \hat{x}_{k-1}\]

This is the Gaussian influence function of a robust M-estimator applied to the Kalman innovation: small innovations (noise) are filtered normally, large ones (motion) pass through nearly unfiltered.

docs.title: 5. Detection Geometry
docs.text:
(5.1)–(5.2) Area and IoU. The intersection of two axis-aligned boxes is the box with corners \((\max x_1, \max y_1, \min x_2, \min y_2)\), empty when either side is non-positive. Then

\[\mathrm{IoU}(A,B) = \frac{|A\cap B|}{|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|}\]

using \(|A\cup B| = |A|+|B|-|A\cap B|\) (inclusion–exclusion).

(5.3) Distance-IoU (Zheng et al., AAAI 2020):

\[\mathrm{DIoU} = \mathrm{IoU} - \frac{\rho^2(c_A,c_B)}{d^2}\]

with \(\rho\) the centre distance and \(d\) the diagonal of the smallest enclosing box. The penalty is non-negative, so \(\mathrm{DIoU}\le\mathrm{IoU}\) always; it separates heavily overlapping boxes with distinct centres, which plain IoU cannot.

(5.4) Soft-NMS (Bodla et al., ICCV 2017): \(s_i \leftarrow s_i\exp(-\mathrm{IoU}^2/\sigma)\). Continuous in IoU, so unlike hard NMS it has no discontinuity at the threshold.

(5.5) Centre ↔ corner forms. \((c_x,c_y,w,h)\leftrightarrow(c_x\mp w/2, c_y\mp h/2)\).

(5.6) Distribution Focal Loss decoding (Li et al., NeurIPS 2020). The head predicts a distribution over integer distances rather than a scalar; the decoded distance is its expectation:

\[d = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} i\,\mathrm{softmax}(\ell)_i\]

Numerical stability. \(\mathrm{softmax}(\ell + c\mathbf{1}) = \mathrm{softmax}(\ell)\) for any constant \(c\), because \(e^{\ell_i+c}/\sum_j e^{\ell_j+c} = e^{c}e^{\ell_i}/(e^{c}\sum_j e^{\ell_j})\). Choosing \(c = -\max_i \ell_i\) bounds every exponential by 1, so no overflow is possible. The test shifts all logits by \(+500\) and requires the result unchanged.

(5.7) Anchor-free reconstruction. For anchor point \((a_x,a_y)\) at stride \(s\) and decoded distances \((l,t,r,b)\) in stride units:

\[x_1 = a_x - ls,\quad y_1 = a_y - ts,\quad x_2 = a_x + rs,\quad y_2 = a_y + bs\]

Anchor points sit at cell centres, \(((c+0.5)s, (r+0.5)s)\).

Greedy NMS and the bitmask sweep. Greedy NMS keeps detection \(i\) (in descending score order) iff no kept \(j<i\) suppresses it. The GPU evaluates the full \(N\times N\) overlap predicate into a bitmask; the host then sweeps in score order, keeping a running OR of the masks of everything kept. Detection \(i\) is kept iff its bit is clear in that union — which is exactly the greedy condition, since the union contains precisely the detections suppressed by survivors. tests/test_tracking.cpp checks the equivalence against a direct implementation over 300 randomised cases.

docs.title: 6. Convolution Arithmetic
docs.text:
(6.1) Definition.

\[y[k,p,q] = b_k + \sum_{c}\sum_{r}\sum_{s} x[c,\,ps_h - P + rd,\,qs_w - P + sd]\; w[k,c,r,s]\]

(6.2) Output extent.

\[O = \left\lfloor\frac{I + 2P - d(k-1) - 1}{s}\right\rfloor + 1\]

The dilated kernel spans \(d(k-1)+1\) samples; the last valid window starts at \(I+2P-\left[d(k-1)+1\right]\), and the floor counts the whole strides that fit.

(6.3) "Same" padding. \(P = \lfloor d(k-1)/2\rfloor\) gives \(O = \lceil I/s\rceil\) for odd \(k\).

(6.4) Lowering to GEMM (im2col). Materialising each receptive field as a column turns the convolution into

\[Y_{[C_{out}\times O_hO_w]} = W_{[C_{out}\times C_{in}k^2]}\;X^{col}_{[C_{in}k^2\times O_hO_w]}\]

Padding taps are written as zeros, so the dense product computes the padded convolution exactly. The \(k^2\)-fold memory expansion buys a dense GEMM, which a tiled shared-memory kernel executes at a far higher fraction of peak than a direct seven-loop convolution. Depthwise layers skip the lowering: their per-channel GEMMs have an inner dimension of 1, too small to amortise it.

(6.5) Batch-norm folding. Inference-time batch norm is affine:

\[y = \gamma\frac{x-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}} + \beta\]

Composed with \(x = w*u + b\), and writing \(\kappa = \gamma/\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}\):

\[y = \kappa(w*u + b - \mu) + \beta = (\kappa w)*u + \left[(b-\mu)\kappa + \beta\right]\]

so \(w' = \kappa w\) and \(b' = (b-\mu)\kappa + \beta\) — an exact identity, not an approximation, using only the linearity of convolution. test_batchnorm_folding checks the folded and unfused paths agree elementwise.

Precision of the accelerated backends. cuDNN and TensorRT evaluate the same equations in reduced precision, which is a numerical choice, not an algorithmic one:

Format Exponent Mantissa Relative resolution Used by FP32 8 bits 23 bits \(\approx 10^{-7}\) native kernels, CPU reference TF32 8 bits 10 bits \(\approx 10^{-3}\) cuDNN on Ampere, by default FP16 5 bits 10 bits \(\approx 10^{-3}\) TensorRT with kFP16

TF32 keeps FP32's exponent, so it cannot overflow where FP32 would not; only the significand is truncated. FP16 narrows the exponent too, which is why TensorRT still places range-sensitive layers in higher precision rather than converting the whole network.

Both resolutions sit far below the input's own quantisation: an 8-bit sensor sample carries \(\approx 4\times10^{-3}\) relative resolution, so the arithmetic is not the limiting error term. This is why the accelerated backends are the default and the strict-FP32 path exists for verification (05_backend_benchmark --strict) rather than for production.

(6.6) Max pooling. \(y[p,q] = \max_{r,s} x[ps_h+r,\, qs_w+s]\).

(6.7) Nearest upsampling. \(y[p,q] = x[\lfloor p/f\rfloor, \lfloor q/f\rfloor]\). Detection necks convolve immediately after upsampling, so bilinear smoothing would be redundant work.

docs.title: 7. Linear Algebra
docs.text:
(7.1) Cholesky factorisation. For symmetric positive definite \(A = LL^{T}\):

\[L_{jj} = \sqrt{A_{jj} - \sum_{k<j}L_{jk}^2},\qquad L_{ij} = \frac{A_{ij} - \sum_{k<j}L_{ik}L_{jk}}{L_{jj}}\ (i>j)\]

Chosen over an explicit inverse because it is backward stable for SPD matrices and needs no pivoting. A non-positive pivot means \(A\) is not numerically positive definite — the failure is itself the diagnostic the Kalman update needs.

(7.2) Solving. \(LL^{T}x=b\) by forward substitution on \(Ly=b\) then back substitution on \(L^{T}x=y\), each \(O(n^2)\).

Symmetrisation. \(A \leftarrow (A+A^{T})/2\) is the orthogonal projection onto the symmetric subspace, hence the smallest Frobenius-norm correction restoring a property rounding has broken.

docs.title: 8. Kalman Filtering
docs.text:
State: \(x = [c_x, c_y, w, h, \dot c_x, \dot c_y, \dot w, \dot h]^{T}\). Measurement: \(z = [c_x,c_y,w,h]^{T}\), so \(H = [I_4\ 0]\).

(8.1) Transition.

\[F = egin{bmatrix} I_4 & \Delta t\,I_4\ 0 & I_4\end{bmatrix}\]

This is exact, not a first-order approximation: the continuous model is \(\dot{x} = Ax\) with \(A = egin{bmatrix}0&I\0&0\end{bmatrix}\), and \(A^2=0\), so \(e^{A\Delta t} = I + A\Delta t\) terminates after two terms.

(8.2) Process noise. Treating unmodelled acceleration as constant over one interval, \(w = Ga\) with \(G = [\Delta t^2/2,\ \Delta t]^{T}\) per axis:

\[Q_{ ext{axis}} = GG^{T}\sigma_a^2 = \sigma_a^2 egin{bmatrix} \Delta t^4/4 & \Delta t^3/2\ \Delta t^3/2 & \Delta t^2\end{bmatrix}\]

Being \(\sigma_a^2\) times an outer product, each block is positive semi-definite by construction and has rank 1 — the test checks \(\det Q_{ ext{axis}} = 0\) and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality on its entries. (Bar-Shalom, Estimation with Applications to Tracking and Navigation, §6.2.2.)

(8.3) Predict. \(\hat{x}^- = F\hat{x}\), \(P^- = FPF^{T} + Q\).

(8.4) Innovation. \( u = z - H\hat{x}^-\), \(S = HP^-H^{T} + R\). Since \(H\) is a selector, \(HP^-H^{T}\) is the leading \(4 imes4\) block of \(P^-\) — no multiplication needed.

(8.5) Mahalanobis gate. \(d^2 = u^{T}S^{-1} u\). Under the filter's Gaussian hypothesis \(d^2\sim\chi^2_4\), so comparing against \(\chi^2_{4,0.95}=9.4877\) is a test with a stated false-rejection rate of 5% — a calibrated statistic, not a tuned pixel threshold. Computed through the Cholesky factor of \(S\) rather than by inverting it.

(8.6)–(8.7) Joseph-form update.

\[K = P^-H^{T}S^{-1},\qquad \hat{x} = \hat{x}^- + K u$$ $$P = (I-KH)P^-(I-KH)^{T} + KRK^{T}\]

Proposition 8.1. The Joseph form preserves symmetry and positive semi-definiteness for any gain \(K\), not only the optimal one.

Proof. Both terms are congruence products \(MP^-M^{T}\) and \(KRK^{T}\). For any \(v\), \(v^{T}MP^-M^{T}v = (M^{T}v)^{T}P^-(M^{T}v)\ge 0\) when \(P^-\succeq 0\), and likewise for \(R\succeq 0\). A sum of PSD matrices is PSD, and each term is manifestly symmetric. ∎

The short form \(P = (I-KH)P^-\) equals this only at the optimal gain and in exact arithmetic; under rounding it can lose symmetry and drift indefinite, at which point the filter diverges. The test runs 400 update cycles and requires \(P\) to stay Cholesky-factorisable throughout.

(8.8) Innovation-based adaptation of R (Mehra, IEEE TAC 15(2), 1970). Track the residual covariance with an EWMA and recover \(R\) from \(S = HP^-H^{T}+R\):

\[\hat{C}_ u \leftarrow (1- eta)\hat{C}_ u + eta\, u u^{T},\qquad \hat{R} = \max\!\left(R_{\min},\ \hat{C}_ u - HP^-H^{T} ight)\]

The floor \(R_{\min}>0\) is essential: the subtraction can drive a diagonal entry negative, which would destroy \(S\succ 0\) and with it the Cholesky factorisation. Only the diagonal is adapted, matching a detector whose four box coordinates are measured independently.

(8.9) Confidence weighting. \(R(c) = R_0/\max(c, c_{\min})\). A half-confidence detection is given twice the variance and moves the state proportionally less — which is how a Kalman filter is meant to weigh a less reliable sensor.

Data association. With \(n\) tracks and \(m\) detections, the cost

\[C_{ij} = \omega\left(1 - \mathrm{IoU}_{ij} ight) + (1-\omega)\min\!\left( rac{d^2_{ij}}{\chi^2_{4,0.95}},1 ight)\]

is minimised over assignments by the Hungarian algorithm in its \(O(n^3)\) shortest-augmenting-path form. It maintains dual potentials \(u_i,v_j\) with \(C_{ij}-u_i-v_j\ge0\), tight on matched pairs; when every row is matched, those duals certify global optimality by complementary slackness.

Greedy nearest-neighbour matching offers no such guarantee. test_assignment includes the canonical counter-example — greedy pays 1.00 where the optimum is 0.35 — and checks the solver against brute-force enumeration on 200 random matrices.

docs.title: 9. Camera Geometry
docs.text:
(9.1) Normalised coordinates. \(x = (u-c_x)/f_x\), \(y = (v-c_y)/f_y\).

Dividing the pixel offset by the focal length gives the tangent of the bearing angle to the point, which is independent of the sensor's resolution. A consumer of this module's detections can therefore reason about direction without knowing the camera format.

(9.2) Depth from apparent height. Similar triangles in the pinhole model give \(h_{px} = f_yH/Z\), hence

\[Z = \frac{f_y H}{h_{px}}\]

for a known physical height \(H\). This is a monocular range estimate: it is only as good as the assumed object height, and it degrades as \(1/h_{px}\), so a one-pixel error at 100 px apparent height is 1% of range while the same error at 10 px is 10%. Where stereo or LiDAR is available, prefer their measurement.

test_camera_geometry checks the round trip — project a known object at a known range, decode the range back — along with resolution independence and the degenerate cases.

docs.title: 10. Exemplar Matching
docs.text: The training-free recognition path. A region is reduced to a fixed-length vector, remembered as a prototype, and anything whose vector is close enough to that prototype is reported as the same object. No dataset, no labels, no gradient step.

docs.title: 10.1 Descriptors live on the unit sphere
docs.text:
(10.1) L2 normalisation. \(\hat{v} = v/\|v\|_2\).

Magnitude in an image descriptor encodes contrast and exposure, not identity, so it is divided out. Every descriptor this module produces is a unit vector, which makes the inner product a similarity directly.

(10.2) Cosine similarity.

\[s(a,b) = \frac{a^{T}b}{\|a\|\,\|b\|} \in [-1,1]\]

(10.3) Equivalence with Euclidean distance. For unit \(u,v\):

\[\|u-v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 - 2u^{T}v = 2(1-s)\]

Ranking by descending cosine similarity and by ascending Euclidean distance give the same order, so the matcher may reason in whichever is convenient.

docs.title: 10.2 Histograms, and why the square root
docs.text:
(10.4) L1 normalisation. \(p_i = v_i/\sum_j v_j\) puts a histogram of counts on the probability simplex, making it independent of how many pixels were sampled.

(10.5) The Hellinger map. \(\phi(p) = \sqrt{p}\), elementwise.

Proposition 10.1. \(\phi\) maps the probability simplex onto the unit sphere, and the inner product of two mapped histograms is the Bhattacharyya coefficient.

Proof. \(\|\phi(p)\|_2^2 = \sum_i(\sqrt{p_i})^2 = \sum_i p_i = 1\), so the image lies on the unit sphere. And \(\phi(p)^{T}\phi(q) = \sum_i\sqrt{p_i}\sqrt{q_i} = \sum_i\sqrt{p_iq_i} = \mathrm{BC}(p,q)\). ∎

(10.6) This is what unifies the two descriptor families: the same cosine routine compares gradient descriptors and colour histograms, and for the histograms it is a statistically meaningful quantity — the Bhattacharyya coefficient, with \(H^2(p,q) = 1 - \mathrm{BC}(p,q)\) the squared Hellinger distance. The square root is not a trick; it is the isometry that puts a distribution on the sphere.

docs.title: 10.3 The prototype is optimal, not just convenient
docs.text:
(10.7) Incremental mean. \(\mu_k = \mu_{k-1} + (x_k-\mu_{k-1})/k\), exact for every \(k\) and numerically stabler than accumulating \(\sum x_i\). A class is refined by showing another view; no history is kept.

(10.8) The prototype. \(c = \mu/\|\mu\|\).

Theorem 10.2. Given exemplars \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) on the unit sphere, the unit vector maximising the total similarity \(\sum_i c^{T}x_i\) is the normalised mean.

Proof. \(\sum_i c^{T}x_i = c^{T}v\) with \(v = \sum_i x_i\). By Cauchy-Schwarz, \(c^{T}v \le \|c\|\|v\| = \|v\|\), with equality iff \(c\) is parallel to \(v\). The maximiser is therefore \(c = v/\|v\| = \mu/\|\mu\|\). ∎

So the prototype is not an arbitrary average: it is the single direction that best explains every example it was built from. This is the nearest-class-mean classifier (Mensink et al., TPAMI 2013), which is Bayes-optimal when the class-conditionals share a covariance.

The test verifies the theorem the hard way — 500 random unit directions, none of which beats the prototype.

docs.title: 10.4 The acceptance gate has a stated error bound
docs.text:
A similarity threshold picked by hand is a guess. This one is calibrated against the scene and carries a bound.

(10.9) Cantelli's inequality. For any random variable with finite mean and variance,

\[P(X - \mu \ge z\sigma) \le \frac{1}{1+z^2}\]

(10.10) The gate. On learning, background regions of the same frame are described and compared with the new prototype, giving \(\mu_{bg}\) and \(\sigma_{bg}\). The threshold is

\[\tau = \max(\tau_{floor},\ \mu_{bg} + z\,\sigma_{bg})\]

By (10.9) the probability that a background region clears \(\tau\) is at most \(1/(1+z^2)\) — without assuming the similarity distribution is Gaussian, which it is not. At \(z=4\) the bound is 5.9%; at \(z=5\), 3.8%. The floor keeps a featureless background, where \(\sigma_{bg}\approx0\), from admitting everything.

test_exemplar_math checks the bound empirically against a deliberately skewed distribution, which is where a Gaussian assumption would have failed.

A second gate covers ambiguity: the winning similarity must exceed the runner-up's by a margin. Two remembered objects that explain a region equally well make the assignment a coin flip, and rejecting is better than guessing.

docs.title: 10.5 The two descriptor families
docs.text:
(10.11) L2-Hys normalisation (Dalal & Triggs, CVPR 2005 §6.4). L2-normalise, clip each component at \(\kappa\), renormalise.

L2 normalisation alone already gives invariance to an affine illumination change \(I \mapsto aI+b\): the gradient removes \(b\) and scales by \(a\), which normalisation divides out. The clip bounds how much any one gradient — a specular highlight, a hard shadow edge — can dominate. Note the renormalisation scales everything back up, so components legitimately end above \(\kappa\): the clip bounds influence, not magnitude.

(10.12) Orientation binning. A gradient angle is mapped to a fractional bin over \([0,\pi)\) for unsigned gradients or \([0,2\pi)\) for signed ones, and its vote is split between the two neighbouring bins. Splitting rather than rounding removes the aliasing that would make the descriptor jump as an edge slowly rotates. The spatial vote is bilinear over neighbouring cells for the same reason, so the full vote is trilinear.

Unsigned is the default: for appearance matching, a dark-to-light edge and its mirror are the same structure.

docs.title: 10.6 What this method can and cannot do
docs.text:
It recognises the instance that was marked. Marking one red mug teaches that mug — not mugs. Category-level generalisation is exactly what training buys, and this is deliberately the other trade: instant, on the spot, for one object.

One measurable limitation, found while testing rather than assumed: pixels below the saturation gate have no usable hue and are pooled into one achromatic bin, so an object that is largely black, white or grey puts most of its colour mass there — and so does every other such object, including background. A pattern of colour-against-black scores 0.5 in colour similarity against a differently coloured pattern of the same construction, purely through shared achromatic mass. For dark or desaturated objects, lower the colour weight and let the gradient half decide.

docs.title: Model Training & Notebooks
docs.text:
Two directories hold Jupyter material: Train_Pytorch/ trains and exports the detectors that run on the robot, and Notebooks/ holds interactive bring-up notebooks for the Jetbot (motion, ROS 2, sensors, stereo calibration).

The deployed inference path is described on Deep Learning (TensorRT / cuDNN / native CUDA backends) and Object Detection (Isaac ROS decoders and NanoOWL).

docs.title: Train_Pytorch/ — training and export
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    D["data_preparation<br/>VOC / COCO → splits,<br/>augmentation"] --> T["training<br/>SSD · Faster R-CNN ·<br/>YOLOv3 · OWL-ViT"]
    T --> E["model_evaluation<br/>mAP · PR / ROC ·<br/>speed · FLOPs"]
    T --> X["export<br/>ONNX · TorchScript"]
    X --> R["trt_export<br/>TensorRT engine"]
    R --> J(("Jetson<br/>isaac_ros_objectdetection"))
Notebook Purpose data_preparation.ipynb ObjectDetectionDataset for bounding-box annotations (Pascal VOC, COCO), train/val/test split with a fixed seed, Albumentations augmentation, dataset statistics and visual inspection custom_detector_training.ipynb Training pipeline for SSD300 (VGG16) and Faster R-CNN (ResNet50-FPN) with learning-rate scheduling, TensorBoard logging and checkpoints ssd_mobilenet_v2.ipynb SSD with a MobileNet v2 backbone on a custom dataset ssdlite320_mobilenet_v3_large.ipynb SSDlite 320 × 320 with a MobileNet v3-Large backbone yolo_training.ipynb YOLOv3 implementation: loss, 13 × 13 grid for 416 × 416 input, multi-scale anchors train_owl-v2.ipynb Fine-tuning OWL-ViT (transformers OwlViTForObjectDetection) model_evaluation.ipynb Confusion matrices, precision-recall and ROC curves, mAP, per-class metrics, inference-speed benchmark, parameter / memory / FLOPs analysis, JSON and HTML reports trt_export.ipynb Export of a trained model towards TensorRT

Shared code lives in Train_Pytorch/scripts/:

Module Content training_helpers.py TrainingConfig, DataConfig, AugmentationConfig, MetricsTracker, ModelCheckpoint, LearningRateScheduler, ModelAnalyzer, get_device(), set_seed(), load_json_annotations() training_utils.py BaseTrainer, MixUp / CutMix augmentation, IoU / AP computation, classification and detection evaluation, ONNX / TorchScript export, dynamic quantization

The change history of the module is in Train_Pytorch/CHANGELOG.md.

From a trained model to the robot

Precision (FP16 / INT8), calibration and engine building for the Orin Nano Super (sm_87) are covered by the Custom Models tutorial and by the TensorRT section of Deep Learning.

docs.title: Notebooks/ — Jetbot bring-up
docs.text:
Directory Notebooks Content basic_motion/ basic_motion.ipynb Motion commands from an rclpy node basic_ros2/ basic_ros2-camera.ipynb, ros2-jupyter_cli.ipynb Camera topic in a notebook; ROS 2 command line from Jupyter teleoperation/ teleoperation.ipynb Teleoperation from the notebook sensor/ imu_show.ipynb, gnss_show.ipynb, mpc-controller.ipynb IMU and GNSS plots; an MPC experiment built with CasADi models/ OWL-VIT.ipynb OWL-ViT open-vocabulary detection on an image calibration_stereo/ 01_intrinsics_lens_dist … 07_calculate_depth, plus capture and depth tests Stereo calibration workflow: chessboard corners and lens distortion, rectification maps, remapping with OpenCV and NVIDIA VPI, depth computation

The stereo calibration notebooks prepare the rig used by Stereo Vision; the printable 10 × 7 chessboard is checkerboard_10x7.pdf (see also the Camera Calibration tutorial).

Notebooks are not the control path

The notebooks are exploration and bring-up tools. The MPC notebook in sensor/ is an experiment; the MPC that flies the vehicle is the one in ros2_control_system, with its derivation, margins and tests.

docs.title: Bandwidth budget
docs.text:
Stream Load Source Sensor link (IMU 1 kHz, 12 encoders 1 kHz, attitude, GNSS) ≈ 1.95 Mbit/s = 2 % of 100 Mbit/s JetOwl Bridge Vision preview, rgb8 160×120 at 5 Hz 2.46 Mbit/s = 2.5 % of 100 Mbit/s Vision micro-ROS Raw camera across boards, 1280×720 RGB8 at 30 Hz ≈ 664 Mbit/s = 66 % of 1 GbE Helm

Raw image streams should therefore be consumed on the board that owns the camera; point clouds and control topics are negligible.

docs.title: Signal chain
docs.text:
Every path that moves hardware follows the chain mandated by the control design standard:

flowchart LR
    S["Sensors<br/>IMU · GNSS · baro · LiDAR · cameras"] --> F["Filters<br/>guards · LPF · Hampel · median"]
    F --> E["Estimators<br/>ESKF · EKF · KF · observers"]
    E --> C["Controllers<br/>MPC · 2-DOF · PID + ESO · SIMC PI"]
    C --> A["Actuator interface<br/>saturation · rate/jerk limit · allocation"]
    A --> P(("Vehicle"))
    P -. "measured state" .-> S

docs.title: Loop hierarchy (UAV)
docs.text:
Loop Rate Location Closed on Rotor speed 1 kHz per rotor FC firmware bidirectional DShot RPM telemetry Angular rate (PID + ESO) 1 kHz FC firmware gyro Attitude 250 Hz FC firmware fused IMU quaternion Translation (MPC) 50 Hz ros2_control_system ESKF estimate Position/yaw reference (2-DOF) 50 Hz ros2_flight_controller filtered odometry Mission supervision event-driven ros2_mission_planner flight status and odometry

Each outer loop is at least 3–5× slower than the loop it commands, so the inner loop can be treated as ideal in the outer loop's design; the residual delay (40 ms for the attitude loop as seen by the MPC) is booked explicitly in the margins.

docs.title: Failsafe hierarchy
docs.text: Event Detected by Response Set-point stale for 0.1 s (Jetson or network lost) FC cmd_guard level attitude (closed loop), bounded open-loop descent, disarm after 1.2·t_fs Odometry stale uav_trajectory_controller level attitude, bounded descent Reference stale uav_trajectory_controller closed-loop position hold Battery low / critical, GNSS lost, geofence flight_controller_node RTH / LAND RF jamming / spoofing failsafe_controller latched, escalate-only RTH / LAND GCS link lost network_bridge_node configurable link_loss policy (RTH, LAND or HOVER) RC link lost while the pilot holds authority FC same bounded landing as a stale set-point

docs.title: Design rules that apply everywhere
docs.text:
• Measured feedback returns to every controller; open loop only where no sensor exists, with a bound and a watchdog.
  • Derivation in the code. Each controller and estimator header carries the design block of the control standard (plant, sensor, filter, estimator, controller, actuator, margins, references).
  • Pure-maths cores. Control and estimation code is separated from ROS and HAL glue (lidar_slam_core, Application/Control/, uav/*.hpp), so it is unit-tested on a host without hardware.
  • Simulation uses the vehicle's own interfaces. The Gazebo virtual MCU sends the same UDP frames to the same driver, so the ROS 2 nodes cannot tell simulation from the vehicle.

docs.title: CUDA — GPU acceleration library (cuda_jetbot_nanoowl)
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from CUDA/README.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in CUDA/.

cuda_jetbot_nanoowl 1.0.0 is a standalone C++17/CUDA library for the Jetson Orin Nano Super (sm_87). It provides GPU device and memory management, a batched multi-channel PID controller, a model-predictive controller for a kinematic vehicle, and a VPI image-processing wrapper. The directory carries COLCON_IGNORE: it is built with plain CMake and is not part of the ROS 2 workspace.

Relation to the flight stack. The controllers here are generic, reusable building blocks with example default parameters. The MPC/MPPI that flies the UAV lives in ros2_control_system, with its plant model, stability margins and SIL evidence; the firmware loops live in JetOwl_FlightControl. Any use of this library in a control path must carry its own derivation, as required by .claude/rules/control-systems.md.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
Module Header Status Content Core common.h, device.h, memory.h built error handling (CUDAException, MemoryException), device query/selection (Device, ScopedDevice, MultiGPUContext), memory pools and RAII guards (MemoryPool, PinnedMemoryPool, DeviceMemoryGuard, ManagedMemoryGuard, StreamGuard) PID pid_controller.h, kernels/pid_control_kernels.cu built PIDController: N independent channels evaluated in one kernel launch; output and integral limits, error deadband, low-pass-filtered derivative, back-calculation anti-windup, optional set-point ramping; position / velocity / adaptive modes MPC mpc_control.h, kernels/mpc_control_kernels.cu built MPCController: kinematic bicycle model [x, y, θ, v] with inputs [a, δ], linearisation, condensed QP (Hessian/gradient built on the GPU), box constraints on inputs and states, projected gradient iterations with warm start; line / circle / spline reference generators VPI vpi_image_processor.h not built by default VPIImageProcessor: format conversion, Gaussian/median/bilateral filters, morphology, Canny/Sobel/Laplacian edges, Harris/FAST corners, stereo disparity, resize/rotate/flip/affine warp, image statistics and blur detection; CPU, CUDA, PVA and VIC back ends

The VPI source is commented out of CORE_SOURCES in CMakeLists.txt ("requires VPI headers"); its example and test are compiled only when CMake finds VPI.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Requirements: CUDA Toolkit (JetPack 6.2 on the Jetson), CMake ≥ 3.20, a C++17 compiler; VPI (optional, shipped with JetPack).

cd CUDA
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j"$(nproc)"
sudo cmake --install build        # optional: headers + libcuda_jetbot_nanoowl
CMake option Default Effect BUILD_SHARED_LIBS ON shared (.so) or static library BUILD_EXAMPLES ON builds the four examples below BUILD_TESTS OFF builds test_mpc_utils (and test_vpi_utils with VPI) ENABLE_PROFILING ON compiles the timing instrumentation (computation_time fields) JETSON_ORIN_NANO ON CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES = 87; OFF uses native

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Executable Shows 01_basic_gpu_check device enumeration, properties, memory pool 02_mpc_control_demo creating an MPCController, cost weights, solving, predicted trajectory, reference generation 03_pid_control_demo multi-channel PID with limits, anti-windup and derivative filtering 04_vpi_image_processing_demo VPI filters, edges and corners (requires VPI) 
./build/01_basic_gpu_check
./build/02_mpc_control_demo

docs.title: C++ usage
docs.text:
#include <cuda_jetbot_nanoowl.h>

cjn::PIDConfig cfg = cjn::create_pid_config(/*kp=*/2.0f, /*ki=*/0.5f, /*kd=*/0.05f);
cfg.sampling_time = 0.01f;                       // must equal the actual loop period
cjn::PIDController pid(cfg);
pid.set_setpoint(0, 1.0f);
cjn::PIDResult r = pid.compute({measured_value});  // r.control_output[0], r.saturated

The gains above are placeholders: gains must come from a named design method against an identified plant (.claude/rules/control-systems.md §2.4.1). The library offers compute_pid_gains_zn() (Ziegler–Nichols) only as a starting point.

docs.title: Python package
docs.text: python/cuda_jetbot_nanoowl (installable with pip install -e .) is a pure-Python facade of the core module (Device, MemoryPool, DeviceGuard, get_available_devices(), …). It does not bind the C++ library and exposes neither the PID nor the MPC controller.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: cmake -B build -DBUILD_TESTS=ON && cmake --build build && ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• CMakeLists.txt declares a test_pid_utils target whose source tests/test_pid_utils.cpp is not in the repository, so -DBUILD_TESTS=ON fails to configure until the target is removed or the test is added.
  • The VPI module is excluded from the library build; enabling it means restoring the two commented lines in CMakeLists.txt on a system with VPI.
  • The MPC uses a kinematic ground-vehicle model and fixed-iteration projected gradient; no stability or convergence certificate is provided with the library.
  • No performance figures have been measured on the target yet.

} catch (const cjn::CUDAException& e) {
    std::cerr << "CUDA error: " << e.what() << std::endl;
    std::cerr << "Error code: " << (int)e.error_code() << std::endl;
}

docs.title: C++ Full Example
docs.text:
#include <cuda_jetbot_nanoowl/cuda_jetbot_nanoowl.h>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    try {
        // Initialize device
        cjn::Device device(0);
        device.print_info();

        // Set as current
        device.set_current();

        // Allocate memory
        const size_t size = 10 * 1024 * 1024;  // 10 MB
        auto gpu_mem = cjn::DeviceMemoryGuard(size);

        // Create pinned memory for transfers
        auto cpu_mem = std::make_unique<float[]>(size / sizeof(float));

        // Transfer data
        gpu_mem.copy_from_host(cpu_mem.get(), size);

        // Create stream
        auto stream = cjn::StreamGuard();

        // Synchronize
        stream.synchronize();

        // Transfer back
        gpu_mem.copy_to_host(cpu_mem.get(), size);

        std::cout << "Success!" << std::endl;
        return 0;

    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cerr << "Error: " << e.what() << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }
}

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import cuda_jetbot_nanoowl as cjn

# Check CUDA
if not cjn.core.is_cuda_available():
    print("CUDA not available!")
    exit(1)

# Print device info
cjn.core.print_device_info()

# Create device
device = cjn.core.Device(0)
print(f"Device: {device.get_id()}")
print(f"Free Memory: {device.get_free_memory() / (1024*1024):.0f} MB")

# Memory pool
pool = cjn.core.MemoryPool(0)
ptr = pool.allocate(1024 * 1024)  # 1 MB
print(f"Allocated at: {ptr}")

# Device guard context
with cjn.core.DeviceGuard(0):
    print("Operations on device 0")

print("Done!")

Item Version On the Jetson Orin Nano Super CUDA Toolkit the one shipped with JetPack 6.2+ pre-installed (/usr/local/cuda) CMake ≥ 3.20 sudo apt install cmake (or pip install cmake if the apt version is older) C++ compiler C++17 (GCC ≥ 9) sudo apt install build-essential VPI optional, for the image-processing module shipped with JetPack (nvidia-vpi) Python ≥ 3.8, optional, for the Python facade sudo apt install python3-dev python3-pip

docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/TNG-Blue/Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL.git
cd Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL/CUDA

cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release        # JETSON_ORIN_NANO=ON → sm_87
cmake --build build -j"$(nproc)"
sudo cmake --install build                       # or: cmake --install build --prefix ~/.local
