docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
How the software reaches the robot, runs there, stays up to date and talks to operators. Each page below is rendered from, or written against, the files that implement it.

  • Docker

    One image per ROS 2 node from a single template, CPU and GPU bases, the runtime contract and Docker Compose for a single Jetson.

    Docker

  • Kubernetes

    Bootstrap of the two-Jetson k3s cluster: network, install scripts, settings and where their numbers come from.

    Kubernetes

  • Helm

    The ros2-jetson chart: node catalogue, scheduling and resource budget, DDS in Kubernetes, failover.

    Helm Charts

  • OTA Updates

    A/B firmware updates for the STM32N6 microcontrollers from the Go OTA server.

    OTA Updates

  • MAVLink Relay Server

    TLS relay that connects the vehicle and operator consoles across NAT without opening a port on the robot.

    MAVLink Relay

  • OTA Web Interface

    Static preview of the OTA server's firmware dashboard.

    Web Interface

docs.title: Deployment targets
docs.text: Target Use How Native build development on the Jetson or a PC ROS/build.sh (Installation) Docker Compose, one Jetson bench work with the production images Docker/compose (Docker) k3s + Helm, two Jetsons the vehicle Kubernetes/ + Helm/ (tutorial) OTA server firmware distribution to the MCUs Server_OTA/ on the cluster, a host or App Engine (Server OTA deployment) MAVLink relay operator consoles on another network Server_Relay/ (MAVLink Relay)

docs.title: Vehicle network
docs.text:
Address (192.168.10.0/24) Device .1 Jetson #1: k3s server, image registry :5000, micro-ROS agent UDP 8888 .2 JetOwl flight controller (STM32N657) .3 JetOwl_Vision camera (STM32N655) .4 Jetson #2: k3s agent .200 OTA server (MetalLB)

The MCUs use static addresses (no DHCP). ROS 2 pods use host networking so that DDS multicast discovery crosses the boards on the physical switch; see Helm.

docs.title: Release flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C["commit on master"] --> CI["CI: lint, tests,<br/>docs build"]
    CI --> IMG["Docker/scripts/build_all.sh<br/>--push --tag vX.Y.Z"]
    IMG --> H["Helm/scripts/deploy.sh<br/>--set global.imageTag=vX.Y.Z"]
    FW["firmware: make ota-upload"] --> OTA["Server_OTA"]
    OTA --> MCU["MCUs: ota/start → ota/apply"]

Roll back the ROS 2 side with helm -n jetowl rollback jetowl; the firmware side rolls back on its own when a new image fails its trial boot. See Release Process.

docs.title: Docker — one image per ROS 2 node
docs.text:
Docker/ builds every ROS 2 package as its own image from one template (Docker/README.md). The list is Docker/images.txt: image, package, base (cpu = ros:humble-ros-base-jammy, gpu = l4t-jetpack r36.4 with CUDA/TensorRT/VPI and the Isaac ROS apt repository) and extra pip packages.

Docker/scripts/build_all.sh --push --tag v0.3.0             # on the master Jetson
Docker/scripts/build_all.sh --only ros2_stereo --skip-base --push --tag v0.3.1

The template builds only the package and its in-repo dependencies (colcon --packages-up-to), resolves system dependencies with rosdep, and ships a runtime stage without sources or compilers that fails to build if any binary has an unresolved shared library.

Containers start from environment variables (ROS_LAUNCH_FILE/ROS_LAUNCH_ARGS or ROS_EXECUTABLE/ROS_ARGS); the entrypoint forwards SIGTERM as SIGINT so ros2 launch shuts its nodes down cleanly on docker stop and Kubernetes pod deletion.

Single board without Kubernetes:

cd Docker/compose && docker compose up -d     # network_mode: host + ipc: host

docs.title: Helm — ROS 2 nodes on two Jetsons
docs.text: The ros2-jetson chart (Helm/charts/ros2-jetson) deploys every ROS 2 node of the robot onto the two-board k3s cluster: one entry in values.yaml → nodes = one ROS 2 package = one image = one Deployment. The full design, with the numbers behind each default, is in Helm/README.md.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Helm/scripts/deploy.sh --set global.imageTag=v0.3.0        # MetalLB, namespace, chart, wait
make -C Helm status                                        # pods and the board each runs on
make -C Helm test                                          # talker on worker → listener on master

docs.title: Placement and load balancing
docs.text:
Kind of node Placement Examples needs a device on one board pinned (placement: master/worker) micro-ROS agent, JetOwl bridge, LiDAR SLAM, stereo/thermal cameras compute only floating (placement: any) — balanced and failed over control system, network bridge, LiDAR AI, object detection, RF classifier, dashboard

The kube-scheduler ranks the two boards for each floating pod by free resources (LeastAllocated), CPU/memory balance (BalancedAllocation), an even ROS 2 pod count (topology spread, maxSkew: 1) and GPU-pod anti-affinity. Requests include GPU memory, since the Orin's GPU shares the 8 GB. No HPA and replicas: 1: a second copy of a ROS 2 node is a second publisher on the same topics, not extra capacity.

Failover of the worker: node-monitor-grace-period 20 s + ≤ 5 s check period + 10 s toleration ≈ 35 s before floating pods restart on the master (images are pre-pulled on both boards). Priority classes (critical → high → normal) decide what runs when one board cannot hold all requests (5.35 CPU / 6.5 GiB requested vs 5.0 CPU / 5.1 GiB allocatable on the master).

docs.title: ROS 2 communication
docs.text: Host networking: DDS multicast discovery (239.255.0.1:7400+250·domain) and unicast data cross the Ethernet switch directly; flannel VXLAN would not carry multicast. The DDS profile binds Fast DDS (default) or Cyclone DDS to the cluster Ethernet addresses, and same-board traffic uses Fast DDS shared memory (hostIPC + host /dev/shm).

docs.title: OTA server
docs.text: Pod network + MetalLB Layer 2 address 192.168.10.200:8080 on the robot Ethernet — the NET_OTA_SERVER_IP of both MCU firmwares.

docs.title: Kubernetes — two-Jetson k3s cluster
docs.text:
Kubernetes/ bootstraps the cluster; workloads come only from Helm. Details: Kubernetes/README.md.

Board Role Ethernet Jetson Orin Nano Super #1 k3s server (master) + image registry :5000 192.168.10.1/24 Jetson Orin Nano Super #2 k3s agent (worker) 192.168.10.4/24 JetOwl FC / Vision MCUs micro-ROS clients → 192.168.10.1:8888 .2 / .3 MetalLB pool LoadBalancer addresses .200–.220 
sudo Kubernetes/cluster/install-master.sh                    # on the master, prints the token
sudo Kubernetes/cluster/install-worker.sh --token <token>    # on the worker
kubectl get nodes -L jetowl.tng-blue.io/role -o wide

The scripts write /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml (node IP and flannel on the Ethernet port, Traefik and ServiceLB off — MetalLB is used — kubelet reservations, 20 s node failure detection), the registry mirror /etc/rancher/k3s/registries.yaml, start the registry, create the nvidia RuntimeClass and label the nodes jetowl.tng-blue.io/role=master|worker.

One k3s server only: an etcd control plane on two boards has quorum ⌊2/2⌋ + 1 = 2 and tolerates no failure, so a second server would add load without availability.

docs.title: Server_Relay — MAVLink relay for robots and consoles on different networks
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from Server_Relay/README.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in Server_Relay/.

ros2_network_bridge and the JetbotNanoOWL console normally share a LAN: the console's UDP heartbeat reaches the bridge and the bridge answers to its address. Put the robot on one network and the phone on another (a 4G phone, a robot behind a home router) and neither can reach the other: both sit behind NAT, the phone usually behind the carrier's (CGNAT), and neither has a port anyone can open.

The relay removes the problem instead of working around NAT: both ends dial out to one server with a public address, over TLS, and the server joins them. Outbound TCP crosses every NAT, CGNAT included; nothing is opened on the robot or the phone.

 Jetson (any network)                    relay (public IP)                 phone (any network)
 network_bridge_node                     relay -listen :5790               JetbotNanoOWL
   transport: relay ──── TLS ──────────▶ ┌──────────────────────┐ ◀────── TLS ──── MAVLink relay
   MAVRELAY/1 vehicle jetbot-01 <tok>    │ robot "jetbot-01"    │      MAVRELAY/1 observer
                                         │  vehicle ──▶ all     │      jetbot-01 <tok>
                                         │  observers ──▶ only  │
                                         │  verified HEARTBEAT  │
                                         └──────────────────────┘

Go 1.21, standard library only. Package relay is the server; main.go is the command.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
1. TLS (1.2 minimum, 1.3 when both ends offer it) to the relay, port 5790 by default.
  2. The client sends one line, at most 512 bytes, within 5 s:
MAVRELAY/1 <vehicle|observer> <robot-id> <token>

robot-id is [A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,64}. 3. The relay answers OK , or ERR auth / ERR malformed / ERR full and closes. 4. From then on, the connection carries raw MAVLink v1/v2 frames both ways.

The relay cuts each stream into whole frames (from the header length, signed frames included) and forwards frames, never byte ranges, so frames from two observers can never interleave into one corrupt frame on the vehicle's stream.

docs.title: Roles and the safety rule
docs.text:
from forwarded to what passes vehicle every observer of that robot every frame observer the vehicle only a HEARTBEAT whose CRC (with CRC_EXTRA 50) verifies, unsigned observer other observers nothing

An observer credential therefore cannot command the robot: no COMMAND_LONG, no set-point, no parameter, no mission item ever reaches the vehicle from it, whatever the client sends — the rule is enforced here, not trusted to the client. It is the network form of the console's own rule (it is an observer and announces itself as MAV_TYPE_LOG, which the bridge never takes for its GCS; see Source/ROS2_Network_Bridge/README.md). A commanding GCS over the relay would need a third role and is deliberately not offered.

  • One vehicle per robot. A new authenticated vehicle replaces the old connection, which can linger after the robot changes network until its idle timeout.
  • Observers per robot: at most -max-observers (default 8).
  • Idle timeout (-idle, default 10 s): both ends send HEARTBEAT at 1 Hz and TCP loses no bytes, so 10 s of silence is a dead path; it also outlasts three TCP retransmission back-offs (1 + 2 + 4 s) of a stalled one.
  • Back-pressure: each peer has a 256-frame send queue. A full queue drops the new frame — a slow observer must not stall the vehicle or the other observers, and to both ends a dropped frame is an ordinary loss that their sequence-gap counters already report.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text: threat what stops it eavesdropping, tampering on the path TLS; the client verifies the server (system CA + host name, or a pinned SHA-256 of the server key) connecting without a credential 256-bit random token per robot and role; the server stores only SHA-256 hashes, compared in constant time guessing tokens 2²⁵⁶ space; every failure waits 1 s and gets the same ERR auth, so nothing tells a wrong robot from a wrong token a leaked observer token the holder can watch, never command (safety rule above); rotate the hash a leaked vehicle token the holder can impersonate the robot to the consoles; it still cannot reach the real robot. Rotate a leaked credentials file it holds hashes, not tokens a relay operator sees telemetry in clear inside the relay; host it yourself. MAVLink signing end to end is not implemented by the bridge (its README, Known limitations)

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text:
Any host with a public address — a small VPS is enough: the console's stream is about 2.5 kB/s per robot (bridge rates.*, 10 Hz ODOMETRY).

# 1. tokens: one per robot and role, kept by the robot / the phone only
VTOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32); OTOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
cd Server_Relay/src && go build -o relay .
cat > ../config/credentials.json <<EOF
[
  {"robot": "jetbot-01", "role": "vehicle",  "sha256": "$(printf %s "$VTOKEN" | ./relay -hash)"},
  {"robot": "jetbot-01", "role": "observer", "sha256": "$(printf %s "$OTOKEN" | ./relay -hash)"}
]
EOF

# 2. a certificate for the relay's name (Let's Encrypt, or self-signed + pin on the clients)
openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -days 825 \
    -subj /CN=relay.example.org -addext subjectAltName=DNS:relay.example.org \
    -keyout privkey.pem -out fullchain.pem
# pin for the clients (SHA-256 of the public key, hex):
openssl x509 -in fullchain.pem -pubkey -noout | openssl pkey -pubin -outform der \
    | openssl dgst -sha256 | cut -d' ' -f2

# 3. run (or: docker build -t mavlink-relay Server_Relay)
./relay -listen :5790 -cert fullchain.pem -key privkey.pem -credentials ../config/credentials.json

Robot side: ros2 launch ros2_network_bridge jetbot_console.launch.py transport:=relay relay_host:=relay.example.org relay_robot:=jetbot-01 relay_token_file:=/etc/jetbot/relay.token (see Source/ROS2_Network_Bridge/README.md). Phone side: Settings → ROS2 Connection → MAVLink relay, with the same host, port, robot id, the observer token and, for a self-signed certificate, the pin.

config/credentials.json and *.pem are git-ignored; config/credentials.example.json shows the format.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
cd Server_Relay/src && gofmt -l . && go vet ./... && go test -race ./...

TLS with a generated certificate, pymavlink golden frames: authentication (wrong token, wrong role), fan-out to two observers, an ARM COMMAND_LONG from an observer dropped while its heartbeat passes, corrupted and signed heartbeats refused, observer limit, vehicle replacement, a stalled observer not holding up the stream of another, the full-queue drop rule, idle timeout. CI: .github/workflows/relay-server-ci.yml.

docs.title: Latency
docs.text: The relay adds the detour through its host, and TCP replaces loss with delay (a retransmitted segment holds back the ones behind it). The console does not assume either away: it estimates each fix's excess delay from its timestamp and predicts the fix forward with its own motion model and process noise before fusing it (JetbotNanoOWL docs/MAVLINK_LINK.md, §8).

docs.title: OTA Web Interface
docs.text: The firmware dashboard shipped with Server_OTA v3.0.0 is published next to this documentation as a static preview, so the UI can be inspected without deploying a server.

docs.title: 🖥️ Open the Preview
docs.text:
🚀 Full-Screen Preview

The complete dashboard — upload zone, firmware grid, statistics and theming — rendered from the real templates.

Open UI → 📦 Server Source

Go backend, templates and deployment scripts under Server_OTA/.

Browse →

Preview, not a deployment

The preview is static and read-only. It is served by GitHub Pages, which has no Go backend, so upload, download and delete are disabled and the API responses are demo payloads. Everything else — layout, theming, filtering, sorting, view switching — is the production UI, byte-for-byte from Server_OTA/web/templates/index.html.

Embedded frame is empty locally

The preview only exists in the deployed dual build. When you run mkdocs serve from a checkout, build it first with the command in Reproduce the dual build locally.

docs.title: 🔌 What the Preview Simulates
docs.text:
Server_OTA/web/static/js/script.js polls three read-only endpoints every 5 seconds. On a static host those paths do not exist, so the preview build injects static/js/preview-demo.js, which answers them with payloads that follow the exact contract of the Go handlers.

Endpoint Go handler data payload Preview source /api/stats handlers.HandleStats total_files, total_size, downloads, server_version derived from the demo dataset /api/health handlers.HandleHealth status, memory_mb, goroutines, timestamp (models.HealthStatus) fixed operational status /api/firmware/list handlers.HandleFirmwareList array of size, mod_time, name, version, device_type, description (models.FirmwareInfo) 5 demo firmware entries

The firmware entries carry exactly the version, device_type and description that services.ListFirmwareFiles() would derive from those file names — see Firmware metadata. The two health counters are illustrative: today the live server reports goroutines: 0 and timestamp: 0 (see Current gaps).

Every response is wrapped in the standard envelope produced by utils.RespondSuccess (models.APIResponse):

{
  "data": { "total_files": 5, "total_size": 272105472, "downloads": 128, "server_version": "3.0.0" },
  "message": "Server statistics",
  "success": true
}

The totals are computed from the demo dataset at runtime rather than hard-coded, so the navbar counters, the dashboard cards and the firmware grid always agree with each other.

Write operations (/upload, /download, delete) have no static equivalent. The shim replaces them with an explanatory notification instead of letting the request fail.

docs.title: 🏗️ Dual Build Pipeline
docs.text:
.github/workflows/docs_deploy.yaml builds two independent artifacts and publishes them as one site to the public documentation repository Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL-Docs.

graph LR
    subgraph "Build (parallel)"
        A["build<br/>MkDocs → site/"]
        B["build-ota-preview<br/>Server_OTA/web → ota-preview/"]
    end

    A --> C["test<br/>6 quality gates"]
    C --> D["deploy-to-public-repo"]
    B --> D
    D --> E["merge:<br/>site/ + site/ota-preview/"]
    E --> F["gh-pages @ Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL-Docs"]
Stage Job Output Documentation build documentation-site-<run_id> artifact Web interface build-ota-preview ota-preview-site-<run_id> artifact Quality gates test HTML, assets, secrets, performance, link checks Publication deploy-to-public-repo merged tree pushed to gh-pages

The preview job is a peer of the docs job, not a step inside it: a failure in the OTA UI build blocks publication, but the two builds do not share state. The deployment step places the preview at ota-preview/ inside the published site and fails if either half is missing.

Workflow triggers — a push to master touching any of:

  • Docs/**, mkdocs.yml — documentation content
  • Server_OTA/web/** — templates, stylesheets, scripts of the dashboard
  • Server_OTA/scripts/build_preview.sh — the preview builder itself
  • .github/workflows/docs_deploy.yaml — the pipeline

docs.title: 💻 Reproduce the Dual Build Locally
docs.text:
# 1. Preview of the OTA UI only (serves it on http://localhost:8081)
./Server_OTA/scripts/build_preview.sh --serve 8081

# 2. Both halves, exactly as CI assembles them
mkdocs build --clean                                      # → site/
./Server_OTA/scripts/build_preview.sh --output site/ota-preview
python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory site              # → http://localhost:8000

build_preview.sh performs the transformations that make the server-rendered template work on a static host:

  1. copies web/templates/index.html, 404.html and web/static/ into the output directory
  2. rewrites the absolute /static/… references the Go server relies on into relative ones
  3. injects window.OTA_PREVIEW_MODE = true and the demo shim before script.js, so the fetch override is installed before the first API call
  4. writes preview-info.json (commit, build time, simulated endpoints)
  5. verifies the result and exits non-zero if an asset, the flag or the shim is missing
Option Default Purpose --source DIR Server_OTA/web Location of templates and static assets --output DIR Server_OTA/preview Output directory (wiped before each build) --serve [PORT] 8081 Serve the result over HTTP after building

docs.title: 🚀 Run the Real Dashboard
docs.text:
The preview replaces a server only for looking at the UI. To exercise uploads, downloads and live statistics, run the actual binary:

From sourceDockerVerify 
cd Server_OTA
./scripts/build.sh        # builds bin/ota-server-3.0.0-linux (+ -rpi)
./scripts/run.sh          # serves http://localhost:8080

docker run -d --name ota-server \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -v $(pwd)/data:/app/data \
  tngblue/server_ota:latest

curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/health  | jq
curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/stats   | jq
curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/firmware/list | jq

Upload limits and accepted extensions come from Server_OTA/config/config.json (50 MB per file; .bin, .hex, .elf, .img, .fw).

docs.title: 🔗 Related Pages
docs.text:
• OTA Updates — the A/B update path end to end
  • Docker Deployment — containerised deployment of the stack
  • REST API — API reference
  • CI/CD — the rest of the automation
**Isaac ROS Jetbot NanoOWL** · OTA Server v3.0.0

docs.title: OTA Updates
docs.text:
Firmware for the two STM32N6 microcontrollers — the JetOwl flight controller (jetowl_fc) and the JetOwl_Vision camera (jetowl_vision) — is updated over the vehicle's Ethernet from the OTA server in this repository. The same OTA layer runs in both firmwares; only the board description differs.

flowchart LR
    B["build machine<br/>make ota-upload VERSION=M.m.p"] -->|"POST /upload<br/>.fw validated"| S["Server_OTA (Go)<br/>:8080"]
    S -->|"GET /api/ota/manifest<br/>GET /download (Range)"| M["MCU 'ota' task<br/>download → SHA-256 →<br/>flash read-back → READY"]
    J["Jetson, ROS 2<br/>/jetowl/ota/start, /apply"] -->|"micro-ROS"| M
    M -->|"pending = other slot,<br/>reset"| F["FSBL<br/>verify copy in RAM,<br/>trial boot with watchdog"]
    F -->|"healthy 30 s"| C(["confirmed"])
    F -->|"3 failed trials /<br/>invalid image"| R(["rollback"])
    M -->|"POST /api/ota/report"| S

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
Property How it is achieved The running image is never overwritten two 4 MB slots (A/B) in the external NOR flash; downloads go to the inactive slot A corrupted image never runs SHA-256 checked four times: downloaded file vs. manifest, slot read back from flash, payload vs. header, and the copy in RAM just before the jump A package cannot overwrite the bootloader every segment must load into a RAM window permitted for the device; the FSBL runs outside all windows The boot record survives a power cut two copies in two sectors, the newer always written to the other sector; read-back yields the old or the new state, never a mixture A bad image cannot loop forever the trial counter is persisted before the jump; after three failed trials the previous image boots A hung image is detected independent watchdog (8.008 s) during the trial session; every blocking network and flash operation is bounded below that The FC is never reset in flight ota/apply is accepted only while disarmed; arming is refused during a trial-boot session

These are proven on the host (504 checks, including a power cut at every flash operation) and end to end against the real Go server over TCP. They have not yet been verified on hardware.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Part Where Reference OTA client, A/B boot control, package format Application/Ota/ (FC), Appli/Ota/ (Vision), FSBL/Boot/ OTA design Packaging tool tools/ota_pack.py in each firmware repository OTA design ROS 2 services and status /jetowl/ota/start, /jetowl/ota/apply, keys fw_version, ota_* of /jetowl/status JetOwl Bridge Server Server_OTA/ (Go): upload validation, manifest, resumable download, device reports Server OTA, API Web interface firmware dashboard of the server OTA Web Interface Cluster deployment Helm, MetalLB address 192.168.10.200:8080, data volume on the master Helm

docs.title: Server address
docs.text: The address is compiled into the firmware (NET_OTA_SERVER_IP and NET_OTA_SERVER_PORT in net_config.h, default 192.168.1.101:8080), and the firmware Makefile uploads to OTA_SERVER (same default). In the two-Jetson cluster the server is exposed at 192.168.10.200:8080, on the MCUs' own subnet; build the firmware with that address for the cluster deployment. When the server is on another subnet, the Jetson must forward and masquerade the MCU traffic (OTA design §7).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Integrity, not authenticity. SHA-256 detects corruption, not a forged package. Signature verification in the FSBL (ECDSA or Ed25519, key in OTP) is the planned next step; until then, keep the server on the vehicle network.
  • Hardware bring-up — XSPI flash, FSBL jump, watchdog, a real network download — is still to be done, in the order listed in the OTA design.

docs.title: Examples — minimal rclcpp reference nodes
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from Examples/README.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in Examples/.

Seven single-file C++ nodes that show one ROS 2 pattern each (publisher with a timer, subscriber, service, image transport with cv_bridge, HTTP calls from a node). They are reference code: the directory carries COLCON_IGNORE, so colcon build skips it.

Node Pattern Subscribes Publishes / serves status_publisher timer → publisher — jetbot_status (std_msgs/String, 500 ms) control_command_publisher timer → publisher — jetbot_cmd_vel (geometry_msgs/Twist, 100 ms) joystick_controller subscriber → publisher joy (sensor_msgs/Joy) cmd_vel (geometry_msgs/Twist) camera_reader image subscriber + OpenCV camera/image_raw (sensor_msgs/Image) OpenCV window parameter_service service server — set_debug_mode (std_srvs/SetBool) firebase_data_handler timer → HTTP (libcurl) — GET/POST Firebase Realtime Database every 5 s firebase_image_uploader image subscriber → HTTP camera/image_raw upload JPEG to Firebase Storage

docs.title: Node graph
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    SP["status_publisher"] --> ST[/"jetbot_status<br/>String"/]
    CCP["control_command_publisher"] --> JCV[/"jetbot_cmd_vel<br/>Twist"/]
    JOYN["joy_node"] --> JOY[/"joy<br/>Joy"/] --> JC["joystick_controller"]
    JC --> CV[/"cmd_vel<br/>Twist"/]
    CAM["camera driver"] --> IMG[/"camera/image_raw<br/>Image"/]
    IMG --> CR["camera_reader"] --> WIN(("OpenCV window"))
    IMG --> FIU["firebase_image_uploader"] -->|"HTTPS POST"| FS[("Firebase Storage")]
    CLI["ros2 service call"] --> SRV{{"set_debug_mode<br/>SetBool"}} --> PS["parameter_service"]
    FDH["firebase_data_handler"] <-->|"HTTPS GET / POST"| RTDB[("Firebase Realtime DB")]

docs.title: Callbacks
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A(["status_publisher: timer 500 ms"]) --> A1["String 'Jetbot is running smoothly!'"] --> A2["publish jetbot_status"]
    B(["control_command_publisher: timer 100 ms"]) --> B1["Twist: linear.x = 0.5, angular.z = 0.1"] --> B2["publish jetbot_cmd_vel"]
    C(["joystick_controller: on joy"]) --> C1["linear.x = axes[1], angular.z = axes[0]"] --> C2["publish cmd_vel"]
    D(["camera_reader: on image"]) --> D1{"cv_bridge → bgr8 ok?"}
    D1 -- yes --> D2["cv::imshow, waitKey(1)"]
    D1 -- no --> D3["log error"]
    E(["parameter_service: set_debug_mode"]) --> E1["debug_mode = request.data"] --> E2["response success + message"]
    F(["firebase_data_handler: timer 5 s"]) --> F1["GET jetbot_data.json"] --> F2["POST status + battery_level"]
    G(["firebase_image_uploader: on image"]) --> G1{"cv_bridge → bgr8 ok?"}
    G1 -- yes --> G2["write /tmp/jetbot_image.jpg"] --> G3["multipart POST to Storage"]
    G1 -- no --> G4["log error"]

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• control_command_publisher and joystick_controller command velocities open loop: no odometry is read and no filter, estimator or limiter sits between the input and cmd_vel. They demonstrate the publisher API only and must not drive a vehicle; closed-loop motion is done by Source/ROS2_Flight_Controller / Source/ROS2_Control_System (see .claude/rules/control-systems.md).
  • The Firebase URL and token are placeholders in the source.
  • CMakeLists.txt lists the Firebase sources as src/firebase_*.cpp, but the files live in firebase_data_handler/ and firebase_image_uploader/; fix the paths before removing COLCON_IGNORE.

docs.title: DFRobot I2C Multiplexer Library
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from Utilities/DFRobot_I2C_Multiplexer/README.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in Utilities/DFRobot_I2C_Multiplexer/.

A professional-grade I2C multiplexer driver library for the Isaac ROS Jetbot NanoOWL platform running on Jetson Orin. Provides both Python and C++ APIs for controlling DFRobot I2C multiplexers with support for port selection, device scanning, and low-level I2C operations.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• 🐍 Python API with smbus2 support for easy scripting
  • ⚙️ C++ API with native Linux i2c-dev support for performance-critical applications
  • 🔍 Device Scanning on each multiplexer port
  • 🎚️ Channel Management with support for up to 8 I2C channels
  • 🔗 Context Manager Support for automatic resource management in Python
  • 🛠️ Command-line Interface for system administration and debugging
  • 📡 Automatic Port Detection and device enumeration
  • 🧪 Comprehensive Testing with unit tests for both Python and C++
  • 📖 Extensive Documentation with examples and API reference

docs.title: Python Package
docs.text: pip install dfrobot-i2c-multiplexer

docs.title: From Source (Development)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/TNG-Blue/Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL.git
cd Utilities/DFRobot_I2C_Multiplexer

# Python
pip install -e .

# C++ (requires CMake 3.10+)
mkdir build && cd build
cmake ..
make
make install
cd ..

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
from dfrobot_i2c_multiplexer import I2CMultiplexer

# Initialize multiplexer on I2C bus 1, address 0x70
mux = I2CMultiplexer(addr=0x70, bus_num=1)

# Scan devices on port 0
devices = mux.scan(port=0)
print(f"Found devices: {devices}")

# Select a specific port
mux.select_port(1)

# Cleanup
mux.close()

Or use context manager for automatic cleanup:

from dfrobot_i2c_multiplexer import I2CMultiplexer

with I2CMultiplexer(addr=0x70, bus_num=1) as mux:
    for port in range(8):
        devices = mux.scan(port)
        print(f"Port {port}: {devices}")

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
#include <dfrobot/i2c_multiplexer.hpp>
#include <iostream>

using namespace DFRobot;

int main() {
    try {
        // Initialize multiplexer
        I2CMultiplexer mux(0x70, 1);

        // Scan port 0
        auto devices = mux.scan(0);
        std::cout << "Found " << devices.size() << " devices\n";

        // Select port 1
        mux.selectPort(1);

    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cerr << "Error: " << e.what() << "\n";
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Command Line Interface
docs.text:
# Scan all ports
i2c-mux-scan -b 1 -a 0x70

# Scan specific port
i2c-mux-scan -b 1 -a 0x70 -p 0

# Use different bus
i2c-mux-scan -b 3 -a 0x70

docs.title: I2CMultiplexer Class
docs.text:
class I2CMultiplexer:
    """I2C Multiplexer driver for Jetson Orin"""

    def __init__(self, addr: int = 0x70, bus_num: int = 1) -> None:
        """Initialize the multiplexer."""

    def scan(self, port: int) -> List[int]:
        """Scan for devices on a specific port."""

    def select_port(self, port: int) -> None:
        """Select an I2C channel."""

    def write_to_device(self, port: int, addr: int, reg: int, data: List[int]) -> None:
        """Write data to a device on a specific port."""

    def read_from_device(self, port: int, addr: int, reg: int, nbytes: int) -> List[int]:
        """Read data from a device on a specific port."""

    def disable_all_ports(self) -> None:
        """Disable all ports."""

    def close(self) -> None:
        """Close the I2C connection."""

    def __enter__(self) -> "I2CMultiplexer":
        """Context manager entry."""

    def __exit__(self, *args) -> None:
        """Context manager exit."""

docs.title: C++ API
docs.text:
namespace DFRobot {

class I2CMultiplexer {
public:
    static constexpr uint8_t DEFAULT_ADDR = 0x70;
    static constexpr uint8_t MAX_CHANNELS = 8;

    // Constructor/Destructor
    I2CMultiplexer(uint8_t addr = DEFAULT_ADDR, int busNum = 1);
    ~I2CMultiplexer();

    // Port control
    std::vector<uint8_t> scan(uint8_t port);
    void selectPort(uint8_t port);
    void disableAllPorts();

    // Device operations
    void writeToDevice(uint8_t port, uint8_t addr, uint8_t reg, 
                      const std::vector<uint8_t>& data);
    std::vector<uint8_t> readFromDevice(uint8_t port, uint8_t addr, 
                                       uint8_t reg, size_t nbytes);

    // Accessors
    int getCurrentChannel() const;
    int getBusNumber() const;
    uint8_t getAddress() const;
};

}  // namespace DFRobot

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text: Our microcontroller platform delivers enterprise-grade capabilities for remotely controlled devices including drones, autonomous robots, and smart navigation systems.

docs.title: Security Capabilities
docs.text: 🔒 Anti-Theft & Anti-Copy ProtectionComprehensive protection mechanisms safeguard source code and firmware from unauthorized access or duplication, ensuring complete system security and intellectual property protection. 🛡️ Anti-Jamming & Anti-SpoofingAdvanced signal protection ensures control communications cannot be interfered with or hijacked by unauthorized sources, maintaining operational safety in contested environments.

docs.title: Communication Systems
docs.text: 📡 Over-the-Air (OTA) UpdatesSeamless remote software updates allow patches or firmware upgrades to be deployed wirelessly via http://jetbot_ros:8081/firmware, enhancing maintainability without physical access. 🌐 Full-duplex LoRa RC link (LR1121)Two Core1121-XF modules per side: commands on 2.4 GHz with frequency hopping (50 Hz), telemetry on a second band (sub-GHz by default, 10 Hz), AES-CMAC authenticated. Ground unit: Remote_UAV (GIGA R1 + Display Shield).

docs.title: Navigation & Control
docs.text: 🌍 Multi-GNSS IntegrationDual GNSS module implementation enhances positioning accuracy and stability, crucial for autonomous navigation and precision localization tasks in various environments. 🤖 ROS2 IntegrationFull compatibility with Robot Operating System 2 enables seamless interaction between system components via standardized topics and services, creating an extensible ecosystem for control applications.

docs.title: Integration with Drone Control
docs.text:
The microcontroller is specifically engineered to support drone control with 6 Degrees of Freedom (6 DOF):

  • X-axis - Lateral movement
  • Y-axis - Forward/backward movement
  • Z-axis - Vertical movement
  • Roll - Rotation around X-axis
  • Pitch - Rotation around Y-axis
  • Yaw - Rotation around Z-axis

This comprehensive control is achieved using only IMU sensors, enhancing the drone's maneuverability while optimizing system performance through integrated data from IMU and GNSS sources.

docs.title: JetOwl_FlightControl
docs.text:
Source

Snapshot of README.md from TNG-Blue/JetOwl_FlightControl at commit 23b5ac3 (submodule Microcontroller/JetOwl_FlightControl). Regenerate with Scripts/mkdocs_hooks/snapshot_submodules.py after updating the submodule.

Flight-control firmware for a multirotor built on the STM32N657X0HxQ (Arm Cortex-M55, TrustZone-M), generated from STM32CubeMX as a four-context project.

The control code in this repository follows one rule: every formula must be traceable to a verifiable source — a peer-reviewed paper, a textbook, or a datasheet — and the source is cited in the header of the file that implements it. No hand-tuned or invented coefficients. The derivations live in docs/CONTROL_DESIGN.md; the code is only their implementation.

Not flight-ready. The airframe constants in Application/Interface/Inc/airframe_config.h (k_f, k_m, arm length, inertia) are placeholder values used by the unit tests. They must be measured on the real airframe (procedure in docs/CONTROL_DESIGN.md §5.4) before propellers are fitted. The CubeMX peripherals (I2C/SPI/UART/TIM) are not enabled yet, so the control tick does not run on hardware — see docs/CUBEMX_SETUP.md and the status table below.

docs.title: Control architecture
docs.text:
sensors → calibration → filter → disturbance observer → controller → mixer → actuators
   ↑                                                                            │
   └───────────────────────── feedback (closed loop) ───────────────────────────┘

Three cascaded tiers, separated by at least a 3–5× time-scale ratio:

Tier Rate Role Implementation MPC 50 Hz primary — look-ahead, explicit constraints mpc.c + qp_solver.c Attitude 250 Hz intermediate — q_sp, q_hat → omega_sp attitude_filter.c PID + ESO 1 kHz secondary — reflex, always running rate_loop.c, pid.c, eso.c FOC ~20 kHz inside the ESC (reference implementation only) foc.c

A supervisor (supervisor.c) arbitrates between MPC and PID. When the tracking error spikes, the ESO-estimated disturbance jumps, or a measurement fails, it discards the MPC plan rather than blending it — a plan computed for a world that no longer exists actively pulls the aircraft toward an infeasible trajectory. Entry and exit use different thresholds plus a dwell time, so the arbiter cannot chatter.

The loop is closed at the IMU/GNSS. The one segment that would otherwise be open — ESC command → actual rotor speed — is closed with bidirectional DShot300 telemetry (dshot.c, docs/CONTROL_DESIGN.md §6).

docs.title: Modules in Application/Control/
docs.text:

docs.title: ROS 2 node jetowl_fc (micro-ROS) — flowcharts
docs.text:
The firmware is a native ROS 2 node behind the micro-ROS agent on the Jetson (Application/Interface/Src/uros_app.c, topic contract in Application/Interface/Inc/uros_app.h, which must match Source/ROS2_JetOwl_Bridge in Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL).

Node graph:

flowchart LR
    subgraph J["Jetson (ROS 2 Humble)"]
        TC["uav_trajectory_controller<br/>(ros2_control_system, MPC 50 Hz)"]
        EST["uav_state_estimator (ESKF)"]
        JB["jetowl_bridge (fc link)"]
        AG["micro_ros_agent<br/>udp4 :8888"]
    end
    TC --> ATT[/"/control/attitude_setpoint<br/>QuaternionStamped"/]
    TC --> THR[/"/control/thrust<br/>Float64 [N]"/]
    JB -->|"SetBool"| ARM{{"/jetowl/arm"}}
    OTA{{"/jetowl/ota/start, /jetowl/ota/apply<br/>Trigger (JETOWL_WITH_OTA)"}}
    ATT --> AG
    THR --> AG
    ARM --> AG
    OTA --> AG
    AG <-->|"XRCE-DDS over UDP,<br/>ETH1 + LAN8742 + lwIP"| FC["jetowl_fc<br/>(STM32N657, FreeRTOS task 'uros')"]
    FC --> IMU[/"/imu/data<br/>Imu ENU/FLU, 200 Hz"/]
    FC --> RPM[/"/jetowl/motor_rpm<br/>50 Hz"/]
    FC --> BARO[/"/baro/pressure<br/>25 Hz"/]
    FC --> ST[/"/jetowl/status<br/>DiagnosticStatus, 2 Hz"/]
    IMU --> EST
    BARO --> EST
    EST -. "odometry/filtered closes the MPC loop" .-> TC
    ST --> JB
    RPM --> JB

uros task — connection state machine and 5 ms publish cycle:

flowchart TD
    S(["uros_task"]) --> N{"Net_Init ok?"}
    N -- no --> N1["idle forever: the aircraft still flies,<br/>only ROS is lost"]
    N -- yes --> T["set custom UDP transport,<br/>FreeRTOS allocator, init messages"]
    T --> W
    W["WAITING_AGENT"] --> W1{"link up and agent<br/>answers ping (50 ms)?"}
    W1 -- no --> W2["osDelay 200 ms"] --> W
    W1 -- yes --> W3{"create node, 4 publishers,<br/>2 subscriptions, services, executor"}
    W3 -- fail --> W4["destroy entities"] --> W2
    W3 -- ok --> W5["time sync with the agent"] --> C
    C["CONNECTED: every 5 ms (osDelayUntil)"] --> C1["executor spin_some 1 ms"]
    C1 --> C2["telemetry snapshot → /imu/data if the estimate is valid<br/>(+ /baro/pressure when a new sample exists)"]
    C2 --> C3["every 4th: /jetowl/motor_rpm<br/>every 100th: /jetowl/status<br/>every 2000th: time sync"]
    C3 --> C4{"every 200th: ping fails 3× in a row?"}
    C4 -- no --> C
    C4 -- yes --> D["DISCONNECTED: destroy entities"] --> W

Command path inside the firmware (callbacks run in the executor):

flowchart TD
    A(["on /control/attitude_setpoint"]) --> A1["q ENU/FLU → NED/FRD (frame_conv.h)"]
    B(["on /control/thrust"]) --> B1["store thrust and tick"]
    A1 --> P{"both parts present and younger<br/>than CMD_TIMEOUT_S?"}
    B1 --> P
    P -- yes --> G["FlightControl_SubmitAttitudeCommand(q, T)"]
    G --> CG["cmd_guard: finite, |q| ≈ 1, tilt limit, T ∈ [0, T_max]"]
    CG --> AT["attitude controller 250 Hz → ω_sp"]
    AT --> RL["rate loop 1 kHz: ESO + PID"]
    RL --> MX["mixer (torque priority) → DShot300"]
    MX --> ESC(("ESC / rotors"))
    ESC -. "bidirectional DShot RPM" .-> MX
    ESC -. "IMU: attitude + rates (closed loop)" .-> AT
    CG -. "setpoint older than 0.1 s" .-> FS["failsafe: level attitude (closed),<br/>bounded open-loop descent, disarm after 1.2·t_fs"]
    R(["on /jetowl/arm"]) --> R1{"OTA trial / IWDG / applying?"}
    R1 -- "yes (arm)" --> R2["refuse with reason"]
    R1 -- no --> R3["FlightControl_RequestArm → ok or reason<br/>(no setpoint, attitude invalid,<br/>thrust too high, not level …)"]

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text:
The four top-level firmware directories are four independent firmware images, not four modules of one program — which is why each has its own main.c. The STM32N6 has no user flash, only boot ROM and RAM, so code must be loaded into RAM (LRUN) or executed from external XSPI flash; that forces a multi-stage boot chain.

Boot ROM (ST, fixed)
   └─> FSBL/            clock, RIF, XSPI      AXISRAM2  0x34180400
        └─> AppliSecure/    SAU/TrustZone, NSC exports  0x34000400
             └─> AppliNonSecure/  <<< the flight application >>>  0x24100400
Directory What it is When you touch it FSBL/ First Stage Boot Loader, runs first clock / boot / XSPI flash configuration AppliSecure/ TrustZone secure application (-mcmse) security services (OTA keys, arming latch) AppliNonSecure/ flight application init + main loop (calls only, no logic) ExtMemLoader/ .stldr tool for STM32CubeProgrammer — does not run on the drone changing the XSPI flash part Application/Control/ pure control math — no HAL includes filters, observers, controllers, mixer Application/Interface/ glue between HAL and Control/: scheduler, airframe/board config tick ISR, device I/O Application/RfLink/ LR1121 driver + full-duplex LoRa link protocol (pure C, identical copy in Remote_UAV/src/rflink/) radio link changes — edit both repos Drivers/JetOwl/ sensor and device drivers (IMU, GNSS, LoRa, FRAM, INA260, PCA9548, OTA) new hardware tests/host/ native unit tests for the control math every control change

0x34… and 0x24… address the same physical RAM through the secure and non-secure aliases — this is standard Arm TrustZone-M behaviour, not a typo. The 0x400 offset at the start of each ROM region is the boot header inserted by ST's signing/packaging tool. Details: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

docs.title: Rules that are not optional
docs.text:
1. Files under Core/ are generated by CubeMX and will be overwritten. Only write between /* USER CODE BEGIN x */ and /* USER CODE END x */.
  2. Never edit mx-generated.cmake (at any level) — it is generated. The per-context CMakeLists.txt files are generated once and are safe to edit.
  3. Build AppliSecure before AppliNonSecure. Secure emits Secure_nsclib/secure_nsclib.o (the CMSE import library) that NonSecure links against; a stale copy produces wrong veneer addresses.
  4. Do not commit build/.
  5. No HAL_Delay() inside the control loop — use a fixed-rate TIM interrupt.
  6. No HAL includes in Application/Control/. That constraint is what makes the host tests possible.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Requires arm-none-eabi-gcc (with libnewlib-arm-none-eabi), CMake ≥ 3.22, and Ninja.

# all four contexts
cmake --preset Debug
cmake --build --preset Debug

# a single context
cmake --preset Debug -DBUILD_CONTEXT=FSBL
cmake --build --preset Debug

docs.title: Make build with micro-ROS over Ethernet (talks ROS 2 to the Jetson)
docs.text:
make microros   # once: build libmicroros.a in docker (microros/micro_ros_static_library_builder:humble)
make            # AppliSecure, then AppliNonSecure with lwIP + micro-ROS (UDP to 192.168.10.1:8888)
make -C Makefile nonsecure MICROROS=0   # without networking

The repository root holds the CubeMX Makefile/ directory, so the root entry point is GNUmakefile. Topic contract, frame conversion, failsafe derivation and build notes: docs/MICROROS_ETHERNET.md. The Jetson side is Source/ROS2_JetOwl_Bridge in Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL.

ExtMemLoader has a CubeMX-generated post-build step that invokes the Windows cmd shell, so it builds only in an STM32CubeIDE environment. It is a programmer tool, not drone firmware.

docs.title: Host tests (no hardware needed)
docs.text:
cmake -S tests/host -B build-host
cmake --build build-host
ctest --test-dir build-host --output-on-failure

13 test binaries, currently 13/13 passing. The control library is compiled with -Wall -Wextra -Werror -Wconversion -Wdouble-promotion -Wshadow, so a warning is a build failure. The tests compare against analytic solutions and independently computed reference values — compiling is not proof that an algorithm is correct.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
.github/workflows/build.yml runs three separate stages so a red build points straight at the cause:

  1. host-tests — actually runs the control math on the host.
  2. arm-compile — compiles every project source with the real ARM compiler (catches width, alignment, float and Cortex-M55/Helium issues the host compiler cannot see).
  3. firmware-link — links FSBL and AppliSecure and reports sizes. AppliNonSecure is not linked yet: its drivers call HAL_I2C_*/HAL_SPI_*/ HAL_UART_* and need the TIM handles CubeMX generates, and those peripherals are not enabled in the .ioc yet.

docs.title: JetOwl_FlightControl architecture (STM32N657X0HxQ)
docs.text:
Source

Snapshot of docs/ARCHITECTURE.md from TNG-Blue/JetOwl_FlightControl at commit 23b5ac3 (submodule Microcontroller/JetOwl_FlightControl). Regenerate with Scripts/mkdocs_hooks/snapshot_submodules.py after updating the submodule.

This document describes the actual structure, verified against the code in this repository, not a theoretical one. Every address and size is taken from the linker scripts and configuration files in the repository.

docs.title: 1. Why there are four directories, each with its own main.c
docs.text:
The four directories FSBL/, AppliSecure/, AppliNonSecure/ and ExtMemLoader/ are not four modules of one program. They are four independent firmware images, each compiled into its own .elf file and loaded at a different location on the chip. Every executable C image needs exactly one main() entry point — so a separate main.c per directory is a necessity, not duplication.

Evidence in the repository:

  • JetOwl_FlightControl.ioc: 

    Mcu.ContextNb=4
Mcu.Context0=FSBL
Mcu.Context1=AppliSecure
Mcu.Context2=AppliNonSecure
Mcu.Context3=ExtMemLoader
Mcu.ContextProject=SecureNSecure

  • mx-generated.cmake (at the root): calls ExternalProject_Add() four times, each pointing to a subdirectory with its own CMakeLists.txt, toolchain and linker script.

docs.title: Root cause: the STM32N657 has no internal user flash
docs.text:
The STM32N6 family has only a Boot ROM (programmed by ST, read-only) and RAM (large AXISRAM/SRAM). Unlike the STM32F4/H7 there is no internal flash for user programs. Code must therefore:

  • reside in external XSPI flash, or
  • be loaded into RAM and run there (LRUN mode — Load & RUN).

Both approaches need an earlier software stage that sets up the clocks and the external memory. That is why a multi-stage boot chain is mandatory.

docs.title: 2. Boot chain
docs.text:
[Boot ROM in the chip]          provided by ST, cannot be changed
          |  finds and loads the FSBL
          v
  [FSBL]  AXISRAM2                configures clocks, RIF, XSPI
          |  jumps to the application
          v
  [AppliSecure]  secure state     configures SAU/TrustZone, exports NSC functions
          |  NonSecure_Init() -> 0x24100400
          v
  [AppliNonSecure]  non-secure    <<< THE FLIGHT APPLICATION RUNS HERE >>>

ExtMemLoader is not part of this chain — see section 4.

docs.title: 3. Memory map
docs.text: Image Linker script ROM (ORIGIN / LENGTH) RAM (ORIGIN / LENGTH) FSBL/ STM32N657XX_AXISRAM2_fsbl.ld 0x34180400 / 255K 0x341C0000 / 256K AppliSecure/ STM32N657XX_LRUN_s.ld 0x34000400 / 399K 0x34064000 / 624K AppliNonSecure/ STM32N657XX_LRUN_ns.ld 0x24100400 / 511K 0x24180000 / 512K

docs.title: The most common confusion: the 0x34… and 0x24… aliases
docs.text:
0x34000000 and 0x24000000 are the same physical RAM, seen through two different address windows:

  • 0x34… = secure alias — accessible only to code running in the secure state.
  • 0x24… = non-secure alias — accessible to non-secure code.

This is the standard Arm TrustZone-M mechanism. In Drivers/CMSIS/Device/ST/STM32N6xx/Include/stm32n657xx.h:3016:

#define SRAM2_AXI_BASE_NS   0x24100000UL

And in AppliSecure/Core/Src/main.c:

#define VECT_TAB_NS_OFFSET       0x00400
#define VTOR_TABLE_NS_START_ADDR (SRAM2_AXI_BASE_NS|VECT_TAB_NS_OFFSET)  /* = 0x24100400 */

0x24100400 is exactly ORIGIN(ROM) in AppliNonSecure/STM32N657XX_LRUN_ns.ld. That is how AppliSecure knows where to jump.

The 0x400 (1 KB) offset at the start of each ROM region is reserved for the boot header that ST's signing/packaging tool inserts in front of the firmware image.

docs.title: LRUN and the other linker scripts
docs.text:
• LRUN = **L**oad & RUN: the image is loaded into RAM and executed from RAM. This is the configuration in use.
  • AppliSecure/ also contains unused alternatives: STM32N657XX_ROMxspi1.ld, STM32N657XX_ROMxspi2_RAMxspi1.ld, STM32N657XX_ROMxspi3_RAMxspi1xspi2.ld, … — these are execute-in-place (XIP) configurations running directly from XSPI1/XSPI2/XSPI3 flash. Switching to XIP means changing the STM32_LINKER_SCRIPT variable in AppliSecure/CMakeLists.txt.

docs.title: FSBL/ — First Stage Boot Loader
docs.text:
The first of your code to run. Its job: configure the system clock, configure RIF (Resource Isolation Framework), initialise XSPI for external-flash access, then hand over to the application.

SystemClock_Config() is at FSBL/Core/Src/main.c:107:

  • Supply: PWR_EXTERNAL_SOURCE_SUPPLY, voltage scale 1
  • HSI on, HSIDiv = 1
  • PLL1: HSI source, M=1, N=25, P1=1, P2=1
  • Distribution through IC2 / IC6 / IC11, each with ClockDivider = 4
  • AHBCLKDivider = DIV2, APB½/⅘ = DIV1

Note: the function temporarily switches back to HSI before moving to the PLL (see the HAL_RCC_GetClockConfig → CPUCLKSOURCE_HSI sequence). This ordering is required on the N6 to avoid losing the clock during the source switch.

When to change it: CPU/bus frequency or clock source changes. The A/B boot-image selection for OTA lives in FSBL/Boot/ (called from USER CODE 2 of main.c) — see docs/OTA.md.

docs.title: AppliSecure/ — secure application (TrustZone secure state)
docs.text:
Compiled with -mcmse (AppliSecure/CMakeLists.txt:28). Its job:

  1. Configure the SAU / security partitioning through AppliSecure/Core/Inc/partition_stm32n657xx.h.
  2. Export NSC (Non-Secure Callable) functions in AppliSecure/Core/Src/secure_nsc.c. There is currently one: 
    CMSE_NS_ENTRY void SECURE_RegisterCallback(SECURE_CallbackIDTypeDef CallbackId, void *func);
    which lets the non-secure side register callbacks for a SecureFault or an illegal-access (IAC) error.
  3. HAL_SuspendTick(), then NonSecure_Init() — sets SCB_NS->VTOR, loads MSP_NS, fetches the non-secure reset handler and jumps to it. It never returns.

When to change it: to place safety/security assets out of reach of bugs in the flight application — for example the OTA authentication key, the motor arm/disarm latch, a safety watchdog. Each such service adds a CMSE_NS_ENTRY function to secure_nsc.c and its declaration to Secure_nsclib/secure_nsc.h.

docs.title: AppliNonSecure/ — flight application
docs.text:
Almost all code is written here. The complete chain: read sensors → filter → disturbance estimation → controller → mixer → ESC/servo → feedback.

AppliNonSecure/Core/Src/main.c is currently an empty template: HAL_Init() then while(1){}. There is no SystemClock_Config() — the clocks have already been configured by the FSBL.

docs.title: ExtMemLoader/ — flash-programming tool, does NOT run on the drone
docs.text:
This is the most frequently misunderstood part. ExtMemLoader builds an external loader (.stldr) for STM32CubeProgrammer / STM32CubeIDE — it teaches the programming tool how to erase/write/read the XSPI flash on your board. It runs temporarily in the chip's RAM while you press the program button, then disappears.

It therefore has no main.c but ExtMemLoader/Core/Src/extmemloader_init.c — an entry point following the external-loader convention, not the application convention.

ExtMemLoader/postbuild.sh copies the .elf file as a .stldr into STM32CubeProgrammer's ExternalLoader/ directory (located through the STM32_PRG_PATH environment variable).

When to change it: when the board's XSPI flash part changes.

docs.title: 5. Build-order constraint
docs.text:
AppliSecure/CMakeLists.txt:31 generates the CMSE import library:

set(STM32_LINKER_OPTION -Wl,--cmse-implib\ -Wl,--out-implib="${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/../Secure_nsclib/secure_nsclib.o")

AppliNonSecure/mx-generated.cmake links that very file:

set (MX_LINK_LIBS
    STM32_Drivers
    ${TOOLCHAIN_LINK_LIBRARIES}
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/../Secure_nsclib/secure_nsclib.o
)

So the root mx-generated.cmake declares:

ExternalProject_Add(JetOwl_FlightControl_AppliNonSecure
    ...
    DEPENDS  JetOwl_FlightControl_AppliSecure
)

Practical consequence: after adding or changing a CMSE_NS_ENTRY function in AppliSecure, you must rebuild AppliSecure first; otherwise AppliNonSecure links against a stale secure_nsclib.o and fails in a way that is very hard to diagnose (calls jump to wrong veneer addresses).

docs.title: 6. Where to write code
docs.text: Task Location Flight logic: filtering, estimation, control, mixer Application/Control/ (pure maths, no HAL) Glue between HAL and flight logic, scheduler, airframe configuration Application/Interface/ New sensor/device driver Drivers/JetOwl/{Inc,Src}/ Driver calls, initialisation, main loop AppliNonSecure/Core/Src/main.c (inside a USER CODE block) Clock / boot / external flash changes FSBL/Core/Src/main.c Security services (OTA key, arming latch) AppliSecure/Core/Src/secure_nsc.c + Secure_nsclib/secure_nsc.h Change of the board's XSPI flash ExtMemLoader/

docs.title: Mandatory rule for CubeMX-generated files
docs.text:
STM32CubeMX overwrites the files under Core/ every time "Generate Code" is pressed. Only the parts between the marker pairs are preserved:

/* USER CODE BEGIN 2 */
   ... your code is safe here ...
/* USER CODE END 2 */

Code outside the markers is lost. That is why the flight logic lives in Application/ and Drivers/JetOwl/ — directories CubeMX never touches — and main.c contains only calls.

Conversely, the CMakeLists.txt files in the four subdirectories are safe to edit — their own header says so:

# This file is generated only once,
# and is not re-generated if converter is called multiple times.
# User is free to modify the file as much as necessary

mx-generated.cmake, however, must not be edited ("File automatically-generated by STM32CubeMX - Do not modify").

docs.title: 6b. The Application/ directory and host tests
docs.text:
Application/Control/{Inc,Src}/     pure control maths — NO HAL includes
Application/Interface/Inc/         airframe_config.h (airframe parameters)
tests/host/                        unit tests built with the native gcc

The rule "Application/Control/ must not include HAL" is not a formality — it is what makes it possible to run the unit tests on an ordinary computer, without a board:

cmake -S tests/host -B build-host
cmake --build build-host
ctest --test-dir build-host --output-on-failure

Modules currently in Application/Control/:

File Content Mathematical source ctrl_math.c vectors, quaternions, attitude integration — attitude_filter.c Mahony filter on SO(3) + gyro-bias estimation Mahony et al., IEEE TAC 53(5), 2008 eso.c Extended State Observer, exact ZOH discretisation Han 2009; Gao 2003; Guo & Zhao 2011 pid.c discrete PID, derivative filtering, back-calculation anti-windup Åström & Hägglund, Advanced PID Control, 2006 mixer.c quad-X control allocation, torque-priority saturation Leishman 2006; Johansen & Fossen 2013 rate_loop.c 1 kHz rate loop: ESO + PID + mixer on three axes, feedback of the achieved torque composition of the above scheduler.c fixed-tick scheduling by rate group, overrun detection — esc_map.c rotor speed → PWM pulse width (fallback, not used on the main path) — dshot.c DShot protocol: framing + CRC + GCR telemetry decoding, DMA bit patterns CONTROL_DESIGN.md §6 rotor_speed.c 1 kHz rotor-speed loop on RPM telemetry: two degrees of freedom (reference model + inverse-model feed-forward) + LPF + SIMC PI, FF_ONLY/STARTUP/STALLED modes Skogestad 2003; Åström & Murray 2021; Bangura & Mahony 2012 — CONTROL_DESIGN.md §6.6 imu_fusion.c dual-IMU fusion by weighted quaternion averaging Markley et al., JGCD 30(4), 2007 foc.c FOC for an encoder-equipped BLDC: Clarke/Park, SVPWM, two current PI loops. Runs in the ESC, not on the MCU — kept as a reference Park 1929; Clarke 1943; van der Broeck 1988 qp_solver.c box-constrained QP, fast gradient with a bounded iteration count Nesterov 1983/2004; Richter et al. 2012; Gershgorin 1931 mpc.c primary MPC at 50 Hz, condensed form, acceleration constraints Rawlings et al. 2017; Maciejowski 2002 supervisor.c MPC/PID arbiter with reflex semantics CONTROL_DESIGN.md §4.1b

Application/Interface/Src/flight_control.c is the only file of the control chain that #includes HAL — it connects the tick TIM ISR to scheduler → rate_loop → rotor_speed → DShot. The TIM-dependent parts sit behind #if defined(BOARD_TIM_*), so the file already compiles (with a #warning reminding that the tick is not running yet).

Derivations: docs/CONTROL_DESIGN.md.

docs.title: 7. Build
docs.text:
# Build all four contexts
cmake --preset Debug
cmake --build --preset Debug

# Build a single context
cmake --preset Debug -DBUILD_CONTEXT=FSBL
cmake --build --preset Debug

The BUILD_CONTEXT variable is tested in the root mx-generated.cmake (if((${BUILD_CONTEXT} MATCHES .*FSBL.*) OR (NOT DEFINED BUILD_CONTEXT))).

Requirements: arm-none-eabi-gcc (toolchain declared in gcc-arm-none-eabi.cmake), CMake ≥ 3.22, Ninja.

docs.title: Make build (with micro-ROS over Ethernet)
docs.text:
make microros     # first time: builds libmicroros.a in docker
make              # GNUmakefile -> Makefile/Makefile: AppliSecure, then AppliNonSecure

The CMake configuration above is the network-less build; lwIP + micro-ROS exist only in Makefile/AppliNonSecure. Details: docs/MICROROS_ETHERNET.md.
