docs.title: OTA
docs.text: The sample STM32N6_OTA driver (never part of the build, no server checksum, no A/B, no bootloader) has been replaced by a complete OTA layer: Application/Ota/ (pure C, host-tested), Application/Ota/Port/ (XSPI2 NOR, lwIP, FreeRTOS task) and an A/B bootloader in FSBL/Boot/. The real XSPI flash map, package format, boot state machine and proofs: docs/OTA.md.

docs.title: Flight control loop design — derivations and references
docs.text:
Source

Snapshot of docs/CONTROL_DESIGN.md from TNG-Blue/JetOwl_FlightControl at commit 23b5ac3 (submodule Microcontroller/JetOwl_FlightControl). Regenerate with Scripts/mkdocs_hooks/snapshot_submodules.py after updating the submodule.

Project principle: every formula in Application/Control/ must be traceable to a verifiable source (peer-reviewed paper, textbook or datasheet). No invented coefficients. This document is the "proof"; the code is only its implementation.

docs.title: 0. Signal diagram
docs.text:
IMU / GNSS / Baro
        |
        v
  [Calibration + bias removal]     calib.c
        |
        v
  [State filter]                   attitude_filter.c   (Mahony on SO(3))
        |  q, omega
        v
  [Disturbance estimator]          eso.c               (Extended State Observer)
        |  f_hat  (total disturbance + model error)
        v
  [Controller]                     pid.c / rate_ctrl   (cascade, compensates f_hat)
        |  [T, tau_x, tau_y, tau_z]
        v
  [Control allocation / mixer]     mixer.c
        |  u_i (per rotor)
        v
  [ESC / servo]                    Application/Interface
        |
        +--------- physical feedback: the IMU measures again -----------> back to the filter

The loop is closed at the IMU/GNSS. The only open segment is ESC command → actual rotor speed (see §6).

docs.title: 1.1 Gyro error model
docs.text:
omega_meas(t) = omega_true(t) + b(t) + n_g(t)
b_dot(t)      = n_b(t)

b = slowly varying bias (random walk), n_g ~ white noise. This is the standard model used throughout the attitude-estimation literature; the parameters sigma_g, sigma_b are measured with the Allan variance.

Source: IEEE Std 952-1997, IEEE Standard Specification Format Guide and Test Procedure for Single-Axis Interferometric Fiber Optic Gyros, Annex C (Allan variance) — the standard definition of angle random walk and rate random walk.

docs.title: 1.2 Accelerometer / magnetometer calibration
docs.text:
Affine model: y = M (x - b), estimated by ellipsoid fitting (a constrained least-squares problem with a closed-form solution through an eigen-decomposition).

Source: Gebre-Egziabher, Elkaim, Powell, Parkinson, "Calibration of Strapdown Magnetometers in Magnetic Field Domain", Journal of Aerospace Engineering 19(2), 2006.

docs.title: 1.3 Conversion from the Adafruit IMU (SH-2)
docs.text: The Adafruit_IMU driver returns fixed-point Q-point values. The conversion factors to SI are taken directly from the "SH-2 Reference Manual" (CEVA/Hillcrest) — cited at Drivers/JetOwl/Inc/Adafruit_IMU.h:9-14. No further derivation is involved.

docs.title: 1.4 IMU read path: mounting frame and calibration gate
docs.text:
Code: Application/Control/Src/imu_frontend.c (maths, host test test_imu_frontend.c) and Application/Interface/Src/imu_acq.c (FreeRTOS task reading I2C — not read inside the 1 kHz interrupt).

q_NB = q_NW ⊗ q_WS ⊗ q_SB            v_B = R(q_SB)⁻¹ v_S        (Diebel 2006 §6)
q_WS : chip → the chip's world frame (ENU, Android convention — SH-2; BNO055 ORI = Android)
q_NW : ENU → NED = (0, 1/√2, 1/√2, 0)
q_SB : FRD body → chip (mounting). Default: chip level, top side up, chip x towards the nose ⇒ (0, 1, 0, 0)

Calibration gate: both chips self-calibrate dynamically (gyro/accel/mag); a sample is accepted only when the accuracy status is > 0 (SH-2 accuracy; BNO055 CALIB_STAT.SYS). Outliers: NaN, | |q|−1 | > 0.1, or any axis ≥ 98 % of the datasheet full scale (saturation) ⇒ the sample is rejected.

Mandatory static check before flight (the default q_SB is an ASSUMPTION, not yet confirmed on the airframe):

Attitude /imu/data must show Firmware state Level, nose pointing (magnetic) north ENU yaw = +90°, roll = pitch = 0, linear_acceleration.z ≈ +9.81 imu_fusion = 3 (BOTH) Right wing down 30° ENU/FLU roll = +30° (right down about the forward x axis) — Nose up 30° FLU pitch = −30° —

If one chip is mounted differently from the assumption, imu_fusion reports a disagreement (> 15°, imu_fusion = 4) and the firmware refuses to arm — a second line of defence, not a substitute for the check above.

docs.title: 1.5 Sampling instant and latency
docs.text:
• BNO08x: t = t_INT + 100 µs·(−BaseDelta + Rebase + delay) (SH-2 Reference Manual 1000-3625: reports 0xFB/0xFA, 14-bit delay field = status[7:2]:byte3). t_INT is captured by EXTI on the INT pin with the control loop's µs clock (FlightControl_NowUs = TIM6 tick × 1000 + TIM6 counter).
  • BNO055: no timestamp; the fusion registers update at 100 Hz with an unknown phase ⇒ data age ~ U(0, 10 ms): unbiased estimate t = t_read − 5 ms, standard deviation 10/√12 = 2.9 ms. Fusing a sample B that is up to Δt older than sample A adds an error ≤ w_B·|ω|·Δt = 0.5·3.5·0.01 rad = 1°.
  • Rate loop: the 200 Hz gyro is held (ZOH) at 1 kHz. Delay = T/2 + I2C ≈ 2.5 + 0.6 ms + chip delay ⇒ Δφ = −ω_c·τ ≈ −2.8° at ω_c = 15.78 rad/s (plus the chip delay; the firmware reports sh2_delay_max_ms).

docs.title: 2.1 Why this filter
docs.text: The filter must (a) have a stability proof, (b) have no singularity at large angles and © be light enough for 1 kHz. Mahony's nonlinear complementary filter meets all three: it operates directly on the group SO(3), so it has no Euler gimbal-lock singularity, and it comes with a Lyapunov proof of almost-global asymptotic stability.

docs.title: 2.2 Formulas (quaternion form, passive complementary filter)
docs.text:
Let q be the attitude estimate (body → inertial) and b_hat the gyro-bias estimate.

The orientation error measured from the reference vectors (gravity v_a, magnetic field v_m):

e = sum_i  k_i * ( v_i_meas  x  v_i_pred )                    (1)

where v_i_pred = R(q)^T * v_i_ref is the reference vector rotated into the body frame and x is the cross product.

Update law:

b_hat_dot = -k_I * e                                          (2)
omega_corr = omega_meas - b_hat + k_P * e                     (3)
q_dot      = 0.5 * q ⊗ [0, omega_corr]                        (4)

docs.title: 2.3 Stability proof (summary)
docs.text:
With the Lyapunov function V = tr(I - R_err) on SO(3) (R_err = R_hat^T R), Mahony et al. prove V_dot <= 0 and that the largest invariant set consists of the desired equilibrium plus three unstable equilibria (the 180° rotations). Convergence is therefore almost global — the region of attraction is all of SO(3) except a set of measure zero.

Source: Mahony R., Hamel T., Pflimlin J.-M., "Nonlinear Complementary Filters on the Special Orthogonal Group", IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 53(5), 2008, pp. 1203–1218. Theorem 5.1 and its proof.

docs.title: 2.4 Choosing k_P, k_I
docs.text:
Linearised around a small error, the system becomes second order:

e_dot_dot + k_P * e_dot + k_I * e = 0

Compared with the standard form s^2 + 2*zeta*wn*s + wn^2:

wn   = sqrt(k_I)
zeta = k_P / (2*sqrt(k_I))

Hence no trial-and-error tuning: choose wn (desired bandwidth, rad/s) and zeta (recommended 1/sqrt(2)), then solve:

k_I = wn^2
k_P = 2 * zeta * wn                                            (5)

The bandwidth wn must lie in between: high enough to track the gyro bias, low enough not to be disturbed by linear acceleration during manoeuvres. In practice 0.5–2 rad/s is a reasonable range for a drone.

docs.title: 2.5 Selected configuration: two IMUs in parallel, this filter NOT used
docs.text:
The project runs both a BNO08x (Adafruit) and a BNO055 (DFRobot). Both perform fusion inside the chip and output a quaternion, so attitude_filter (Mahony) is not used on the main flight path — stacking two filters only adds delay and breaks the statistical assumptions.

The module is kept, fully tested, for cases that require fusion from raw data (for example to control the latency completely, or after switching to an IMU without internal fusion).

Fusing the two quaternions is described in §2.7.

docs.title: 2.6 Accuracy benefit of two sensors
docs.text:
If two sensors have independent errors with the same variance σ², the equally weighted mean has variance σ²/2, i.e. the standard deviation is reduced by √2 (~29 %).

This has been measured numerically in tests/host/test_imu_fusion.c::test_noise_reduction: injecting independent noise into both inputs around the same true value gives a single/fused RMS-error ratio in the range 1.2–1.7.

The "independent" condition really matters. Two IMUs placed side by side on the same board share the same vibration and the same thermal drift; that common part of the error is not removed. The √2 benefit applies only to the truly independent part. Placing the two IMUs far apart and with different orientations increases the independent part.

The optimal weights are inversely proportional to the variance of each sensor. The current default uses equal weights because the real variance of each unit has not been measured yet.

docs.title: 2.7 Fusing two quaternions — why not average component-wise
docs.text:
Unit quaternions live on the sphere S³, not in a flat vector space. Averaging component-wise and normalising is an unfounded approximation, increasingly wrong as the two rotations differ, and it is even ill-defined because q and −q represent the same rotation — flipping the sign of one input gives a completely different result, and two nearly identical estimates can even cancel each other out.

Markley et al. define the mean as the solution of the optimisation problem:

q_mean = argmax  Σ w_i (qᵀ q_i)²      subject to |q| = 1

The solution is the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue of M = Σ w_i q_i q_iᵀ. The squared form (qᵀq_i)² is precisely what removes the sign ambiguity.

Closed form for two quaternions (the eigenvector lies in the plane spanned by {q₁, q₂}, which reduces the problem to the eigenvalues of a 2×2 matrix):

c = q₁ · q₂                                (after aligning signs so that c ≥ 0)
z = √( (w₁ − w₂)² + 4 w₁ w₂ c² )
a = (w₁ − w₂ + z) / 2
b = w₂ c
q_mean = normalize(a q₁ + b q₂)

Check with w₁ = w₂ = ½: z = c, a = b = c/2 → the equally weighted mean, as expected.

Source: Markley F. L., Cheng Y., Crassidis J. L., Oshman Y., "Averaging Quaternions", Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics, 30(4), 2007, pp. 1193–1197.

Implementation: Application/Control/Src/imu_fusion.c.

docs.title: 2.8 Disagreement detection
docs.text:
Angle between the two estimates: θ = 2·arccos(|q₁·q₂|). Above the threshold (default 15°) the estimates are not fused: the result would be a value in between that matches neither. Nor does this layer pick one of the two on its own — that needs external information (magnetometer, dynamic model) it does not have. It keeps the previous cycle's value and reports upwards.

imu_fusion_disagreement() is well worth logging: it rises before a sensor fails completely and can serve as an early warning.

The 15° threshold is a starting value, not yet measured on a real airframe. The correct way to set it: log imu_fusion_disagreement() over a few minutes of test flight, take the 99th percentile and double it.

docs.title: 2.9 Heavier alternative: MEKF
docs.text:
If higher accuracy is needed and the computational budget allows it, use a Multiplicative EKF (estimating the error in the 3-dimensional tangent space, which avoids the quaternion normalisation constraint).

Sources: Markley F. L., "Attitude Error Representations for Kalman Filtering", Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics, 26(2), 2003. Survey: Crassidis, Markley, Cheng, "Survey of Nonlinear Attitude Estimation Methods", JGCD 30(1), 2007.

The matrix implementation uses CMSIS-DSP's arm_mat_* (Drivers/CMSIS/DSP/Source/MatrixFunctions/).

docs.title: 3.1 Why it is needed
docs.text: The filter of §2 estimates the state. It does not estimate the disturbance: gusts, a centre-of-gravity offset, thrust-model error, a sagging battery that reduces thrust. With PID alone these must be "chased" by the integral term — slowly and with overshoot. The ESO estimates them directly and compensates them in the control law.

docs.title: 3.2 Formulas
docs.text:
Consider one axis (for example the roll rate) of the form:

y_dot = b0 * u + f(t)                                          (6)

f(t) = total disturbance (everything not modelled), b0 = known nominal gain.

Extend f as a state: x1 = y, x2 = f. Second-order observer:

x1_hat_dot = x2_hat + b0*u + l1*(y - x1_hat)                   (7)
x2_hat_dot =                 l2*(y - x1_hat)                   (8)

docs.title: 3.3 Choosing l1, l2 — closed form, no trial-and-error
docs.text:
Characteristic polynomial of the observer error: s^2 + l1*s + l2. Place all poles at -wo (Gao's bandwidth parameterisation):

s^2 + l1*s + l2 = (s + wo)^2
=>  l1 = 2*wo
    l2 = wo^2                                                  (9)

Only one tuning parameter remains: wo (observer bandwidth, rad/s). Rule of thumb: set wo ≈ 3..10 times the control-loop bandwidth, and keep wo well below the sampling frequency (wo << 2*pi*fs) so that the discretisation remains valid.

Sources:

  • Han J., "From PID to Active Disturbance Rejection Control", IEEE Transactions on Industrial Electronics, 56(3), 2009, pp. 900–906 — the ESO and total-disturbance concepts.
  • Gao Z., "Scaling and Bandwidth-Parameterization Based Controller Tuning", Proceedings of the American Control Conference, 2003, pp. 4989–4996 — formula (9).
  • Guo B.-Z., Zhao Z.-L., "On the convergence of an extended state observer for nonlinear systems with uncertainty", Systems & Control Letters, 60(6), 2011, pp. 420–430 — convergence proof.

docs.title: 3.4 Compensation law
docs.text:
u = ( u0 - x2_hat ) / b0                                       (10)

u0 is the output of the controller of §4. Substituting (10) into (6):

y_dot = b0 * (u0 - f_hat)/b0 + f  =  u0 + (f - f_hat)  ≈  u0

After compensation the plant becomes a pure integrator — the controller of §4 only needs to be designed for that simple nominal system. That is why the ESO is worth using.

docs.title: 3.5 Discretisation
docs.text:
Application/Control/Src/eso.c uses an exact ZOH, with coefficients precomputed at configuration time. The full derivation is in that file's header comment; the key point is that A has the double eigenvalue -wo, so A + wo*I is nilpotent (its square is zero), which truncates the exponential series after the first-order term:

Ad = exp(-wo*Ts) * [[1 - wo*Ts,  Ts       ],
                    [-wo^2*Ts,   1 + wo*Ts]]
Bd = [ b0*E*Ts ;  b0*(E*(1 + wo*Ts) - 1) ]           E = exp(-wo*Ts)
Ld = [ 1 - E*(1 - wo*Ts) ;  wo^2*Ts*E ]

Expanding to first order in Ts gives back exactly the forward-Euler formulas — checked in tests/host/test_eso.c.

docs.title: 3.6 The wo*Ts constraint — stable does NOT mean accurate
docs.text:
This is the most common pitfall with an ESO, and it has been measured numerically in tests/host/test_eso.c::test_accuracy_requires_small_wo_ts:

wo*Ts f_hat (true disturbance = 1.0) Error 5.00 0.17 83 % 0.50 0.98 2 % 0.05 1.0001 0.01 %

Why: the eigenvalue of Ad is exp(-wo*Ts) < 1 for every Ts > 0, so the observer never diverges — the advantage of ZOH over forward Euler (which goes unstable for wo*Ts > 2). But the ZOH discretisation treats y as an input held constant over each period, while the real y varies continuously. When wo*Ts is large the observer converges within a single period and never "sees" the intra-period variation, so the disturbance estimate is systematically low.

Practical consequence: an ESO that "runs stably, with no NaN and no divergence" can still be 80 % wrong. wo*Ts must be checked numerically, not by looking at a plot. Rule: keep wo*Ts <= 0.1. At 1 kHz (Ts = 1 ms) this limits wo <= 100 rad/s.

Application/Interface/Inc/airframe_config.h sets ESO_WO_RATE = 100.0f, i.e. wo*Ts = 0.1 at 1 kHz — exactly at the limit. A higher wo requires a correspondingly faster rate loop.

docs.title: 4.1 Three-tier architecture: primary MPC — reflex PID — motor FOC
docs.text:
[MPC]  primary, 50 Hz          planning, explicit constraint handling
     │    Application/Control/mpc.c
     │    produces the desired acceleration → converted to tilt + thrust
     ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  [SUPERVISOR]  arbiter                      │  supervisor.c
 │  MPC fresh & nominal → follow the MPC       │
 │  surprise → DISCARD the plan, PID handles it│
 │  MPC stale → PID runs alone                 │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │
     ▼
   [PID]  secondary = REFLEX, 1 kHz    always running, never plans
     │    attitude_filter → eso → rate_loop (pid.c)
     ▼
   [mixer] → [ESC, bidirectional DShot300]
                    │
                    └─ [FOC]  inside the ESC, with an encoder
                              foc.c is a reference implementation, not run on the MCU

Time-scale separation principle: an inner loop must be at least 3–5 times faster than the outer loop before it can be treated as "ideal" when designing the outer loop. The ratios 1000/250/50 Hz all satisfy this.

Tier Rate Role In Out MPC 50 Hz primary — look-ahead, constraints p, v, reference trajectory desired acceleration Attitude 250 Hz intermediate q_sp, q_hat omega_sp PID + ESO 1000 Hz secondary — reflex omega_sp, omega_meas torque tau FOC ~20 kHz inside the ESC iq_ref, encoder 3 duty cycles

Attitude loop (250 Hz) — attitude_ctrl.c: a P law on the error quaternion Ω = sat(2 sgn(q_e.w) K ⊙ q_e.v), q_e = q̂⁻¹ ⊗ q_sp (Wie, Weiss & Arapostathis 1989), Lyapunov function V = 1 − |q_e.w|, K_i = ω_c,rate,i / 5 with ω_c,rate computed exactly from the PID + b0. The set-point comes from the MPC on the Jetson through micro-ROS and passes through cmd_guard.c (validation, 0.1 s timeout, bounded failsafe). Full derivation and proof: docs/MICROROS_ETHERNET.md §4–5.

docs.title: 4.1b Why the PID is a "reflex" and not merely the inner loop
docs.text:
The MPC looks ahead and respects constraints, but it is slow and can miss its deadline. The PID does not look ahead but is always present and reacts instantly.

supervisor.c decides whom to follow. Three modes:

Mode When Set-point given to the PID MPC_ACTIVE the plan is fresh and the situation is nominal the MPC's REFLEX the error jumps, or the estimated disturbance jumps, or a measurement fails a safe value PID_ONLY MPC stale / no plan yet the last good value

The easiest thing to get wrong — why the plan must be DISCARDED in a reflex:

When something unexpected happens (a strong gust, a collision, a lost rotor), the current MPC plan was computed for a world that no longer exists. Continuing to execute it is not just useless but harmful: it pulls the aircraft towards a trajectory that is no longer feasible.

So REFLEX is not "blending MPC and PID" — it drops the MPC output entirely, lets the PID handle the situation, and forces the MPC to re-plan from scratch (supervisor_should_reset_plan() signals this for exactly one cycle).

Hysteresis and dwell time: entering the reflex mode uses a high threshold; leaving it uses a lower one, which must be held continuously for dwell_cycles cycles. These two mechanisms prevent toggling when the error oscillates around a threshold — chattering at the arbiter level is more dangerous than choosing the wrong mode, because it makes the output jump continuously. supervisor_init() rejects a configuration with an exit threshold ≥ the entry threshold for exactly this reason.

The estimated disturbance is also a reflex input, not only the tracking error: a jump in the ESO disturbance signals that the world has just changed even before the tracking error has had time to grow. Catching it one cycle earlier is worth it.

docs.title: 4.1c MPC — condensed form and time budget
docs.text:
Implementation: Application/Control/Src/mpc.c + qp_solver.c.

Model: a double integrator per axis, with acceleration as the input. The three axes decouple at small tilt angles — true in normal flight. During aggressive manoeuvres the decoupling assumption no longer holds, and that is precisely one of the moments when the reflex tier must take over.

Condensed form: the state variables are eliminated, leaving only the input sequence as the decision variable:

X = Ψ x₀ + Φ U
J = (X − X_ref)ᵀ Q̄ (X − X_ref) + Uᵀ R̄ U  =  ½ Uᵀ H U + gᵀ U + const

H = 2(ΦᵀQ̄Φ + R̄)          ← depends only on parameters, COMPUTED ONCE at initialisation
g = 2ΦᵀQ̄(Ψx₀ − X_ref)     ← rebuilt every cycle, O(N²)

For a double integrator, Ψ and Φ have a closed form; no matrix powers are needed:

Ψ:  p_k = p₀ + k·Ts·v₀ ,  v_k = v₀
Φ:  effect of u_j on state k (k > j), with m = k−j−1:
    on position = Ts²(m + 0.5)
    on velocity = Ts

The reference trajectory must be consistent over the whole horizon: p_ref_k = p_ref + k·Ts·v_ref. Holding p_ref fixed while v_ref ≠ 0 is a self-contradictory request (one cannot both stay at p_ref and move at v_ref) and causes a constant tracking lag that can never be removed — not because an integral term is missing but because the problem is posed wrongly. Locked in by test_mpc.c::test_tracks_moving_reference.

Constraints: box constraints on the input (|u| ≤ a_max, derived from the maximum tilt: a_max = g·tan(θ_max)) are handled exactly. Constraints on the state (for example |v| ≤ v_max) are not boxes in U and cannot be included — the velocity is penalised in the cost through q_vel instead. This is a real limitation of the approach, not an oversight: adding state constraints would break the iteration bound and with it the real-time guarantee.

docs.title: 4.1d QP solution with a bounded iteration count
docs.text:
An interior-point or active-set solver is fast in most cases, but nobody can bound its worst case. In a flight control loop what matters is not the average but the ceiling: one overrun cycle is one cycle without a control command.

Nesterov's fast gradient method with a constant step has a provable linear convergence rate:

f(z_k) − f* ≤ (1 − √(μ/L))ᵏ · (f(z₀) − f*)

From this the number of iterations needed for a given accuracy can be derived (qp_required_iterations()) and — more importantly — a fixed iteration count can be set directly with the maximum error known in advance. That trades bounded accuracy for a deterministic run time.

Eigenvalue bounds by Gershgorin instead of computing the true eigenvalues (too expensive every cycle):

λ_max ≤ max_i ( H_ii + Σ_{j≠i} |H_ij| )
λ_min ≥ min_i ( H_ii − Σ_{j≠i} |H_ij| )

Using the upper bound as L is safe: a step smaller than the optimal step converges more slowly but still converges. Conversely, a step larger than 1/λ_max makes the method diverge.

The most important safety property: the fast gradient method projects every iterate onto the box, so the returned solution is always feasible even when the iterations run out — it may only be sub-optimal. In flight control, a feasible, slightly sub-optimal command is far better than no command at all.

Sources:

  • Nesterov Y., "A method of solving a convex programming problem with convergence rate O(1/k²)", Soviet Math. Doklady, 27(2), 1983.
  • Nesterov Y., Introductory Lectures on Convex Optimization, Kluwer, 2004, §2.2.
  • Richter S., Jones C. N., Morari M., "Computational Complexity Certification for Real-Time MPC With Input Constraints Based on the Fast Gradient Method", IEEE TAC, 57(6), 2012.
  • Gershgorin S. A., "Über die Abgrenzung der Eigenwerte einer Matrix", Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR, 1931.
  • Maciejowski J. M., Predictive Control with Constraints, Prentice Hall, 2002, Ch. 3.

docs.title: 4.2 Discrete PID — implementation form
docs.text:
Parallel form with a filtered derivative (a pure derivative amplifies high-frequency noise without bound):

P(k) = Kp * e(k)
I(k) = I(k-1) + Ki * Ts * e(k)                     (rectangular integration)
D(k) = (Td/(Td + N*Ts)) * D(k-1)
       - (Kp*Td*N/(Td + N*Ts)) * (y(k) - y(k-1))   (derivative on the MEASUREMENT, not on the ERROR)

with Td = Kd/Kp (derivative time). The high-frequency gain of the D term is bounded at Kp*N.

Two mandatory details:

  1. The derivative acts on the measured signal y, not on the error e. On e, every set-point change would produce an unbounded derivative spike ("derivative kick").
  2. The filter coefficient N (typically 8–20) bounds the high-frequency gain of the D term at Kp*Kd*N. Without N, gyro noise is amplified straight into the motors.

docs.title: 4.3 Integrator anti-windup — back-calculation
docs.text:
When the output saturates, the integral keeps accumulating and the system loses control when it leaves saturation. Back-calculation is used:

u_unsat = P + I + D
u       = sat(u_unsat, u_min, u_max)
I       = I + (Ts/Tt) * (u - u_unsat)                          (11)

Tt = tracking time constant, recommended Tt = sqrt(Ti * Td) (geometric mean).

Source: Åström K. J., Hägglund T., Advanced PID Control, ISA, 2006 — Chapter 3 (implementation form, derivative filtering, coefficient N) and Section 3.5 (back-calculation anti-windup, formula (11) and the choice of Tt).

docs.title: 4.4 Tustin discretisation of the filter stages
docs.text:
Every linear filter in the chain uses the bilinear transform:

s  ->  (2/Ts) * (z-1)/(z+1)

Tustin preserves stability (it maps the left half-plane into the unit circle) — the decisive advantage over forward Euler, which can turn a stable continuous system into an unstable discrete one when Ts is large. When the cut-off frequency must match exactly, pre-warping is used: w_d = (2/Ts)*tan(w_a*Ts/2).

Source: Franklin, Powell, Workman, Digital Control of Dynamic Systems, 3rd ed., Chapter 4.

docs.title: 4.5 Other controller options
docs.text:
The project is not limited to PID. Choose according to the requirements and the computational budget:

Controller When to use it Source Cascade PID Default, lightweight, good enough for stable flight Åström & Hägglund, Advanced PID Control, 2006 LQR Optimal error/energy trade-off around hover; the DARE is solved offline and the online part is just the matrix product u = -K x Anderson B.D.O., Moore J.B., Optimal Control: Linear Quadratic Methods, Prentice-Hall, 1990 Geometric control on SE(3) Large angles, aerobatics, aggressive trajectory tracking — avoids Euler singularities entirely, with an exponential stability proof Lee T., Leok M., McClamroch N.H., "Geometric Tracking Control of a Quadrotor UAV on SE(3)", IEEE CDC, 2010 NMPC Explicit constraints (thrust limits, no-fly zones, angle limits) and prediction are required Rawlings, Mayne, Diehl, Model Predictive Control: Theory, Computation, and Design, 2nd ed., Nob Hill, 2017 ADRC (ESO + PD) Strong wind disturbance, inaccurate model Han 2009; Gao 2003 (see §3) FOC Motor tier, see §4.6 Park 1929; Clarke 1943; van der Broeck et al. 1988; Bose 2002

On computational capacity: the Cortex-M55 has a double-precision FPU and Helium (MVE). LQR runs comfortably at 1 kHz. Short-horizon NMPC is feasible at 50–100 Hz for the position loop, not at 1 kHz for the rate loop.

docs.title: 4.6 FOC — control tier of an encoder-equipped BLDC motor
docs.text:
Implementation: Application/Control/Src/foc.c, verified in tests/host/test_foc.c.

Why FOC rather than six-step control: six-step (trapezoidal) control energises only 2 of the 3 phases at any time, so the current vector jumps in 60° steps → noticeable torque ripple and acoustic noise. FOC keeps the current vector always perpendicular to the rotor flux, giving smooth torque and maximum torque per ampere.

Why an encoder is mandatory: the Park transform needs the electrical angle of the rotor. Sensorless estimation (based on the back-EMF) does not work at very low speed and at start-up, because the back-EMF is proportional to speed and tends to zero. An encoder gives the absolute angle at every speed, standstill included.

docs.title: Transform chain
docs.text:
ia, ib (ADC) → [Clarke] → α,β → [Park θ] → d,q
                                             ↓
                              [d-axis PI: id_ref = 0]
                              [q-axis PI: iq_ref ∝ torque]
                                             ↓
                           [limit |v| ≤ Vdc/√3] → [Park⁻¹] → [SVPWM] → 3 duty cycles
                                             ↓
                        inverter bridge → motor → encoder → back to Park

docs.title: Clarke convention: amplitude-invariant
docs.text:
iα = ia
iβ = (ia + 2·ib) / √3          (using ia + ib + ic = 0)

Only two phases need to be measured — which is why the circuit needs only two shunt resistors.

There are two Clarke conventions. The project uses the amplitude-invariant one: the magnitude of the α-β vector equals the phase-current amplitude, readable directly in real amperes. The power-invariant convention (an extra factor √(2/3)) gives an orthogonal matrix but scales the torque differently. Mixing the two conventions is a classic bug that makes the torque constant wrong by a factor of √(3/2).

docs.title: SVPWM by zero-sequence injection (min–max)
docs.text:
Instead of determining the sector and computing dwell times as in classical SVPWM, compute the three phase voltages and subtract the midpoint of their maximum and minimum:

vcom = (max(va,vb,vc) + min(va,vb,vc)) / 2
duty_x = 0.5 + (v_x − vcom) / Vdc

The result is identical to classical SVPWM, with no sector determination and no trigonometric tables.

The subtraction shifts all three phase voltages by the same amount, so the line-to-line voltages are unchanged — and the motor only sees line-to-line voltages — while the required amplitude decreases. The maximum phase amplitude therefore reaches Vdc/√3 instead of Vdc/2 for sinusoidal PWM, i.e. a bus utilisation 2/√3 = 1.1547 times better (+15.47 %).

This figure is measured numerically in test_foc.c::test_svpwm_bus_utilisation: the amplitude is increased until the modulation index reaches its limit at an arbitrary angle, and the result lands exactly on Vdc/√3.

docs.title: Voltage limiting by vector magnitude
docs.text: Beyond Vdc/√3 the inverter enters over-modulation: distorted waveforms, high-order harmonics, torque no longer proportional to iq. When the vector must be shrunk, it is scaled by its magnitude rather than clamping each component separately — separate clamping changes the angle of the voltage vector, i.e. the direction of the torque. Locked in by a test.

docs.title: Encoder angle-offset calibration
docs.text:
The encoder's zero does not coincide with the rotor's d axis. Procedure (run once, motor unloaded):

  1. Force a voltage vector along a fixed d direction (vd > 0, vq = 0, θ = 0).
  2. The rotor aligns itself with the d axis and comes to rest.
  3. Read the encoder count at that position → that is the offset.

With a wrong value the torque falls as cos(error) and reverses beyond 90° electrical. The value obtained should be stored in FRAM (already on the board) so that calibration is not repeated at every start-up.

docs.title: Known limitation
docs.text: At high speed the d and q axes are coupled through the ω·L·i terms (cross-coupling). Feed-forward decoupling of those terms is the next upgrade; for now the two PI loops have to reject them as a disturbance. This is acceptable over a drone's normal operating speed range.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Park R. H., "Two-reaction theory of synchronous machines", AIEE Transactions, 48, 1929 — the original d-q transform.
  • Clarke E., "Circuit Analysis of A-C Power Systems", Vol. I, Wiley, 1943 — the α-β transform.
  • van der Broeck, Skudelny, Stanke, "Analysis and Realization of a Pulsewidth Modulator Based on Voltage Space Vectors", IEEE Trans. Industry Applications, 24(1), 1988 — SVPWM.
  • Bose B. K., Modern Power Electronics and AC Drives, Prentice-Hall, 2002, Chapter 8.

docs.title: 5.1 Rotor model
docs.text:
For each rotor i spinning at angular speed w_i:

thrust        T_i  = k_f * w_i^2
drag torque   Q_i  = k_m * w_i^2

This quadratic relation comes from propeller momentum theory: thrust is proportional to rho * A * (w*R)^2 with a thrust coefficient C_T that is nearly constant in normal operation.

Source: Leishman J. G., Principles of Helicopter Aerodynamics, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press, 2006, Chapter 2 (momentum theory, definitions of C_T, C_Q).

k_f and k_m must be MEASURED; guessed values are not acceptable. See §5.4.

docs.title: 5.2 Allocation matrix for a quad-X
docs.text:
Standard rotor numbering: 1 = front-right (CCW), 2 = rear-left (CCW), 3 = front-left (CW), 4 = rear-right (CW). Arm length l (centre → rotor), projected half-diagonal d = l/sqrt(2).

With x_i = w_i^2:

[ T     ]   [  k_f      k_f      k_f      k_f   ] [ x1 ]
[ tau_x ] = [ -d*k_f    d*k_f    d*k_f   -d*k_f ] [ x2 ]        (12)
[ tau_y ]   [  d*k_f   -d*k_f    d*k_f   -d*k_f ] [ x3 ]
[ tau_z ]   [ -k_m     -k_m      k_m      k_m   ] [ x4 ]

(The signs of the tau_z row follow the direction of rotation: a CCW rotor produces a reaction torque in the negative z direction, a CW rotor in the positive direction.)

For a quad-X this matrix M is invertible (det M != 0 when k_f, k_m, d != 0), so:

x = M^(-1) * [T, tau_x, tau_y, tau_z]^T                        (13)
w_i = sqrt( max(x_i, 0) )                                       (14)

M^(-1) is computed once at initialisation, never inside the loop.

docs.title: 5.3 General case and saturation
docs.text:
With more than 4 rotors (hexa, octo), M is 4 x n and the problem is under-determined. The Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse M^+ = M^T (M M^T)^(-1) gives the minimum 2-norm solution, equivalent to minimising the sum of w_i^2 (an approximation of the energy).

When the solution violates the bounds [x_min, x_max], the elements must not be clipped independently — that breaks the ratios between the torques and can reverse a torque. An allocation algorithm with saturation handling is required (giving priority to tau over T, because losing torque flips the aircraft whereas losing thrust only costs altitude).

Source: Johansen T. A., Fossen T. I., "Control allocation — A survey", Automatica, 49(5), 2013, pp. 1087–1103.

docs.title: 5.4 Measuring k_f, k_m — mandatory before flight
docs.text:
A thrust stand with load cells for force and torque is required, plus a rotor-speed sensor (or an ESC with telemetry).

  1. Run the rotor at a series of steady speeds w_j (for example 10 points covering the whole range).
  2. Record (w_j, T_j, Q_j) in steady state.

  3. Fit a linear least-squares line through the origin in the variable u = w^2: 

    k_f = sum(u_j * T_j) / sum(u_j^2)
k_m = sum(u_j * Q_j) / sum(u_j^2)

  4. Check R^2 > 0.98. If lower, the quadratic assumption does not hold over that range (usually because of ground effect or the rotor entering the vortex-ring state) — narrow the range or use a higher-order model.

Record the results in Application/Interface/Inc/airframe_config.h. Never commit sample values as if they were measured values.

docs.title: 6. Closed loop — the open segment closed by bidirectional DShot
docs.text: Design update. The first version of this document stated that ESC command → rotor speed was the only open segment of the system, because with PWM/OneShot the firmware cannot know whether a rotor reached the requested speed. The project has adopted bidirectional DShot, so that open segment no longer exists.

docs.title: 6.1 How the loop is closed
docs.text:
Bidirectional DShot makes the ESC return the actual electrical period after every frame. From it:

period [µs] = mantissa << exponent          (12 bits: eee mmmmmmmmm)
eRPM        = 60e6 / period
mech. RPM   = eRPM / (pole count / 2)

Implementation: Application/Control/Src/dshot.c, verified in tests/host/test_dshot.c against reference values computed independently from the specification.

The chain thereby becomes fully closed at every tier:

throttle command → ESC → rotor → measured actual RPM → back to the controller

docs.title: 6.2 Consequence for the speed → throttle map
docs.text: A linear w ↔ throttle map is still only an approximation (ESCs are linear in throttle, not in rotor speed, and the characteristic depends on load, battery voltage and temperature). But its error no longer matters: the actual RPM is read back every cycle, so the map serves only as a feed-forward — a starting point for the feedback loop to correct, not an assumption that has to be right. That feedback loop is designed in §6.6.

docs.title: 6.3 Three states that must be distinguished, never merged
docs.text:
This is the easiest place to make a mistake, and it is pinned down by a test:

State Meaning Required behaviour valid && !stopped actual RPM read used by the feedback loop valid && stopped the ESC reports the rotor has stopped RPM = 0, treated as a genuinely stopped rotor !valid wrong CRC / corrupted GCR quintet — nothing is known must not be treated as RPM = 0

Treating a corrupted frame as RPM = 0 would make the controller believe the rotor had stopped and drive the command to full scale — exactly when nothing is known about that rotor. test_dshot.c::test_stopped_vs_invalid locks this behaviour in.

docs.title: 6.4 Additional feedback sources
docs.text:
• INA260 (Drivers/JetOwl/Inc/Adafruit_INA260.h): current is a proxy for torque (Q ≈ k_t · I for a BLDC). It cannot replace the RPM measurement but detects a jammed or lost rotor.
  • The outer loop through the IMU remains independently closed: a rotor that does not reach its speed shows up as an angular-rate error that the rate loop compensates. This is the second line of protection and keeps working even if the telemetry fails completely.

docs.title: 6.5 Conditions for the telemetry to work
docs.text:
The ESC must run firmware with bidirectional DShot enabled (BLHeli_32, Bluejay). Otherwise:

  • the ESC never answers, and
  • the inverted CRC of bidirectional mode makes the ESC drop every frame → the motor does not turn at all.

That is the typical symptom of a wrong BOARD_ESC_BIDIRECTIONAL flag, easily mistaken for a wiring fault.

docs.title: 6.6 Rotor-speed loop from RPM telemetry
docs.text:
Implementation: Application/Control/Src/rotor_speed.c (pure maths, host test tests/host/test_rotor_speed.c), called from the 1 kHz tick interrupt in flight_control.c::rotor_step right after rate_loop_update. One instance per rotor.

w_ref (mixer) ─► reference model r_m ─► FF = model inverse ────────┐
                     │                                               ▼
                     └► delay D, LPF ─► r_cmp ─(+)─► PI (SIMC) ─(+)─► clamp ─► DShot ─► ESC ─► rotor
                                          ▲(−)                                                 │
                                          └── LPF 150 Hz ◄── RPM telemetry (previous frame) ◄──┘

docs.title: Plant model
docs.text:
Torque balance on the rotor shaft [35]: J ẇ = a_u (u − u0) − b w − k_m w² (b = K_t K_e / R, k_m the propeller drag-torque coefficient). Linearised around w0:

G(s) = K e^(−θs) / (τ s + 1),   τ = J / (b + 2 k_m w0),   K = a_u / (b + 2 k_m w0)

An important consequence: K/τ = a_u/J does not depend on the operating point. At the crossover frequency (ω ≫ 1/τ) L(jω) ≈ Kc K / (τ jω) depends only on K/τ, so one set of gains serves the whole speed range — the operating point only changes the low-frequency part, which the integrator takes care of. A non-linear simulation at 200, 500 and 1100 rad/s (τ varying 20–58 ms, K varying 0.37–1.07) confirms this.

Delay θ = Ts/2 (command ZOH) + Ts (the RPM used in cycle k is the response to frame k−1) + T_e/2 (the ESC averages over one electrical period, ~0.43 ms at 10 000 RPM with 14 poles) ≈ 1.9 ms → 2 ms is used.

docs.title: Measurement filter
docs.text: The RPM is quantised (1 µs electrical period, 9-bit mantissa) → white noise of a few rad/s, multiplied by Kc ≈ 8 count/(rad/s). First-order filter f_c = 150 Hz, ZOH discretisation [8]: y[k] = y[k−1] + a (x[k] − y[k−1]), a = 1 − e^(−Ts/τ_f). Criteria: f_c ≥ 5·f_crossover,rotor (24.7 Hz) → phase lag at crossover atan(1/5) ≤ 11.3° (9.4° in practice), and f_c < f_s/2. τ_f is the smallest neglected time constant, so by Skogestad's half rule [33]: τ_eff = τ + τ_f/2, θ_eff = θ + τ_f/2 — and SIMC uses (τ_eff, θ_eff).

docs.title: Controller — two degrees of freedom
docs.text:
The first version used u = u_ff(w_ref) + PI(w_ref − w_meas). Simulation showed 17–20 % overshoot even with a correct feed-forward: the FF already supplied the throttle needed for the step, and the P term added Kc·Δw on top for the same step. The standard solution is a two-degree-of-freedom structure [36], [7]:

(a) reference model:   r_m[k+1] = r_m[k] + a_m (w_ref[k] − r_m[k]),   a_m = 1 − e^(−Ts/τ_c)
(b) FF = exact inverse of the ZOH model  w[k+1] = p w[k] + (1−p) K u[k],  p = e^(−Ts/τ):
        u_ff[k] = S(r_m[k+1]) + g_d (r_m[k+1] − r_m[k]),     g_d = p / ((1−p) K)
(c) r_cmp = LPF( r_m delayed by D = θ/Ts + ½ sample, linear interpolation )   — the EXPECTED measurement
(d) PI on e = r_cmp − w_filtered:
        u = u_ff + Kc e + I,   u_sat = clamp(u, 48, 2047)
        I ← I + (Kc/Ti) Ts e + (Ts/Tt)(u_sat − u)                 (back-calculation [7], Tt = Ti/2)

S is the static inverse of the model: in steady state a_u (u − u0) = b w + k_m w², so S(w) = c0 + c1 w + c2 w² with c0 = u0, c1 = b/a_u, c2 = k_m/a_u. It must be monotonically increasing on [w_min, w_max] (rotor_speed_init checks both end points). g_d ≈ τ/(K Ts) = J/(a_u Ts) — also independent of the operating point. With a correct model, r_cmp matches the measurement and the feedback barely acts (test: |e| ≤ 0.05 rad/s after a 50 rad/s step); (a)–© are outside the loop and do not change the stability margins.

SIMC gains [33], [34]:

Kc = τ_eff / (K (τ_c + θ_eff)),     Ti = min(τ_eff, 4 (τ_c + θ_eff))

τ_c is squeezed between two constraints:

Constraint Reason Value τ_c ≥ θ_eff SIMC recommendation for a fast/robust compromise [33] θ_eff = 2.53 ms τ_c + θ_eff ≤ 1/(5 ω_c,rate) the rate loop treats the actuator as ideal (5× separation, [27]) 1/(5·15.78) = 12.7 ms

τ_c = 4 ms is chosen → Kc = 8.50 count/(rad/s), Ti = 26.1 ms.

docs.title: Stability margins — computed on the actual DISCRETE loop
docs.text:
test_rotor_speed.c::test_margins evaluates L(e^{jωTs}) = C(z)·F(z)·G(z)·e^{−jω·0.43 ms} with a forward-Euler PI, a ZOH LPF, the exact ZOH plant and the z⁻¹ of previous-frame telemetry — using the very macros in airframe_config.h:

Case ω_c [rad/s] PM GM Nominal 152 65.6° 13.8 dB Worst of the 4 corners ±20 % K, τ — 58.0° 10.4 dB Worst ±20 %, 1 telemetry frame lost (+1 Ts delay) — 45.2° 6.6 dB Worst ±20 %, 2 frames lost (+2 Ts delay) — 32.4° ✗ 4.1 dB ✗

Requirement of control-systems §4: GM ≥ 6 dB, PM ≥ 45° — met by the first three rows.

The sample-age limit ROTOR_MEAS_TIMEOUT_S = 2.5 ms follows directly from the last two rows: the normal age is 1 Ts and each lost frame adds 1 Ts of delay; one lost frame still meets the requirement, two do not → only ages ≤ 2 Ts are accepted. The limit sits between 2 Ts and 3 Ts so that it does not depend on floating-point rounding; beyond it → FF_ONLY.

docs.title: Time response (non-linear plant, test_nonlinear_steps)
docs.text:
Identified FF, plant a_u off by ±10 % (battery sag):

Step Overshoot 2 % settling Steady-state error 200 → 400 rad/s ≤ 0.3 % 18 ms < 0.03 rad/s 500 → 800 rad/s 0 % 39–44 ms (dynamic FF saturates — a physical limit) < 0.03 rad/s 1100 → 900 rad/s 0 % 19–22 ms < 0.03 rad/s

Default linear FF (not identified, c2 = 0): overshoot ≤ 3.8 %, settling ≤ 49 ms — the integrator absorbs the mismatch. Quantisation noise ±3 rad/s: peak-to-peak throttle ripple 41 counts (< Kc·6 = 51 without filtering). Saturation for 0.5 s at w_ref = W_MAX, then back to 600 rad/s: I is bounded (back-calculation) and recovers in 69 ms.

docs.title: When no usable feedback exists
docs.text:
Condition Mode Behaviour RPM valid, age ≤ timeout, not stopped CLOSED (a)–(d) No RPM / stale (wrong CRC, ESC not answering, plain DShot) FF_ONLY u = u_ff + I, I frozen; the filter re-initialises from the first sample when telemetry returns ESC reports stopped (below the measurable range, during sensorless start-up) STARTUP as FF_ONLY — the model G(s) does not hold in this region stopped continuously for > ROTOR_STALL_TIME_S while armed STALLED S(w_ref) only, no PI — no throttle pushed into a jammed motor; cleared only on disarm; /jetowl/status reports ERROR rotor stalled

FF_ONLY with BOARD_ESC_BIDIRECTIONAL = 0 is a justified open loop: no rotor-speed sensor exists. The rate loop on the IMU remains closed around it (§6.4). Monitoring: rotor_closed_mask, rotor_stall_mask in /jetowl/status; fc_telemetry_t carries rotor_mode, rotor_w_ref, rotor_err, rotor_u for logging.

docs.title: Identification procedure — mandatory before flight
docs.text:
On a thrust stand, propeller fitted, battery full, reading the RPM through /jetowl/motor_rpm (50 Hz) or a 1 kHz log:

  1. Static map S: ≥ 10 throttle levels u_j evenly spread over 10–90 %, each held ≥ 5τ (≥ 0.3 s), averaging w_j over the last 0.2 s. Least squares u_j ≈ c0 + c1 w_j + c2 w_j² (linear in the parameters). Check R² > 0.99 and monotonicity → ROTOR_FF_C0/C1/C2.
  2. K, τ, θ: ±5 % throttle steps around mid-range; fit w(t) = w0 + K Δu (1 − e^{−(t−θ)/τ}) (tfest/procest or non-linear least squares); report the fit (%). Repeat at 3 operating points and check that K/τ is nearly constant (the assumption of §6.6) → ROTOR_K_PLANT, ROTOR_TAU, ROTOR_THETA.
  3. ROTOR_STALL_TIME_S: measure the time from arming until rotor_mode leaves STARTUP over 20 arming cycles; set it to ≥ 2× the largest value.
  4. Re-run ctest — test_rotor_speed recomputes the margins with the new constants and must still PASS.

docs.title: 7. Timing and discretisation
docs.text:
Every discrete formula above assumes a fixed Ts. That assumption breaks if HAL_Delay() or a free-running loop is used.

Mandatory requirements:

  • The tick comes from a TIM interrupt, not from a while(1) loop.
  • Never call HAL_Delay() in any function that runs in the control loop.
  • Measure the actual jitter (record max|Ts(k) - Ts_nominal|). If the jitter exceeds ~1 % of Ts, it must be fixed before trusting the control results.
  • Blocking I2C/UART/SPI transfers must not be placed in the control-loop ISR — use DMA and read the result in the next cycle.

Rate groups (Application/Interface/Src/app_scheduler.c):

Group Rate Work A 1000 Hz gyro read, ESO, rate loop, mixer, ESC write B 250 Hz accel/mag read, attitude filter, attitude loop C 50 Hz baro, position/velocity loop D 10 Hz GNSS, battery measurement (INA260), LoRa telemetry E 1 Hz FRAM logging, system health checks

docs.title: 9. Limitations of this design
docs.text:
An honest account of what has not been done yet:

  • k_f, k_m, l and the inertia matrix J have no real values yet — they must be measured on the specific airframe (§5.4). Every constant in airframe_config.h is currently a sample value for testing, not for flight.
  • The PID/LQR gains are not tuned — an identified model or bench experiments are required.
  • The rotor-speed loop (§6.6) uses sample K, τ, θ, S — the stability margins are computed correctly for those numbers, but they must be re-identified on the real motor + propeller with the procedure of §6.6.
  • There is no detailed aerodynamic model yet (body drag, ground effect, rotor interaction).
  • Safety logic is not implemented yet: signal-loss failsafe, low-battery detection, geofence.
  • The mathematics is tested on the host (tests/host/); the parts running on hardware are not yet verified.

docs.title: Peripheral configuration in STM32CubeMX
docs.text:
Source

Snapshot of docs/CUBEMX_SETUP.md from TNG-Blue/JetOwl_FlightControl at commit 23b5ac3 (submodule Microcontroller/JetOwl_FlightControl). Regenerate with Scripts/mkdocs_hooks/snapshot_submodules.py after updating the submodule.

This list is derived from the actual driver code in Drivers/JetOwl/, not from guesswork. Every line can be traced to a specific function signature or #define.

docs.title: 0a. Board: NUCLEO-N657X0-Q — pinout looked up
docs.text:
The .ioc is set to board=custom, but the real hardware is a NUCLEO-N657X0-Q (STM32N657X0H3Q, VFBGA264) with ARDUINO Uno V3 / ST Zio and ST morpho headers.

So the pinout does not have to be guessed. The complete pin assignment is in Application/Interface/Inc/board_config.h, taken from the Zephyr Project board support (boards/st/nucleo_n657x0_q) — a verifiable source.

Summary of the assignment:

Function Peripheral Pins Arduino Sensors (2 IMUs, baro, INA260) I2C1 SCL=PH9, SDA=PC1 D15 / D14 GNSS USART3 + DMA + IDLE interrupt TX=PD8, RX=PD9 D1 / D0 Debug (VCP through ST-LINK) USART1 TX=PE5, RX=PE6 — FRAM + 2 × LoRa LR1121 SPI5 (prescaler 16 = 12.5 MHz) SCK=PE15, MISO=PG1, MOSI=PG2; CS FRAM=PA3, LoRa UL=PD7, DL=PA10 D13/D12/D11/D10, D9, A2 DShot to 4 ESCs TIM1 CH1–CH4 PE9, PE11, PE13, PE14 D3, D7, —, — 1 kHz control tick TIM6 no pins —

Do not change board=custom to the Nucleo board in CubeMX — that pulls in the board's default configuration and overwrites the existing 4-context configuration. Only the pins above need to be assigned.

docs.title: Three points to confirm before wiring
docs.text:
1. TIM1 CH1–CH4 on PE9/PE11/PE13/PE14 — lower confidence than the other rows. This mapping is the common STM32 convention and matches the STM32N6570-DK board documentation, but it could not be taken directly from the STM32N657 datasheet's alternate-function table. Verified in the repository: TIM1 is an advanced timer on APB2 (stm32n657xx.h:3106, :42139) and GPIO_AF1_TIM1 exists (stm32n6xx_hal_gpio_ex.h:65). In CubeMX select TIM1 → 4 PWM channels: if the pins shown match the table, the table is correct.
  2. The two LoRa LR1121 modules share SPI5 with the FRAM — see §2.1 below and docs/RFLINK.md.
  3. TIM1's 400 MHz clock — check it in the Clock Configuration tab after enabling TIM1/TIM6, since TIM1 is on APB2 and the timer multiplier depends on the APB divider.

docs.title: 0. Current state: the .ioc is almost empty
docs.text:
JetOwl_FlightControl.ioc currently enables only:

Mcu.IP0=CORTEX_M55_FSBL   Mcu.IP1=CORTEX_M55_NS   Mcu.IP2=CORTEX_M55_S
Mcu.IP3=NVIC1             Mcu.IP4=NVIC2           Mcu.IP5=NVIC
Mcu.IP6=RCC               Mcu.IP7=RIF             Mcu.IP8=SYS
Mcu.PinsNb=2              (VP_RIF_VS_RIF1, VP_SYS_VS_Systick)

No I2C, UART, SPI, TIM or ETH at all. Consequence: the 9 driver files just added to the build in AppliNonSecure/CMakeLists.txt compile but do not link, because they call HAL_I2C_*, HAL_UART* and HAL_SPI_* while those HAL modules are not in STM32_Drivers_Src (see AppliNonSecure/mx-generated.cmake — currently only hal, cortex, pwr, pwr_ex, rcc, rcc_ex, gpio, dma, dma_ex, exti, tim, tim_ex).

CubeMX adds the corresponding HAL modules to mx-generated.cmake when the peripherals are enabled. Do not edit that file by hand.

docs.title: 1. Peripherals to enable
docs.text: Peripheral Used by Evidence in the code I2C (≥ 1 bus) Adafruit_IMU, Adafruit_INA260, Adafruit_PCA9548, DFRobot_IMU, DFRobot_GNSS, WaveShare_GNSS (optional) Adafruit_IMU_Init(..., I2C_HandleTypeDef *hi2c, ...) UART/USART (1–3) Adafruit_GPS, WaveShare_GNSS GPS_Init(gps, UART_HandleTypeDef *huart); WSGNSS_Init_UART(h, huart_nmea, huart_rtcm) DMA (for the UART) WaveShare_GNSS HAL_UARTEx_ReceiveToIdle_DMA() in WaveShare_GNSS.c SPI (1–2) Adafruit_FRAM, WaveShare_LoRa FRAM_Init(dev, SPI_HandleTypeDef *hspi, cs_port, cs_pin) GPIO IMU RESET/INT, GNSS RST/PWR, FRAM CS, LoRa NSS/RST/DIO Adafruit_IMU_Init(..., reset_port, reset_pin, int_port, int_pin) TIM Control-loop tick + PWM to the ESCs docs/CONTROL_DESIGN.md ETH + LwIP micro-ROS, OTA integrated outside CubeMX: Application/Network, docs/MICROROS_ETHERNET.md XSPI2 + IWDG OTA (Application/Ota/Port/xspi_nor.c), FSBL HAL modules enabled by compile flags; clocks/pins configured by the FSBL and AppliSecure — docs/OTA.md

docs.title: I2C address of each device (7-bit, from the headers)
docs.text:
Device Address Source Adafruit IMU (BNO08x / SH-2) 0x4A (DI=0) or 0x4B (DI=1) Adafruit_IMU.h:32-33 INA260 (current/voltage) 0x40 default Adafruit_INA260.h:37 PCA9548 (I2C mux) 0x70 with A2=A1=A0=0 Adafruit_PCA9548.h:30 BNO055 (DFRobot IMU) 0x28 (COM3=GND) or 0x29 DFRobot_IMU.h:44-45 BMP280 (pressure) 0x76 (SDO=GND) or 0x77 DFRobot_IMU.h:189-190 DFRobot GNSS 0x20 DFRobot_GNSS.h:47

There is no address conflict among these devices → one hardware I2C bus is sufficient. The PCA9548 is only needed when several devices share an address (for example two BNO08x IMUs both at 0x4A).

Note: the headers already shift the addresses to 8-bit (0x4A << 1) for the HAL, except INA260_I2C_ADDRESS_DEFAULT and PCA9548_BASE_ADDR_7BIT, which are raw 7-bit values. Check how each driver uses its address before passing it to HAL_I2C_Master_Transmit() (the HAL always expects the address shifted left by one bit).

docs.title: 2.1 Two Core1121-XF (LR1121) LoRa modules on SPI5
docs.text:
The full-duplex control link to Remote_UAV (docs/RFLINK.md) uses the driver Application/RfLink/Src/lr1121.c — the driver takes a port layer (function pointers), so it works on any bus. Drivers/JetOwl/WaveShare_LoRa is a driver for the LR2021 chip (Core2021-XF module) and is not used for this link.

Signal UL module (receives 2.4 GHz commands) DL module (transmits telemetry) NSS (GPIO out, idle high) PD7 (D9) PA10 (A2) BUSY (GPIO in) PA8 (A0) PA12 (A3) DIO9 / IRQ (rising-edge EXTI) PE10 (D5) PF3 (A4) NRESET (GPIO out, idle high) PA9 (A1) PG15 (A5)
  • SPI5: mode 0, MSB first, 8 bit, prescaler 16 (12.5 MHz ≤ 16 MHz for the LR1121, ≤ 33 MHz for the FRAM).
  • The two EXTIs have different line numbers (EXTI10, EXTI3), so they do not share a vector.
  • Every other SPI5 user must take RfLinkApp_SpiLock() (rflink_app.h).
  • RfLinkApp_Start() is already called in app_freertos.c; it returns false until BOARD_CUBEMX_PERIPHERALS_READY = 1.

docs.title: 2.2 SPI parameters for the FRAM
docs.text:
Adafruit_FRAM.h (comment of FRAM_Init) requires:

  • SPI mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0)
  • MSB first
  • 8-bit data size
  • a baud-rate prescaler giving ≤ 33 MHz

docs.title: 2.3 The GNSS UART must enable DMA + the IDLE interrupt
docs.text:
WaveShare_GNSS.c uses HAL_UARTEx_ReceiveToIdle_DMA(). In CubeMX:

  1. Enable USARTx in Asynchronous mode.
  2. DMA Settings tab → Add → select USARTx_RX, mode Circular.
  3. NVIC Settings tab → enable USARTx global interrupt and the corresponding DMA channel interrupt.

If any step is missing the driver runs but never receives data.

The driver also requires forwarding from the HAL callbacks:

void HAL_UARTEx_RxEventCallback(UART_HandleTypeDef *huart, uint16_t Size) {
    WSGNSS_UART_RxEventCallback(&h_gnss, huart, Size);
}
void HAL_UART_ErrorCallback(UART_HandleTypeDef *huart) {
    WSGNSS_UART_ErrorCallback(&h_gnss, huart);
}

The module's default baud rate is 460800 (supported range 4800–921600) — WaveShare_GNSS.h:305. The Adafruit GPS uses PMTK, 9600 by default, with a command to switch to 115200 (Adafruit_GPS.h:69-70).

docs.title: 2.4 WaveShare_GNSS over I2C is currently unusable
docs.text: The header states it explicitly: Waveshare has not published the LG290P's I2C protocol, so WSGNSS_Init_I2C() only prepares the handle and every transfer returns WSGNSS_NOT_SUPPORTED. In addition, RTCM is only available on UART2. Use WSGNSS_Init_UART() when RTK is needed.

docs.title: 2.5 CubeMX's "CoupleFile" option
docs.text:
The .ioc sets ProjectManager.CoupleFile=false, i.e. CubeMX does not generate i2c.c/i2c.h, spi.c/spi.h… pairs but puts everything into main.c.

DFRobot_IMU.h used to #include "i2c.h" → it would not compile. It now includes "stm32n6xx_hal.h" (the driver receives its handle as a parameter, so no global variable is needed).

If you enable CoupleFile=true in CubeMX (Project Manager → Code Generator → Generate peripheral initialization as a pair of .c/.h files per peripheral), keep that choice consistently and update AppliNonSecure/CMakeLists.txt if needed — but do not go back to including i2c.h in the drivers, because that would make the drivers depend on an IDE configuration option.

docs.title: 2.6 Parameters precomputed from the clock tree
docs.text:
The following values are derived directly from JetOwl_FlightControl.ioc (RCC.TIMGFreq_Value = 400 MHz, RCC.SPI1Freq_Value = RCC.I2C1Freq_Value = RCC.USART1Freq_Value = 200 MHz) and all divide exactly, so the frequencies obtained are exact, with no rounding error. This matters because all the discretisation in Application/Control/ assumes a fixed Ts exactly equal to its design value.

They are in Application/Interface/Inc/board_config.h — enter exactly these numbers in CubeMX:

Item Value Derivation Control tick TIM (TIM6/TIM7) PSC = 399, ARR = 999 400 MHz / 400 = 1 MHz; 1 MHz / 1000 = exactly 1000 Hz TIM1 for DShot300 PSC = 0, ARR = 1332, T0H=500, T1H=1000 see the table in §2.7 SPI for the FRAM Prescaler = 8 → 25 MHz 200 MHz / 8 = 25 MHz ≤ the required 33 MHz. Prescaler 4 gives 50 MHz — over the limit GNSS UART 460800 baud USARTDIV = 200e6/460800 = 434.03 → error 0.0064 %, well within tolerance I2C Fast Mode 400 kHz Do not set TIMINGR by hand — let CubeMX compute it, because the value depends on the bus's actual edge times

docs.title: 2.7 DShot — the selected ESC protocol
docs.text:
DShot encodes each bit as a pulse width within a fixed period: bit 0 → high for 37.5 % of the period, bit 1 → 75 %. Hence PSC = 0 (counting at the full 400 MHz) and ARR set from the bit rate:

Variant ARR Actual frequency Error T0H T1H 16-bit frame % of a 1 kHz period DShot150 2666 149 981 Hz −0.0125 % 1000 2000 107 µs 10.7 % DShot300 1332 300 075 Hz +0.0250 % 500 1000 53 µs 5.3 % DShot600 666 599 700 Hz −0.0500 % 250 500 27 µs 2.7 %

DShot300 is the default because: T0H/T1H fall on round numbers (500/1000), so the 37.5 %/75 % ratios are practically exact; the 53 µs frame takes only 5.3 % of the 1 kHz period, leaving ample room for the turnaround and the ~30 µs telemetry reply; and the lower bit rate tolerates long wires and noise better — decisive when ESCs are connected to the Nucleo with jumper wires. Switching to DShot600 only means changing three constants in board_config.h.

docs.title: CubeMX configuration of TIM1
docs.text:
1. Move the AppliNonSecure HAL timebase away from TIM1 (SYS → Timebase Source, e.g. TIM16/TIM17). CubeMX currently uses TIM1 as the 1 kHz timebase. If this is forgotten, FlightControl_Start() refuses to start (esc_prepare() sees TIM1's PSC/ARR do not match DShot) rather than sending malformed frames.
  2. TIM1 → Channel1..4 = PWM Generation CHx (not CHxN), context NonSecure.
  3. Counter Period (ARR) = 1332, Prescaler = 0, auto-reload preload = Enable, Output compare preload = Enable (the firmware also re-enables it). Pulse = 0.
  4. GPDMA1: add a channel (context NonSecure), request TIM1_UP, Memory→Peripheral, Source: increment, Word; Destination: fixed, Word; Normal (not circular, not linked-list). Link the DMA to TIM1 (hdma[TIM_DMA_ID_UPDATE]) — CubeMX generates __HAL_LINKDMA when the TIM1_UP request is selected.
  5. NVIC: enable the GPDMA channel interrupt with priority ≥ 5 (the callback runs in the DMA ISR).
  6. Set BOARD_CUBEMX_PERIPHERALS_READY = 1.

What the firmware does every 1 ms (flight_control.c, esc_write_dshot):

mixer → throttle 48..2047 → 16-bit frame (inverted CRC if bidirectional)
  → dshot_build_dma_burst_u32(): 4 channels × (16 bits + 2 idle slots), WORD, interleaved  (host-tested)
  → SCB_CleanDCache_by_Addr (D-cache enabled; 32 B-aligned buffer, 288 B)
  → [bidir] pins PE9/11/13/14 back to AF
  → HAL_TIM_DMABurst_MultiWriteStart(TIM1, DBA = CCR1, DBL = 4, req = UPDATE, 288 BYTE)
TC (GPDMA ISR → HAL_TIM_PeriodElapsedCallback(TIM1) → esc_dma_done):
  → [bidir] pins back to input + pull-up (release the line for the ESC's reply)
  → HAL_TIM_DMABurst_WriteStop

Why 2 idle slots: the CCRs are preloaded, so slot k written by the DMA at update u_k is output only during [u_(k+1), u_(k+2)). With N slots, TC occurs right after u_(N−1); the last bit (slot 15) has completed when N − 2 ≥ 16 ⇒ ≥ 2 idle slots are needed to release the line at TC without truncating the last bit (dshot.h).

Time budget: frame (16 + 2) × 3.33 µs = 60 µs; a bidirectional ESC replies after ~30 µs, 21 bits × 2.67 µs = 56 µs ⇒ ~146 µs ≪ 1 ms. If the previous transaction has not finished at the next tick, the frame is dropped and counted (dshot_skipped on /jetowl/status, which must always be 0); DMA errors are counted in dshot_errors.

DMA burst mode (registers DMAR/DCR) lets one DMA transaction update all four CCRs, so the four ESCs receive their frames in phase — no skew of tens of µs as with four separate timers.

docs.title: Bidirectional — mandatory condition
docs.text:
The ESC must run firmware with bidirectional DShot enabled (BLHeli_32 / Bluejay). Otherwise the ESC never answers and the inverted CRC of bidirectional mode makes it drop every frame → the motor does not turn at all. This symptom is easily mistaken for a wiring fault.

The bidirectional signal is inverted (idle high, each bit a low pulse T0H/T1H): the firmware sets low polarity on CC1..CC4 and pull-ups on the 4 pins; after each frame the pins are released to inputs so that the ESC can drive the line — there is no push-pull contention between MCU and ESC.

docs.title: Receiving bidirectional telemetry — GPIO sampling through DMA
docs.text:
Pin-level sampling was chosen over 4-channel input capture: it needs only 1 timer + 1 DMA channel, all 4 ESCs are received simultaneously in one stream, and all decoding is pure software with host tests (dshot_rx_decode_samples, Application/Control/Src/dshot.c).

Item Configuration Reason TIM3 Internal clock, PSC = 0, ARR = 355, no channels, context NonSecure update 400 MHz / 356 = 1.1236 MHz ≈ 3 samples per telemetry bit (r = 2.9955) GPDMA1 (second channel) Request TIM3_UP, Peripheral→Memory, Source fixed Word, Destination increment Word, Normal; NonSecure captures GPIOE->IDR at every update; esc_prepare() checks direction/width and refuses to start if they are wrong NVIC for that channel priority ≥ 5 decoding runs in the TC ISR (~a few µs)

Sequence every 1 ms: transmit the frame (60 µs) → TC: release the 4 pins to input + pull-up, start TIM3 + DMA for 192 samples (171 µs) → receive TC: decode each pin → telemetry_apply (GCR + CRC checks) → RPM. Total 231 µs < 1 ms. A channel that does not answer is counted in esc_telem_missing; a corrupted frame in telem_errors; both make that rotor's RPM "unknown", not 0.

Run-length decoding: from the first falling edge, each run of m samples at the same level = round(m/r) bits. Runs inside a frame must be 1..3 bits long (the GCR table never has more than 2 consecutive zeros — a test enumerating the whole table proves it); otherwise the whole frame is dropped. Correct while the ESC/FC clock mismatch is < 5.5 % (dshot.h); the test checks ±4 % at 7 phases.

docs.title: 3. Secure / non-secure assignment through RIF — DECISION: KEEP TrustZone
docs.text: Decided: keep the 4-context architecture. Mcu.ContextProject=SecureNSecure stays; the project structure is not regenerated.

docs.title: 3.1 How the .ioc represents context assignment
docs.text:
Each context has a key listing the peripherals that belong to it:

FSBL.IPs           = CORTEX_M55_FSBL,GPDMA1,HDP,HPDMA1,LINKEDLIST,RCC,GPIO,NVIC:I,DEBUG,THREADX
AppliSecure.IPs    = CORTEX_M55_S,GPDMA1,HPDMA1,LINKEDLIST,RCC,RIF,SAU,GPIO,NVIC1:I,DEBUG,THREADX
AppliNonSecure.IPs = CORTEX_M55_NS,GPDMA1:I,HDP,HPDMA1:I,LINKEDLIST,RCC,SYS:I,GPIO:I,NVIC2:I,DEBUG,THREADX
ExtMemLoader.IPs   = EXTMEM_LOADER,EXTMEM_MANAGER,RCC:I,GPIO,DEBUG

The :I suffix marks the context that generates the initialisation code for that peripheral. For example GPDMA1 appears in both AppliSecure and AppliNonSecure, but only NonSecure has :I — so MX_GPDMA1_Init() is generated in AppliNonSecure.

In addition, RIF.RIFAWARE.* (554 lines) covers only GPDMA1, GPIO, HPDMA1, LTDC, PWR, RCC, RTC — the peripherals with per-feature access control. I2C/SPI/USART/TIM are not in that group; they are partitioned as whole blocks through RISUP, i.e. through the context assignment above.

docs.title: 3.2 Boundary principle
docs.text:
The whole 1 kHz control loop runs entirely in the non-secure state, with no NSC calls inside the loop. The secure side keeps only three jobs, all at very low rates, so the NSC veneer cost is not measurable:

Secure job Call rate Why it is secure Motor arm/disarm latch a few times per flight A bug in the NMEA/LoRa/OTA parsers must never spin the motors OTA image signature verification once per update The authentication key must not share memory with code that processes network data Safety watchdog 1–10 Hz If the non-secure application hangs, the secure side cuts the motor output

Reason for this boundary: the three parsers in Drivers/JetOwl/ — NMEA from the GNSS, LoRa packets from the ground, firmware from the OTA network — all process data controlled by outside parties. That is precisely the kind of risk TrustZone exists to contain.

Default rule:

Peripheral Assigned to Reason I2C (IMU, baro, INA260, mux) Non-secure In the 1 kHz control loop; must not go through an NSC veneer UART (GNSS, GPS) Non-secure As above SPI (FRAM, LoRa) Non-secure As above TIM (control tick + ESC PWM) Non-secure As above Ordinary GPIO Non-secure Motor safety-latch GPIO (if implemented) Secure Out of reach of bugs in the flight application OTA key/authentication (RNG, PKA, HASH if used) Secure Security assets

docs.title: Symptoms of a wrong assignment
docs.text:
If a peripheral is left Secure and non-secure code accesses it, RIF/IAC raises an Illegal Access Interrupt. It shows up as the callback registered through

SECURE_RegisterCallback(IAC_ERROR_CB_ID, my_handler);   /* AppliSecure/Core/Src/secure_nsc.c */

being called, or as the program hanging in Error_Handler for no apparent reason. This is the most common error when starting with TrustZone on the N6 — if a peripheral "does not respond" despite a correct configuration, check RIF first.

Recommendation: register both callbacks right in AppliNonSecure's main() so that a fault yields diagnostic information instead of a silent hang.

docs.title: 3.3 Which peripheral is enabled in which context
docs.text:
Peripheral Context :I (generates init code) I2C (IMU, baro, INA260, mux) AppliNonSecure yes USART/UART (GNSS, GPS) + DMA AppliNonSecure yes SPI5 (FRAM + 2 × LoRa LR1121) AppliNonSecure yes Control tick TIM (TIM6/TIM7) AppliNonSecure yes ESC PWM TIM AppliNonSecure yes GPIO (sensor reset/int/CS) AppliNonSecure yes (already GPIO:I) Motor safety-latch GPIO (if implemented) AppliSecure yes RNG / PKA / HASH (if signed OTA is implemented) AppliSecure yes

The FSBL stays as it is — it only needs RCC/GPIO to bring up the clocks and XSPI.

Order of work: enable TIM6 (control tick) first. It is the only peripheral that needs no pinout — a basic timer has no output pins. That lets you verify the whole build + boot + 1 kHz tick chain before touching any sensor.

docs.title: 3.4 IMU read path (Application/Interface/Src/imu_acq.c)
docs.text:
Item Configuration Reason I2C1 Fast Mode 400 kHz, PH9 SCL / PC1 SDA (board_config.h §2.1), context NonSecure bus budget ~41 % (airframe_config.h §6.3) PE0 GPIO_EXTI0, falling edge, pull-up the BNO08x's active-low INT; HAL_GPIO_EXTI_Falling_Callback is in imu_acq.c NVIC EXTI0 priority ≥ 5 (e.g. 6) the ISR calls osThreadFlagsSet — must be ≥ configLIBRARY_MAX_SYSCALL_INTERRUPT_PRIORITY PD0, PD5 GPIO_Output BNO08x / BNO055 RESET

After generating: set BOARD_CUBEMX_PERIPHERALS_READY = 1 and build with make DRIVERS=1 (Make) — the CMake build already includes Drivers/JetOwl. Check ros2 topic echo /jetowl/status: imu_fusion = 3, imu_rejected not increasing, then perform the static check of CONTROL_DESIGN.md §1.4.

docs.title: 4. After configuring CubeMX
docs.text:
1. Generate Code.
  2. Check that AppliNonSecure/mx-generated.cmake has added stm32n6xx_hal_i2c.c, _uart.c, _spi.c and _tim.c to STM32_Drivers_Src.
  3. Check that AppliNonSecure/Core/Src/main.c still contains your code inside the USER CODE blocks.
  4. Check that AppliNonSecure/CMakeLists.txt still contains the Drivers/JetOwl driver section (CubeMX does not regenerate this file, but check it after every generation).
  5. Build: cmake --preset Debug && cmake --build --preset Debug.

docs.title: micro-ROS over UDP/Ethernet: JetOwl ↔ Jetson (Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL)
docs.text:
Source

Snapshot of docs/MICROROS_ETHERNET.md from TNG-Blue/JetOwl_FlightControl at commit 23b5ac3 (submodule Microcontroller/JetOwl_FlightControl). Regenerate with Scripts/mkdocs_hooks/snapshot_submodules.py after updating the submodule.

This document describes what has been built and verified in the repository (compiled, linked, host-tested), and separates out what is not yet verified on hardware. Read section 9 before flashing a board.

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
Jetson Orin (ROS 2 Humble)                              STM32N657 — AppliNonSecure (FreeRTOS)
 ┌──────────────────────────────┐                       ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ uav_trajectory_controller    │ /control/attitude_    │ "uros" task (uros_app.c, 200 Hz)        │
 │  (MPC, 50 Hz, ENU/FLU)       │  setpoint, /control/  │   ENU/FLU → NED/FRD (frame_conv.c)      │
 │                              │  thrust ────────────▶ │   FlightControl_SubmitAttitudeCommand   │
 │ uav_state_estimator (ESKF)   │ ◀──── /imu/data ───── │ ┌─ TIM interrupt 1 kHz (flight_control.c)┐│
 │ flight_controller (modes)    │ ◀─ /jetowl/status ─── │ │ cmd_guard → attitude_ctrl (250 Hz)    ││
 │ jetowl_bridge ─ /jetowl/arm ▶│                       │ │ → rate_loop PID+ESO (1 kHz) → mixer   ││
 └──────────┬───────────────────┘                       │ │ → DShot → ESC → RPM (bidirectional)   ││
            │ micro_ros_agent udp4 :8888                │ └──────────── IMU feedback ────────────┘│
            └──────── UDP/IPv4, 100BASE-TX RMII ────────│ lwIP 2.2.1 ← ethernetif.c ← ETH1+LAN8742│
                                                        └───────────────────────────────────────┘

Two design principles:

  1. The attitude and rate loops are always closed on the firmware's IMU. Commands from the Jetson are only set-points. A slow network or lost packets never open a loop; they only make the set-point stale → handled by cmd_guard (section 4).
  2. No intermediate node on the command path. The firmware subscribes to exactly the topics that ros2_control_system publishes and publishes exactly the topics the ESKF listens to — the Jetson stack runs unchanged.

docs.title: 2. Topic contract
docs.text:
Direction Name Type QoS Rate FC→J /imu/data sensor_msgs/Imu (ENU/FLU, frame imu_link) best effort 200 Hz FC→J /jetowl/status diagnostic_msgs/DiagnosticStatus reliable 2 Hz FC→J /jetowl/motor_rpm std_msgs/Float32MultiArray (NaN = unknown) best effort 50 Hz FC→J /baro/pressure sensor_msgs/FluidPressure [Pa], BMP280, variance 1.44 Pa² (BST-BMP280-DS001 table 8; airframe_config.h section 6.4) → ESKF on the Jetson best effort 25 Hz J→FC /control/attitude_setpoint geometry_msgs/QuaternionStamped best effort 50 Hz J→FC /control/thrust std_msgs/Float64 [N] best effort 50 Hz J→FC /jetowl/arm std_srvs/SetBool (service) — on request J→FC /jetowl/ota/start, /jetowl/ota/apply std_srvs/Trigger (service) — on request, docs/OTA.md

QoS compatibility: a reliable publisher (MPC) → best-effort subscriber (FC) is valid; a best-effort publisher (FC /imu/data) → SensorDataQoS subscriber (ESKF) is valid. A serialised Imu is ≈ 330 B and fits the custom transport's 512 B MTU (best effort does not fragment).

docs.title: 3. Frame conversion (frame_conv.c)
docs.text:
Firmware: NED (world) / FRD (body). ROS (REP-103): ENU / FLU. With q_ab the rotation taking a vector from frame b to frame a, q_ac = q_ab ⊗ q_bc (Diebel 2006 §6):

ENU→NED:  M = [[0,1,0],[1,0,0],[0,0,-1]], det M = +1  →  q_NE = (0, 1/√2, 1/√2, 0)   (π about (1,1,0)/√2)
FRD→FLU:  diag(1,-1,-1)                                →  q_LB = (0, 1, 0, 0)        (π about x)

q_ned_frd = q_NE ⊗ q_enu_flu ⊗ q_LB
q_enu_flu = q_NE⁻¹ ⊗ q_ned_frd ⊗ q_LB⁻¹
ω_flu = diag(1,-1,-1) ω_frd,   a_flu = diag(1,-1,-1) a_frd

tests/host/test_frame_conv.c checks the geometric definition: for every q and v, R(q_enu) v_flu = M_EN R(q_ned) v_frd (error < 1e-5), and a level FC heading north ⇒ ROS yaw = +90°.

docs.title: 4. Command gate cmd_guard (Application/Control)
docs.text:
Command validation: NaN/Inf → rejected; | |q|−1 | > 0.1 → rejected (a corrupted packet or wrong type, not a rounding error); commanded tilt limited to 35° (more than the Jetson MPC's 30°, so valid commands are never clipped); thrust clamped to [0, 4 k_f ω_max²] (actuator saturation).

Pairing the two topics: /control/attitude_setpoint and /control/thrust are published back to back every MPC cycle; a command is submitted only when both are fresh (≤ 0.1 s). If one topic stops ⇒ nothing is submitted ⇒ failsafe.

Link loss (timeout = 0.1 s = 5 MPC cycles; losing 1–2 UDP packets does not trigger it):

Axis Action Loop roll/pitch return to level closed (IMU) yaw hold the heading (twist) of the last valid command closed (IMU) vertical landing profile, see below open — the FC has no altitude sensor in its loop

The open vertical loop is a permitted exception (control-systems §1: no feedback sensor exists in the FC's loop). Model m z̈ = T cos θ − m g; at equilibrium T cos θ = m g, so the weight estimate is W = T_last cos θ_last:

phase 1, 0 ≤ t < t1 = v_d/a_d :  T = W (1 − a_d/g)   ⇒  z̈ = −a_d
phase 2, t ≥ t1               :  T = W              ⇒  ż = −v_d
t_fs = v_d/a_d + max(0, h_max − v_d²/(2a_d)) / v_d     (= 31 s with a_d = 0.5, v_d = 1, h_max = 30 m)

If the link has not returned after 1.2 t_fs ⇒ disarm (a defined safe state). Error bound: a relative error ε in W ⇒ z̈ off by ε g (ε = 5 % ⇒ 0.49 m/s²) — which is why the time limit is required. The profile (0.5 m/s², 1 m/s) matches the "stale odometry" failsafe of ros2_control_system.

Arming conditions: fresh command, valid IMU (sample < 20 ms old), commanded thrust ≤ 20 % of maximum thrust, measured tilt < 20°, TIM loop running. Disarm is always accepted. Automatic disarm: t_fs elapsed, IMU lost in flight, tilt > 75° for 0.25 s (flipped).

tests/host/test_cmd_guard.c: 36 checks (rejection/clamping, ACTIVE→FAILSAFE→ACTIVE, the exact values W(1−a/g) then W, heading hold, disarm after 37.2 s, 32-bit tick-counter wrap-around, every arming refusal reason).

docs.title: 5. Attitude loop attitude_ctrl (Application/Control)
docs.text:
q_e = q̂⁻¹ ⊗ q_sp,   s = sgn(q_e.w),   Ω_i = sat_i(2 s K_i q_e.v_i)

Source: Wie, Weiss & Arapostathis, JGCD 12(3), 1989 — the same law as the simulated attitude loop in Gazebo/ROS2_Hexacopter_Control on the Jetson side.

Proof (assuming an ideal rate loop ω = Ω, valid with a bandwidth separation ≥ 5, Khalil ch. 11): q̇_e = −½ [0,ω] ⊗ q_e ⇒ q̇_e.w = ½ ω·q_e.v. With V = 1 − s q_e.w ≥ 0: V̇ = −½ s Σ Ω_i q_e.v_i. Saturation preserves the sign, so each term s Ω_i q_e.v_i ≥ 0 ⇒ V̇ ≤ 0, zero only when q_e.v = 0 (LaSalle ⇒ convergence; s selects the short arc ⇒ no unwinding). Without saturation: V̇ = −Σ K_i q_e.v_i².

Choice of K: at small angles q_e.v ≈ θ/2 ⇒ Ω = Kθ, L_att = K/s · T_rate(s). K_i = ω_c,rate,i / 5; ω_c,rate is computed exactly from the configured PID + b0 (L_r(jω) = C_pid(jω) b0/(jω), bisection on a log scale) rather than approximated by b0 Kp. With the current sample values: ω_c = 15.78 rad/s ⇒ K = 3.16 s⁻¹ (roll/pitch). With T_rate ≈ ω_c/(s+ω_c): PM = 90° − atan(⅕) = 78.7°.

tests/host/test_attitude_ctrl.c: Ω = Kθ at small angles; q and −q give the same command; saturation preserves the sign; V never increases along a trajectory starting from a 170° error, and converges; with a first-order rate loop (ω_c = 15) overshoot < 1 %; the tilt limit preserves direction and axis; ω_c matches an independent double-precision complex computation (error 1e-4).

docs.title: 6. Network: ETH1 + LAN8742 + lwIP
docs.text:
Item Value Source PHY, interface LAN8742, RMII STM32CubeN6 Projects/NUCLEO-N657X0-Q/Applications/NetXDuo/Nx_UDP_Echo_Client Pins PF4 MDIO, PF5 CLK, PF7 REF_CLK, PF10 CRS_DV, PF11 TX_EN, PF12/13 TXD0/1, PF14/15 RXD0/1, PG11 MDC — AF11 as above (HAL_ETH_MspInit) ETH1 clock source HCLK as above PHY driver Drivers/BSP/Components/lan8742 github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32-lan8742 (BSD-3) Stack lwIP STABLE-2_2_1, FreeRTOS sys_arch, socket API github.com/lwip-tcpip/lwip (BSD) Addresses FC 192.168.10.2/24, agent 192.168.10.1:8888, static IP Application/Network/Inc/net_config.h

TrustZone/RIF (AppliSecure/Core/Src/main.c, JetOwl_EthernetToNonSecure, inside USER CODE): ETH1 clock, RISC ETH1 = NSEC, RIMC master ETH1 = NSEC (DMA issues NS transactions), the 10 RMII pins = NSEC, NVIC_SetTargetState(ETH1_IRQn). Without this step a non-secure access to ETH1 raises an IAC/fault.

Cache: the NS D-cache is enabled and the HAL ETH driver does not maintain the descriptor cache. The RX/TX descriptors + 12 RX buffers live in one static block aligned to 32 B, sized to a multiple of 32 and declared non-cacheable through MPU_NS region 0 (ARMv8-M allows 32 B regions). TX buffers are lwIP pbufs ⇒ SCB_CleanDCache_by_Addr before DMA.

Interrupts: ETH1 priority 7 ≥ configLIBRARY_MAX_SYSCALL_INTERRUPT_PRIORITY (5) — required for the ISR to call xSemaphoreGiveFromISR.

Transport: net_if.c replaces the original udp_transport.c (which fixed port 8888 at both ends and called recv(MSG_WAITALL) on a datagram socket). Framing is disabled (UDP is packet-oriented).

docs.title: 7. Timestamps
docs.text: header.stamp = t0 + t_sample: t_sample is the instant the chip sampled (INT pin + SH-2 time field, CONTROL_DESIGN.md §1.5) on the control loop's µs clock; t0 comes from rmw_uros_sync_session (agent clock = Jetson clock) and is re-synchronised every 10 s. Intervals between stamps are exact to the µs; the absolute origin is off by at most ~1 ms (the micro-ROS clock follows the FreeRTOS tick) — a constant offset between two synchronisations. Latency budget of the set-point path: MPC period 20 ms + UDP/agent < 1 ms (direct 100 Mbit/s link) + 250 Hz sampling ≤ 4 ms; the MPC already budgets 40 ms for the attitude loop.

docs.title: 8. Build
docs.text:
make microros              # first time: builds libmicroros.a in docker (micro_ros_static_library_builder:humble)
make                       # AppliSecure → AppliNonSecure (mandatory order)
make -C Makefile nonsecure MICROROS=0   # network-less build
make agent                 # runs the micro-ROS agent (docker) on the Jetson/host
  • The repository root contains a CubeMX-generated directory Makefile/, so the entry point is GNUmakefile (GNU make reads it first).
  • The builder runs make print_cflags at the repository root; print_cflags prints exactly the firmware's ABI flags (-mcpu=cortex-m55 -mthumb -mfpu=fpv5-d16 -mfloat-abi=hard …) — the library and the firmware must share the ABI.
  • Makefile/AppliSecure writes the import library to Makefile/AppliSecure/build/secure_nsclib.o and Makefile/AppliNonSecure links that exact file. It deliberately does not write Secure_nsclib/secure_nsclib.o (used by the CMake build): sharing one file between the two builds could make the NS image link against the veneers of a secure image other than the one flashed.
  • Measured results: AppliSecure ROM 14.0 KB / RAM 13.1 KB; AppliNonSecure (micro-ROS) ROM 181.6 KB / 511 KB, RAM 224.2 KB / 512 KB (two 64 KB heaps: FreeRTOS + micro-ROS).

docs.title: Pre-existing defects found during integration
