docs.title: MIPI CSI-2 camera on FreeRTOS: STM32N655 + IMX335
docs.text:
Source

Snapshot of docs/camera/CAMERA_CSI_RTOS.md from TNG-Blue/JetOwl_Vision at commit 09cd68c (submodule Microcontroller/JetOwl_Vision). Regenerate with Scripts/mkdocs_hooks/snapshot_submodules.py after updating the submodule.

This document describes the Appli/Camera module: it reads a MIPI CSI-2 camera through the CSI host and DCMIPP of the STM32N655, runs on FreeRTOS (CMSIS-RTOS2), and closes auto-exposure (AE) and auto-white-balance (AWB) loops. Every formula has a reference (section 8) and is verified by unit tests (tests/host) and an analysis script (logloop_analysis.py).

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
+------------------------- feedback loop (every frame) ------------------------+
                |                                                                              |
 IMX335 --CSI-2 2 lane RAW10--> CSI host --> DCMIPP pipe1 ISP:                                 |
  ^  (I2C: exposure, gain)                   black level -> WB gain -> demosaic -> [statistics]|
  |                                          -> downsize 2592x1944→640x480 -> gamma -> RGB565 |
  |                                                  |                         |              |
  |                                                  | AXI                     | frame IRQ    |
  |                                                  v                         v              |
  |                                          frame buffers (AXISRAM3..6)   camera thread      |
  |                                                  ^                     (High priority)    |
  |                                                  |                         |              |
  |                                  CAM_AcquireFrame/ReleaseFrame      measure R̄,Ḡ,B̄ ------+
  |                                          (consumer thread)                 |
  |                                                                            v
  +-------------------- actuator <-- quantisation <-- controller <-- Kalman (estimation)
File Role Camera/Inc/camera_conf.h Board pins, sensor, pipeline, control-loop parameters Camera/Src/camera.c DCMIPP/CSI/ISP, IRQ, buffer ring, camera thread, API Camera/Src/camera_io.c Sensor I2C, EN/NRST pins, power-up sequence Camera/Src/cam_i2c_timing.c Computes the TIMINGR register from the I2C standard (section 6) Camera/Src/cam_logloop.c Kalman filter + common control law (section 4) Camera/Src/cam_isp_ctrl.c AE, AWB, actuator quantisation (sections 4, 5) Drivers/BSP/Components/imx335 ST's IMX335 driver (stm32-imx335 v1.3.2, BSD-3) Drivers/STM32N6xx_HAL_Driver/*dcmipp*, *i2c* ST HAL v1.4.0, the same version as the existing HAL

Application API (camera.h):

CAM_WaitReady(timeout_ms);                 // wait until the camera is streaming
CAM_AcquireFrame(&frame, timeout_ms);      // take the newest frame, RGB565 640x480
/* ... use frame.data (AI, display) ... */
CAM_ReleaseFrame(&frame);                  // return the buffer
CAM_GetStatus(&st);                        // frame, drop and error counts, exposure, gain

defaultTask in app_freertos.c is an example consumer thread.

docs.title: 2. Data path and hardware configuration
docs.text:
• Clocks (PLL1 = 64 MHz / 2 × 25 = 800 MHz, configured by the FSBL): DCMIPP = IC17 = 800/4 = 200 MHz (matches RCC.DCMIPPFreq_Value in the .ioc), CSI D-PHY reference = IC18 = 800/40 = 20 MHz.
  • CSI-2: 2 lanes, no lane swap, D-PHY band DCMIPP_CSI_PHY_BT_1600, VC0, data type RAW10 (0x2B): the same IMX335 configuration as ST's camera middleware.
  • Downsize (RM0486, same formula as CMW_UTILS_get_down_config): \(\text{ratio} = \lfloor 8192 \cdot W_{in}/W_{out} \rfloor = 33177\), \(\text{div} = \lfloor (1024\cdot 8192 - 1)/\text{ratio} \rfloor = 252\). HAL constraints: \(\text{ratio} \le 65535\), \(128 \le \text{div} \le 1023\); a ratio < 8 is checked with #error at compile time.
  • Buffers: CAM_NUM_BUFFERS × 614 400 B at 0x34200000 (AXISRAM3..6, secure alias). These banks are powered down after reset; cam_axisram_enable() enables their clocks and clears SRAMSD. The linker script does not use this region. An #error fires if the buffers exceed 1 792 KiB.
  • RIF: the DCMIPP is a bus master (RIMC CID1, secure, privileged); the DCMIPP, CSI and I2C1 slaves are set secure/privileged (CAM_RIF_Config(), called from SystemIsolation_Config).
  • Cache: the DCMIPP writes to RAM without going through the D-cache, so CAM_AcquireFrame() invalidates the buffer region when the D-cache is enabled.

docs.title: 3. RTOS synchronisation and buffer protocol
docs.text:
RTOS objects are statically allocated (the project's heap_5 has only 8 KiB):

  • Pipe1 frame ISR → osThreadFlagsSet(camera, FRAME): wakes the AE/AWB loop.
  • ISR → osSemaphoreRelease(frame_sem) (binary): signals a new frame to the consumer thread.
  • The consumer thread changes buffer state inside taskENTER_CRITICAL(). The critical section masks the DCMIPP IRQ because its priority is 6, not higher than configLIBRARY_MAX_SYSCALL_INTERRUPT_PRIORITY = 5, so it is blocked by BASEPRI.

Invariant: the DCMIPP never writes into a buffer held by the consumer thread.

Proof. The state consists of capture (the buffer the DCMIPP is writing), ready (the newest complete frame) and held (the set of buffers being held). Only the ISR changes capture, and before changing it, it picks next ∉ held ∪ {capture}. If no such buffer exists, capture is kept and the frame is dropped (dropped++). The consumer thread only adds the element ready to held, and ready ≠ capture because the ISR sets ready = done and capture = next ≠ done in the same run. The two state changes are mutually exclusive thanks to the critical section. Therefore capture ∉ held always holds. The new address is a shadow register latched at the next frame. At 30 fps the IMX335's vertical blanking is (4500 − 1944) lines × 7.4 µs ≈ 18 ms, far longer than the ISR latency. ∎

With 2 buffers, if the consumer holds a buffer for longer than one frame, new frames are dropped (never torn). Increase CAM_NUM_BUFFERS if memory allows.

docs.title: 4. Log-domain control loop: filter → estimation → control → actuator → feedback
4.1 Model
docs.text:
A CMOS sensor is linear below saturation. The measured mean brightness is \(y = L\cdot t\cdot g\), where \(L\) is the scene luminance, \(t\) the exposure time and \(g\) the gain. Taking the logarithm turns the product into a sum:

\[z_k = u_{k-D} + d_k + v_k,\qquad u=\ln(t\,g),\; d=\ln L,\; v_k\sim\mathcal N(0,R)\]

\(D\) is the number of frames between writing the actuator and the statistics reflecting that value (IMX335: \(D=3\), equal to sensorDelay in ST's tuning; ISP registers: \(D=1\)). The changing scene is modelled as a random walk: \(d_{k+1} = d_k + w_k\), \(w_k\sim\mathcal N(0,Q)\).

AWB has exactly this form. The green ISP gain is held at 1 and measured after demosaicing: \(\ln(\bar R/\bar G) = \ln g_R + \ln(R_{raw}/G_{raw})\). So \(u=\ln g_R\) and \(d\) is the colour of the illuminant. All three loops (AE, AWB-R, AWB-B) therefore share CAM_LogLoop_t.

Decoupling. AE measures \(\bar G\), which does not depend on the AWB gains (G gain = 1). The ratio \(\bar R/\bar G\) does not depend on \(t\,g\) in the linear region. The interaction matrix is therefore diagonal, and each loop's stability can be analysed separately.

docs.title: 4.2 Kalman filter (estimating \(d\))
docs.text:
With \(u_{k-D}\) known (the value actually written, stored in a ring buffer), the measurement is \(\tilde z_k = z_k - u_{k-D} = d_k + v_k\). Scalar Kalman filter:

\[P^-_k = P_{k-1}+Q,\quad K_k=\frac{P^-_k}{P^-_k+R},\quad \hat d_k=\hat d_{k-1}+K_k(\tilde z_k-\hat d_{k-1}),\quad P_k=(1-K_k)P^-_k\]

The fixed point of the Riccati equation, \(P^-=(1-K)P^- + Q\), gives \(P^{-2} - QP^- - QR = 0\), hence

\[P^-_\infty=\frac{Q+\sqrt{Q^2+4QR}}{2},\qquad K_\infty=\frac{P^-_\infty}{P^-_\infty+R}\in(0,1).\]

The code initialises at \(P_\infty\), so the system is LTI from the first frame and the proofs below apply without considering a transient. AE (\(Q=2.5\cdot10^{-3}\), \(R=10^{-2}\)) gives \(K_\infty = 0.3904\). AWB (\(Q=10^{-3}\), \(R=10^{-2}\)) gives \(K_\infty=0.2702\). The test test_riccati compares this closed-form solution with the Riccati iteration.

docs.title: 4.3 Control law (certainty equivalence)
docs.text:
The plant has the form \(z=u+d\), so the input that reaches the set-point is \(u_k = z_{ref} - \hat d_k\). The command is then rate-limited \(|u_k-u_{k-1}|\le\Delta\) (AE: \(\Delta=\ln 2\) per frame), saturated to \([u_{min},u_{max}]\) and quantised (4.6).

No windup. The estimator uses the applied \(u\) (after saturation and quantisation). Hence \(\tilde z_k = d_k+v_k\) holds for every \(u\): no integral of the control error accumulates while the actuator is saturated.

docs.title: 4.4 Stability and steady-state error
docs.text:
Consider a plant with model errors: a gain \(\alpha\) (pixel saturation, non-linearity) and a true delay \(D_p\) different from the model delay \(D_m\): \(z_k=\alpha u_{k-D_p}+d\). Substituting \(u=z_{ref}-\hat d\) into the steady-state filter, the homogeneous part gives the characteristic polynomial

\[\chi(\lambda)=\lambda^N-(1-K)\lambda^{N-1}+K\alpha\,\lambda^{N-D_p}-K\,\lambda^{N-D_m},\quad N=\max(D_p,D_m).\]

When \(D_p=D_m=D\): \(\chi(\lambda)=\lambda^{D}-(1-K)\lambda^{D-1}+K(\alpha-1)\).

  • \(D=1\): \(\lambda=1-K\alpha\), stable if and only if \(0<\alpha<2/K\).
  • \(D=2\): Jury's criterion for \(\lambda^2+a_1\lambda+a_0\) with \(a_1=-(1-K)\), \(a_0=K(\alpha-1)\): \(|a_0|<1\), \(1+a_1+a_0=K\alpha>0\), \(1-a_1+a_0=2-2K+K\alpha>0\). Hence stable if and only if \(0<\alpha<1+1/K\).
  • \(D\ge3\): checked with the Schur–Cohn criterion (script).

Zero steady-state error for every \(\alpha\) in the stability region. At equilibrium, \(\hat d = d+(\alpha-1)(z_{ref}-\hat d)\), so \(\alpha\hat d = d+(\alpha-1)z_{ref}\) and \(z=\alpha(z_{ref}-\hat d)+d=z_{ref}\). The random walk in the model is equivalent to an integrator, so the system has integral action.

Results of python3 docs/camera/logloop_analysis.py. The analytical and Schur–Cohn margins agree:

Loop \(K_\infty\) \(D=1\) \(D=2\) \(D=3\) AE 0.3904 \(\alpha<5.12\) (theory 5.123) \(\alpha<3.56\) (theory 3.562) \(\alpha<2.895\) AWB 0.2702 \(\alpha<7.40\) \(\alpha<4.70\) \(\alpha<3.585\)

Delay error for AE (\(D_m=3\)): a true delay of 1…4 frames is still stable for \(\alpha\in(0;\,2.23]\) and beyond. The nominal model is \(\alpha=1\), so the gain margin is more than a factor of 2.

docs.title: 4.5 Saturated (censored) measurements
docs.text:
When \(\bar G\ge Y_{clip}\) (240), we only know that \(z\ge\ln Y_{clip}\), i.e. \(d\ge \ln Y_{clip}-u_{k-D}\); when \(\bar G\le Y_{floor}\), the opposite. A normal Kalman update would then produce a biased estimate. The code projects \(\hat d\) onto the feasible set:

\[\hat d \leftarrow \max\bigl(\hat d,\ \ln Y_{clip}-u_{k-D}\bigr)\]

The covariance only receives the time update, and at the first unsaturated sample \(\hat d\) is re-initialised to \(z-u_{k-D}\).

No overshoot when the model is exact (\(\alpha=1\), \(D_p=D_m\), constant \(d\)). Assume \(\hat d\le d\) beforehand. This holds right after a step up in brightness, since \(\hat d\) still carries the dark scene's value. The projection bound satisfies \(\ln Y_{clip}-u_{k-D}\le d\), so \(\max(\hat d,\text{bound})\le d\) and the inequality is preserved. Then \(u=z_{ref}-\hat d\ge z_{ref}-d\); the rate limit only makes \(u\) decrease more slowly, so \(z=u+d\ge z_{ref}\). Throughout the saturated phase the image approaches the set-point from the bright side and is never driven too dark. The residual deviation in simulation (≈ 8 %) comes from measurement noise and quantisation. Simulation (dark → very bright scene, \(D=3\)): the ±20 % settling time drops from 19 to 13 frames. Trade-off: when \(\alpha>1\) or the true delay exceeds the model delay, the lower bound is no longer tight, so the temporary darkening can be larger (up to −50 % at \(\alpha=1.5\)). The stability region is unchanged because the projection acts only during saturation.

docs.title: 4.6 AE actuator allocation and quantisation
docs.text:
\(E=e^u\) [µs × gain]. Exposure time is preferred (less noisy than gain): \(t=\mathrm{clamp}(E, 7, t_{max})\), line count \(n=\lfloor t/7\rfloor\), \(t_q=7n\). The remainder \(E/t_q\ge1\) goes into the gain, rounded to the IMX335's 0.3 dB step (72 dB maximum). The value of \(u\) written to the estimator is \(\ln(t_q\,g_q)\).

\(t_{max} = (4500-9)\cdot 7 = 31\,437\) µs. ST's driver computes SHR0 = VMAX − t/7 and requires SHR0 ≥ 9. A larger \(t\) makes the unsigned subtraction wrap around (the driver's own 33 266 µs exceeds this limit). The line constant is 7 µs, not 7.407 µs, because the driver uses (uint32_t)IMX335_1H_PERIOD_USEC. This fixed multiplicative error only adds a constant to \(d\), so the filter absorbs it.

docs.title: 4.7 AWB (gray world)
docs.text: Set-point \(z_{ref}=0\), i.e. \(\bar R=\bar G=\bar B\) after the gains. Updates happen only when \(10\le\bar G\le200\) (linear region, no dark noise, no clipping). Outside that range the loop only performs the time update (gains held). Gains are bounded to \([1;\,3.5]\), the envelope of ST's IMX335 calibration points from 2800 K to 6650 K (R 1.24…2.44; B 1.43…2.82) plus a margin. This constraint keeps gray world from drifting on monochromatic scenes. The ISP gain is encoded as \(g = \text{MULT}/128\cdot 2^{\text{SHF}}\), with an error ≤ ½ LSB (≤ 0.39 % for \(g\ge1\)).

docs.title: 5. Why this estimator + controller instead of PID
docs.text: In the log domain the plant is a unit gain plus a pure delay. With Gaussian noise and a random-walk scene, the Kalman filter is the optimal linear (MMSE) estimator. The certainty-equivalence law separates from the estimator (separation principle), and because the delay \(D\) is compensated explicitly through the history of \(u\) (equivalent to a Smith predictor), the loop gain is not limited by the delay when the model is exact. A PI on the image error would have to reduce its gain with \(D\) to stay stable and would need an additional anti-windup mechanism. Here the absence of windup follows from the structure (section 4.3).

docs.title: 6. I2C timing (CAM_IO_I2C_ComputeTiming)
docs.text:
The TIMINGR register is computed from the actual I2C kernel clock (HAL_RCCEx_GetPeriphCLKFreq) instead of a "magic" constant. For PRESC = 0…15 the first value satisfying every constraint is selected (UM10204 table 10, RM0486 formulas, analog filter on, \(t_{AF}\in[50,260]\) ns):

  • \((SCLDEL+1)t_{PRESC}\ge t_r+t_{SU;DAT}\)
  • \(t_f+t_{HD;DAT,min}-t_{AF,min}-3t_{I2CCLK}\le SDADEL\cdot t_{PRESC}\le t_{VD;DAT}-t_r-t_{AF,max}-4t_{I2CCLK}\)
  • \((SCLL+1)t_{PRESC}\ge t_{LOW}\), \((SCLH+1)t_{PRESC}\ge t_{HIGH}\), \((SCLL+SCLH+2)t_{PRESC}+2(t_{AF,min}+2t_{I2CCLK})\ge 1/f_{SCL}\), so \(f_{SCL}\) never exceeds the target.

The test decodes TIMINGR at 16…200 MHz × 100/400 kHz and checks each inequality. It also confirms that 400 MHz at 100 kHz has no solution, because \(t_{PRESC}\le40\) ns while \(t_{SCLDEL}\) needs ≥ 78 ns per step.

docs.title: 7. Testing
docs.text:
make -C tests/host                     # 3047 checks: Riccati, stability, saturation,
                                       # quantisation, AE+AWB simulation, I2C timing
python3 docs/camera/logloop_analysis.py  # Schur–Cohn stability region + non-linear simulation

The firmware has been cross-compiled with arm-none-eabi-gcc 13.2 in Debug and Release (ROM 86 KB / 46 KB, RAM 12 KB, frame buffers outside). CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) re-runs both commands above and builds the FSBL + Appli on every push/PR. X-CUBE-AI/App is currently a placeholder without a model: the header no longer declares the ai_* buffers, and X-CUBE-AI will regenerate them when a model is added in CubeMX.

docs.title: To do on the real board
docs.text:
1. Check every [BOARD] item in camera_conf.h against the JetOwl schematic (I2C1 PH9/PC1, EN = PD2, NRST = PC8 are the defaults of the STM32N6570-DK + MB1854 module).
  2. If the sensor is not an IMX335, replace the driver and the sensor constants. The control loop stays the same; only \(D\) needs to be measured again.
  3. Measure the real delay \(D\) by applying an exposure step and counting the frames until \(\bar G\) changes, then set CAM_AE_DELAY. Per 4.4, an error of ±1 frame is still stable.

docs.title: micro-ROS over UDP/Ethernet: JetOwl_Vision → Jetson (Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL)
docs.text:
Source

Snapshot of docs/network/MICROROS_ETHERNET.md from TNG-Blue/JetOwl_Vision at commit 09cd68c (submodule Microcontroller/JetOwl_Vision). Regenerate with Scripts/mkdocs_hooks/snapshot_submodules.py after updating the submodule.

This document describes what has been built, linked and host-tested in the repository, and separates out what is not yet verified on hardware (section 8). Read section 8 before flashing a board.

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
STM32N655 — Appli (secure, FreeRTOS)                              Jetson Orin (ROS 2 Humble)
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐                ┌──────────────────────────────┐
 │ IMX335 ─CSI-2─▶ DCMIPP pipe 1 ─▶ RGB565 640×480│                │ micro_ros_agent udp4 :8888   │
 │   ▲ closed AE/AWB (cam_isp_ctrl, "cam" thread,│                │   (shared with JetOwl FC)    │
 │   │  priority 40, ISP statistics → sensor I2C) │                │             │ DDS            │
 │   └──────── feedback: next frame's statistics ─│                │             ▼                │
 │                                               │                │ jetowl_bridge (vision_mcu):  │
 │ defaultTask: CAM_AcquireFrame                 │                │  checks image, rate, latency,│
 │   └▶ UrosApp_OfferFrame (5 Hz):               │                │  lost samples → /diagnostics  │
 │       D×D box filter → decimation D → rgb8    │                │  valid image → camera/image   │
 │ "uros" task (10 ms): reliable rcl_publish ────┼── UDP 1472 B ─▶│                              │
 │ lwIP 2.2.1 ← ethernetif ← ETH1 + LAN8742 RMII  │  192.168.10.0/24│                              │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘                └──────────────────────────────┘

Principle: the only control loop on this MCU is AE/AWB, and it is always closed on the ISP statistics (docs/camera/CAMERA_CSI_RTOS.md). The micro-ROS path is a best-effort output — every network thread has a lower priority than the camera thread (lwipopts.h): camera 40 > eth_rx 34 > tcpip 33 > uros 24. Losing the network never opens a loop; it only means the Jetson receives no images.

docs.title: 2. Topic contract
docs.text:
Must match Source/ROS2_JetOwl_Bridge/include/ros2_jetowl_bridge/vision_mcu.hpp on the Jetson.

Direction Name Type QoS Rate V→J /jetowl_vision/image_preview sensor_msgs/Image, rgb8 160×120 (or mono8), frame jetowl_vision_optical_frame reliable 5 Hz V→J /jetowl_vision/status diagnostic_msgs/DiagnosticStatus reliable 1 Hz

Keys of /jetowl_vision/status: streaming, frames, fps, dropped, errors, ctrl_steps, exposure_us, gain_db, mean_r/g/b, preview_made, preview_sent, preview_pub_errors, preview_busy_skips, preview_errors, preview_last_seq, pub_time_ms, pub_time_ms_max, status_pub_errors, eth_rx_drops, uptime_s. Levels: ERROR = camera failure, WARN = camera starting / no new frame within 1 s, OK otherwise.

Why reliable: XRCE-DDS fragments a sample larger than the MTU only on a reliable stream (rmw_microxrcedds humble, src/rmw_publish.c: uxr_prepare_output_stream_fragmented + flush_session). A reliable publisher is QoS-compatible with both reliable and best-effort subscribers.

Timestamps: stamp = t0 + tick_ms, tick_ms = the HAL tick in the DCMIPP end-of-frame interrupt, t0 from rmw_uros_sync_session (agent clock = Jetson clock), re-synchronised every 10 s. Resolution 1 ms; the stamp is the end of the frame, later than the exposure centre by ≈ the sensor read-out time + t_exp/2.

docs.title: 3. Network
docs.text: Item Value Source Addresses Vision 192.168.10.3/24, MAC 00:80:E1:4A:4F:02; agent 192.168.10.1:8888 Appli/Network/Inc/net_config.h Topology Switch: Jetson + JetOwl FC (.2) + JetOwl Vision (.3); one agent serves both MCUs (one XRCE session per client) PHY, pins LAN8742 RMII, PF⅘/7/10–15 + PG11, AF11 — [BOARD], see section 8 STM32CubeN6 NUCLEO-N657X0-Q/.../Nx_UDP_Echo_Client Stack lwIP STABLE-2_2_1, FreeRTOS sys_arch, socket API, static IP same as JetOwl_FlightControl TrustZone/RIF Appli runs secure: ETH1 slave + RIMC master = SEC, PRIV (as for the DCMIPP), pins secure (default) ethernetif_rif_config() Interrupts ETH1 priority 7 ≥ configLIBRARY_MAX_SYSCALL_INTERRUPT_PRIORITY (5), below the DCMIPP (6) net_config.h Cache descriptors + RX buffers in one 32 B-aligned block, MPU non-cacheable; TX cleans the D-cache before DMA ethernetif.c

docs.title: 4. Preview image — anti-aliasing filter and decimation
docs.text:
Chain: RGB565 frame (sensor → ISP with calibrated black level/WB/gamma) → D×D box filter → decimation by D → 8-bit quantisation (Appli/Camera/Src/cam_preview.c, pure C, tested on the host).

  • Down-sampling requires low-pass filtering first (Oppenheim & Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed., §4.6): X_d(e^{jω}) = (1/D) Σ_k X(e^{j(ω−2πk)/D}) — every component at ω = 2πk/D folds onto DC.
  • The box filter y[m,n] = D⁻² Σ_{i,j<D} x[Dm+i, Dn+j] has the separable response |H(ω)| = |sin(Dω/2) / (D sin(ω/2))|: zeros exactly at ω = 2πk/D, DC gain = 1. The largest gain beyond the first zero (2π/D < ω ≤ π): −11.3 dB for D = 4, −12.8 dB for D = 8, → −13.3 dB (single-stage CIC, Hogenauer, IEEE TASSP 29(2), 1981). It is not an ideal filter; residual aliasing is bounded by that side-lobe level — sufficient for a monitoring image, not for photometric measurement.
  • Quantisation: the ideal 8-bit value of a c-bit code k is 255k/(2^c−1); averaging and the linear map commute, so each output is computed from an exact integer sum with one rounding: c8 = ⌊(2·255·S + D²(2^c−1)) / (2D²(2^c−1))⌋ ⇒ error ≤ 0.5 LSB.
  • mono8 = BT.601 luma on gamma-encoded R'G'B' (ITU-R BT.601-7 §2.5.1: Y' = 0.299R' + 0.587G' + 0.114B'), also with a single rounding (64-bit integers).

Verification (make -C tests/host, test_cam_preview.c, 177 checks; gcc, clang, ASan+UBSan): all 65 536 RGB565 codes map exactly to round(255k/(2^c−1)); luma error ≤ 0.5 LSB; a constant image is preserved for every D = 1…8 (DC gain = 1); every pattern periodic in D (including the Nyquist checkerboard with D = 2) yields exactly its constant mean (zeros at 2πk/D); random frames: every channel and the luma are within 0.5 LSB of the exact mean; unaligned sources / padded pitch give the same result.

Phase-locked preview schedule (uros_app.c): image k is taken from the first camera frame with tick ≥ kT (t_{k+1} = t_k + T, T = 200 ms), not "previous image tick + T" — the latter makes the period drift up to a multiple of the frame period (7 frames = 233 ms ⇒ 4.3 Hz at 30 fps). The lag behind the grid is 0 ≤ j < one frame period (33 ms), so the long-term rate is exactly 5 Hz and the Jetson side counts lost images exactly, m = round(Δt/T) − 1, when |j₂ − j₁| < T/2 (vision_mcu.hpp). More than one period late (just reconnected to the agent) ⇒ the grid is re-anchored; no burst of catch-up images.

Buffer hand-over (uros_app.c): one 57 600 B buffer whose FREE/WRITING/READY/SENDING state changes inside a critical section of a few instructions. defaultTask (the only consumer of CAM_AcquireFrame) filters a frame when the 200 ms period is due and the buffer is not SENDING; the uros task sends a READY image. No long-held locks, no allocation; an image being sent is never overwritten (counted in preview_busy_skips).

docs.title: 5. Bandwidth budget and send time
docs.text:
Library configuration (microros_static_library/library_generation/colcon.meta, changed from the upstream defaults): UCLIENT_CUSTOM_TRANSPORT_MTU = 1472 (= 1500 − 20 IP − 8 UDP: no IP fragmentation), RMW_UXRCE_STREAM_HISTORY_OUTPUT = 16 (= the agent's default UAGENT_CONFIG_RELIABLE_STREAM_DEPTH), …_INPUT = 4. The agent accepts datagrams up to UAGENT_SERVER_BUFFER_SIZE = 65535 B and uses the MTU the client sends in CREATE_CLIENT (ProxyClient.cpp).

Quantity Value rgb8 160×120 image payload 57 600 B (+ ≈ 70 B of CDR Image fields) XRCE fragments (≈ 12 B header per fragment) N = ⌈57 670 / 1460⌉ = 40 Windows (16 fragments per window) 3 (16 + 16 + 8) Wire time per fragment 1538 B·8 / 100 Mbit/s = 123 µs (incl. Ethernet header, FCS, preamble, IFG) Wire time per image 40 × 123 µs = 4.9 ms Link load at 5 Hz 40·1538·8·5 = 2.46 Mbit/s = 2.5 % of 100 Mbit/s

Blocking-time model of rcl_publish: the agent sends an ACKNACK after every reliable message it receives (Processor.cpp), so each window costs 16·t_wire + RTT: T_pub ≈ N·(t_wire + t_sw) + ⌈N/16⌉·RTT. With RTT < 1 ms on a direct link, T_pub is about 5–10 ms ≪ the 200 ms period (the uros task is busy < 5 % of the time). t_sw (the lwIP/HAL cost per packet) is not yet measured — which is why the firmware reports pub_time_ms and pub_time_ms_max in its status, for verification on the bench. One lost packet triggers the heartbeat path: UXR_CONFIG_MIN_HEARTBEAT_TIME_INTERVAL = 100 ms, so an image with a lost packet costs ≥ 100 ms more (still < the 1 s RMW_UXRCE_PUBLISH_RELIABLE_TIMEOUT).

Memory (measured with arm-none-eabi-size, Debug -Og): Appli ROM 181.4 KB / 511 KB, RAM 324.9 KB / 1536 KB (two 64 KB heaps: FreeRTOS + micro-ROS; 57.6 KB preview buffer; XRCE output buffer 1472 × 16 B). Without micro-ROS: ROM 54.8 KB, RAM 20.5 KB.

docs.title: 6. Build
docs.text:
make microros              # first time: builds libmicroros.a in docker (micro_ros_static_library_builder:humble)
make                       # FSBL + Appli (micro-ROS enabled)
make appli MICROROS=0      # network-less build
make agent                 # micro-ROS agent (docker) on the Jetson/host — one agent for both FC and Vision
  • The repository root contains a directory Makefile/, so the entry point is GNUmakefile. The builder runs make print_cflags at the repository root, which prints exactly the firmware's ABI flags (-mcpu=cortex-m55 -mthumb -mfpu=fpv5-d16 -mfloat-abi=hard …).
  • Makefile/common.mk comes from JetOwl_FlightControl: .o files are named after their source path (lwIP, FreeRTOS and the HAL have files with the same name).
  • CMake still works: cd Appli && cmake --preset Debug -DJETOWL_WITH_MICROROS=ON (OFF by default; CI builds CMake without micro-ROS, and a separate job builds the Makefile with micro-ROS).

docs.title: 7. Jetson side
docs.text:
ros2_jetowl_bridge (vision_mcu link) — see Source/ROS2_JetOwl_Bridge/README.md:

ros2 launch ros2_jetowl_bridge jetowl_bridge.launch.py vision_mcu:=true            # + FC (default)
ros2 launch ros2_jetowl_bridge jetowl_bridge.launch.py fc:=false vision_mcu:=true  # camera only

docs.title: 8. Not yet verified / open items
docs.text:
• Not yet run on hardware. In order: ping 192.168.10.3 → the agent sees a second session → ros2 topic hz /jetowl_vision/image_preview → read pub_time_ms_max to verify section 5.
  • [BOARD] PHY and RMII pins currently follow the NUCLEO-N657X0-Q (LAN8742). The STM32N6570-DK board (the camera module's default in camera_conf.h) uses a different PHY over RGMII — that would require a different PHY driver and MediaInterface configuration, not just different pins. Check the JetOwl_Vision schematic before flashing.
  • ETH1 is not enabled in the .ioc (CubeMX) yet. HAL_ETH_MODULE_ENABLED is defined by a compile flag so that stm32n6xx_hal_conf.h need not be edited; when ETH1 is enabled in CubeMX, define JETOWL_ETH_MSP_FROM_CUBEMX / JETOWL_ETH_HANDLE_FROM_CUBEMX to use the MSP/handle generated by CubeMX.
  • MPU region 0 is used by ethernetif.c for the DMA block; if CubeMX configures the MPU later, the two must be merged.
  • While a frame is held for filtering (~a few ms every 200 ms) the DCMIPP may have to drop a frame if the other buffer is ready (two buffers) — counted in dropped; the AE/AWB loop does not depend on the frame buffers.

docs.title: Coexistence
docs.text: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on the ground controller share the 2.4 GHz band with the LoRa uplink; they are locked while the aircraft is armed (UI §5). On the vehicle the Ethernet links are wired and do not share spectrum with the RC link.

docs.title: Jetson Orin Nano Super
docs.text: The project targets the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit (8 GB) exclusively. CUDA code is compiled for compute capability 8.7 (sm_87); the original Jetson Nano cannot run JetPack 6 or ROS 2 Humble natively and is not supported.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Flash JetPack 6.2 or newer with NVIDIA SDK Manager or the SD-card image. JetPack 6.2 is the release that enables the Super power modes on the Orin Nano.
  2. Prefer an NVMe SSD over a microSD card for the root file system: container images, TensorRT engines and ROS bags are large and write-intensive.
  3. Install ROS 2 Humble and the build tools — see Installation.
  4. Configure the Ethernet address of the robot network (192.168.10.1/24 on the master board) — see Kubernetes for the netplan settings used by the cluster.

docs.title: Power modes
docs.text:
Select the mode with nvpmodel and lock the clocks for benchmarking with jetson_clocks:

sudo nvpmodel -q                 # current mode
sudo nvpmodel -m <id>            # select a mode (ids are listed in /etc/nvpmodel.conf)
sudo jetson_clocks               # pin clocks to the mode's maximum (benchmarks only)
tegrastats                       # live CPU/GPU load, memory, temperatures, rail power

Measure timing-sensitive code (detector latency, MPPI, SLAM) in the power mode the vehicle will fly with, and record the mode next to the result. See Power.

docs.title: OpenMV RT1062 — API Audit & Fix Report
docs.text: Files audited: Microcontroller/OpenMV/OpenMV_RT1062.py (§2–6) and Source/ROS2_Microcontroller/ (§7) Reference: OpenMV firmware v5.0.0 API docs (MicroPython v1.28) — https://docs.openmv.io/v5.0.0/ Verdict of the original file: ❌ it does not run. It aborts during the import block, before a single frame is captured, and it never brings the Ethernet interface up.

docs.title: 1. Verdict summary
docs.text: Question Answer Does it use the current OpenMV API? No. The script targets the tf module and the legacy net.detect() signature, both removed in firmware v4.5.6. Does the code run once flashed? No. import _thread and import urequests both raise ImportError at load time; tf.load() no longer exists either. Does it use the Ethernet shield? No. network is imported but network.LAN() is never constructed, so the PHY is never brought up and no socket can ever connect. It also opened a TCP client, while the ROS2 node is also a client — nobody was listening.

docs.title: 2. Blocking defects (script cannot start)
docs.text:
# Line (original) Defect Evidence B1 30 import _thread — threading is disabled in the OpenMV fork of MicroPython. _thread is not in the v5.0.0 module index. Module-level _thread.allocate_lock() therefore kills the script at import. OpenMV forum, maintainer: "Threading is disabled in our fork." B2 31 import urequests — the module is named requests; there is no urequests. requests — HTTP client B3 32–33 uhashlib / ubinascii — the u-prefixed aliases are gone; use hashlib / binascii. Python Module Index B4 25, 165 import tf + tf.load(path, load_to_fb=True) — the tf C module was replaced by the ml package in v4.5.6; tf.load, detect(), segment() and classification() were removed. load_to_fb was then removed from ml.Model in v5.0.0. v4.5.6 changelog, v5.0.0 changelog

Any one of B1–B4 is fatal on its own.

docs.title: 3. Runtime defects (would fail even after the imports were fixed)
docs.text: # Line Defect Correct API R1 — Ethernet is never initialised. network is imported and never used. lan = network.LAN(); lan.active(True); while not lan.isconnected(): ... — DHCP starts automatically once the link is up. (RT1062 quick reference) R2 173–187 The cam opens a TCP client to 192.168.1.100:8080, but ros2_microcontroller/openmv_communication.py is also a client (it dials openmv_ip = 192.168.1.104:8080). Two clients, zero servers → the link can never come up. The cam must bind() / listen() / accept(). R3 671–675 net.detect(img, threshold=…, nms=…) — no such method, and that was never the tf.detect signature either. model.predict([img]) with a post-processor from ml.postprocessing. (ml) R4 681–684 obj.classid(), obj.value(), obj.rect() — not part of any OpenMV detection API. Post-processors return per-class lists of ((x, y, w, h), score); the list index is the class id. R5 42 ssd_mobilenet_v1.tflite — OpenMV ships decoders for darknet (YOLOv2), ultralytics (YOLOv5/v8), mediapipe and edgeimpulse (FOMO) only. SSD's TFLite_Detection_PostProcess is a custom op that TFLM does not implement. Use FOMO / YOLOv5 / YOLOv8, or write your own postprocess callable. (Post-processors) R6 731 except socket.timeout: — MicroPython has no socket.timeout; it raises plain OSError. Evaluating the except clause raises AttributeError, which the outer handler treated as a dead socket → the loop closed and reopened the socket on every single frame. except OSError as e: if e.args[0] in (errno.EAGAIN, errno.ETIMEDOUT): ... (socket.settimeout) R7 252, 339 urequests.get(url, timeout=…) — requests.request() has no timeout parameter. Use socket-level timeouts. R8 346 response.raw.read(chunk_size) — Response exposes status_code, reason, headers, content, json(). There is no .raw, and stream= is "accepted for API compatibility; not used". content is a decoded str, so it corrupts binary payloads. Stream the body over a raw socket (implemented in the fix). R9 246 OTA queries /api/v1/firmware/latest?device_type=… — Server_OTA exposes /api/firmware/list, /api/firmware/info?file=, /download?file=, /api/health, /api/stats. The old URL returns 404 on your own server. See Server_OTA/src/handlers/handlers.go:81. R10 386, 409, 440 apply_update() / rollback() call self._dir_exists(...) on files, and download writes {filename} while apply reads a hard-coded firmware.py — the names never match, so an update could never be applied. Fixed: staged name is carried through, .part → atomic rename, previous file kept as .bak. R11 57–58, 144–158 sensor is deprecated since v4.5 and every example moved to csi in v5.0.0. Still functional, but alloc_extra_fb/dealloc_extra_fb now raise OSError. csi.CSI() with pixformat() / framesize() / snapshot(time=…). R12 87–88 pyb.LED(2) — the RT1062 is an NXP i.MXRT (mimxrt) part; the portable API is machine.LED("LED_GREEN"), shipped as a frozen module on every board. machine.LED R13 76 UPDATE_DIR = "/flash/updates" — the RT1062 flash root is /, the SD card is /sdcard. Relative path under the flash root. R14 769 Run as OpenMV_RT1062.py, the script only executes from the IDE. OpenMV auto-runs main.py at boot. Copy the script to the cam as main.py.

docs.title: 4. Design / algorithm defects
docs.text: # Defect Fix D1 ObjectTracker mutated self.tracks while iterating it, and re-keyed tracks so ids were not stable. Rewritten. D2 Association was greedy "first track with IoU > 0.3" — order dependent, no optimality guarantee, and it drops the identity of crossing targets. Minimum-cost assignment (Jonker–Volgenant/Hungarian) on 1 − IoU, with gating. Provably optimal for the linear assignment problem. D3 No filtering at all: raw detector boxes were published straight to the controller, so the ROS2 side would have to differentiate a noisy signal to get velocity. Per-track α–β estimator on a constant-velocity model, gains from Kalata's tracking index (see below). Position and velocity are published. D4 avg_fps = 0.9*avg + 0.1*fps — a magic weight whose bandwidth depends on the (variable) frame rate. First-order IIR with g = 1 − exp(−T/τ), the exact ZOH discretisation of τ·ẏ + y = u, so τ is a real time constant in seconds. D5 send_detection_data compared whole dicts to decide "changed", including the confidence float, so essentially every frame was transmitted. Unchanged behaviour, but payload now comes from filtered tracks, which are stable while a target is tracked.

docs.title: Estimator design (D3)
docs.text:
State per axis: x = [p, v], constant-velocity model.

predict:  p⁻ = p + T·v            v⁻ = v
update:   p  = p⁻ + α·r           v  = v⁻ + (β/T)·r ,   r = z − p⁻

Gains are not hand-tuned. With σ_a the manoeuvre (acceleration) noise std [px/s²] and σ_m the detector position noise std [px], Kalata's tracking index and the steady-state solution of the associated Riccati equation give

λ = σ_a·T² / σ_m
r = (4 + λ − √(8λ + λ²)) / 4
α = 1 − r²          β = 2(1 − r)²  ≡  2(2 − α) − 4√(1 − α)

P. R. Kalata, The Tracking Index: A Generalized Parameter for α-β and α-β-γ Target Trackers, IEEE Trans. AES-20(2), 1984.

Limits check out: λ → 0 ⇒ (α, β) → (0, 0) (pure coasting, ignore the measurement); λ → ∞ ⇒ (α, β) → (1, 2) (full trust in the measurement). Because the frame period jitters, the gains are recomputed from the measured T on every update instead of being frozen at design time.

Gating uses the normalised squared residual d² = (Δx² + Δy²)/σ_g² against χ²(2 dof, p=0.99) = 9.21, under the stated assumption that the residual is zero-mean Gaussian with std σ_g.

Box size (w, h) is smoothed by the same first-order lag as D4, with τ = SIZE_TAU_S.

docs.title: 5. What the rewritten file does
docs.text:
CSI frame → ml.Model.predict() → confidence gate → gated Hungarian association
          → α–β estimator (position + velocity) → line-framed JSON over TCP
          → ROS2 controller node (closes the loop; this script never actuates)
  • csi.CSI with an automatic fallback to sensor on firmware < v5.
  • ml.Model + a selectable post-processor (fomo / yolov5 / yolov8 / yolov2 / none), labels from the model's sidecar .txt or labels.txt.
  • network.LAN() brought up explicitly, DHCP by default, optional static ipconfig(addr4=…, gw4=…), link loss detected and re-established in-loop.
  • TCP server by default (TCP_MODE), non-blocking accept/recv/send, proper errno.EAGAIN handling, \n-framed JSON reassembled across TCP segments.
  • Single-threaded cooperative loop — no _thread, no locks.
  • OTA rewritten against the real Server_OTA API, binary-safe raw-socket download, size check, SHA-256 logged, .part staging, atomic swap with .bak, and it refuses to "apply" a DFU-only image from MicroPython.

docs.title: Verification performed
docs.text:
Algorithm and protocol layers were exercised on the host (the camera, ml and network.LAN layers need the board):

  • α–β gains: limit behaviour, the β identity, monotonicity in T, range.
  • Assignment solver: 300 random matrices vs. brute-force optimum — exact match on every case, including non-square ones.
  • Tracker: constant-velocity target with σ=3 px measurement noise → mean position error 1.2 px, velocity estimate 124.6 vs 120.0 px/s true; crossing targets keep distinct ids; stale tracks are deleted.
  • TCP channel over real sockets: framing across segment boundaries, split commands, disconnect detection, reconnect.
  • OTA against a mock of the Go API: device-type filtering, byte-identical 10 kB binary download, SHA-256 match, atomic apply + rollback, size-mismatch rejection with no partial file left behind.

docs.title: 6. Still to do before the board will run it
docs.text:
1. Check the firmware version on the cam (import omv; print(omv.version_string())) and flash ≥ v4.5.6 — ideally v5.0.0 — from OpenMV IDE.
  2. Provide a real model. Config.MODEL_FILE defaults to trained.tflite; copy your FOMO/YOLO model and its labels to the cam and set Config.POSTPROCESSOR to the matching decoder. ssd_mobilenet_v1.tflite will not work (§R5).
  3. Copy the script as main.py if it should run standalone at boot.
  4. Wire Ethernet through magnetics — the MDI pads must not be wired straight to an RJ45; use the PoE shield or a magjack.
  5. Set Config.STATIC_ADDR4 to 192.168.1.104/24 if you want to keep the IP hard-coded in the ROS2 node, or switch that node to DHCP + mDNS.
  6. Server_OTA only serves .bin/.hex/.elf/.img/.fw (services.isAllowedFileType). To ship .py or .tflite payloads, extend that allow-list server-side first.

docs.title: 7. ROS2 side (ros2_microcontroller) — also fixed
docs.text:
Update (October 2026). ros2_microcontroller was merged into the single MCU node ros2_jetowl_bridge/jetowl_bridge (C++): its vision link (vision_link.cpp, enabled with vision.enabled / vision:=true) keeps every behaviour below — TCP client to the listening camera or USB CDC, newline framing with remainder and flood discard, exponential back-off, OK/WARN/ERROR diagnostics, optional CSV log, target / target_velocity normalisation — with gtests in Source/ROS2_JetOwl_Bridge/test/test_vision_link.cpp. The table is kept as the record of the original audit.

The bridge node had its own blocking defects and is rewritten in the same change.

File Defect Fix openmv_communication.py @rclpy.callback — no such decorator in rclpy; the module raised AttributeError at import, so the node could never start. Removed; plain callbacks on ROS timers. openmv_communication.py rclpy.lifecycle.Node with on_configure, but main() never triggered any transition and there is no lifecycle manager in the repo → the socket was never opened. Plain rclpy.node.Node with an explicit connection state machine. Switching back to LifecycleNode is easy once a manager exists. openmv_communication.py main() looped spin_once() (blocking, no timeout) plus read_from_openmv() — a busy loop that starves either the callbacks or the socket. rclpy.spin() + a poll timer (poll_rate_hz) and a diagnostics timer. openmv_communication.py reconnect() was a @staticmethod using self (NameError), and nothing ever called it. Exponential backoff t←min(2t, t_max) inside the poll timer, reset on success. openmv_communication.py recv() output published as-is: a payload split across TCP segments became a truncated message. Byte buffer split on \n, remainder retained, oversized unframed buffers dropped. openmv_communication.py Diagnostics tested if self.socket: — a socket object is always truthy, so a dead link still reported "Operational". OK / WARN (connected but silent > rx_timeout_s) / ERROR (disconnected), plus rx/tx counters and the last error. openmv_communication.py analyze_data() called on every received line, but it parses comma-separated numbers while the camera sends JSON → it failed on every message and pulled pandas/numpy (undeclared) into the hot path. Off by default (analyze_numeric_lines), imported lazily, only for non-JSON lines. openmv_communication.py Held the I/O lock across a blocking recv(); settimeout(0.1) re-applied per read. Non-blocking sockets; the lock covers only the I/O call, dispatch happens outside it. openmv_communication.py CSV log opened in the cwd and never flushed or closed. Optional (log_file, empty disables), header written once, flushed periodically, closed on shutdown. openmv_communication.py USB default /dev/ttyUSB0; the OpenMV cam enumerates as /dev/ttyACM*. Default /dev/ttyACM0, transport selected by the transport parameter. dynamic_reconfigure.py rclpy.parameter.ParameterCallbackResult does not exist (it is rcl_interfaces.msg.SetParametersResult), and Parameter.Type.FLOAT is DOUBLE. Both corrected; validation extended to the new parameters. This is what the existing tests/test_dynamic_reconfigure.py already expected. health_monitor.py Used rclpy.ok() without importing rclpy → NameError on the first iteration, and a non-daemon thread. rclpy imported, daemon thread with a stop event, reports the real link state via node.link_healthy(). logging_utils.py from rclpy.logger import Logger — the module is rclpy.logging, and the import was unused. Removed. openmv_rt1062.launch.py Node imported from launch.actions (it lives in launch_ros.actions); condition=LaunchConfiguration(...) == 'usb' is a Python bool, not a launch condition; package='your_package' placeholders. Rewritten with launch_ros.actions.Node and IfCondition(PythonExpression(...)), real package/executable, and launch arguments. setup.py console_scripts for microcontroller_node and diagnostics_node, neither of which exists. Removed. package.xml pyserial, rcl_interfaces, launch, launch_ros used but not declared. Declared.

docs.title: New published interfaces
docs.text:
openmv_out_topic (raw JSON String) is unchanged. Added:

  • target — geometry_msgs/PointStamped, the highest-confidence target in normalised image coordinates x = 2cx/W − 1, y = 2cy/H − 1, z = √(wh/WH). z is a range proxy: for a pinhole camera s = f·S/Z, so Z = f·S/s and range is inversely proportional to z.
  • target_velocity — geometry_msgs/Vector3Stamped, the same target's image-plane velocity in normalised units per second. The camera already filters it (α–β), so the controller should use it as a feed-forward term rather than differentiating target.

image_width / image_height must match the camera's framesize (QVGA 320×240 by default).

docs.title: Verification performed
docs.text:
Firmware TcpChannel and the ROS2 bridge were run against each other over a loopback socket with the ROS layer stubbed (no ROS2 in this environment): connect both ways, two payloads in one TCP segment plus a split third reassembled, correct normalised target (x=+0.200 y=+0.200 z=0.200, v=(+0.188, −0.100)/s), command round trip answered by the real firmware command handler, diagnostics OK → ERROR on disconnect → WARN when silent, backoff 0.02 → 0.04 → 0.08 → capped, automatic reconnect with backoff reset, and parameter validation accepting/rejecting the right values. tests/test_openmv_communication.py was added for the framing and normalisation paths; it needs a real rclpy, so it was not executed here.

docs.title: Jetson
docs.text:
The Orin Nano Super's power mode sets the CPU/GPU clock limits and therefore the latency of every GPU and CPU workload. Use nvpmodel to select it and tegrastats to read the rail power, load and temperatures — see Jetson.

Benchmark and verification results must state the power mode they were measured in. No power measurement of the full stack has been recorded yet (Performance and Verification).

docs.title: Vehicle battery monitoring
docs.text:
Signal Producer Consumer Behaviour battery/state (sensor_msgs/BatteryState) power-monitor driver flight_controller_node, mission_planner_node, network_bridge_node, Qt dashboard warning → return to home; critical → land State of charge mission_planner_node mission feasibility and supervision first-order low-pass, τ = 5 s; measured/model power ratio low-pass, τ = 20 s Pack current and voltage INA260 on the FC (I2C1, 0x40) FC current as a torque proxy for jammed-rotor detection

The battery failsafes are part of the flight controller's safety monitor (Flight Controller); the mission planner checks before take-off that the mission's energy, including wind, fits the battery (Mission Planner).

Topic without a publisher

No package in the three repositories publishes battery/state yet; it is listed among the unconnected inputs of the System Node Graph. The vehicle's power monitor must provide it before flight.

docs.title: Ground controller
docs.text: The Remote UAV measures its 2S Li-ion pack through a 20 k / 10 k divider on A4, filters it with a first-order low-pass (τ = 1 s) and warns below 7.0 V (3.5 V per cell, about 10 % capacity left) (Signal Chain §8).

docs.title: Isaac ROS Jetbot NanoOWL
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from MATLAB/README.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in MATLAB/.

Simulation and data visualization framework for autonomous robotics using NVIDIA Isaac ROS, Jetbot platform, and NanoOWL vision model.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This project provides a comprehensive MATLAB/Simulink environment for simulating, testing, and analyzing autonomous robot behaviors. It integrates NVIDIA Isaac ROS framework with Jetbot hardware platform, utilizing the lightweight NanoOWL model for efficient object detection and navigation algorithms.

MATLAB is used for:

  • Simulating robot dynamics and control algorithms
  • Rendering and visualizing sensor data (camera, IMU, encoders)
  • Analyzing experimental results and system performance
  • Prototyping computer vision and navigation algorithms
  • Hardware-in-the-loop testing before hardware deployment

docs.title: MathWorks Products
docs.text:
• MATLAB R2021b or later
  • Simulink
  • Computer Vision Toolbox
  • Robotics System Toolbox
  • ROS Toolbox
  • Image Processing Toolbox (recommended)
  • Navigation Toolbox (recommended)

docs.title: 3<sup>rd</sup> Party Products
docs.text:
• Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (for hardware deployment, shipped by JetPack 6.2)
  • ROS 2 Humble
  • NVIDIA Isaac ROS packages
  • Python 3.10
  • CUDA Toolkit 12.6+ (for hardware deployment)

docs.title: Hardware Requirements (Optional - for deployment)
docs.text:
• NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super (8GB Developer Kit)
  • Jetbot chassis with differential drive
  • CSI/USB camera module
  • IMU sensor
  • USB-C PD power supply, 5V/5A (25W)

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Clone or download this repository to your local machine
  2. Open MATLAB and navigate to the project folder
  3. Open the project file: Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL.prj
  4. MATLAB will automatically configure paths and dependencies

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Run the main example scripts located in the scripts/ folder or open Simulink models directly from the simulink/ folder.

docs.title: Robot Trajectory Simulation
docs.text: Simulate differential drive robot following predefined paths with realistic physics and sensor models.

docs.text: Load and visualize recorded sensor data including camera frames, IMU readings, and wheel encoder measurements.

docs.text: Test object detection pipeline with NanoOWL model integration for real-time performance analysis.

docs.text: Run comprehensive Simulink models for robot dynamics, sensor fusion, and navigation control.

docs.title: ROS 2 toolkit: read, subscribe, publish, 3-D / 2-D view
docs.text:
scripts/ros2/ and utilities/ros2/ connect MATLAB to the JetOwl ROS 2 graph (Humble). With them you can list topics, subscribe to them, record into ring buffers, and send navigation commands. The data is drawn on one dashboard with 3-D and 2-D views plus time series.

addpath('scripts/ros2');
jetowl_ros2_viz();                                   % demo: synthetic flight, no ROS needed
[h, s] = jetowl_ros2_viz('live', 0);                 % ROS_DOMAIN_ID = 0
s.list_topics()                                      % topic list of the graph
s.publish_nav_command('HOVER');                      % flight/nav_command (std_msgs/String)
s.publish_waypoints([0 0 3; 10 0 3; 10 10 3]);       % flight/waypoints (PoseArray, frame odom)
jetowl_ros2_viz('bag', 'rosbag2_2026_10_02', struct('speed', 4));   % replay a ros2 bag
jetowl_ros2_viz('live', 0, struct('views', {{'slam'}}, 'rate_hz', 10));  % SLAM view only

Two figures update in real time from the same history snapshot: the flight dashboard and the SLAM view (opts.views, default both).

Panel Content Topics 3-D (odom, ENU) ESKF trail, body axes, ground truth, GNSS, setpoint, MPC path, mission, obstacles (bounding spheres), map, scan /odometry/filtered, /hexa/ground_truth/odometry, /gps/fix, /flight/setpoint, /control/predicted_path, /mission/preview, /tracked/markers, /map, /scan 2-D (top view) Occupancy grid, SLAM path, LiDAR points, pose, 95 % position ellipse /map, /slam/path, /slam/pose, /scan Altitude ESKF z, barometric height, GNSS height /odometry/filtered, /baro/pressure, /gps/fix Position / attitude / RPM x y z, roll pitch yaw vs. attitude setpoint, rotor speeds /odometry/filtered, /imu/data, /control/attitude_setpoint, /jetowl/motor_rpm

SLAM view (jetowl_slam_view_create / jetowl_slam_data / jetowl_slam_view_draw), from /map, /slam/pose, /slam/path, /slam/debug and /scan:

Panel Content Map occupancy grid (unknown cells not drawn), keyframes, pose with 95 % ellipse and ±2σ yaw wedge, scan in the map frame, newest ICP measurement vs EKF prior NIS per scan (accepted / rejected), mean over the last 50 accepted updates, exact 95 % bounds of that mean, gate χ²₃(0.99) = 11.34; verdict CONSISTENT / NOT CONSISTENT Innovation ν_x, ν_y, ν_yaw with ±2√S_ii ICP inlier ratio, reduced χ², rejected scans; eigenvalues of the scaled information H' (log) with the degeneracy flag Health pose σ (x, y, yaw), processing time per scan vs the 100 ms scan period, EKF v, ω, gyro bias Statistics the numbers above plus explored / occupied / free area of the map (Nav2 thresholds)

The topic list, with types and QoS, lives in utilities/ros2/jetowl_topic_catalog.m.

QoS. Subscriptions are best-effort, which matches any publisher. The exceptions are the latched topics (/map, /slam/path, /mission/preview). These are subscribed reliable + transient-local, so the last sample is delivered on connection.

Safety gate. JetOwlRos2Session.publish refuses actuator topics (/control/*, /cmd_vel*, /hexa/*, /jetowl/arm*) unless AllowActuatorTopics = true is set explicitly. From MATLAB the normal path is a navigation command or waypoints. These go through ros2_flight_controller, which keeps its own closed loop, watchdog and failsafe.

Mathematics (each function cites its source in its header):

Function Formula Source jetowl_quat_to_rotm, jetowl_quat_to_euler, jetowl_euler_to_rotm Hamilton quaternion → R; ZYX Euler, R = Rz(ψ)·Ry(θ)·Rx(φ) Kuipers, Quaternions and Rotation Sequences §5.14, §7.8; REP-103 jetowl_decode_msg (odometry) v_world = R(q)·v_child (twist is in the child frame) REP-105, nav_msgs/Odometry jetowl_geodetic_to_enu WGS-84 geodetic → ECEF → ENU NIMA TR8350.2; Groves eq. 2.112, 2.150 jetowl_baro_altitude h = 44330.77·(1 − (p/p0)^0.190263) ICAO Doc 7488 (ISA), the same constants as the ESKF jetowl_scan_to_points θ_i = θ_min + i·Δθ; Inf/NaN or out-of-limit ranges dropped REP-117; planar rigid transform, Siciliano et al. §2.7 jetowl_grid_geometry Row-major OccupancyGrid, origin rotated by its yaw nav_msgs/OccupancyGrid jetowl_cov_ellipse k² = −2·ln(1 − p) (χ² quantile, 2 dof), eigen-decomposition of P Bar-Shalom, Li & Kirubarajan §1.4.17, §3.7 jetowl_marker_radius Bounding sphere for a box, cylinder or sphere Same as ros2_control_system obstacle_geometry.hpp jetowl_chi2_quantile Solves gammainc(x/2, n/2) = p by bisection (exact χ² quantile, no toolbox) Abramowitz & Stegun 26.4.19, 6.5.1 jetowl_nis_bounds m·NIS_avg ~ χ²(m·k): bounds χ²_{mk}(0.025, 0.975)/m Bar-Shalom, Li & Kirubarajan §5.4.2 jetowl_slam_window_stats NIS mean over the last 50 accepted EKF updates (the nis_window of the SLAM node), ICP acceptance, degenerate share as above; slam_params.yaml jetowl_grid_fit Map into a fixed N×N grid by integer max-pool (an occupied cell stays occupied) nav_msgs/OccupancyGrid jetowl_map_stats Explored / occupied (v ≥ 65) / free (v ≤ 25) area Nav2 map_server trinary thresholds

The dashboard only shows data. It does not filter or estimate anything itself. The state it draws is the one the ESKF and SLAM already estimate on the Jetson, so the view is the robot's own closed loop, not a second copy of it.

The demo (jetowl_viz_demo_state) is a synthetic coordinated-turn helix. It uses the bank angle φ = −atan(v·ω/g) and a hover RPM scale that is only illustrative. Its /slam/debug draws the innovation as ν = S^½·z, z ~ N(0, I₃), so the NIS is χ²(3) by construction, as for a consistent filter. It uses a deterministic Park–Miller + Box–Muller generator. The map is revealed within 12 m of the visited positions.

Requirements. live and bag need ROS Toolbox (ROS 2). demo and the tests run in base MATLAB and in GNU Octave ≥ 8:

cd test/tests && octave --eval "test_ros2_viz_suite()"         # 11 groups
cd test/tests && octave --eval "test_simulink_blocks_suite()"  # 9 groups

docs.title: Simulink: MATLAB Function blocks for ROS 2 monitoring
docs.text:
simulink/blocks/ holds one .m file per MATLAB Function block. A model is built only from MATLAB Function blocks whose code is a single call such as [odo, n] = jetowl_blk_sub_odometry(t);. No other Simulink library block is needed.

  • 15 ROS 2 sources: odometry, IMU, GNSS, baro, setpoints, rpm, SLAM pose / debug / map / path, scan, markers, and more.
  • 7 processing blocks: GNSS → ENU, baro height, scan → map points, 95 % ellipse, obstacles → odom, SLAM NIS consistency, map area.
  • 2 real-time views: flight dashboard and SLAM view.
addpath('simulink');  jetowl_sl_setup_path();
jetowl_build_monitor_model();                                   % builds jetowl_ros2_monitor.slx
sim('jetowl_ros2_monitor');                                     % demo source, real-time pacing
jetowl_build_monitor_model(struct('source', 'live', 'arg', 0)); % robot on ROS_DOMAIN_ID 0
out = jetowl_monitor_sil(struct('duration', 30));               % same graph without Simulink

Block reference, ports, sizes and the real-time model settings: simulink/README.md.

docs.title: robot_dynamics.slx
docs.text:
Simulates the kinematics and dynamics of a differential drive robot. Includes wheel encoders, motor models, and physics-based motion.

Inputs:

  • Left wheel velocity command (rad/s)
  • Right wheel velocity command (rad/s)

Outputs:

  • Robot pose (x, y, theta)
  • Wheel encoder ticks
  • Linear and angular velocities

docs.title: sensor_fusion.slx
docs.text:
Fuses data from multiple sensors (camera, IMU, encoders) for robust state estimation.

Features:

  • Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for pose estimation
  • Complementary filter for IMU data
  • Outlier rejection and sensor validation

docs.title: vision_pipeline.slx
docs.text:
Complete image processing pipeline from raw camera input to object detection.

Pipeline stages:

  1. Image preprocessing (resize, normalize)
  2. Feature extraction
  3. Object detection (NanoOWL)
  4. Post-processing and tracking

docs.title: navigation_controller.slx
docs.text:
Path planning and motion control for autonomous navigation.

Components:

  • A* path planning algorithm
  • Pure pursuit controller
  • Obstacle avoidance
  • Dynamic replanning

docs.title: Data Analysis Utilities
docs.text: The project includes comprehensive utilities for loading experimental data, analyzing detection performance, calculating metrics (precision, recall, F1 score), plotting confusion matrices, and exporting data to ROS bag format.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Run all tests using MATLAB's testing framework. Individual test files are available in the test/ folder for specific components like kinematics, vision pipeline, and navigation.

docs.title: Hardware Deployment
docs.text:
While MATLAB is primarily used for simulation, you can deploy algorithms to hardware using:

  1. Simulink Coder to generate C++ code from Simulink models
  2. ROS Toolbox to interface with Isaac ROS nodes
  3. GPU Coder to deploy to NVIDIA Jetson platforms

The project supports ROS connection to real hardware for testing and validation.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration files are located in resources/config/ and include:

robot_params.json - Robot physical parameters (wheel radius, track width, max velocity, acceleration limits)

vision_config.json - Vision system settings (camera resolution, frame rate, detection thresholds)

docs.title: JetOwl Simulink blocks (MATLAB Function blocks only)
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from MATLAB/simulink/README.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in MATLAB/simulink/.

Every block of the JetOwl ROS 2 monitor is a MATLAB Function block whose code is one call of a .m file in blocks/. To build a model you place MATLAB Function blocks and connect them. No other Simulink library block is needed: no ROS Toolbox Subscribe block, no Scope, no Clock.

                ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐
 jetowl_blk_    │ clock        │──►│ 15 ROS 2 sources     │──►│ 7 processing blocks  │──► 2 views
 clock ─────────┘ t = k·Ts     │   │ /odometry/filtered … │   │ ENU, baro, scan,     │   flight
                               │   │ /map /slam/* /scan   │   │ ellipse, NIS window, │   SLAM
                               │   └──────────────────────┘   │ obstacles, map area  │
                               │                              └──────────────────────┘

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
addpath('MATLAB/simulink');  jetowl_sl_setup_path();
jetowl_build_monitor_model();                                    % demo source, no ROS needed
sim('jetowl_ros2_monitor');                                      % two figures update in real time

jetowl_build_monitor_model(struct('source', 'live', 'arg', 0));  % robot, ROS_DOMAIN_ID = 0
jetowl_build_monitor_model(struct('source', 'bag', 'arg', 'rosbag2_2026_10_02'));

Without Simulink (base MATLAB or GNU Octave), the same block graph runs in a fixed-step loop:

out = jetowl_monitor_sil(struct('source', 'demo', 'duration', 30));
out = jetowl_monitor_sil(struct('source', 'live', 'arg', 0, 'duration', 600));   % paced

docs.title: Assembling a block by hand
docs.text:
1. Add a MATLAB Function block (Simulink › User-Defined Functions).
  2. Replace its code with the call given in the header of the .m file, for example:
function [odo, n] = fcn(t)
[odo, n] = jetowl_blk_sub_odometry(t);
  1. Connect the ports by name: they are the argument names of the function. Keep the fixed-step discrete solver with every block on an inherited sample time, and run jetowl_sl_setup_path() plus jetowl_sl_bridge('open', …) in the model InitFcn.

jetowl_monitor_wiring.m is the complete wiring of the reference model. The builder and the Simulink-free runner both read it.

docs.title: Block reference
docs.text: Sizes come from blocks/jetowl_blk_sizes.m: NSCAN = 1024, GMAX = 512, NPATH = 2000, NTRAJ = 128, NOBS = 32, NELL = 65. Variable-length messages are NaN-padded (−1 for the grid) to these sizes and carry their valid count.

docs.title: Sources (ROS 2 → signals)
docs.text:
Each source returns the newest sample with time ≤ t (zero-order hold) and n, the number of messages received so far. A change of n means a new sample.

Block Topic Outputs jetowl_blk_clock(Ts) — t = k·Ts jetowl_blk_sub_odometry /odometry/filtered odo [1×12] p, v_world, rpy, Pxx Pxy Pyy jetowl_blk_sub_ground_truth /hexa/ground_truth/odometry gt [1×12] jetowl_blk_sub_imu /imu/data imu [1×9] rpy, ω, a jetowl_blk_sub_gnss /gps/fix lla [1×3] jetowl_blk_sub_baro /baro/pressure p_pa jetowl_blk_sub_attitude_setpoint /control/attitude_setpoint rpy_sp [1×3] jetowl_blk_sub_thrust /control/thrust thrust [N] jetowl_blk_sub_motor_rpm /jetowl/motor_rpm rpm [1×4] jetowl_blk_sub_range /range range_m (NaN outside limits, REP-117) jetowl_blk_sub_slam_pose /slam/pose pose [1×7] x y yaw Pxx Pxy Pyy Pyaw jetowl_blk_sub_slam_debug /slam/debug dbg [1×29] (jetowl_slam_debug_index) jetowl_blk_sub_map /map G [GMAX² int8], meta [w h res ox oy oyaw] jetowl_blk_sub_slam_path /slam/path P_path [NPATH×3], np jetowl_blk_sub_setpoint /flight/setpoint P_sp [NTRAJ×3], np jetowl_blk_sub_predicted_path /control/predicted_path P_pred [NTRAJ×3], np jetowl_blk_sub_mission_preview /mission/preview P_mis [NPATH×3], np jetowl_blk_sub_scan /scan r [NSCAN×1], meta [θmin Δθ rmin rmax beams] jetowl_blk_sub_markers /tracked/markers obs [NOBS×5] cx cy cz r in_base, no

docs.title: Processing (pure maths, %#codegen, no ROS)
docs.text: Block Computes Source of the formula jetowl_blk_gnss_enu(lla, n) WGS-84 → ENU about the mean of the first 10 fixes (ESKF datum) NIMA TR8350.2; Groves eq. 2.150 jetowl_blk_baro_height(p, n, odo) h = 44330.77·(1 − (p/p0)^0.190263) + z_ESKF(first sample) ICAO Doc 7488 jetowl_blk_scan_points(r, meta, pose) beams gated by REP-117, sensor → base (mount) → map (SLAM pose) REP-117; Siciliano §2.7 jetowl_blk_cov_ellipse(pose) 95 % ellipse, k² = −2 ln 0.05, closed-form 2×2 eigen-decomposition Bar-Shalom §1.4.17; Strang §6.4 jetowl_blk_obstacles_world(obs, no, odo) base_link markers → odom: p + R(rpy)·c Siciliano §2.7; same as the MPC jetowl_blk_slam_consistency(dbg, n) NIS mean over the last 50 accepted updates, exact 95 % χ² bounds, ICP acceptance, degenerate share, worst time Bar-Shalom §5.4.2 jetowl_blk_map_stats(G, meta, n) explored / occupied / free area (Nav2 trinary thresholds) Nav2 map_server

docs.title: Views (sinks) and commands
docs.text:
Block Shows jetowl_blk_view_flight(t, odo, gt, imu, rpy_sp, enu, h_baro, rpm, P_sp, P_pred, W) 3-D trail, axes, GNSS, setpoint, MPC path, obstacles; 2-D SLAM panel; position, altitude (ESKF / baro / GNSS), attitude vs setpoint, rpm jetowl_blk_view_slam(t, G, meta, n_map, pose, n_pose, P_path, pts, ell, dbg, n_dbg, cons, ms) map, keyframes, pose with 95 % ellipse and ±2σ yaw, scan, ICP vs prior; NIS with window mean, bounds and gate; innovations ±2√S; ICP quality; eigenvalues and degeneracy; σ; processing time vs 100 ms; EKF v, ω, b_g; statistics panel with the NIS verdict jetowl_blk_command_step(t, t_on, cmd_id) 0 before t_on, cmd_id after jetowl_blk_pub_nav_command(cmd) publishes flight/nav_command once per change; only on a live source

The views are the figures of jetowl_ros2_viz (jetowl_viz_draw, jetowl_slam_view_draw), fed with the same data structs. A model, a bag replay and a live MATLAB session therefore show identical plots.

docs.title: Real time
docs.text:
• Model time = wall time. The builder turns on simulation pacing (rate 1). The scope redraws every 1/redraw_hz (default 10 Hz) of model time and keeps every sample in ring buffers (12 000 samples = 10 min at 20 Hz).
  • Live data. The bridge reads the newest message of each topic once per step from JetOwlRos2Session. Playback of a bag or the demo maps model time to data time (t_data = t0 + t), so a run is reproducible.
  • Execution modes. ROS I/O and graphics run in MATLAB through coder.extrinsic. Use the Normal or Accelerator simulation mode. Rapid Accelerator and embedded code generation cannot call MATLAB, and the processing blocks are the only part that would generate standalone code.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: The blocks only read, except jetowl_blk_pub_nav_command. That block sends a navigation command name from JetOwlRos2Session.NAV_COMMANDS to flight_controller_node. The controller checks the command against its state machine and keeps its own closed loop, watchdog and failsafe. No block writes an actuator topic (/control/*, /cmd_vel, /hexa/*). The reference model contains no command block.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
MATLAB/test/tests/test_simulink_blocks_suite.m (9 groups) checks the following, in MATLAB or GNU Octave without Simulink:

  • the chi-square quantile against its CDF and against the closed form for 2 degrees of freedom;
  • the NIS bounds against the Wilson–Hilferty bounds of lidar_slam_node (< 1 %);
  • the grid fit against a direct max-pool, including that occupied cells stay occupied;
  • every processing block against the MATLAB function it mirrors;
  • the bridge cursor, padding, decimation and publish gate;
  • the wiring (order, ports, nargin / nargout);
  • the code the builder writes into each block, executed and compared with direct calls;
  • a run of the block graph against the dashboard and SLAM data computed from the same history.

jetowl_build_monitor_model itself needs Simulink. Its dry_run output, meaning every block body and every line, is what the test executes.

cd MATLAB/test/tests && octave --eval "test_simulink_blocks_suite()"
