docs.title: Jetbot NanoOWL
docs.text:
Advanced Android Control Interface for Jetbot Nano with ROS2 Integration

Features • Installation • Usage • Architecture • Contributing

docs.title: 📋 Overview
docs.text:
Jetbot NanoOWL is an Android monitoring and remote-access console for NVIDIA Jetbot Nano robots. The estimation stack — sensor conditioning, state estimation, mapping and the transport — runs in C++ on a native thread; Kotlin is the user interface and nothing else.

This app observes; it does not drive. The guidance laws, velocity loops and operator controls were removed: nothing computed here is written back to the robot. What remains is a console that shows where the robot is and what its sensors say, a SLAM front end, remote access (SSH, SFTP, VNC), and a Linux environment that runs on the phone itself.

Every block in the sensor-to-state path is a discretisation of a named continuous-time design, derived in docs/ESTIMATION_DESIGN.md and checked by a host test suite that asserts the derived property rather than a recorded output.

docs.title: Key Highlights
docs.text:
• 🧮 Provable estimation chain — sensor → median → low-pass → noise ID → EKF → pose fix, with the derivation and a test for each stage
  • 🗺️ Real SLAM plumbing — log-odds occupancy grid, Bresenham ray casting, ICP scan matching feeding an absolute pose fix back into the EKF
  • 🐧 Linux environment on the phone — a guest rootfs, a real terminal on a pseudo-terminal so apt and nano behave, its package manager, shortcuts to the apps you install, and their windows rendered on the Android display the way WSLg does it — each app on its own display, so it gets its own entry in Recents and closing it closes that app alone. The container runtime is fetched by the phone itself, so a stock APK works with no build machine and no bundled GPL code
  • ⚙️ Native heavy lifting — 50 Hz estimator loop, map rasterisation and VNC pixel decoding all in C++; the UI thread only blits and draws text
  • 📊 Live diagnostics — raw odometry against the fused estimate, innovation consistency (NIS), online noise estimates, loop jitter, link counters
  • 🖥️ Remote access — multi-tab SSH terminal, SFTP browser and editor, and a native RFB client

docs.title: Estimation chain (native C++)
docs.text: stage implementation reference spike rejection sliding median, rejects bursts of ≤ (w−1)/2 samples exactly Tukey 1977 linear filtering first-order low-pass, pre-warped bilinear (−3 dB exactly at f_c), Butterworth/notch biquads §2 noise identification Welford moments + innovation-based R̂ with positivity projection Mehra 1970, Myers & Tapley 1976 odometry forward differential-drive kinematics with variance propagation §6 state estimation EKF on [x y θ v ω], exact constant-twist arc, Joseph-form update, NIS monitor Bar-Shalom §5.2.3, §6.2 absolute fix ICP scan match, or a pose from the Isaac ROS graph, weighted by its covariance §8

docs.title: Mapping and localisation
docs.text:
• Log-odds Bayesian occupancy grid; integrating a scan costs one addition per traversed cell (360 beams into a 200×200 grid: 0.21 ms)
  • Bresenham ray casting, clamped log-odds, binary map save/load
  • Point-to-point ICP scan matching seeded with the odometry prior, feeding DiffDriveEKF::updatePose with a variance taken from the match residual — the measurement that bounds dead-reckoning drift
  • Map rasterised to ARGB in C++, straight into the Android bitmap

docs.title: Monitoring console (Kotlin)
docs.text:
• Custom occupancy-map and strip-chart views; pinch zoom, pan, long-press to measure range and bearing from the robot
  • Charts draw raw wheel odometry against the fused estimate, so the filter's contribution is the gap between the two traces
  • Live state estimate and its 1σ uncertainty, NIS consistency, online noise estimates, loop rate and jitter, link packet counters

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
• Binary UDP link with CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE framing, sequence-gap accounting and a robot-side command watchdog (protocol)
  • Reference ROS2 bridge in tools/jetbot_bridge.py, with a --dry-run mode that needs no ROS2
  • ROS2Manager still publishes geometry_msgs/Twist when built against rclcpp

docs.title: Isaac ROS integration
docs.text:
• tools/isaac_ros_bridge.py connects the console to the Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL graph without modifying that repository — it subscribes to what the graph already publishes and publishes to what it already subscribes to, with every topic name a command-line argument
  • Absolute pose from /odometry folded into the EKF as a covariance-weighted Kalman update — the exteroceptive fix that bounds dead-reckoning drift
  • NanoOWL detections from /output_detections drawn live in the camera frame
  • The detector's prompt set from the console and republished on /input_query: NanoOWL is open vocabulary, so the prompt is the class list
  • Graph health from /diagnostics, plus the Jetson's CPU, GPU and temperature
  • Full guide: docs/ISAAC_ROS_INTEGRATION.md

docs.title: MAVLink link to the Isaac ROS graph
docs.text:
• A second transport. It reads ros2_network_bridge, the MAVLink v2 node of Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL: ros2 launch ros2_network_bridge jetbot_console.launch.py phone_host:=<phone>. Pick it in Settings → ROS2 Connection → MAVLink
  • Native C++ codec: CRC-16/MCRF4XX with CRC_EXTRA, byte-wise resync, v1 and v2. It is byte-exact against pymavlink
  • ODOMETRY (#331) fused as two Kalman updates with the covariances the robot reported, full 3×3 for the pose and 2×2 for the twist. The NED → ENU map is exact, not linearised. An unknown or non-positive-definite covariance is not fused, rather than weighted by a guess
  • The console is an observer. Its heartbeat is MAV_TYPE_LOG, so the bridge never takes it for the GCS, and closing the app cannot trip the vehicle's link-loss failsafe
  • Vehicle state, battery, status texts, and loss in both directions are shown in the diagnostics drawer
  • Robot on another network: both ends dial out over TLS to Server_Relay, a small Go server in the Isaac repository, so the link works through any NAT, the carrier's included. Pick Settings → ROS2 Connection → Relay. The relay passes nothing from the phone but its heartbeat, so an observer token cannot command the robot
  • Each fix's delay is measured from its timestamp without clock sync. The fix is then carried to the present with the EKF's own motion model and process noise before it is fused
  • Design and proofs: docs/MAVLINK_LINK.md

docs.title: UAV flight console (3-D)
docs.text:
• The vehicle is a multirotor, so on the MAVLink source the console tracks a 6-DoF state. A Kalman filter runs on [p; v] in ENU with the continuous white-noise acceleration model. Its noise density q̃ = a_max² T_m = 1.6 m²/s³ comes from the vehicle's own limits in uav_control.yaml, not from tuning. The attitude is carried to the present on the body rate
  • 3-D map from the LD19. The bridge sends each scan as standard OBSTACLE_DISTANCE. The console places every fan with the pose interpolated to the fan's own timestamp, so slices taken at different heights and attitudes stack into a log-odds voxel map (5 cm voxels, Amanatides–Woo traversal, the same model as the desktop dashboard)
  • Native renderer (orbit, pinch zoom, two-finger pan, oblique / top / chase presets). It draws the voxels coloured by height, the flight path and a hexarotor glyph
  • Primary flight display: attitude with roll arc and pitch ladder, speed and altitude tapes with a vertical-speed bar, and a heading tape
  • Maps save, load and clear as .vox files
  • Design and proofs: docs/UAV_3D.md

docs.title: Remote access
docs.text:
• Native RFB decoding (Raw, CopyRect, RRE) writing directly into the bitmap; the pixel format is negotiated so the wire byte order matches the bitmap and the raw path is one word per pixel
  • Multi-tab SSH terminal (xterm.js), SFTP browser and file editor

docs.title: Linux environment (WSLg-style)
docs.text:
• Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, and only that: the base image is downloaded, verified against Canonical's published digest, and run under PRoot. 22.04 is the same userspace a Jetson running JetPack 6 has and the release ROS 2 Humble is built for, so a package name resolves on the phone the way it does on the robot
  • Setup is a four-step checklist — runtime, guest, desktop base, and optionally a window manager that gives one app the whole display — and nothing else is offered as a bundle: anything beyond setup is installed by name with apt or from the terminal
  • Installed apps are discovered from the guest's .desktop files, so anything installed from a shell shows up too; each can be pinned in the app or handed to the Android launcher as a home-screen shortcut
  • The guest signs you in as jetbot_owl@Blue, with a working sudo — a shim, because the guest already runs with every privilege the app has and a setuid binary cannot work under PRoot at all
  • One folder is visible to both sides — /mnt/android in the guest — so an Android file can be opened in Linux and a file written in Linux can be saved back out. Getting files in and out uses the system document picker, so no storage permission is asked for and nothing beyond the chosen file is reached
  • Their windows render on the phone with no display protocol in between: Xvfb -fbdir keeps its screen in a memory-mapped file inside the guest's /tmp, which is a directory this app owns, so a frame is one copy rather than an encode, a loopback socket and a decode. Input and damage go back over X11 itself (XTEST, DAMAGE). Measured at 1280×720: 0.328 ms mean per frame, 26% of the screen touched. The X server is started -nolisten tcp, so there is no port for anything to reach

  • The screen is laid out as a settings console:

    • setup folds to one line of ticks once it is done;
    • Terminal, Shared folder, Desktop and Linux apps are launch tiles;
    • display options are a grouped list with switches;
    • a storage bar shows the guest against the free space on its volume;
    • the console reports how many lines it holds.

    - See docs/LINUX_ENVIRONMENT.md

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Emergency stop that dumps every integrator, so releasing it cannot kick
  • Feedback watchdog: no telemetry → the inner loop drops to feed-forward and says so, instead of integrating against a stale sample
  • Envelope limits on velocity, acceleration and jerk; wheel-speed saturation that preserves the commanded path curvature
  • Gain-stability conditions enforced in code, not left to the operator

docs.title: Frontend (Android)
docs.text:
• Language: Kotlin
  • Min SDK: 24 (Android 7.0)
  • Target SDK: 36 (Android 14+)
  • UI Framework: Material Components, ViewBinding
  • Architecture: MVVM-inspired single-activity

docs.title: Control core (native)
docs.text:
• Language: C++17, no third-party dependencies
  • Build System: CMake 3.22.1 (if(ANDROID) switches between the APK library and a host build with the test runner)
  • Threading: control loop on its own native thread; UDP receive thread; telemetry handed to the UI under one mutex
  • Optional: rclcpp / geometry_msgs when built inside a ROS2 workspace
  • Tested on the host: cmake -S app/src/main/cpp -B build-host && ./build-host/jetbot_core_tests

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Android Studio Ladybug or later
  • Android SDK 24+
  • NDK r25 or later
  • CMake 3.22.1+
  • (Optional) ROS2 Humble/Foxy for full functionality

This build targets API 28 on purpose. The Linux environment needs the W^X exemption that targetSdk <= 28 grants, which is what lets the app execute a runtime it downloaded — the same trade Termux makes. The consequence is that Google Play will not accept or update this app; it is for sideloading and GitHub releases. A build that would rather keep a modern targetSdk can bundle PRoot instead with tools/fetch-proot.sh and raise the target back. Both paths are described in docs/LINUX_ENVIRONMENT.md §3.

docs.title: Build Steps
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository 

    git clone https://github.com/TNG-Blue/jetbot-nanoowl.git
cd jetbot-nanoowl

  2. Open in Android Studio 

    studio .

  3. Sync Gradle

  4. Android Studio will automatically sync dependencies

  5. Ensure NDK and CMake are installed via SDK Manager

  6. Build the project 

    ./gradlew assembleDebug

  7. Install on device 

    ./gradlew installDebug

docs.title: Release builds
docs.text:
Builds meant to be handed out must be signed with a stable release key, not the shared debug key, and must carry a strictly increasing versionCode:

./gradlew verifyReleaseSigning assembleRelease -PappVersionCode=<n>

The key is read from keystore/keystore.properties (git-ignored) or from the RELEASE_STORE_FILE / RELEASE_STORE_PASSWORD / RELEASE_KEY_ALIAS / RELEASE_KEY_PASSWORD environment variables. Keeping one certificate across releases is what lets Android install a new APK as an update and what stops Google Play Protect from treating every build as an unknown app — see docs/APP_SIGNING_AND_PLAY_PROTECT.md.

docs.title: Quick start without a robot
docs.text: Without a robot there is no telemetry, so the console has nothing to estimate from. What is usable offline is the rest of the app: the Linux environment (menu → Linux), the SSH and SFTP tools, and the VNC client. The estimation chain itself is exercised by the host test suite rather than by a simulator — see Testing.

docs.title: With the Isaac ROS graph
docs.text:
1. On the Jetson, with the Isaac ROS graph already running: 
    python3 tools/isaac_ros_bridge.py --phone <phone-ip>
    (--dry-run emits synthetic Isaac ROS traffic if the graph is not up yet, and needs no ROS2 installed at all.)
  2. In the app: menu → Connections, enter the robot's IP and press CONNECT.
  3. The status strip turns green and reads ROS2 live · pose fixed once odometry arrives; the perception card fills with NanoOWL detections. Tap 🔍 on that card to change what the detector looks for.

See docs/ISAAC_ROS_INTEGRATION.md for the full topic map, remapping, and troubleshooting.

docs.title: With a bare robot
docs.text:
For a robot that is not running the Isaac ROS graph, the minimal bridge speaks the original packet set:

python3 tools/jetbot_bridge.py --phone <phone-ip>

docs.title: Reading the console
docs.text:
The status strip says where the estimate comes from and how fresh it is: no link, link up · no telemetry, ROS2 live · odometry, or ROS2 live · pose fixed when an absolute fix landed in the last two seconds.

The diagnostics drawer (📈) shows the pose and its 1σ uncertainty, the NIS consistency monitor, the identified sensor noise, the map counters, the link counters and the loop period with its jitter. The two charts draw raw wheel odometry against the fused estimate: the gap between the traces is exactly what the gyro and the pose fixes contributed.

Long-press anywhere on the map to measure — it reports the range and bearing from the robot's estimated pose to the point you picked.

docs.title: Maps
docs.text: Save, load and clear from the tool column on the right. Maps are written as log-odds snapshots under the app's private storage and reload with their geometry intact.

docs.title: Native layer (C++)
docs.text:
EstimationPipeline — owns every block and steps them in order: sensor conditioning, noise identification, EKF predict/update, telemetry. One method (step) is the whole estimator cycle.

DiffDriveEKF — EKF over [x y θ v ω] with the exact constant-twist arc, analytic Jacobians, Q = G diag(σ_a², σ_α²) Gᵗ, Joseph-form update and a NIS consistency monitor.

AdaptiveNoiseEstimator — identifies each measurement variance online from the innovation sequence, so the filter weighs the sensors the robot actually has.

PIDController — the one controller still in the tree. It no longer drives the robot; its consumer is FramePacer.

FramePacer — closes the loop on the Linux desktop's frame latency: an M/G/1 setpoint and an IMC-tuned PI with back-calculation anti-wind-up (derivation).

OccupancyGrid — log-odds mapping, Bresenham ray casting, ARGB rasterisation into the Android bitmap, binary persistence.

alignScans — 2-D ICP with the closed-form Kabsch step, seeded with the odometry prior, producing the absolute pose fix that bounds drift.

JetbotLink — UDP transport with CRC framing and a receive thread.

AlphaBetaTracker — steady-state Kalman filter for the Linux rootfs bootstrap's progress readout (derivation).

JNI bridges — native_core_jni.cpp (estimation, map, telemetry, transport), rfb_jni.cpp (VNC pixels), linux_display_jni.cpp (frame pacing, bootstrap progress), ros2_stub_jni.cpp / ros2_jni.cpp (legacy ROS2Manager, UDP or DDS depending on the build).

docs.title: Application layer (Kotlin)
docs.text:
NativeCore — the only place Kotlin talks to the core. Verifies at startup that both sides agree on the telemetry and config array layouts, then exchanges one double[] per frame.

MainActivity — console: binds views, forwards operator intent, renders the telemetry snapshot at 25 Hz. No control logic.

LinuxEnvActivity / LinuxAppsActivity / LinuxLaunchActivity — the Linux environment: bootstrap, packages, session control, the app drawer, and the one launch path every shortcut goes through.

PRootRuntime — downloads the container runtime from the official Termux repository, verifies each package against the digest that repository publishes, unpacks ar → tar.xz into private storage, and self-tests by running proot --version so a device that refuses to execute it says so immediately.

Custom views — OccupancyMapView (hands its bitmap to the native rasteriser), TelemetryChartView (draws pre-decimated min/max pairs) and DetectionOverlayView.

docs.title: UDP link (default)
docs.text:
rclcpp cannot be cross-compiled into the APK for a normal Android build, so the app speaks a small binary UDP protocol to a bridge node on the robot. Full wire format: docs/JETBOT_LINK_PROTOCOL.md.

type direction payload 0x01 CmdWheel app → robot left, right wheel rate [rad/s] 0x02 CmdTwist app → robot v [m/s], ω [rad/s] 0x03 Heartbeat app → robot — 0x04 OwlQuery app → robot open-vocabulary detector prompt 0x05 SafetyCmd app → robot latch or release the emergency stop 0x10 StateOdom robot → app wheel rates, gyro z, yaw, battery, validity flags 0x11 Scan robot → app angle_min, angle_increment, ranges 0x12 PoseFix robot → app absolute pose with its covariance 0x13 Detections robot → app NanoOWL boxes, normalised to [0,1], with labels 0x14 NodeStatus robot → app graph health, detector rate, CPU/GPU/temperature

Types 0x04, 0x05 and 0x12–0x14 were added rather than changing any existing layout, so an older bridge and a newer app interoperate in both directions; tools/jetbot_bridge.py stays at the original set as the proof.

Framing is CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE; bad frames and sequence gaps are counted and shown in the console. The bridge must implement its own ~200 ms command watchdog, as the reference implementation does.

docs.title: ROS2 topics
docs.text:
When the native library is built inside a ROS2 workspace (find_package(rclcpp) succeeds for the target ABI), ROS2Manager publishes directly:

Topic Type Direction Description /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/Twist publish body twist command

Otherwise the same Kotlin API routes through the UDP transport, and the bridge republishes it. With tools/isaac_ros_bridge.py the full map is:

Topic Type Direction /jetbot/cmd_vel geometry_msgs/Twist bridge publishes /input_query std_msgs/String bridge publishes /safety/emergency_stop std_msgs/Bool bridge publishes /odometry nav_msgs/Odometry bridge subscribes /joint_states sensor_msgs/JointState bridge subscribes /imu sensor_msgs/Imu bridge subscribes /scan sensor_msgs/LaserScan bridge subscribes /output_detections vision_msgs/Detection2DArray bridge subscribes /input_image/camera_info sensor_msgs/CameraInfo bridge subscribes /diagnostics diagnostic_msgs/DiagnosticArray bridge subscribes

Every name is a command-line argument, so a remapped graph needs a different launch line rather than a code change.

docs.title: 🎨 Console layout
docs.text:
Watching a robot needs four answers at a glance — where is it, how fast is it going, is the link alive, what does it see. Everything that is not one of those is a number you consult, not one you monitor, so it lives in a drawer.

The console opens in UAV mode, because the vehicle is a multirotor, and the default link is MAVLink. It stays in UAV mode with no link at all:

  • the 3-D map replaces the floor plan;
  • the primary flight display sits bottom-left;
  • the strip under the map shows altitude, vertical speed, ground speed, heading, position σ and the voxel count;
  • the mode chip shows the vehicle state.

It switches to the ground-robot layout below only once a JetBot actually streams telemetry over JBL1. That switch is latched, so a short dropout does not swap the layout back. Picking JBL1 without a ground robot keeps the UAV layout, and the vehicle line says that JBL1 carries no flight data.

Always on screen

  • Map — full-screen occupancy grid with the travelled path and the robot pose; pinch to zoom, drag to pan, long-press to measure
  • Status strip — one dot and one phrase: ROS2 live · pose fixed, ROS2 live · odometry, link up · no telemetry or no link, plus battery
  • Speed — estimated v large, ω beside it
  • Perception card — live NanoOWL boxes in the camera frame, the strongest label, and the current prompt; 🔍 changes it, tapping the card opens VNC
  • Tool row — recentre, zoom, and a menu for save / load / clear map

Diagnostics drawer (the ⌃ button; closed by default, and while it is closed these values are not even formatted, so the UI thread does less work)

  • Pose, heading, position uncertainty, NIS, identified sensor noise, map counts
  • Raw wheel odometry against the fused estimate, for v and ω
  • Charts: the same pair drawn from natively decimated min/max envelopes
  • Isaac ROS graph: health and the node that reported it, detector rate, CPU, GPU, temperature, pose-fix count and age
  • Link: packet counters, loop rate and jitter, estimator consistency

Connections overlay — VNC and SSH endpoints, and the Linux environment (menu button)

docs.title: Control loop
docs.text:
Defaults live in jetbot::pipeline::PipelineConfig and are surfaced to the UI through NativeCore.defaultConfig(), so there is one source of truth:

parameter default meaning control period 20 ms nominal Ts; the loop measures its real period and uses that max linear / yaw 0.5 m/s, 2.0 rad/s envelope max accel 1.2 m/s², 6 rad/s² applied to the reference encoder / gyro cutoff 8 Hz, 12 Hz −3 dB points of the low-pass stage median window 5 rejects bursts of ≤ 2 bad samples σ accel / σ angular accel 0.8 m/s², 3.0 rad/s² EKF process noise watchdog 0.6 s telemetry silence before the loop opens wheel radius / base 32.5 mm / 112 mm stock Jetbot chassis

docs.title: Network setup
docs.text:
1. Phone and Jetson on the same network.
  2. Bridge listens on UDP 9600, app on UDP 9601 (both configurable).
  3. Permissions (INTERNET, ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE, ACCESS_WIFI_STATE) are declared in the manifest.

docs.title: Native core (no Android toolchain needed)
docs.text:
cmake -S app/src/main/cpp -B build-host
cmake --build build-host -j
./build-host/jetbot_core_tests        # 381 checks, 0 failures

Each check asserts a property that is derived by hand in docs/ESTIMATION_DESIGN.md or docs/LINUX_ENVIRONMENT.md: the exact −3 dB point of the pre-warped bilinear low-pass, Mehra's R̂ recovered from a known innovation sequence, the PID anti-wind-up fixed point, log-odds linearity, exact ICP recovery of a known transform, the CRC check value, an unbiased estimate against an exactly integrated unicycle, the alpha-beta pole modulus √(1−α), and the M/G/1 optimum ρ* = 1/(1+√(1+C_v²)). See app/src/main/cpp/tests/README.md.

docs.title: Link interoperability
docs.text:
python3 tools/jetbot_bridge.py --phone 127.0.0.1 --phone-port 9611 \
        --listen-port 9610 --dry-run &
./build-host/link_interop_test 9610 9611

Runs the app's transport and the robot bridge as two processes over real sockets, and checks the loop converges against a robot in another process.

The same test with --isaac additionally requires the pose fix, the detections and the graph status to survive the round trip, which is what keeps the Python codec in tools/jetbot_link.py and the C++ one in src/core/udp_link.cpp from drifting apart:

python3 tools/isaac_ros_bridge.py --phone 127.0.0.1 --phone-port 9611 \
        --listen-port 9610 --dry-run &
./build-host/link_interop_test 9610 9611 --isaac

docs.title: Isaac ROS message conversion (no ROS2 needed)
docs.text: python3 tools/test_isaac_ros_bridge.py   # 26 tests

docs.title: Android
docs.text:
./gradlew test                  # JVM unit tests
./gradlew connectedAndroidTest  # instrumented tests
./gradlew assembleDebug         # APK (requires SDK + NDK)

docs.title: Manual checklist
docs.text:
• Link comes up against the bridge; counters advance, no gaps
  • With the Isaac ROS bridge: status reads ROS2 live · pose fixed
  • The map fills in as scans arrive and the trail follows the estimate
  • Changing the detector prompt changes the labels that come back
  • Diagnostics drawer opens, shows graph health, and closes
  • Pulling the link trips the watchdog and the console says so
  • Map save / load round-trips
  • Linux: a guest installs, the desktop base installs, an app launches and its window renders

docs.title: Done in this revision
docs.text:
• Heavy processing moved to C++; Kotlin is the UI layer
  • Estimation chain with derivations and a property-based test suite
  • EKF state estimation with online noise identification
  • Log-odds occupancy mapping, ICP scan matching, map save/load
  • UDP transport with a reference ROS2 bridge
  • Native VNC pixel decoding
  • Linux environment with a WSLg-style display path
  • Robot control removed: this end observes and no longer commands

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Fix the adaptive noise-estimator collapse described under Known Limitations, so the gyro contributes to the fused yaw rate again
  • Camera stream into the minimap (MJPEG or H.264 over the link)
  • Loop closure and pose-graph optimisation on top of the scan matcher
  • Hextile / Tight RFB encodings (needs the decoder to drive the socket)
  • Recorded-telemetry replay for offline analysis

docs.title: 🐛 Known Limitations
docs.text:
• ICP along featureless walls — point-to-point correspondences slide along a long straight wall, so such a scan constrains the pose well across the wall and weakly along it. Mitigated by the odometry prior and by deriving the fix variance from the match residual; see §8 of the design document.
  • No ROS2 inside the APK — rclcpp is not cross-compiled for Android, so the default transport is the UDP link with a bridge node on the robot.
  • RFB encodings — only Raw, CopyRect and RRE are advertised, because those are the ones whose payload length follows from the rectangle header.
  • The adaptive noise estimator collapses on the odometry channels — Mehra's identity assumes white innovations, but the wheel rates are low-passed before forward kinematics, so consecutive innovations are correlated, R̂ is driven onto its positivity floor, and the EKF then treats odometry as near-exact. The measured consequence is that the gyro contributes nothing to the fused yaw rate. The host suite prints the numbers and deliberately asserts nothing; see §9 of the design document. This pre-dates the removal of the controllers.
  • The map has no loop closure — drift is bounded by scan matching but not eliminated over long traverses.
  • No simulator — the plant model went with the controllers, so the estimation chain is exercised by the host test suite rather than in the app.
  • targetSdk = 28 — a deliberate reduction in platform hardening, taken so the Linux environment can execute a runtime the phone downloaded. It rules out Google Play distribution and opts the whole app out of the Android 10+ behaviour changes, scoped storage included. See §3 of the Linux document; the alternative is to bundle PRoot and raise the target again.
  • An X server per Linux window — per-app windows give each app its own display, which is what makes Recents list them separately, and each one costs an X server. Eight run at a time; past that the launcher says so instead of thrashing. Turning the setting off puts everything back on one shared desktop.

docs.title: Estimation and perception design — Jetbot NanoOWL
docs.text:
Source

Snapshot of docs/ESTIMATION_DESIGN.md from TNG-Blue/JetbotNanoOWL at commit f2ccd4b (submodule Mobile/Android/JetbotNanoOWL). Regenerate with Scripts/mkdocs_hooks/snapshot_submodules.py after updating the submodule.

Every block in the app's sensor-to-state path is a discretisation of a named continuous-time design, with the derivation written out here and a property test in app/src/main/cpp/tests/test_main.cpp that checks the implementation still matches the mathematics. Nothing in the chain is tuned by feel alone: where a gain has a stability condition, the condition is enforced in code.

The app no longer controls the robot. The guidance laws (Kanayama tracker, polar pose stabiliser, cross-track LQR), the inner velocity loops (PID, MPC), the reference shaper, the inverse kinematics, the plant simulator and the operator surfaces that drove them were removed; this end observes. The sections they occupied are gone from this document and their derivations are in the git history. What is left is what still runs: conditioning, noise identification, estimation, odometry and mapping.

The PID of §5 survives because the Linux environment's display pacing loop uses it — see docs/LINUX_ENVIRONMENT.md §6.2, which together with §6.1 is derived in the same style and covered by the same host suite.

Section numbers are referenced from the source comments (§2, §5, …).

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
encoders ─┐
  gyro ─────┼─► median ─► low-pass ─► noise ID ─► EKF ─────────┐
  lidar ────┴────────────────────► ICP scan match ─► pose fix ─┤
                                                              │
                                        x̂ = [x y θ v ω] ◄──────┘
                                                              │
                          occupancy grid ◄── scan, at the estimated pose
                                                              │
                                 console: map, charts, diagnostics
                                                              ▲
                      UDP link  ◄── telemetry ◄── robot ───────┘

Implementation: jetbot::pipeline::EstimationPipeline (src/core/estimation_pipeline.cpp).

One loop, and it is an observer. The estimator runs at a fixed rate (50 Hz by default) and consumes whatever the link delivers. There is no actuator path: nothing this app computes is written back to the robot, and the link's wheel command and safety-stop messages, though still part of the wire protocol, are never sent from here.

Staleness is reported, not hidden. When telemetry stops arriving (time_since_sample > watchdog_timeout) the EKF keeps propagating its motion model, because that is still the best available prediction — but the output is flagged (feedback_valid = false, the source dot turns amber), because a pose that is pure dead reckoning is a different claim from one a measurement just corrected.

Why the heavy work is native. The loop must keep a fixed period regardless of what the Android UI thread is doing, so it runs on a native thread (nativeStartLoop). Per second, at the default settings, the core performs ~50 EKF predict/update cycles (5×5 matrices), ~10 ICP alignments, ~10 scan integrations touching ~10⁵ grid cells, and one full-viewport map rasterisation per UI frame. Measured on the host test machine, integrating a 360-beam scan into a 200×200 grid takes 0.21 ms, i.e. ~2 % of one 10 Hz period.

docs.title: 2. Sensor conditioning
docs.text: jetbot::filter — include/jetbot/filter/filters.h, src/core/filters.cpp.

docs.title: 2.1 Median pre-filter
docs.text: A window of length w = 2k+1 rejects any burst of at most k corrupted samples exactly. The median minimises Σ|x_i − m|, so a single arbitrarily large outlier cannot move it past its neighbours — no linear filter has this property, because a linear filter's output is an affine function of every input. Encoder counters produce exactly this kind of impulsive fault (a missed or doubled tick), which is why the non-linear stage comes first.

docs.title: 2.2 First-order low-pass, pre-warped bilinear
docs.text:
Target: H(s) = ω_c / (s + ω_c). Substituting the pre-warped bilinear map s = K(z−1)/(z+1) with K = ω_c / tan(ω_c T/2), and writing α = tan(ω_c T/2):

H(z) = α(1 + z⁻¹) / ((1+α) − (1−α)z⁻¹)

y[n] = a(x[n] + x[n−1]) + b y[n−1],   a = α/(1+α),  b = (1−α)/(1+α)

Properties, all verified in the tests:

  • DC gain exactly 1: 2a/(1−b) = 1 algebraically, so the filter cannot bias a velocity measurement.
  • −3 dB exactly at f_c: pre-warping maps the digital frequency ω_c to the analogue frequency ω_c, so |H(e^{jω_c T})| = 1/√2 with no frequency warping error. Without pre-warping the cutoff lands at (2/T)tan(ω_c T/2), which at f_c = 8 Hz, T = 20 ms is a 4 % error — small, but free to avoid.
  • Unconditionally stable: b ∈ (0,1) for every ω_c > 0.

OnePoleLowPass::magnitudeAt() evaluates the realised difference equation on the unit circle, so the UI and the tests read the true response of the code rather than of the ideal prototype.

docs.title: 2.3 Second-order Butterworth / notch
docs.text: Standard RBJ bilinear realisation with Q = 1/√2 (maximally flat). Available for chassis-resonance rejection; magnitudeAt() confirms unity DC gain, 1/√2 at the cutoff and monotone roll-off.

docs.title: 3. Noise identification
docs.text: jetbot::estimation — include/jetbot/estimation/noise_estimator.h.

docs.title: 3.1 Welford moments
docs.text:
mean_k = mean_{k−1} + (x_k − mean_{k−1})/k
M2_k   = M2_{k−1} + (x_k − mean_{k−1})(x_k − mean_k)
var    = M2_k/(k−1)

One pass, no catastrophic cancellation (Welford 1962; Knuth TAOCP vol. 2 §4.2.2). Used for the loop-period jitter monitor, where the mean dominates the variance by four orders of magnitude and the naive sum-of-squares form would lose all significance.

docs.title: 3.2 Innovation-based measurement-noise identification
docs.text:
For a Kalman filter the innovation ν_k = z_k − H x̂_k⁻ is zero-mean white with

C_ν = H P⁻ Hᵗ + R                                     (Mehra 1970)

so averaging the empirical innovation power over a sliding window and subtracting the model term identifies R without ever observing the true state:

R̂ = (1/N) Σ ν_k²  −  (1/N) Σ H P_k⁻ Hᵗ,    projected onto [floor, ceiling]

The projection is the Myers & Tapley (1976) positivity safeguard: without it a window where the innovations happen to be small would make R̂ negative and destroy the positive definiteness of the filter.

The same identity gives a consistency monitor, NIS = E[ν²/(HP⁻Hᵗ + R)] ≈ 1 for a correctly tuned filter; the console shows it, and the estimator indicator turns amber outside [0.2, 4].

A rejected alternative, for the record. The first implementation estimated the wheel-rate variance from the raw-minus-filtered residual. That residual contains the signal's high-frequency content as well as the noise, so under a manoeuvre it over-estimated the variance by ~70×, the filter stopped trusting odometry, and the velocity estimate became both laggy and noisy — which then destabilised the inner loop. The innovation-based estimator has no such coupling because the model term H P⁻ Hᵗ is subtracted explicitly.

docs.title: 4. State estimation — EKF
docs.text: jetbot::estimation::DiffDriveEKF — src/core/diff_drive_ekf.cpp. State x = [x, y, θ, v, ω]ᵗ.

docs.title: 4.1 Motion model
docs.text:
Exact integration of a constant twist over one sample (a circular arc), with the straight-line branch for |ω| ≤ 10⁻⁴ rad/s:

|ω| > ε:   x⁺ = x + (v/ω)(sin(θ + ωT) − sin θ)
           y⁺ = y − (v/ω)(cos(θ + ωT) − cos θ)
|ω| ≤ ε:   x⁺ = x + vT cos θ,   y⁺ = y + vT sin θ
           θ⁺ = wrap(θ + ωT),   v⁺ = v,   ω⁺ = ω

v and ω are random walks driven by white acceleration noise. Using the exact arc rather than an Euler step removes a systematic cross-track error of ½ v ω T² per step — at v = 0.3 m/s, ω = 1 rad/s, T = 20 ms that is 60 µm/step, i.e. 3 mm/s of accumulating bias, which dead reckoning would integrate without bound.

docs.title: 4.2 Jacobian
docs.text:
For the arc branch, with θ₁ = θ + ωT:

∂x⁺/∂θ = (v/ω)(cos θ₁ − cos θ)
∂x⁺/∂v = (sin θ₁ − sin θ)/ω
∂x⁺/∂ω = −(v/ω²)(sin θ₁ − sin θ) + (v/ω)T cos θ₁
∂y⁺/∂θ = (v/ω)(sin θ₁ − sin θ)
∂y⁺/∂v = −(cos θ₁ − cos θ)/ω
∂y⁺/∂ω =  (v/ω²)(cos θ₁ − cos θ) + (v/ω)T sin θ₁
∂θ⁺/∂ω = T

The straight-line branch uses the leading terms of the same expansion (∂x⁺/∂ω = −½vT² sin θ), which is why the threshold can be small without the Jacobian becoming singular.

docs.title: 4.3 Process noise
docs.text:
With σ_a, σ_α the 1-σ unmodelled linear and angular accelerations,

G = [½T²cos θ   0   ;  ½T²sin θ   0  ;  0   ½T²  ;  T   0  ;  0   T]
Q = G · diag(σ_a², σ_α²) · Gᵗ

the standard discretised continuous-white-noise-acceleration model (Bar-Shalom §6.2). Two parameters with physical units replace five covariance entries, which is what makes the filter tunable from the UI.

docs.title: 4.4 Measurement models
docs.text:
source H R wheel odometry (v, ω) rows selecting v, ω identified per §3.2 rate gyro row selecting ω identified per §3.2 absolute yaw row selecting θ, wrapped residual fixed ICP pose fix rows selecting x, y, θ from the match RMSE (§11) MAVLink ODOMETRY I₅, θ residual wrapped blockdiag(R_pose 3×3, R_twist 2×2) from the source, mapped exactly (MAVLINK_LINK.md §5), carried forward over the measured delay: F R Fᵀ + Q(τ) (§8 there)

A part of ODOMETRY whose covariance is unknown or not positive definite is not fused, and it is never replaced by a constant. Positive definiteness is tested by Cholesky with pivots above float32 round-off. With one valid part, that part alone is fused through the 3×3 or 2×2 rows, without compensation.

docs.title: 4.5 Joseph-form update
docs.text:
S = H P⁻ Hᵗ + R,   K = P⁻ Hᵗ S⁻¹
P⁺ = (I − KH) P⁻ (I − KH)ᵗ + K R Kᵗ

Algebraically equal to (I−KH)P⁻, but positive semi-definite even under round-off (Bar-Shalom §5.2.3). Every angular residual passes through wrapAngle, and the covariance diagonal has a 10⁻⁹ floor so the filter cannot become so confident that it ignores new measurements.

Verified: over a 60 s noisy arc, estimated velocity error is <25 % of raw odometry error and yaw-rate error <10 %; the time-averaged estimate is unbiased to 0.01; mean NIS stays in the consistency band; P stays symmetric and positive on the diagonal; a pose fix moves the estimate toward the measurement.

docs.title: 5. PID
docs.text:
jetbot::control::PIDController — src/core/pid.cpp.

This is the one controller still in the tree. It no longer drives the robot; its only consumer is the IMC-tuned loop that paces the Linux desktop's frame requests (docs/LINUX_ENVIRONMENT.md §6.2). The derivation is kept here because that loop depends on every property below.

Continuous law (Åström & Hägglund, Advanced PID Control, ch. 3):

u = Kp(b·r − y) + (Ki/s)(r − y) − (Kd·s/(1 + Tf·s))·y
  • derivative on −y only: a setpoint step cannot produce a derivative kick;
  • the derivative is low-passed with Tf, bounding its high-frequency gain at Kd/Tf instead of letting measurement noise through with gain Kd·ω;
  • b < 1 softens the response to setpoint steps without changing the disturbance-rejection loop shape.

Discretisation (backward Euler, exact at DC):

D[k] = (Tf/(Tf+T))·D[k−1] − (Kd/(Tf+T))·(y[k] − y[k−1])
I[k] = I[k−1] + Ki·T·e[k] + (T/Tt)·(u_applied[k−1] − u_unsat[k−1])

docs.title: 5.1 Anti-wind-up, with a closed-form check
docs.text:
The last term is back-calculation. While the actuator is saturated the integrator is driven toward the value that makes the controller output achievable, with time constant Tt. At steady state the update is zero, so

0 = Ki·e + (1/Tt)(u_sat − u_unsat)   ⟹   I* = u_sat − Kp·b·r + Kp·y + Ki·Tt·e

For the test case (Kp=1, Ki=5, Tt=0.1, e=r=10, y=0, u_sat=1) this predicts I* = 1 − 10 + 5 = −4, and the implementation lands on −4 to 10⁻⁶. The same run without anti-wind-up (Tt → ∞) charges the integrator to Ki·e·t = 500, i.e. 125× further, and takes 100× longer to leave saturation.

u_applied is an optional input: the pipeline passes the command that actually reached the actuator, so the integrator back-calculates against reality (external anti-wind-up / tracking mode) rather than against the controller's own clamp. This is what keeps the integrator honest when the reference shaper or the wheel-speed saturation of §6 has reduced the command.

docs.title: 6. Differential-drive odometry
docs.text:
jetbot::control — src/core/diff_drive_kinematics.cpp.

inverse:  v_r = v + ωL/2,  v_l = v − ωL/2,   ω_i = v_i/r
forward:  v   = r(ω_r + ω_l)/2,  ω = r(ω_r − ω_l)/L

docs.title: 6.1 Variance propagation
docs.text:
With independent wheel-rate noise of variance σ_ω²:

var(v) = r²σ_ω²/2,      var(ω) = 2r²σ_ω²/L²

so the ratio between the two channels is var(ω)/var(v) = 4/L². For the stock Jetbot (L = 112 mm) that is 319 rad²/m²: the same wheel-rate noise is amplified into the yaw channel far more strongly than into the linear one, because a narrow wheel base means a small rate difference implies a large yaw rate. That is the quantitative reason the gyro carries most of the weight on ω in §4.4, and it falls out of the kinematics rather than out of a tuning session.

docs.title: 7. Occupancy mapping
docs.text:
jetbot::mapping::OccupancyGrid — src/core/occupancy_grid.cpp.

Under the standard assumptions of cell independence and a static world, recursive Bayes over measurements z_{1:t} gives, in odds form,

odds(m_i | z_{1:t}) = odds(m_i | z_t) · odds(m_i | z_{1:t−1}) / odds(m_i)

and taking logarithms turns the product into a sum:

l_{i,t} = l_{i,t−1} + log( p(m_i|z_t)/(1 − p(m_i|z_t)) ) − l_{i,0}

With a uniform prior (l_{i,0} = 0) the increments are the two constants log(p_hit/(1−p_hit)) for the beam endpoint and log(p_miss/(1−p_miss)) for every cell the beam passed through, so integrating a scan costs one addition per traversed cell (Thrun, Burgard & Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, §9.2). That is the whole reason for the log-odds parameterisation, and it is what makes a 360-beam scan affordable at 10 Hz on a phone.

Cells along a beam are selected with Bresenham's integer line algorithm: exact, symmetric, and free of floating-point drift. Log-odds are clamped to [l_min, l_max] so the map stays responsive to change instead of saturating permanently. Recovering the probability is p = 1 − 1/(1 + e^l).

Verified: the prior reads 0.5 everywhere; the endpoint becomes occupied and the traversed cells free; k repeated hits give exactly k·log(p_hit/(1−p_hit)) until the clamp; the clamp holds; save/load round-trips geometry and log-odds bit-for-bit; the rasteriser writes an opaque ARGB word for every pixel of the viewport, and its device-byte-order path is exactly the red/blue swap of the logical one.

docs.title: 8. Scan matching (ICP)
docs.text:
jetbot::mapping::alignScans — src/core/scan_matcher.cpp.

Alternates the two standard steps (Besl & McKay 1992):

  1. correspondence — nearest target point per source point, with a gating radius that rejects outliers;
  2. minimisation — the rigid transform minimising Σ‖R(θ)q_i + t − p_i‖². Removing both centroids decouples translation from rotation, and the rotation has the closed form (the 2-D case of Kabsch/Umeyama)
θ* = atan2( Σ(q_ix p_iy − q_iy p_ix),  Σ(q_ix p_ix + q_iy p_iy) )
t* = mean(p) − R(θ*)·mean(q)

Each iteration is therefore exactly optimal for its correspondence set, and the cost is monotonically non-increasing.

ICP is a local method, so the pipeline always seeds it with the odometry prior — the relative motion the EKF believes has happened since the previous scan, expressed in the previous scan's frame. The result is composed back onto the previous scan pose and fed to DiffDriveEKF::updatePose with a variance taken from the match RMSE, so a loose fit cannot drag the estimate around. This is the measurement that bounds odometry drift: without an exteroceptive fix the position error of any dead-reckoning chain grows without bound.

Known limitation, stated rather than hidden: point-to-point correspondences slide along long featureless walls, so a wall-only scan is well constrained in the normal direction and weakly constrained along it. That is a property of the cost function; the prior plus the RMSE-derived variance is what keeps it from hurting the estimate. The tests check both cases — exact recovery of a known transform on a well-conditioned cloud, and a bounded residual on a wall-like scan seeded with the prior.

docs.title: 9. Verification
docs.text:
The native core is platform independent, so the same code that runs on the phone is exercised by a host test suite:

cmake -S app/src/main/cpp -B build-host
cmake --build build-host -j
./build-host/jetbot_core_tests

381 checks, 0 failures at the time of writing. Coverage by area:

area what is asserted filters analytic DC gain and −3 dB point, roll-off, notch rejection, median outlier rejection noise ID Welford mean/variance recovery, Mehra R̂ recovery from a known innovation sequence, NIS ≈ 1 EKF error reduction vs raw odometry, unbiasedness, NIS consistency band, covariance symmetry and positivity, pose-fix correction PID integral action, proportional path, clamping, analytic anti-wind-up fixed point, 50× improvement over the naive form, external anti-wind-up fixed point, bounded derivative gain (kept for the display pacer of §6.2 in LINUX_ENVIRONMENT.md) odometry forward map against its closed form, in-place rotation, variance propagation mapping log-odds linearity and clamping, ray-cast free/occupied classification, timing, save/load round trip, rasteriser output ICP exact transform recovery, residual RMSE, inlier count, wall-like scan with prior transport CRC-16/CCITT check value, packet round trip, single-bit corruption detection, loopback delivery MAVLink CRC-16/MCRF4XX check value, ODOMETRY and observer HEARTBEAT byte-exact against pymavlink, resync and noise immunity, exact heading map over 500 attitudes, Σ_enu = J Σ_ned Jᵀ, refusal of unknown/zero/singular covariances, posterior (P⁻¹+R⁻¹)⁻¹, watchdog fed by ODOMETRY, loopback with vehicle lock and gap counting, excess-delay estimate with the clock offset cancelled, latency compensation landing on the present state with E[NIS] = 5, stream mode for the relay (MAVLINK_LINK.md §10) UAV (6-DoF) OBSTACLE_DISTANCE byte-exact against pymavlink, ODOMETRY → 6-DoF measurement (frames, Euler-rate Jacobian, twist signs), SO(3) Exp/Shepperd/ZYX/slerp, exact CWNA Q composition, velocity Jacobian by finite differences, Monte-Carlo NEES/NIS = 6, latency compensation, attitude carried forward, voxel traversal properties, log-odds model, fan placement on a tilted vehicle, renderer projection and depth test (UAV_3D.md §6) RFB raw/copyrect/RRE decoding, bounds rejection, RGB565 scaling, device byte order pipeline unbiased velocity and yaw-rate estimates over a settled window against an exactly integrated unicycle, online noise identification, watchdog staleness, covariance shrinking on a pose fix, bounded dead-reckoning drift, map built from the estimated pose progress tracker Kalata's gain pairing, complex pole pair of modulus exactly √(1−α), Jury region, exact convergence on a ramp, noise rejection against the raw difference quotient, stall handling (docs/LINUX_ENVIRONMENT.md §6.1) display pacing ρ* at its analytic anchors, grid search reproducing ρ* and L* (confirming the convexity argument), closed-loop settling point against a mis-modelled plant, utilisation guard through a stall, anti-wind-up recovery, spike rejection (docs/LINUX_ENVIRONMENT.md §6.2)

Known issue, surfaced by the estimator test. The adaptive measurement-noise estimator of §3.2 collapses onto its positivity floor for the odometry channels. Mehra's identity assumes a white innovation sequence, but the wheel rates are low-passed before forward kinematics, so consecutive innovations are strongly correlated: mean(ν²) then measures the step-to-step change rather than the measurement noise, comes out below H P⁻ Hᵀ, and the difference is projected onto the floor. The odometry channel is thereafter treated as near-exact, its Kalman gain goes to one, the state follows odometry, the innovations stay small, and the collapse sustains itself — so the gyro contributes nothing to the fused yaw rate. The test prints the numbers (ratio 1.0000) and deliberately asserts nothing, since the only honest assertion would pin the defect in place. This pre-dates the removal of the controllers.

The Android build itself (./gradlew assembleDebug) requires the Android SDK and NDK and is not run by this suite.

docs.title: Driving the Isaac ROS graph from the console
docs.text:
Source

Snapshot of docs/ISAAC_ROS_INTEGRATION.md from TNG-Blue/JetbotNanoOWL at commit f2ccd4b (submodule Mobile/Android/JetbotNanoOWL). Regenerate with Scripts/mkdocs_hooks/snapshot_submodules.py after updating the submodule.

How the Android console gets its data from Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL and sends commands back, without a single change to that repository.

Two transports. This page covers JBL1 through tools/isaac_ros_bridge.py. The Isaac repository also has its own MAVLink node, ros2_network_bridge, and the console can read it instead. That path gives pose and twist with full covariances, battery and status texts, but no scan or detections. See MAVLINK_LINK.md. Only one transport is open at a time; the choice is in Settings → ROS2 Connection.

docs.title: Why a bridge and not rclcpp on the phone
docs.text:
ROS2 is a peer-to-peer DDS network. Putting a participant on a phone means cross-compiling rclcpp and the type support for the Android ABI, and then relying on multicast discovery across a Wi-Fi link that usually blocks it. The app can be built that way — app/src/main/cpp/CMakeLists.txt uses rclcpp when it finds it — but the supported path is a small node on the Jetson that subscribes with DDS, where DDS works well, and forwards over one UDP socket, where a phone works well.

The bridge is tools/isaac_ros_bridge.py. It is an ordinary ROS2 node: it subscribes to topics the Isaac ROS graph already publishes and publishes to topics it already subscribes to. Every topic name is a command-line argument, so a remapped graph needs a different launch line, not a different bridge.

docs.title: Topic map
docs.text:
Direction Link packet ROS2 topic (default) Type console → robot 0x02 CmdTwist /jetbot/cmd_vel geometry_msgs/Twist console → robot 0x04 OwlQuery /input_query std_msgs/String console → robot 0x05 SafetyCmd /safety/emergency_stop std_msgs/Bool robot → console 0x10 StateOdom /joint_states, /imu sensor_msgs/JointState, sensor_msgs/Imu robot → console 0x11 Scan /scan sensor_msgs/LaserScan robot → console 0x12 PoseFix /odometry nav_msgs/Odometry robot → console 0x13 Detections /output_detections vision_msgs/Detection2DArray robot → console 0x14 NodeStatus /diagnostics diagnostic_msgs/DiagnosticArray robot → console (image size only) /input_image/camera_info sensor_msgs/CameraInfo

The defaults come from the Isaac ROS repository itself:

  • /jetbot/cmd_vel and /odometry are the remapped names in Source/ROS2_Control_System/launch/control_system.launch.py;
  • /input_query, /output_detections and /output_image are the NanoOWL node's own topics in Source/Isaac_ROS-Object_Detection/isaac_ros_objectdetection/OWL/;
  • /safety/emergency_stop and /diagnostics are published by Source/ROS2_Lidar_AI_Solution/src/safety/safety_zone_node.cpp.

docs.title: Where the data goes once it arrives
docs.text:
/joint_states ─┐
        /imu ────┼─▶ median ─▶ low-pass ─▶ noise ID ─▶ ┌──────┐
                 │                                     │ EKF  │─▶ state estimate
   /odometry ────┼──────────── pose fix (with R) ─────▶│      │       │
       /scan ────┴──▶ ICP scan match ─▶ pose fix ─────▶└──────┘       │
                                    └─▶ occupancy grid                │
                                                                      ▼
  operator ──▶ guidance (Manual │ Kanayama │ polar │ LQR) ──▶ inner loop (PID │ MPC)
                                                                      │
                                    rate & jerk limit ─▶ inverse kinematics
                                                                      │
                                                          /jetbot/cmd_vel ─▶ robot
                                                                      │
                          measured wheel rates close both loops ◀─────┘

The chain is unchanged from ESTIMATION_DESIGN.md; what the Isaac ROS graph adds is the pose fix, and it matters more than the topic count suggests.

A differential drive that integrates wheel rates has heading variance growing linearly in time and position error growing with its integral — the estimate drifts without bound, and no amount of filtering fixes that, because the information simply is not there. /odometry is an exteroceptive measurement in a fixed frame, so it bounds the error. It is applied as an ordinary Kalman update (ControlPipeline::applyPoseFix), weighted by the covariance the publisher supplied.

That last part is why the bridge floors the variance. A node that leaves pose.covariance at zero — a common placeholder — is claiming a perfect measurement; taken literally the Kalman gain goes to 1, the filter throws away its own prediction, and the estimate jumps to the fix on every message. --min-var-xy and --min-var-yaw (default 1e-4) are the floor, and the receiver rejects a non-positive variance outright.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
On the Jetson, with the Isaac ROS graph already up:

# workspace sourced as usual, e.g.
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
source ~/workspaces/isaac_ros-dev/install/setup.bash

python3 tools/isaac_ros_bridge.py --phone 192.168.1.50

tools/jetbot_link.py must sit next to it — it holds the wire format shared with the C++ side.

In the console: ☰ → Settings → ROS2 Connection, choose JBL1, set the Jetson's address and Save. Ports default to 9600 on the robot and 9601 on the phone.

A graph with different names:

python3 tools/isaac_ros_bridge.py --phone 192.168.1.50 \
    --cmd-vel-topic /jetbot/cmd_vel \
    --odom-topic /odometry/filtered \
    --scan-topic /ld19/scan \
    --detections-topic /output_detections

A chassis that is not the stock Jetbot:

python3 tools/isaac_ros_bridge.py --phone 192.168.1.50 \
    --wheel-radius 0.0325 --wheel-base 0.112 \
    --left-joint wheel_left_joint --right-joint wheel_right_joint

--help lists every topic and chassis parameter.

docs.title: Trying it without a robot
docs.text:
python3 tools/isaac_ros_bridge.py --phone 192.168.1.50 --dry-run

No ROS2 needed. The bridge simulates a differential drive, a lidar in a square room and a detector watching two landmarks, and emits the full packet set — enough to bring up the link, the estimator, the map, the detection overlay and the graph-health panel before any of it meets the Jetson.

The console has its own simulation as well, and the two answer different questions. Simulation mode in the console (Settings → simulation) runs the plant model inside the app, so nothing leaves the phone: it exercises the control chain and the perception overlay with no network at all. --dry-run exercises the transport as well, over real sockets.

docs.title: The detector prompt
docs.text:
NanoOWL is open vocabulary: there is no fixed class list, and the prompt on the query topic is the class list. The console's 🔍 button on the perception card sets it, sends it as 0x04, and the bridge republishes it on /input_query.

Two details about the Isaac ROS node shape how the bridge handles the result:

  • it publishes boxes in pixels, so the bridge normalises them against the camera resolution — from /input_image/camera_info when that is available, otherwise from --image-width / --image-height;
  • it sets hypothesis.class_id to the index of the matched phrase in the query, and leaves hypothesis.score unset. The bridge resolves the index back to the phrase by splitting the query exactly the way the node does (prompt.strip("][()").split(",")), and forwards the missing score as 0, which the console renders as a label with no percentage rather than as 0 %.

If the graph is restarted the prompt has to be restated, so the app resends it on every connect.

docs.title: Checking the two codecs still agree
docs.text:
The wire format has two implementations — udp_link.cpp and jetbot_link.py — and they are checked against each other over real sockets:

cmake -S app/src/main/cpp -B build-host && cmake --build build-host -j
g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Iapp/src/main/cpp/include -Iapp/src/main/cpp \
    tools/link_interop_test.cpp -Lbuild-host -ljetbot_core -lpthread -o link_interop_test

python3 tools/isaac_ros_bridge.py --phone 127.0.0.1 --dry-run &
./link_interop_test 9600 9601 --isaac

--isaac requires the pose fix, the detections and the graph status as well as the original packet types. The message conversion itself is covered separately, without ROS2:

python3 tools/test_isaac_ros_bridge.py
