docs.title: HexacopterSystem::PreUpdate — one physics step
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A(["PreUpdate(info, ecm)"]) --> B{"configured and not paused?"}
    B -- no --> Z(["return"])
    B -- yes --> C["read pose, v, ω, a from the ECM"]
    C --> D["apply queued faults and commands<br/>(arm refused until at-rest calibration done)"]
    D --> E["BMI088 IMU + MS5611 baro models<br/>(σ = N·√f_s, biases)"]
    E --> F{"autopilot?"}
    F -- yes --> G["FlightController.step: gyro LPF · Mahony · KF[z, v, b]<br/>altitude → climb PI → thrust; attitude P → rate PI → torque<br/>allocation (min-norm, priorities, failed rotors) → ω_ref × 12"]
    F -- no --> H["ω_ref from /hexa/motor_speed_cmd"]
    G --> I["12 × ESC/BLDC at 20 kHz over the step:<br/>FOC current IMC, Luenberger observer, speed PI + FF,<br/>fault detection"]
    H --> I
    I --> J["AddWorldWrench: thrust, reaction,<br/>gyroscopic torque, drag"]
    J --> K{"mcu_link?"}
    K -- yes --> L["virtual MCU: IMU 1 kHz, encoders 1 kHz,<br/>attitude 100 Hz, GNSS 10 Hz → UDP frames"]
    K -- no --> M
    L --> M["publish /hexa/motor_speeds, state_estimate, status<br/>(at the publish rate) + optional CSV log"]
    I -. "rotor failed flags" .-> G
    J -. "body motion → next ECM state (closed loop)" .-> C

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
# ROS 2 Humble + Gazebo Harmonic
sudo apt install ros-humble-ros-gzharmonic libeigen3-dev libyaml-cpp-dev
colcon build --packages-up-to ros2_hexacopter_gazebo
source install/setup.bash                       # sets GZ_SIM_SYSTEM_PLUGIN_PATH

ros2 launch ros2_hexacopter_gazebo hexacopter_sim.launch.py      # gui:=false for headless
# wait ~2 s (at-rest gyro/accel calibration), then:
ros2 topic pub --once /hexa/arm std_msgs/msg/Bool "{data: true}"
ros2 topic pub -r 20 /hexa/cmd geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {z: 1.0}}"          # climb
ros2 topic pub -r 20 /hexa/cmd geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{angular: {x: 0.15}}"        # roll
ros2 topic pub --once /hexa/fault/open_circuit std_msgs/msg/Int32 "{data: 4}"       # kill motor 4
ros2 topic echo /hexa/status          # [armed, calibrated, healthy rotors, rp scale, yaw scale, NIS]
ros2 topic hz /imu/data               # MCU link → jetowl_bridge: 1 kHz
ros2 topic echo /gps/fix --once       # WGS-84 fix with covariance
ros2 topic echo /diagnostics          # link loss, clock, per-stream watchdogs

ros2 run ros2_hexacopter_control hexa_design_report                 # gains, margins, SIL: PASS/FAIL
colcon test --packages-select ros2_hexacopter_control ros2_hexacopter_description ros2_hexacopter_gazebo

Without ROS (plain CMake, e.g. on a CI runner with libgz-sim8-dev):

cmake -S Gazebo/ROS2_Hexacopter_Gazebo -B build && cmake --build build -j
HEXA_PLUGIN_DIR=$PWD/build python3 -m pytest Gazebo/ROS2_Hexacopter_Gazebo/test -q   # both SIL tests

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
gz topic (ROS topic via bridge) Type Dir Meaning /hexa/cmd Twist in angular.x roll [rad], angular.y pitch [rad], angular.z yaw rate [rad/s], linear.z climb rate [m/s] /hexa/arm Boolean / std_msgs/Bool in refused until the 2 s at-rest calibration completes /hexa/fault/open_circuit, /hexa/fault/propeller Int32 in fault injection, rotor index 0–11 /hexa/motor_speed_cmd Actuators in 12 speeds [rad/s] when autopilot:=false (external autopilot) /hexa/motor_speeds Actuators out ESC speed estimates (gz side) /hexa/state_estimate Pose out estimated attitude, altitude in position.z /hexa/status Float_V / ros_gz_interfaces/Float32Array out armed, calibrated, healthy rotors, allocation scales, baro NIS /hexa/ground_truth/odometry nav_msgs/Odometry out evaluation only UDP 9870 → jetowl_bridge sensor-link frames out IMU, IMU info, GNSS, 12 encoders, attitude, heartbeat (mcu_link:=true) UDP 9871 TIME_SYNC_REQUEST in time-sync service of the virtual MCU

Rotor numbering: arm i at azimuth 30° + 60°·i (nose between arms 0 and 5); rotor 2i is the upper rotor, 2i+1 the lower one; upper rotors spin CCW on even arms.

docs.title: Control design (summary — full derivations in the headers of ros2_hexacopter_control)
docs.text:
Stage Choice Numbers (from hexa_design_report) Propulsion momentum-theory k_T = C_T ρ D⁴/4π², k_Q = C_P ρ D⁵/8π³; lower rotor ×0.8 T/W = 3.46 (6S); 2.28 with the 4S of the MATLAB config Motor surface PMSM dq model, ω_e L cross-coupling, voltage circle V_bus/√2 ω_max 855 / 909 rad/s ESC current IMC PI K_p = ω_ci L, K_i = ω_ci R, decoupling, 1-PWM delay ω_ci = 6283 rad/s, PM 63° ESC speed Luenberger observer on the 14-bit encoder (triple pole 600 rad/s) + PI pole placement + exact FF PM ≥ 69.5°, GM ≥ 24 dB (±20 %) ESC failsafe speed-error, observer-load and observer-residual tests healthy residual ≤ 0.33 counts, prop-loss ≥ 70 → threshold 5 Allocation min-norm pseudo-inverse, priority roll/pitch > yaw > thrust rank 4 with any single rotor removed Rate PI, crossover placed exactly (30 / 30 / 12 rad/s), gyroscopic FF, yaw-torque LPF worst GM 17.3 dB, PM 65.3° (±20 % I, m, k_T, J_r) Attitude quaternion P (Lyapunov V = 1 − |q_w|), separation 5 PM ≥ 53° Vertical KF [z, v, b_a] + climb PI pole placement + slew/FF, altitude P PM ≥ 71.8° / 88.7° Attitude estimate Mahony, K_P = 2ζω_c, K_I = ω_c², ω_c = 0.05 rad/s, gyro bias calibrated at rest see limits

Two findings of the analysis that changed the design:

  1. Yaw is actuated by the motor reaction torque −s(J ω̇ + k_Q ω²), not by the aerodynamic torque the allocator assumes. That adds a zero at 2.4 rad/s. Above it the yaw actuator behaves like a differentiator, and without a yaw-torque low-pass the yaw loop drops below GM = 6 dB at −20 % inertia (test_design.cpp: YawFilterIsNecessary).
  2. On a multirotor the accelerometer measures thrust, not gravity, during horizontal acceleration, so tilt is not observable from it (Martin & Salaün 2010). With the sensor-noise-optimal crossover of 1.4 rad/s the attitude estimate was pulled level during a 0.2 rad roll and the vehicle kept rolling. With ω_c = 0.05 rad/s and the gyro bias calibrated at rest, the pull is ≤ 10 % after 2 s.

docs.title: Verification evidence
docs.text: Level What Result Frequency domain 171 loop checks: every loop nominal + 16 corners of ±20 % (I, m, k_T, J_rotor) all GM ≥ 6 dB, PM ≥ 45° (current loop ≥ 30°) Unit (gtest, 6 suites) airframe, allocation, ESC, design, estimators, flight SIL all pass 6-DOF SIL (no Gazebo) hover RMS 4.9 cm; roll step 0.2 rad 7.2 % overshoot; climb 1 m/s < 10 % overshoot; each of the 12 motors failed in turn; propeller loss; plant ±20 % all pass Gazebo SIL (headless gz sim, test_gazebo_sil.py) take-off, climb 1 m/s, hover (RMS 0.56 cm), roll step, motor 4 open-circuit at 15 s all pass: detected in 0.31 s, 3.1 cm altitude loss, max tilt 0.049 rad Gazebo, live topics arm/cmd/fault over gz-transport; propeller loss on rotor 7 2.3 cm altitude dip, tilt 0.043 rad, status reports 11 healthy Gazebo SIL, MCU link (test_mcu_link_sil.py) take-off and hover received by the Jetson-side decoder over UDP IMU/encoders 1000 Hz, GNSS 10 Hz, attitude 100 Hz, 0 lost, 0 CRC errors; hover speeds 448.6 / 501.5 rad/s (design 449 / 502); GNSS fix at the origin ROS 2 launch, headless (ROS 2 Jazzy + Harmonic) hexacopter_sim.launch.py gui:=false /imu/data 996 Hz, /encoders/joint_states 998 Hz, /gps/fix STATUS_FIX, /diagnostics loss 0.00 %

docs.title: Assumptions and limits
docs.text:
• Airframe mass/inertia, lower-rotor efficiency, rotor drag, pole pairs and the 6S bus are assumptions ([A] in the YAML). Identify them on a thrust stand and with a bifilar pendulum, then re-run hexa_design_report. The gains follow automatically.
  • The MATLAB configs (MATLAB/scripts/control/Config*_Hexacopter.m) describe a 6-motor/1.5 kg vehicle with hand-set gains. They are not used here and are not consistent with this model.
  • Tilt/accelerometer-bias and yaw are not observable without velocity or heading aiding. In Gazebo the true tilt differs from the estimate by ≈ 0.027 rad (20 mg bias) and yaw drifts slowly. Horizontal position/velocity hold therefore needs GNSS or optical flow and a magnetometer (not in scope). The interface is attitude + climb rate, for a pilot or for the outer loops of Source/ROS2_Flight_Controller.
  • Rotor wake interaction is a constant efficiency; ground effect, blade flapping, battery sag and ESC thermal limits are not modelled.
  • Verified with gz-sim 8.15 (OSRF packages) on Ubuntu 24.04; the ROS 2 launch file was run with ROS 2 Jazzy (same launch/rclcpp API as Humble), not with Humble.
  • The MCU link has been verified in simulation only; the STM32N6 firmware side is not written yet (see ros2_jetowl_bridge "MCU firmware integration").

docs.title: ros2_mcu_emulator — virtual MCU for Gazebo
docs.text:
Source

This page is rendered from Gazebo/ROS2_Mcu_Emulator/README.md, the authoritative description kept next to the code in Gazebo/ROS2_Mcu_Emulator/.

On the vehicle the IMU, GNSS receiver and encoders are read by the MCU, which sends them to the Jetson over Ethernet (ros2_jetowl_bridge, sensor link). In simulation this package takes the MCU's place: it samples Gazebo ground truth through datasheet error models and sends the same UDP frames (same C encoder, protocol.c) to the same Jetson driver. The ROS nodes in Source/ cannot tell simulation from the vehicle.

Part Content geodesy.hpp WGS-84 geodetic ⇄ ECEF ⇄ local ENU (exact; Groves §2.4) sensor_models.hpp IMU (Allan white noise, turn-on + Gauss–Markov bias, saturation), GNSS (Gauss–Markov position error, velocity noise, latency, epoch stamping), encoder quantiser virtual_mcu.hpp MCU link firmware: frames with protocol.c, non-blocking UDP, time-sync service, MCU clock with optional offset/skew McuEmulatorSystem gz-sim 8 system plugin for any model: link IMU/GNSS + joint encoders

The hexacopter plugin (HexacopterSystem) links the library directly, so the frames carry the very IMU sample its flight controller used and the ESC rotor angles.

docs.title: Use with any model
docs.text:
<plugin filename="McuEmulatorSystem" name="mcu_emulator::McuEmulatorSystem">
  <link_name>base_link</link_name>
  <remote_host>127.0.0.1</remote_host> <remote_port>9870</remote_port>
  <command_port>9871</command_port>
  <imu>
    <rate>1000</rate>
    <gyro_noise_density>2.443e-4</gyro_noise_density>
    <accel_noise_density>1.716e-3</accel_noise_density>
    <mount_rpy>3.14159 0 0</mount_rpy>        <!-- IMU upside down: announced to the Jetson -->
  </imu>
  <gnss>
    <rate>10</rate> <latency>0.05</latency>
    <reference_latitude>10.7769</reference_latitude>
    <reference_longitude>106.7009</reference_longitude>
    <reference_height>10.0</reference_height>
  </gnss>
  <encoders>
    <rate>200</rate> <counts_per_rev>4096</counts_per_rev>
    <joint>left_wheel_joint</joint> <joint>right_wheel_joint</joint>
  </encoders>
</plugin>

then ros2 launch ros2_jetowl_bridge jetowl_bridge.launch.py fc:=false sensor_link:=true sim:=true (set sensor_link.encoder.joint_names and sensor_link.encoder.accel_std for the vehicle). All SDF elements and their defaults are listed at the top of src/mcu_emulator_system.cpp. GZ_SIM_SYSTEM_PLUGIN_PATH is set by this package's environment hook.

docs.title: Error models
docs.text:
Sensor Model Parameters (defaults) Reference Gyro / accel white noise n ~ N(0, N²·f_s) per sample BMI088: N_g = 2.443e-4 rad/s/√Hz, N_a = 1.716e-3 m/s²/√Hz, 1 kHz IEEE Std 952-1997 Annex C Turn-on bias b₀ ~ N(0, σ_b0²) 0.5 °/s, 20 mg BMI088 datasheet In-run bias b[k+1] = φb[k] + w, φ = e^{−T/τ}, w ~ N(0, B²(1−φ²)) ⇒ stationary σ = B τ = 100 s, B_g = 9.7e-6 rad/s, B_a = 3.9e-4 m/s² [A] first-order Gauss–Markov Saturation clip at full scale, status flag ±2000 °/s, ±24 g BMI088 GNSS position per ENU axis e[k+1] = φe[k] + w, exact discretisation σ_h = 1.27 m (1.5 m CEP / 1.1774), σ_v = 2.5 m [A], τ = 60 s [A] Rankin, IEEE PLANS 1994; u-blox NEO-M9N GNSS velocity white 0.05 m/s NEO-M9N GNSS timing epoch k/f, delivered after latency L, stamped at the epoch f = 10 Hz, L = 50 ms [A] time-pulse capture GNSS geodesy ENU → ECEF → (φ, λ, h), 1e-7 deg / mm wire resolution reference point in SDF WGS-84, Groves §2.4 Encoder ⌊θ/Δ⌋ into an int32 counter CPR from SDF / physical YAML —

The GNSS receiver reports h_acc = σ_h, v_acc = σ_v, s_acc = σ_vel; the test ConsistentWithDriverCovariance closes the loop through the Jetson driver's covariance: the NIS of position and velocity averages 3.0 ± 0.3 (χ²₃) over 50 000 epochs.

docs.title: MCU clock
docs.text: t_mcu = (1 + skew)·t_sim + offset in µs. With the defaults (0, 0) the MCU clock is the simulation clock and the driver uses clock.mode: passthrough. Setting <clock_offset> / <clock_skew_ppm> exercises the driver's Kalman clock synchronisation in SIL (test_virtual_mcu: ClockSynchronisationThroughTheTimeSyncService, 7.25 s / 30 ppm → stamp error < 20 µs).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
colcon test --packages-select ros2_mcu_emulator    # 3 gtest suites + headless Gazebo test
# or: cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build -j && (cd build && ctest)
Suite Checks test_geodesy known points (equator, pole = b), 2000 random round trips < 1e-11 rad / 0.1 mm, 1 m north = 1/M rad test_sensor_models GNSS stationary variance and ρ(τ) = e⁻¹, latency/epoch stamping, NIS vs. driver covariance, outage; IMU noise variance and bias, saturation; encoder quantisation and int32 wrap test_virtual_mcu virtual MCU → UDP → LinkDecoder: IMU with mounting rotation from IMU_INFO, GNSS, 2 encoders, 0 loss; time-sync service with offset/skew test_mcu_emulator_gazebo.py gz sim -s with McuEmulatorSystem on a box + wheel (JointController 10 rad/s), IMU mounted upside down: 1 kHz IMU, 200 Hz encoder, 5 Hz GNSS, 0 loss; +g in base_link after the announced mount rotation; wheel speed within 3σ of 10 rad/s; fix at the reference

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• No lever arm: the IMU is at the link origin (add ω×(ω×r) + ω̇×r if it matters).
  • No magnetometer, barometer or multipath/outage statistics (outage only on command).
  • The GNSS error τ and vertical σ are assumptions, not receiver measurements.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Choose the path that matches what you have. All paths share the same workspace: the repository root is a colcon workspace that contains Source/ and Gazebo/.

Path You need You get Start Simulation Ubuntu 22.04 PC with ROS 2 Humble and Gazebo Harmonic the X12 hexacopter in Gazebo, streaming through the real MCU driver; the full UAV stack in SIL Quick Start → Simulation Jetson, native Jetson Orin Nano Super with JetPack 6.2+ the ROS 2 packages built on the target Installation Jetson, containers Jetson with Docker one container per ROS 2 node with Docker Compose Quick Start → Containers Two-Jetson cluster two Jetsons, an Ethernet switch k3s + Helm placement and failover Production Setup

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
• Platform. The Jetson code targets the Orin Nano Super only (sm_87). The original Jetson Nano is not supported.
  • Submodules. Clone with --recurse-submodules: the flight-control and camera firmware, the Android app and NVIDIA's Lidar_AI_Solution are submodules.
  • Safety. The firmware is not flight-ready: airframe constants are sample values and no control loop has been verified on hardware. Work in simulation or on a bench without propellers until the verification order has been completed.

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
1. Quick Start — run something in minutes: simulation, a native build, or containers.
  2. Installation — set up ROS 2, Isaac ROS and the workspace on the Jetson.
  3. Hardware Setup — network addresses, sensors, MCUs and the RC link.
  4. First Steps — check that every part is alive and the loops are closed.
  5. Troubleshooting — known problems and their fixes.

docs.title: First Steps
docs.text:
A health check of the system after installation, from the MCU links up to the operator tools. Every node marked 📊 in the System Node Graph reports on /diagnostics, so most checks read that topic.

source install/setup.bash
ROS/run.sh list          # every executable built in the workspace

docs.title: 1. Watch the system
docs.text:
ros2 run ros2_monitoring ros2_monitoring --start-page nodes     # terminal node manager
ros2 launch ros2_qt ros2_qt.launch.py                           # Qt operator dashboard

The node manager shows nodes appearing and disappearing, lifecycle states and CPU trends; the dashboard shows the flight-stack topics with their measured rate, jitter and staleness.

docs.title: 2. MCU links
docs.text:
VehicleSimulation 
ros2 launch ros2_jetowl_bridge jetowl_bridge.launch.py vision_mcu:=true
ros2 topic hz /imu/data                  # 200 Hz from the flight controller
ros2 topic echo /jetowl/status --once    # firmware status, OTA and RC-link keys

ros2 launch ros2_hexacopter_gazebo hexacopter_sim.launch.py gui:=false
ros2 topic hz /imu/data                  # ≈ 1 kHz through the virtual MCU
ros2 topic echo /gps/fix --once

In /diagnostics, the entries jetowl_bridge/fc: link, jetowl_bridge/vision_mcu: link | image or jetowl_bridge/sensor_link: link | clock | imu | gnss | encoders must be OK.

docs.title: 3. Estimation
docs.text:
ros2 launch ros2_control_system control_system.launch.py
ros2 topic hz /odometry/filtered
ros2 topic echo /estimator/diagnostics --once

The estimator diagnostics report the position uncertainty, the NIS and the rejected-sample counters. A NIS persistently above its χ² band means the noise model does not match the sensors and must be fixed before the controller is trusted.

docs.title: 4. Flight stack
docs.text:
ros2 launch ros2_mission_planner autonomous_mission.launch.py
ros2 topic echo /flight/status

flight/status reports the flight mode measured by the flight controller. Commands sent by the mission planner, the network bridge or the dashboard are acknowledged only when this status confirms them.

docs.title: 5. Perception
docs.text:
# Thermal pipeline on a synthetic scene (no camera needed)
ros2 launch ros2_night_vision_owl night_vision_owl_pipeline.launch.py
ros2 topic echo /thermal/tracks --once

# LiDAR SLAM on the Jetbot sensors
ros2 launch ros2_lidar_slam dual_lidar_slam.launch.py ld19_port:=/dev/ld19 lpb40b_port:=/dev/lpb40b
ros2 topic hz /scan
ros2 topic echo /slam/pose --once

docs.title: 6. Check that the loops are closed
docs.text:
Each controller publishes its loop signals for review — set-point, measurement, estimate, error, each controller term and the pre/post-saturation command:

Loop Topic Translational MPC control/diagnostics, control/predicted_path Flight controller flight/diagnostics Flight firmware /jetowl/status (rotor_closed_mask, rotor_stall_mask, dshot_skipped, …)

A loop is closed when its measurement follows its set-point in these logs — not when the command merely changes.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Tutorials — fly a mission in simulation, calibrate the stereo rig, configure SLAM.
  • Troubleshooting — when a check above fails.

docs.title: Hardware Setup
docs.text:
Bring-up order for the vehicle hardware. Each step links to the page with the full procedure.

Propellers off

Until the airframe constants are measured and the loops have passed HIL and bench tests, run every motor test without propellers and with a current-limited supply.

docs.title: 1. Robot network
docs.text:
Connect the Jetson(s) and the MCUs to one Ethernet switch and give them the static addresses of the robot network:

Device Address Jetson #1 (agent, k3s master) 192.168.10.1/24 JetOwl FC 192.168.10.2/24 (firmware net_config.h) JetOwl Vision 192.168.10.3/24 (firmware net_config.h) Jetson #2 (k3s worker, optional) 192.168.10.4/24

See Network Architecture. The netplan settings used by the cluster scripts are in Kubernetes.

docs.title: 2. Flight controller (STM32N657)
docs.text:
1. Enable the peripherals in STM32CubeMX following CubeMX Setup (I2C1, USART3 + DMA, SPI5, TIM1 + GPDMA, TIM3, TIM6, EXTI) and set BOARD_CUBEMX_PERIPHERALS_READY = 1.
  2. Build AppliSecure before AppliNonSecure, then flash the signed FSBL and the first .fw package (OTA §6).
  3. Measure k_f, k_m on a thrust stand and identify the rotor-speed model before fitting propellers (Control Design §5.4, §6.6).
  4. Perform the static IMU mounting check (§1.4 of the control design).

docs.title: 3. Camera MCU (STM32N655)
docs.text: Check the [BOARD] items of camera_conf.h and net_config.h against the schematic, build with micro-ROS and verify the preview stream (JetOwl Vision).

docs.title: 4. RC link
docs.text:
1. Generate a private link key: python3 tools/rflink_keygen.py in JetOwl_FlightControl (writes the key into both repositories).
  2. Build both firmwares with the same RFLINK_PLAN / RFLINK_REGION.
  3. Wire the ground controller (Wiring) — each module with the antenna for its own band, antennas as far apart as possible.
  4. Calibrate the sticks on the ground controller (Signal Chain §4).

docs.title: 5. Jetbot sensors
docs.text: Sensor Connection Bring-up LD19 LiDAR, LPB40B ToF USB-serial Sensor Setup tutorial 2 × IMX219 CSI Camera Calibration tutorial MI48 thermal camera USB Night Vision OpenMV RT1062 Ethernet or USB OpenMV audit

docs.title: 6. Ground station
docs.text: Connect QGroundControl or the Android console through the network bridge (Network Bridge); for a console on another network use the MAVLink Relay.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Native installation on a Jetson Orin Nano Super. The same steps work on an Ubuntu 22.04 PC for everything that does not need the Jetson GPU (simulation, estimation and control packages, tools).

Component Version JetPack 6.2 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04, L4T 36.4) ROS 2 Humble Hawksbill Python 3.10 Build tools colcon, CMake ≥ 3.16 (≥ 3.20 for CUDA/), rosdep, vcstool, git

docs.title: 0. Flash JetPack
docs.text: Flash JetPack 6.2+ and configure storage and networking as described in Jetson Orin Nano Super.

docs.title: 1. ROS 2 Humble
docs.text:
ROS/install.sh follows the official Ubuntu (deb packages) procedure: UTF-8 locale, the universe component, the ros2-apt-source package, the ROS packages with ros-dev-tools, and rosdep init/update.

ROS/install.sh --distro humble --variant ros-base -y     # Jetson (no GUI)
ROS/install.sh --distro humble --variant desktop -y      # PC with RViz

The chosen distribution is remembered by ROS/tag.sh and used by ROS/build.sh and ROS/run.sh.

docs.title: 2. Isaac ROS (object detection only)
docs.text: isaac_ros_objectdetection uses the Isaac ROS DNN image encoder, TensorRT and Triton nodes. They are installed as ros-humble-* packages from NVIDIA's Isaac ROS apt repository; add that repository following the Isaac ROS documentation, after which rosdep resolves the keys. The GPU container base image (Docker/images/ros2_base_gpu) already contains it.

docs.title: 3. Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/TNG-Blue/Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL.git
cd Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL
# already cloned without submodules:
git submodule update --init --recursive

docs.title: 4. Build the workspace
docs.text:
The repository root is the colcon workspace; COLCON_IGNORE excludes the non-ROS trees.

ROS/build.sh --rosdep                      # install dependencies, build everything (Release)
source install/setup.bash

Useful variants:

ROS/build.sh -p ros2_control_system --test     # one package and its tests
ROS/build.sh -u ros2_jetowl_bridge             # a package and its dependencies
ROS/build.sh -- --packages-skip ros2_qt        # skip a package
ROS/build.sh --clean                           # remove build/, install/, log/ first

docs.title: 5. Optional components
docs.text: Component Extra installation Page Gazebo simulation sudo apt install ros-humble-ros-gzharmonic libeigen3-dev libyaml-cpp-dev Simulation Qt dashboard sudo apt install qtbase5-dev libqt5serialport5-dev qtwebengine5-dev libqt5opengl5-dev libcurl4-openssl-dev libjsoncpp-dev pkg-config Qt Dashboard micro-ROS agent built once with micro_ros_setup, or run as a container (agent:=docker) JetOwl Bridge MAVLink tests pip install pymavlink Network Bridge CUDA library CMake build in CUDA/ CUDA Library Deep-learning pipeline CMake build in DeepLearning/ Deep Learning installation Firmware toolchains arm-none-eabi-gcc 13.2, CMake ≥ 3.22, Ninja; arduino-cli for the Remote UAV Firmware Documentation site pip install -r Docs/requirements.txt (+ libcairo2-dev for social cards) Contributing

docs.title: 6. Verify
docs.text:
python3 -m pytest Tests/ -q                     # repository checks
colcon test --packages-select ros2_control_system ros2_flight_controller
colcon test-result --verbose

Continue with Hardware Setup or the First Steps.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Three ways to see the system running. Option A needs no robot.

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/TNG-Blue/Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL.git
cd Isaac_ROS-Jetbot_NanoOWL

docs.title: Option A: simulation on a PC
docs.text:
Requirements: Ubuntu 22.04, ROS 2 Humble, Gazebo Harmonic.

sudo apt install ros-humble-ros-gzharmonic libeigen3-dev libyaml-cpp-dev
ROS/build.sh --rosdep -u ros2_hexacopter_gazebo -u ros2_jetowl_bridge
source install/setup.bash

ros2 launch ros2_hexacopter_gazebo hexacopter_sim.launch.py        # gui:=false for headless

Wait about 2 s for the at-rest IMU calibration, then in a second terminal:

source install/setup.bash
ros2 topic pub --once /hexa/arm std_msgs/msg/Bool "{data: true}"
ros2 topic pub -r 20 /hexa/cmd geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {z: 1.0}}"   # climb
ros2 topic hz /imu/data          # ≈ 1 kHz through the virtual MCU and jetowl_bridge
ros2 topic echo /hexa/status     # armed, calibrated, healthy rotors, NIS

The sensor topics reach ROS 2 through the same UDP protocol and driver as on the vehicle — see Simulation.

docs.title: The full UAV stack in software-in-the-loop
docs.text:
ROS/build.sh -u ros2_mission_planner -u ros2_network_bridge
python3 Source/ROS2_Control_System/tests/sil/uav_stack_sil.py \
  --estimator  install/ros2_control_system/lib/ros2_control_system/uav_state_estimator \
  --controller install/ros2_control_system/lib/ros2_control_system/uav_trajectory_controller \
  --flight     install/ros2_flight_controller/lib/ros2_flight_controller/flight_controller_node \
  --control-params install/ros2_control_system/share/ros2_control_system/config/uav_control.yaml

The script flies arm → take-off → a four-waypoint mission → RTH → land against a simulated vehicle with +10 % mass and wind, and checks every phase. Options for the mission planner and the MAVLink link are described on the Control System page.

docs.title: Architecture at a Glance
docs.text:
The system is split across three kinds of compute, each doing what it is best at: the microcontrollers run the hard real-time loops next to the sensors and motors, the Jetson runs estimation, planning and GPU perception under ROS 2, and operator devices observe and command over bounded-bandwidth links.

flowchart TB
    subgraph OPS["Operators"]
        GCS["Ground station<br/>(MAVLink v2)"]
        APP["Android console"]
        QT["Qt dashboard"]
        RC["Remote UAV<br/>LoRa ground controller"]
    end
    subgraph JETSON["Jetson Orin Nano Super · ROS 2 Humble"]
        PER["Perception<br/>NanoOWL · YOLOv5 · LiDAR AI · stereo · thermal"]
        EST["Estimation<br/>ESKF · SLAM · tracking"]
        PLAN["Planning<br/>mission planner · flight controller"]
        CTRL["Control<br/>MPC / MPPI"]
        BR["Bridges<br/>jetowl_bridge · network_bridge"]
    end
    subgraph MCU["Microcontrollers"]
        FC["JetOwl FC · STM32N657<br/>attitude 250 Hz · rate 1 kHz · DShot"]
        VIS["JetOwl Vision · STM32N655<br/>IMX335 · AE/AWB"]
        SENS["Sensor MCU / virtual MCU<br/>IMU · GNSS · encoders"]
    end
    PER --> EST --> PLAN --> CTRL
    CTRL -- "attitude set-point, thrust<br/>(micro-ROS, UDP)" --> FC
    FC -- "IMU, barometer, status" --> EST
    SENS -- "CRC-32 UDP frames" --> BR --> EST
    VIS -- "preview image, status" --> BR
    BR <--> GCS
    BR <--> APP
    QT --- JETSON
    RC <-- "LoRa 2.4 GHz / sub-GHz" --> FC

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Layer Runs on Rate Responsibility Rotor speed, angular rate, attitude flight-controller MCU 1 kHz / 1 kHz / 250 Hz Keep the airframe stable; always closed on the firmware's IMU Command guard and failsafe flight-controller MCU 1 kHz Validate set-points, bounded landing on link loss Translational control Jetson (ros2_control_system) 50 Hz Offset-free MPC on the ESKF estimate; MPPI near obstacles Guidance and modes Jetson (ros2_flight_controller) 50 Hz Flight-mode state machine, minimum-jerk references, safety monitor Missions Jetson (ros2_mission_planner) event-driven Feasibility, sequencing, supervision Perception Jetson GPU sensor rate Detection, tracking, depth, mapping Operations Jetson + operator devices ≤ 10 Hz Telemetry, commands with acknowledgement, monitoring

The time-scale separation between nested loops is at least 3–5×, which is what allows each outer loop to treat the inner one as ideal in its design.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Isaac ROS Jetbot NanoOWL is a ROS 2 Humble platform for the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super: GPU perception, state estimation, closed-loop control, embedded firmware, a Gazebo simulation that runs the same driver code as the vehicle, and the tooling to deploy and update it. Every card below links to the page that documents that part in detail.

15 ROS 2 packages in Source/ 4 Gazebo simulation packages 12 BLDC motors in the X12 sim 1 kHz Simulation lock-step rate

docs.title: Perception
docs.text:
• Open-vocabulary object detection

    NanoOWL and YOLO decoders accelerated with TensorRT. With tracking enabled, detections are treated as a noisy measurement and pass through a recursive estimator whose prediction gates the next association.

    Object Detection

  • LiDAR SLAM

    LD19 and LPB40B drivers with CRC checks, Hampel outlier rejection and gyro de-skew, feeding an EKF with PL-ICP scan matching against a submap and a χ² innovation gate.

    SLAM & Navigation

  • Thermal night vision

    Bad-pixel repair, temporal low-pass filtering and CA-CFAR detection, followed by a constant-velocity Kalman tracker with NIS consistency monitoring.

    Night Vision

  • Stereo depth

    Two IMX219 cameras, VPI semi-global matching on the GPU and a per-pixel Kalman filter on disparity: metric depth published together with its 1σ uncertainty.

    Stereo Vision

  • CUDA library

    cuda_jetbot_nanoowl for sm_87: GPU device and memory management, a batched multi-channel PID, a kinematic MPC and a VPI image-processing wrapper.

    CUDA Library

  • RF spectrum monitoring

    2.4–2.5 GHz SDR monitoring on the GPU, jamming and spoofing detection, and an escalate-only RF failsafe that commands RTH or LAND.

    RF Spectrum

docs.title: Estimation and control
docs.text:
Every path that moves hardware follows the same closed-loop chain, and each stage is derived, not tuned by feel (control-systems rule):

flowchart LR
    S[Sensor] --> F[Filter]
    F --> E[Estimator]
    E --> C[Controller]
    C --> A[Actuator]
    A --> P[Plant]
    P -- measured state --> S
FilterEstimatorController

A first-order low-pass \(H(s) = \dfrac{1}{\tau s + 1}\), \(\tau = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f_c}\), discretised with the backward-Euler rule \(s \approx (1 - z^{-1})/T_s\):

\[ y[k] = y[k-1] + \alpha\,\bigl(x[k] - y[k-1]\bigr), \qquad \alpha = \frac{T_s}{\tau + T_s} \]

Its phase lag \(\varphi(\omega) \approx -\arctan(\omega\tau)\) at the loop crossover is charged against the phase-margin budget.

Kalman filter predict / update, with \(Q\) and \(R\) taken from measured noise densities:

\[ \begin{aligned} \hat{x}_{k|k-1} &= F\,\hat{x}_{k-1|k-1} + B\,u_{k-1}, & P_{k|k-1} &= F P_{k-1|k-1} F^\top + Q \\ K_k &= P_{k|k-1} H^\top \bigl(H P_{k|k-1} H^\top + R\bigr)^{-1}, & \hat{x}_{k|k} &= \hat{x}_{k|k-1} + K_k\bigl(y_k - H\hat{x}_{k|k-1}\bigr) \end{aligned} \]

Consistency is checked with the normalised innovation squared \(\nu_k^\top S_k^{-1} \nu_k \sim \chi^2_m\).

PID with a filtered derivative on the measurement and back-calculation anti-windup:

\[ u = K_p e + K_i \!\int e\,dt - \frac{K_d\, s}{1 + s\,T_d/N}\,y, \qquad \dot{I} = K_i e + \frac{1}{T_t}\bigl(u_\text{sat} - u\bigr) \]

LQR, MPC, FOC and sliding-mode designs are used where the plant calls for them.

References: K. J. Åström, T. Hägglund, Advanced PID Control; D. Simon, Optimal State Estimation; G. F. Franklin, J. D. Powell, M. Workman, Digital Control of Dynamic Systems.

  • Sensor fusion

    A 15-state error-state Kalman filter over IMU, GNSS, barometer and heading, plus the estimators of each sensor pipeline, with covariances carried through to the consumers.

    Sensor Fusion & Estimation

  • Motion and flight control

    Offset-free linear MPC with MPPI near obstacles, a flight-mode state machine with a 2-DOF position loop, and firmware attitude/rate loops — each with its margins.

    Control System · Flight Controller

  • Coaxial X12 hexacopter simulation

    Gazebo Harmonic plugin at a 1 kHz lock-step with 12 BLDC motors, FOC ESC models, control allocation and gain synthesis with margin reports.

    Simulation

  • MCU ⇄ Jetson sensor link

    IMU, GNSS and encoders stream over Ethernet/UDP with CRC-32 frames and a clock-sync Kalman filter. A virtual MCU sends the same frames in simulation, so every node downstream runs unchanged in SIL and on the vehicle.

    JetOwl Bridge

docs.title: Embedded firmware
docs.text:
• JetOwl flight control and vision

    STM32N6 (Cortex-M55, TrustZone) firmware: MPC + reflex PID/ESO + DShot on the flight controller, closed-loop AE/AWB on the camera MCU, both native micro-ROS nodes with A/B OTA.

    JetOwl Flight Control · JetOwl Vision

  • OpenMV vision

    OpenMV RT1062 detection server (ml API, firmware ≥ v4.5.6): Hungarian association and an α-β tracker on the camera, tracks sent as JSON lines over TCP to the JetOwl bridge.

    OpenMV RT1062 API audit

  • Long-range links

    A full-duplex LR1121 LoRa RC link to the ground controller, and a MAVLink v2 ground-station link over UDP, TCP, telemetry radio or a TLS relay.

    Remote UAV · Network Bridge

docs.title: Deployment and operations
docs.text:
• Containers

    Docker images for the Jetson and the host tools, orchestrated with Kubernetes and Helm charts.

    Docker · Kubernetes · Helm

  • Over-the-air updates

    A Go OTA server with firmware metadata, device detection and a web dashboard that is also published as a live preview with this site.

    Server OTA · Web interface

  • Monitoring

    A terminal node manager (graph changes, lifecycle and parameter services, CPU trends) and a Qt operator dashboard with topic-rate and staleness estimation.

    Monitoring · Qt Dashboard

  • MAVLink relay

    A TLS relay that both the robot and the console dial out to, so a ground station on another network (4G, CGNAT) can reach the robot.

    MAVLink Relay Server

docs.title: Project Overview
docs.text: Isaac ROS Jetbot NanoOWL is an open-source autonomy platform for the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super. It covers the complete path from sensor input to actuator command — GPU perception, state estimation, planning, closed-loop control, embedded firmware, simulation, operator tools and deployment — for a ground robot (Jetbot) and a multirotor UAV (JetOwl).

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Area What the repository provides Where Perception Open-vocabulary detection (NanoOWL), YOLOv5 / SSD-MobileNet, 3-D LiDAR detection, stereo depth, thermal detection and tracking ROS 2 Modules Estimation 15-state error-state Kalman filter, LiDAR SLAM, per-sensor estimators with consistency checks Sensor Fusion & Estimation Planning and control Mission planner, flight-mode state machine, offset-free MPC with MPPI near obstacles Control System Embedded firmware STM32N6 flight controller and camera MCU (micro-ROS, A/B OTA), LoRa ground controller Firmware Simulation Coaxial X12 hexacopter in Gazebo Harmonic and a virtual MCU on the real sensor protocol Simulation Operator tools Qt dashboard, terminal node manager, MAVLink ground-station link, Android console Qt Dashboard · Mobile App Deployment One container image per ROS 2 node, a two-Jetson k3s cluster with Helm, OTA server, MAVLink relay Deployment Design tooling MATLAB/Simulink models and monitoring blocks, PyTorch training notebooks MATLAB · Training

docs.title: Engineering principles
docs.text:
Closed loop by construction. Every path that moves hardware runs sensor → filter → estimator → controller → actuator, and the measured — not the commanded — state returns to the controller. Open loop is allowed only where no feedback sensor exists, and is then bounded and guarded by a watchdog. See the control design standard.

Derived, not tuned. Filter cut-offs, noise covariances, gains and thresholds come from a named method and a cited source (datasheet, textbook or paper); each controller documents its plant model, margins including delays, and its failsafe.

Evidence before claims. Packages ship unit tests, software-in-the-loop tests and stated limitations. The Performance and Verification page lists only measured or proven figures and says what has not been measured yet.

One source of truth. Component documentation lives next to the code, and this site renders it directly, so the site cannot drift from the implementation.

docs.title: Performance and Verification
docs.text:
This page collects the figures that the repository has measured or proven, each with the level at which it was obtained and the page that records the evidence. Nothing here is a target or an estimate: where a measurement does not exist yet, the table says so.

The project's verification order is fixed by the control design standard:

flowchart LR
    M["Model<br/>(MATLAB / analysis)"] --> S["SIL<br/>(ROS 2 / Gazebo)"]
    S --> H["HIL"]
    H --> B["Bench<br/>(current limits)"]
    B --> V["Vehicle"]

Current maturity

Every figure below comes from analysis, unit tests or software-in-the-loop simulation. No component has completed hardware-in-the-loop or bench verification yet, and the firmware airframe constants are sample values. The system is not flight-ready.

docs.title: 🧭 How It Fits the Fleet
docs.text:
graph LR
    Dev["Developer / CI"] -->|upload firmware| OTA["Server OTA<br/>:8080"]
    OTA -->|"GET /api/firmware/list"| Jetson["Jetson Orin Nano Super"]
    OTA -->|"GET /download?file="| STM32["STM32 motor control"]
    OTA -->|"GET /download?file="| OpenMV["OpenMV RT1062"]
    Jetson -->|"GET /api/health"| OTA
    STM32 -->|"GET /api/health"| OTA

A device polls /api/firmware/list, compares the version field against what it is running, and pulls the new image from /download?file=<name>. Version and device type are derived from the file name by the server — see Firmware metadata for the exact rules, which determine how you must name the files you upload.

docs.title: Server OTA — API Reference
docs.text:
Every route registered by setupRoutes() in Server_OTA/src/main.go, with the exact payloads produced by Server_OTA/src/handlers/handlers.go.

Base URL in a local run: http://localhost:8080

docs.title: 📋 Route Table
docs.text:
Method Path Handler Purpose GET / HandleHome Renders the dashboard (web/templates/index.html) GET /api/stats HandleStats Storage and download counters GET /api/health HandleHealth Liveness / readiness probe GET /api/firmware/list HandleFirmwareList All firmware files with metadata GET /api/firmware/info?file= HandleFirmwareInfo Metadata for one file GET /download?file= HandleDownload Firmware binary download (HTTP Range supported) POST /upload HandleUpload Store a firmware file (.fw packages are validated) GET /api/ota/manifest?device= HandleOTAManifest Newest valid JetOwl MCU release, key=value text POST /api/ota/report?device=&version=&state=&detail= HandleOTAReport MCU reports its OTA state GET /api/ota/devices HandleOTADevices Last report of every MCU GET /static/* http.FileServer CSS, JS, images from web/static GET /404 HandleNotFound 404 page

All routes except /static/* pass through utils.WithRateLimit: at most 5 concurrent requests, others wait up to 5 s and then receive 503 Server busy as text/plain.

docs.title: 📦 Response Envelope
docs.text:
Every JSON route answers with models.APIResponse:

{
  "data": { },
  "message": "human readable string",
  "success": true
}

data is omitted on errors (omitempty), and success is false with the HTTP status carrying the reason.

docs.title: GET /api/health
docs.text:
Liveness probe. Used by the Docker HEALTHCHECK and by both App Engine manifests.

curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/health

{
  "data": { "status": "operational", "memory_mb": 24, "goroutines": 0, "timestamp": 0 },
  "message": "Server is healthy",
  "success": true
}
Field Type Meaning status string Always operational while the handler is reachable memory_mb uint64 MemoryManager.GetMemoryStats().Alloc converted to MB goroutines int Currently always 0 — see Current gaps timestamp int64 Currently always 0 — GetUnixTime() is a stub

Probe on status, not on payload

Because two fields are placeholders, health checks should assert HTTP 200 and success == true, not the numeric values.

docs.title: GET /api/stats
docs.text:
curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/stats

{
  "data": { "total_files": 5, "total_size": 272105472, "downloads": 12, "server_version": "3.0.0" },
  "message": "Server statistics",
  "success": true
}
Field Type Meaning total_files int Number of allowed files in data/firmware/, counted on this request total_size int64 Sum of their sizes in bytes downloads int32 Downloads served since process start (in-memory, reset on restart) server_version string Hard-coded "3.0.0" in the handler

The handler calls ListFirmwareFiles() first, so the counters always reflect the same directory scan as /api/firmware/list.

docs.title: GET /api/firmware/list
docs.text:
curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/firmware/list

{
  "data": [
    {
      "size": 262144,
      "mod_time": "2026-09-14T08:31:07.482Z",
      "name": "stm32f407_motor_control_v183.bin",
      "version": "v183",
      "device_type": "STM32",
      "description": "Firmware for STM32"
    }
  ],
  "message": "Firmware list",
  "success": true
}
Field Type Source size int64 os.FileInfo.Size() mod_time RFC 3339 os.FileInfo.ModTime() name string File name version string Parsed from the name after _v device_type string ESP32, ESP8266, Arduino, STM32 or Generic description string "Firmware for " + device_type

Directories and files whose extension is not .bin, .hex, .elf, .img or .fw are skipped. Naming rules are in Firmware metadata.

Errors: 500 with "Unable to list files" if data/firmware/ cannot be read (for example when it does not exist).

docs.title: GET /api/firmware/info?file=<name>
docs.text:
curl -s "http://localhost:8080/api/firmware/info?file=stm32f407_motor_control_v183.bin"

{
  "data": { "name": "stm32f407_motor_control_v183.bin", "size": 262144, "size_fmt": "256.0KB" },
  "message": "Firmware info",
  "success": true
}
Status Condition message 400 file query parameter missing File parameter required 404 File not in data/firmware/ File not found

size_fmt comes from utils.FormatFileSize: bytes below 1024 render as 512B, larger values as one decimal with no space (256.0KB, 1.5MB, 2.0GB).

docs.title: GET /download?file=<name>
docs.text:
Streams the binary with http.ServeFile and increments the download counter.

curl -OJ "http://localhost:8080/download?file=stm32f407_motor_control_v183.bin"

Response headers

Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=stm32f407_motor_control_v183.bin
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Status Condition message 400 file missing File parameter required 403 Not a plain file name (/, .., leading ., characters outside [A-Za-z0-9._-]) or extension not in the allow-list File name or type not allowed 404 File does not exist File not found

Range: bytes=<n>- returns 206 Partial Content with Content-Range: bytes n-last/size (http.ServeFile); the JetOwl MCUs resume an interrupted download this way.

Write timeout bounds the transfer

WriteTimeout is 30 s, so a download that cannot complete within that window is cut off. For large images, raise the timeout or place a proxy in front of the service.

docs.title: POST /upload
docs.text:
curl -X POST -F "firmware=@stm32f407_motor_control_v183.bin" http://localhost:8080/upload

{ "data": { "file": "jetowl_fc_v1.2.3.fw", "size": 235980, "device": "jetowl_fc",
            "version": "1.2.3", "sha256": "1dc0…0b0b" },
  "message": "Firmware stored", "success": true }

The file is written to a temporary file, validated, then linked to its final name, so a failed or partial upload never appears in data/firmware/.

Status Condition 400 no firmware field, or file name/type not allowed 409 a file with that name already exists (published versions are immutable) 413 larger than max_upload_size 422 .fw package invalid: header, size, payload SHA-256, or name ≠ <device>_v<M.m.p>.fw

docs.title: 🛩️ JetOwl MCU OTA
docs.text:
Firmware updates for the vehicle's STM32N6 microcontrollers — jetowl_fc (JetOwl_FlightControl) and jetowl_vision (JetOwl_Vision). The MCUs reach the server at 192.168.10.200:8080 (MetalLB address of the OTA Service in the k3s cluster). The full design (A/B slots, bootloader, rollback, proofs) is in docs/OTA.md of JetOwl_FlightControl.

Release = a JOWL v1 package named <device>_v<M.m.p>.fw, produced by tools/ota_pack.py in the firmware repositories (make ota-upload VERSION=M.m.p). Header (256 B): magic, device, version, segments {load_addr, offset, size}, payload SHA-256, CRC-32 — checked identically by the firmware (C), this server (Go, ParsePackageHeader) and the packer (Python).

docs.title: GET /api/ota/manifest?device=<id>
docs.text:
device=jetowl_fc
version=1.2.3
file=jetowl_fc_v1.2.3.fw
size=235980
sha256=1dc074ff929a4614e59ccc0c1c08861552af6dd23d2c659818843ee3ab210b0b

The newest version (compared numerically: 1.10.0 > 1.9.99) whose package passes validation; a package that fails (corrupt payload, header ≠ name) is skipped and logged. 404 when the device has no release, 400 for a malformed device id. sha256 is over the whole file and is cached by (name, size, mtime).

docs.title: POST /api/ota/report
docs.text: Query parameters device, version (M.m.p), state and detail ([a-z0-9_]{1,32}): the MCU reports running, trial, downloaded, staged, confirmed, up_to_date, error. At most 64 devices are kept. GET /api/ota/devices lists them with the remote address and last_seen.

docs.title: 🤖 Device-Side Polling
docs.text:
A minimal update check, using the fields the server actually provides:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

OTA_URL="http://ota-server.local:8080"
DEVICE="STM32"
CURRENT="v183"

latest=$(curl -fsS "${OTA_URL}/api/firmware/list" \
  | jq -r --arg dev "$DEVICE" '
      .data
      | map(select(.device_type == $dev))
      | sort_by(.mod_time)
      | last')

name=$(jq -r '.name'    <<<"$latest")
version=$(jq -r '.version' <<<"$latest")

if [[ "$version" != "$CURRENT" ]]; then
    curl -fsS -o "/tmp/${name}" "${OTA_URL}/download?file=${name}"
    echo "downloaded ${name} (${version})"
fi

Selection is by mod_time rather than by comparing version strings, because extractVersion truncates at the first separator and cannot be ordered reliably — see the warning in Firmware metadata.

docs.title: Server OTA — Architecture
docs.text: How the Go service is put together: packages, request pipeline, and the resource budget it runs under.

docs.title: 📦 Packages
docs.text: Package File(s) Responsibility main src/main.go Resolves the working directory, creates data dirs, loads config, starts the memory manager, registers routes, runs http.Server config src/config/config.go Loads config/config.json once (sync.Once), falls back to built-in defaults and writes the file if it is missing; guarded by an RWMutex handlers src/handlers/handlers.go HTTP handlers and the route → handler map models src/models/models.go Config, FirmwareInfo, ServerStats, APIResponse, PageData, UploadResult, HealthStatus services src/services/firmware.go, logger.go, memory.go Firmware listing and metadata, logging, periodic GC utils src/utils/cache.go, format.go, middleware.go Template LRU cache, size/time formatting, rate limiting and JSON responses

docs.title: 🔁 Request Pipeline
docs.text:
graph TB
    Client["Device / Browser"] --> Mux["net/http DefaultServeMux"]
    Mux -->|"/static/*"| FS["http.FileServer<br/>web/static"]
    Mux -->|"all other routes"| RL["utils.WithRateLimit"]
    RL -->|"slot acquired"| H["handlers.*"]
    RL -->|"5 s timeout"| Busy["503 Server busy<br/>errorCount++"]
    H --> S["services.*<br/>data/firmware"]
    H --> R["utils.RespondSuccess / RespondError<br/>models.APIResponse"]
    S --> R
    R --> Client

setupRoutes() registers the static file server under /static/, every entry of handlers.HandleAPI() (each already wrapped in WithRateLimit), and /404.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text:
var requestSemaphore = make(chan struct{}, 5)   // utils/middleware.go

Each request tries to take a slot from a buffered channel of size 5. If no slot frees up within 5 seconds, the request is answered with 503 Server busy and the global error counter is incremented. SetMaxConcurrent(n) replaces the semaphore for deployments that can afford more parallelism — App Engine Flexible sets MAX_CONCURRENT_REQS: "10".

Why a semaphore and not a token bucket

The limit protects memory, not fairness: firmware transfers are large relative to the 256–512 MB instance sizes this service targets, so the bound that matters is "how many transfers may be in flight at once", which a counting semaphore expresses directly.

docs.title: ⏱️ Runtime Budget
docs.text:
Setting Value Where ReadTimeout 10 s src/main.go WriteTimeout 30 s src/main.go IdleTimeout 60 s src/main.go MaxHeaderBytes 1 MB (1 << 20) src/main.go GC interval 30 s services/memory.go Memory cleanup threshold 80 % services/memory.go Template cache 4 templates, LRU eviction by last-use timestamp utils/cache.go

services.OptimizeForEmbedded() runs before anything else, and MemoryManager (started in main, stopped via defer) reads runtime.MemStats on every tick and forces a collection when the threshold is crossed. WriteTimeout (30 s) is the practical ceiling on a single firmware download — size your images accordingly or put a proxy in front for very large transfers.

docs.title: 🗂️ Firmware Metadata
docs.text:
services.ListFirmwareFiles() reads data/firmware/, skips directories and disallowed extensions, and derives three fields from the file name. Naming matters:

Field Rule Example version Text after the first _v, up to the next . or _; otherwise Unknown motor_v1.8.3.bin → v1 … see note below device_type Case-insensitive substring match: esp32, esp8266, arduino, stm32; otherwise Generic stm32f407_control.bin → STM32 description "Firmware for " + device_type → Firmware for STM32

Version parsing stops at the first separator

extractVersion cuts at the first . or _ after _v, so fw_v1.8.3.bin yields v1, not v1.8.3. Use a separator-free version segment (fw_v183.bin) or treat the field as informational and keep the authoritative version inside the image header until the parser is extended.

Listing also refreshes the shared counters (UpdateTotalSize, UpdateTotalFiles), which is why /api/stats is consistent with /api/firmware/list.

docs.title: 📤 Response Envelope
docs.text:
Every JSON endpoint answers with models.APIResponse:

type APIResponse struct {
    Data    interface{} `json:"data,omitempty"`
    Message string      `json:"message"`
    Success bool        `json:"success"`
}

RespondSuccess(w, data, message) sets success: true; RespondError(w, message, code) writes the status code, sets success: false (no data) and increments errorCount. JSON is encoded with SetEscapeHTML(false) so file names keep their literal characters.

docs.title: ⚠️ Current Gaps
docs.text:
Documented because they affect what clients can rely on today:

Area Behaviour in the code Consequence HandleUpload Returns RespondSuccess(w, nil, "Upload endpoint placeholder") without reading the multipart body Uploads must be staged into data/firmware/ by other means (scp, volume mount, CI) services.GetUnixTime() return int64(0) // TODO ServerStats.LastUpload stays 0, and HealthStatus.Timestamp is 0 HandleHealth Goroutines is read from a local struct that is never populated goroutines is always 0; memory_mb is real (MemoryManager.GetMemoryStats) gracefulShutdown Defined in main.go but not wired to a signal handler The process exits without draining in-flight transfers

The static Web Interface preview mirrors the JSON schema of these endpoints — field names and types — not these placeholder values, so it shows a populated dashboard.

docs.title: Server OTA — Deployment
docs.text: Four ways to run the service, plus the CI pipeline that validates every change.

docs.title: 💻 Local Binary
docs.text:
cd Server_OTA

./scripts/build.sh     # → bin/ota-server-3.0.0-linux and -rpi
./scripts/run.sh       # → http://localhost:8080

build.sh cross-compiles two targets from src/main.go with -ldflags "-X main.Version=3.0.0 -s -w": linux/amd64 (-linux) and linux/arm GOARM=7 for Raspberry Pi (-rpi); on MSYS/Cygwin it adds a -windows.exe build.

run.sh honours PORT (default 8080), creates data/firmware, data/logs and the web/ asset directories, and logs to data/logs/server.log. If Go is installed but no binary exists, it falls back to go run ./src/main.go.

The process resolves its own base directory: started from src/, it walks up until it finds web/templates, so relative paths (config/config.json, data/firmware) keep working. A missing config/config.json is written from the built-in defaults on first start.

Stage firmware manually for now

POST /upload is still a placeholder (see API Reference), so copy images into data/firmware/ directly. Only .bin, .hex, .elf, .img and .fw are listed and downloadable.

docs.title: 🐳 Docker
docs.text:
The image is built from the repository root, because the Dockerfile copies from Server_OTA/:

docker build \
  -f Docker/images/server_ota/Dockerfile \
  -t tngblue/server_ota:3.0.0 \
  .

docker run -d --name ota-server \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -v "$(pwd)/firmware:/app/data/firmware" \
  -v "$(pwd)/ota-logs:/app/data/logs" \
  tngblue/server_ota:3.0.0
Stage Base Contents builder golang:1.20-alpine Builds main.go with CGO_ENABLED=0, -ldflags="-s -w -X main.Version=3.0.0" runtime alpine:latest Static binary, config/, web/, empty data/firmware and data/logs

The runtime stage declares a health check that polls /api/health every 30 s (10 s timeout, 5 s start period, 3 retries), so docker ps reports the container unhealthy when the API stops answering.

Mount the firmware directory

data/firmware lives in the container layer. Without a volume, every image uploaded or copied in is lost when the container is replaced.

docs.title: ☁️ App Engine
docs.text:
Two manifests ship with the service:

Standard (app.yaml)Flexible (app-flexible.yaml) 
cd Server_OTA
gcloud app deploy app.yaml
Setting Value Runtime go120, service ota-server, version v3-0-0 Instance class F2 Scaling 1–10 instances, CPU target 60 %, throughput target 70 % Firmware dir /tmp/firmware (ephemeral) Probes liveness and readiness on /api/health Static /static/.* served from web/static, secure: always 
cd Server_OTA
gcloud app deploy app-flexible.yaml
Setting Value Runtime custom / env: flex, service ota-server-flex Resources 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, 5 GB disk + 10 GB firmware-storage volume at /firmware Scaling 1–20 instances, CPU 65 %, memory 70 %, 120 s cooldown Concurrency MAX_CONCURRENT_REQS: "10" Session affinity enabled

Standard uses ephemeral storage

app.yaml points FIRMWARE_DIR at /tmp/firmware, which does not survive an instance restart and is not shared between instances. For a fleet that must pull the same image from any instance, use the Flexible manifest's mounted volume or move firmware to Cloud Storage.

Environment variables are declared twice in app.yaml

The manifest contains two env_variables: blocks (the second holds the timeout values); YAML keeps the last one, so PORT, ENVIRONMENT, LOG_LEVEL, FIRMWARE_DIR and MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE from the first block are dropped at deploy time. Merge them into a single block before relying on those values.

docs.title: 🏗️ Cloud Build
docs.text:
cloudbuild.yaml builds, pushes and deploys:

gcloud builds submit --config Server_OTA/cloudbuild.yaml
  1. docker build tagged latest, $SHORT_SHA and 3.0.0
  2. docker push of the $SHORT_SHA tag
  3. gae-deploy with --appyaml=app.yaml and the pushed image
  4. Health check against https://$PROJECT_ID.appspot.com/api/health

Machine type N1_HIGHCPU_8, timeout 3600 s, Cloud Logging only. The Flexible deployment step is present but commented out.

docs.title: ✅ CI Pipeline
docs.text:
.github/workflows/ota-server-ci.yml runs on every push and pull request touching Server_OTA/**:

Job Checks code-quality gofmt -l . must be empty, then go vet ./... build-and-test go mod download, go build -ldflags="-s -w", go test -race -coverprofile, uploads binary + config/config.json and the coverage report integration-test Downloads the artifact, prepares the runtime directory layout, verifies the binary summary Aggregates the three results into the job summary

Changes under Server_OTA/web/** additionally trigger the documentation workflow, which rebuilds the Web Interface preview and republishes it with the docs site.

docs.title: 🩺 Post-Deploy Checklist
docs.text:
BASE=https://your-deployment.example.com

curl -fsS "$BASE/api/health"        | jq '.success'          # expect true
curl -fsS "$BASE/api/stats"         | jq '.data'             # counters present
curl -fsS "$BASE/api/firmware/list" | jq '.data | length'    # staged files visible
  • /api/health returns 200 with success: true
  • data/firmware is a persistent volume, not container-local storage
  • data/logs is writable (the logger opens it at startup)
  • Firmware names follow the _v<version> and device-keyword rules in Firmware metadata
  • Concurrency limit raised via SetMaxConcurrent if more than 5 devices may pull simultaneously
  • Reverse proxy or raised WriteTimeout if images take longer than 30 s to transfer

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Task-oriented walkthroughs. Each tutorial states what you need, gives commands you can run from a fresh checkout, and ends with measurable checks: an expected rate, a consistency statistic, an acceptance threshold or a test that passes. Every procedure comes from the README or design record of the package it uses, which remains the reference.

Verification status

Most of the stack is verified by unit tests and software-in-the-loop simulation. Hardware-in-the-loop and vehicle evidence is still being produced for several components; the tutorials say where. Follow the verification order of the Control Design Standard — model, SIL, HIL, bench with current limits, vehicle — and never skip ahead.

docs.text:

    Write a mission file and fly it end to end in the full-stack SIL against wind and model error; avoid keep-out zones; re-task in flight. No hardware.

    Start

    Start

    Start

    One image per node, k3s on two boards, Helm, DDS across the boards, and a measured failover.
