docs.title: Suggested order
docs.text: If you want to… Follow see the system work without hardware Quick Start → Fly Your First Mission bring up a vehicle Hardware Setup → Connect the Flight Controller and Sensors → Monitor a Running Robot → Connect a Ground Control Station work on perception Calibrate the Stereo Camera → Configure and Validate 2-D LiDAR SLAM → Deploy a Custom Detection Model ship to the robot Deploy the Stack on a Two-Jetson Cluster → Update MCU Firmware Over the Air

docs.title: Writing a tutorial
docs.text: New tutorials follow the same structure: a table of time, prerequisites and outcomes; numbered steps with commands that run as written; a verifiable check after each step; links to the reference page. Claims about performance must come from a measurement in the repository, with its conditions. See Contributing.

docs.title: Deploy a Custom Detection Model
docs.text:
Take a detector from training to the robot: export it to ONNX, compile a TensorRT engine for the Orin Nano Super (sm_87), run it in the Isaac ROS pipeline, and add the Kalman tracker so the detections leave the pipeline as a filtered estimate rather than raw per-frame measurements.

Before you start

  • Time: 1–2 hours, excluding training
  • You need: the Jetson with JetPack 6.2 and the Isaac ROS container, a trained PyTorch detector (or a public YOLOv5 ONNX), a camera topic
  • You learn: ONNX export, TensorRT precision choices, the geometry the decoder must know, detection tracking as state estimation

docs.title: Choose the path first
docs.text:
Training is not always the right answer. The repository offers three ways to detect an object:

Path Needs Recognises Where Open vocabulary (NanoOWL) a text query any category you can name nano_owl_detector.launch.py Exemplar matching one drawn box the specific instance you marked DeepLearning/ ExemplarMatcher Trained detector a labelled dataset and a training run the categories it was trained on this tutorial

Try NanoOWL first; train only when a fixed set of categories must be detected faster or more reliably than an open-vocabulary query allows:

ros2 launch isaac_ros_objectdetection nano_owl_detector.launch.py \
    image_encoder_engine:=/workspaces/isaac_ros-dev/data/owl_image_encoder_patch32.engine
ros2 topic pub --once /input_query std_msgs/String "{data: 'a person, a mug'}"

docs.title: 1. Train and evaluate
docs.text:
The notebooks in Train_Pytorch/ cover data preparation (Pascal VOC, COCO, fixed-seed splits, Albumentations), training (SSD, SSDlite/MobileNet, Faster R-CNN, YOLOv3, OWL-ViT fine-tuning) and evaluation (mAP, precision-recall, per-class metrics, inference speed). See Model Training & Notebooks.

Before exporting, record in the model's notes:

  • the input resolution and normalisation (mean, standard deviation, RGB/BGR, value range);
  • whether the training resize preserved the aspect ratio (letterbox) or stretched the image;
  • the class list in output order;
  • the validation mAP and the dataset version it was measured on.

The deployment parameters in step 4 must reproduce those choices exactly.

docs.title: 2. Export to ONNX
docs.text:
import torch

model.eval()
dummy = torch.randn(1, 3, 640, 640)          # the training input shape
torch.onnx.export(
    model, dummy, "detector.onnx",
    input_names=["images"], output_names=["output0"],
    opset_version=17,
)

Train_Pytorch/scripts/training_utils.py and trt_export.ipynb contain the same export with checks. Verify the graph before going further:

python3 -c "import onnx; m = onnx.load('detector.onnx'); onnx.checker.check_model(m); \
print([i.name for i in m.graph.input], [o.name for o in m.graph.output])"

The printed names are the binding names used in step 4.

docs.title: 3. Build the TensorRT engine on the target
docs.text:
Build the engine on the Jetson: TensorRT benchmarks kernel tactics on the actual GPU, so an engine built on another GPU or TensorRT version will not load.

/usr/src/tensorrt/bin/trtexec --onnx=detector.onnx --saveEngine=detector.plan --fp16
Precision When Note FP32 reference, accuracy checks slowest FP16 default for deployment uses the Ampere tensor cores; re-check mAP on the validation set INT8 only with an ONNX that carries Q/DQ nodes (quantisation-aware training) this repository ships no INT8 calibrator

The Orin Nano Super has no DLA cores, so there is no DLA offload option.

Alternatively, the Isaac ROS TensorRT node builds the engine itself from model_file_path on first start and caches it at engine_file_path (force_engine_update:=True rebuilds it).

docs.title: 4. Run it in the Isaac ROS pipeline
docs.text:
For a YOLOv5-style head:

ros2 launch isaac_ros_objectdetection isaac_ros_yolov5_tensor_rt.launch.py \
    model_file_path:=/workspaces/isaac_ros-dev/models/detector.onnx \
    engine_file_path:=/workspaces/isaac_ros-dev/models/detector.plan \
    image_topic:=/camera/color/image_raw \
    network_image_width:=640 network_image_height:=640 \
    source_image_width:=1280 source_image_height:=720 \
    input_binding_names:='["images"]' output_binding_names:='["output0"]'

Geometry that must match

The decoder maps boxes from the network frame back to the camera frame by inverting the encoder's resize. network_image_* must equal the encoder resolution and source_image_* the camera resolution; letterbox must say whether the resize preserved the aspect ratio. A mismatch shifts every box without any error message. The YOLOv5 launch files pass the same arguments to the encoder and the decoder so the two cannot drift apart.

Set encoder_image_mean and encoder_image_stddev to the normalisation used in training, and replace config/coco_labels.txt (or pass your own label_file to the visualizer) with your class list.

Check the output:

ros2 topic hz /object_detections
ros2 topic echo /object_detections --once

docs.title: 5. Turn detections into estimates
docs.text:
A detector is a noisy, intermittent sensor: boxes jitter, objects are missed for a frame, and identities are not preserved. Before anything downstream uses the boxes, enable the tracker in the decoder's parameter file:

yolov5_decoder_node:
  ros__parameters:
    enable_tracking: true
    track_iou_thres: 0.3
    track_max_age: 8
    track_min_hits: 3

Each track is a nearly-constant-velocity Kalman filter over x = [cx, cy, w, h, ẋ, ẏ]ᵀ:

Q_pv = q_a · [[T³/3, T²/2], [T²/2, T]]           (continuous white-noise acceleration, exact discretisation)
P    = (I − KH)P⁻(I − KH)ᵀ + KRKᵀ                (Joseph form: stays symmetric positive semi-definite)
d²   = νᵀ S⁻¹ ν  ≤ χ²₄(0.99) = 13.277            (gate before IoU association)

T comes from the message stamps, not wall time, so bags replayed at any speed give correct velocities. With tracking on, Detection2D.id carries the track identifier.

track_max_age and track_min_hits are frame counts. Set them from your camera rate and the longest occlusion you want to bridge, and state the choice in your configuration.

docs.title: 6. Validate on the robot
docs.text: Check How Accuracy unchanged by FP16 run the evaluation notebook on the validation set with the engine's outputs Box geometry draw /object_detections with yolov5_visualizer_node and compare with known object positions Throughput ros2 topic hz on the detections at the camera rate; GPU load with tegrastats Tracker consistency innovations of confirmed tracks inside the χ² gate on a recorded bag

docs.title: The C++ path without ROS
docs.text:
DeepLearning/ provides the same chain as a C++/CUDA library with three back ends (TensorRT, cuDNN, native CUDA) behind one Detector interface:

TrtBuildConfig config;
config.precision = TrtPrecision::FP16;
config.timing_cache_path = "timing.cache";

TrtEngine engine;
engine.build_from_onnx("detector.onnx", config);
engine.save_engine("detector.engine");

Its examples run on synthetic GPU frames with analytic ground truth, so the pipeline can be checked without a camera or a model. See Deep Learning.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Object Detection: decoders, post-processing library and tests.
  • Deep Learning mathematics: derivations behind the pre-processing, NMS, Kalman tracker and Hungarian association.

docs.title: Connect a Ground Control Station
docs.text:
Link QGroundControl (or any MAVLink v2 ground station) to the UAV stack through ros2_network_bridge, check the telemetry against the estimator, command the vehicle with acknowledged commands, and configure what happens when the link is lost.

Before you start

  • Time: about 45 minutes
  • You need: a built workspace (Fly Your First Mission), QGroundControl on the same machine or network, pip install pymavlink for the SIL check
  • You learn: the MAVLink downlink budget, the command/acknowledge protocol, datalink-loss failsafe design, the relay for consoles behind NAT

docs.title: What the bridge does
docs.text:
Direction Content Downlink HEARTBEAT 1 Hz, SYS_STATUS 1 Hz, ATTITUDE 10 Hz, LOCAL_POSITION_NED 10 Hz, GLOBAL_POSITION_INT 5 Hz, ODOMETRY 5 Hz (with covariances), STATUSTEXT; converted from ENU/FLU to NED/FRD Uplink discrete commands only (arm, take-off, land, RTL, loiter, mission start); no set-points cross the lossy link Supervision GCS heartbeat watchdog and the datalink-loss failsafe

A command is acknowledged ACCEPTED only when the flight controller's measured mode confirms it, not when the message was delivered.

docs.title: 1. Verify the link in SIL first
docs.text:
The full-stack SIL can run a pymavlink ground station against the real nodes:

ROS/build.sh -u ros2_mission_planner -u ros2_network_bridge
source install/setup.bash
python3 Source/ROS2_Control_System/tests/sil/uav_stack_sil.py \
  --estimator  install/ros2_control_system/lib/ros2_control_system/uav_state_estimator \
  --controller install/ros2_control_system/lib/ros2_control_system/uav_trajectory_controller \
  --flight     install/ros2_flight_controller/lib/ros2_flight_controller/flight_controller_node \
  --control-params install/ros2_control_system/share/ros2_control_system/config/uav_control.yaml \
  --mission-planner install/ros2_mission_planner/lib/ros2_mission_planner/mission_planner_node \
  --mission-params  install/ros2_mission_planner/share/ros2_mission_planner/config/mission_planner_params.yaml \
  --mission-file    install/ros2_mission_planner/share/ros2_mission_planner/config/waypoint_mission.yaml \
  --network-bridge  install/ros2_network_bridge/lib/ros2_network_bridge/network_bridge_node

The test starts the mission with MAV_CMD_MISSION_START, compares the downlinked position with the truth, and silences the GCS heartbeat for 8 s mid-mission. Expected: MISSION_START acknowledged ACCEPTED, LOCAL_POSITION_NED within 0.18 m RMS of the truth, 15 mission events as STATUSTEXT, and the mission continuing under the planner through the link loss (14/14 checks).

docs.title: 2. Connect QGroundControl
docs.text:
QGroundControl listens on UDP 14550 by default; the bridge binds 14555 and sends to 14550.

# GCS on this machine, stack already running
ros2 launch ros2_network_bridge network_bridge.launch.py

# Whole stack + bridge, GCS on another host
ros2 launch ros2_network_bridge uav_with_gcs.launch.py gcs_host:=192.168.2.10

# SiK telemetry radio (57 600 Bd)
ros2 launch ros2_network_bridge network_bridge.launch.py transport:=serial

With udp.learn_remote: true the bridge answers whichever host sends it MAVLink. Restrict it in config/network_bridge_params.yaml:

    udp:
      allowed_hosts: ["192.168.2.10"]
    mavlink:
      gcs_system_id: 255          # QGroundControl

No message signing

MAVLink signing is not implemented; signed frames are rejected. Use a trusted network with allowed_hosts and gcs_system_id set.

docs.title: 3. Check the telemetry
docs.text:
ros2 topic echo /network/gcs_connected          # true once GCS heartbeats arrive
ros2 topic echo /network/diagnostics            # loss, false-trip rate, rx/tx B/s, CRC errors

In QGroundControl the vehicle appears as a hexarotor. The flight mode is the heartbeat custom_mode, an index into the flight-controller mode table (0 DISARMED, 2 ARMED_IDLE, 3 TAKEOFF, 4 HOVER, 5 WAYPOINT_FOLLOW, 9 RETURN_TO_HOME, 10 LANDING, 13 EMERGENCY_STOP, …).

docs.title: Fit the link budget
docs.text:
The downlink load at the default rates is

B = Σ f_i · (12 + len_i) = 2301 B/s

which is 1.8 % of a 1 Mbit/s IP link and 40 % of a 57 600 Bd radio (5760 B/s). The bridge keeps the load under link.max_utilization (50 %); above it, every periodic rate is scaled by s = (u_max·C − B_hb) / (B − B_hb), heartbeats excepted. If you raise a rate, recompute B for your radio.

docs.title: 4. Command the vehicle
docs.text:
QGroundControl action MAV_CMD ACCEPTED when the FC mode is Arm / Disarm 400 COMPONENT_ARM_DISARM ARMED_IDLE / DISARMED (disarm refused while flying) Take off 22 NAV_TAKEOFF TAKEOFF or HOVER Land 21 NAV_LAND LANDING, LANDED or DISARMED Return 20 NAV_RETURN_TO_LAUNCH RETURN_TO_HOME or LANDING (aborts the planner's mission, whose return respects keep-out zones) Pause 17 NAV_LOITER_UNLIM HOVER Start mission 300 MISSION_START mission/start succeeded

Every accepted command is first answered IN_PROGRESS, then ACCEPTED, or FAILED after commands.ack_timeout_s (3 s). Flight termination (185) maps to EMERGENCY_STOP only with commands.allow_termination: true.

Missions are not uploaded through the MAVLink mission protocol. Upload them to the planner (mission/upload) and start them from the GCS.

docs.title: 5. Configure the datalink-loss failsafe
docs.text:
The link is declared lost after link_loss.timeout_s without a GCS heartbeat. For heartbeat rate f_hb and independent frame loss probability p, the false-loss rate is

λ_ft = 3600 · f_hb · (1 − p) · p^⌈T·f_hb⌉   per hour

At T = 5 s, 1 Hz: 0.032/h for p = 0.1, 6.1/h for p = 0.3. /network/diagnostics reports the live value from the measured loss. Increase T if it is too high for your radio.

Parameter Default Effect link_loss.action rth none, hover, rth or land when the link is lost while flying link_loss.continue_mission true a mission already validated by the planner continues link_loss.retry_s, retries 2 s, 3 the action is re-sent until the flight mode confirms it

The failsafe does not act while the vehicle is already returning, landing or under manual control.

docs.title: 6. Consoles on another network
docs.text:
When the console and the vehicle are both behind NAT (a phone on a mobile network), use the TLS relay: both sides dial out to Server_Relay, so no port is opened on the robot.

ros2 launch ros2_network_bridge jetbot_console.launch.py transport:=relay \
    relay_host:=<relay host> relay_robot:=jetbot-01 \
    relay_token_file:=/etc/jetbot/relay.token relay_pin:=<sha256 of the relay key>

The token is read from a file (never a parameter, so it does not show in ros2 param), and relay_pin pins the relay's public key so a self-signed relay works and an impostor is refused before the token is sent. The relay forwards nothing from an observer to the vehicle except a verified heartbeat.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Network Bridge: frame conversions, covariance mapping, OBSTACLE_DISTANCE and tests.
  • MAVLink Relay: deploying Server_Relay.
  • Mobile App: the JetbotNanoOWL console that reads the same downlink.

docs.title: Configure and Validate 2-D LiDAR SLAM
docs.text:
Wire the LDROBOT LD19 scanner and the DFRobot LPB40B range finder, give them stable device names, calibrate the parameters that come from your own sensors, build a map, and check that the estimator is consistent before anything navigates on it.

Before you start

  • Time: about 2 hours, including bench measurements
  • You need: the Jetbot with an LD19 and an LPB40B on USB-serial adapters, the IMU stream on /imu/data (Connect the Flight Controller and Sensors), a tape measure, a matte wall and a thin post
  • You learn: sensor parameters from datasheets and bench data, the EKF + PL-ICP + pose-graph pipeline, NIS-based consistency checks

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
LD19 ──UART 230400──▶ ld19_node ── /scan ──┐
 LPB40B ─UART 115200─▶ lpb40b_node ─ /range ─┤
 IMU ── /imu/data (gyro = EKF input) ─────────┼──▶ lidar_slam_node
 wheel odometry ── /odom (optional) ──────────┘     gate · Hampel · de-skew → EKF ↔ PL-ICP
                                                     → pose graph + loop closure → /map, slam/pose

The estimation loop is closed: the fused pose and velocity feed the next scan's de-skew, correspondence gate and ICP initial guess. The package commands no actuator; its pose and map feed the planners and controllers.

docs.title: 1. Stable device names
docs.text:
USB-serial adapters change /dev/ttyUSB* numbers between boots. Read the vendor, product and serial of each adapter:

udevadm info -a /dev/ttyUSB0 | grep -E 'idVendor|idProduct|serial' | head -3

Create /etc/udev/rules.d/99-lidar.rules with your values:

SUBSYSTEM=="tty", ATTRS{idVendor}=="10c4", ATTRS{idProduct}=="ea60", ATTRS{serial}=="<ld19>",   SYMLINK+="ld19"
SUBSYSTEM=="tty", ATTRS{idVendor}=="1a86", ATTRS{idProduct}=="7523", ATTRS{serial}=="<lpb40b>", SYMLINK+="lpb40b"

sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger
ls -l /dev/ld19 /dev/lpb40b

docs.title: 2. Build and check the drivers
docs.text:
ROS/build.sh -p ros2_lidar_slam
source install/setup.bash
ros2 launch ros2_lidar_slam dual_lidar_slam.launch.py ld19_port:=/dev/ld19 lpb40b_port:=/dev/lpb40b
Check Expected ros2 topic hz /scan 10 Hz (the LD19's in-device rotation loop), 450 rays per scan ros2 topic echo /range --once a finite range; +inf = nothing within 40 m, NaN = invalid /diagnostics no CRC errors, rotation 10 ± 0.1 Hz

The LD19 turns clockwise; the driver mirrors it to REP-103 (counter-clockwise), so an object to the robot's left must appear at a positive angle.

docs.title: 3. Set the sensor mounts
docs.text:
The mounts are static transforms from launch arguments ld19_{x,y,z,yaw} and lpb40b_{x,y,z,yaw} [m, rad]. Measure the positions from base_link. Use publish_mounts:=false if your URDF already provides them.

LD19 yaw. Place a single thin post in front of the robot on its x axis. In RViz (fixed frame base_link), the post must appear at 0°. Correct ld19_yaw until it does.

docs.title: 4. Calibrate the range noise
docs.text:
Every default in config/slam_params.yaml is tagged with its source: [D] datasheet, [C] computed, [A] assumption. The LD19 random range noise σ_rand = 0.01 m is an assumption. Measure it:

  1. Park the robot facing a matte wall at 1, 3 and 6 m.
  2. At each distance record 100 scans: ros2 bag record /scan.
  3. Take the standard deviation of the ray normal to the wall.

  4. Set

    sensor.sigma_range = √((0.045/√3)² + σ_rand²)

    The first term is the datasheet's ±45 mm accuracy bound treated as a uniform distribution.

LPB40B. Compare /range with a tape measure at 1, 5 and 10 m. The mean error must be within ±5 cm (datasheet accuracy); otherwise correct the mount or latency_s.

docs.title: 5. Build a map
docs.text:
ros2 launch ros2_lidar_slam lidar_visualization.launch.py      # RViz, on a laptop

Drive slowly through the area and return to the start so that loop closures can correct drift. Keyframes are taken every 0.2 m or 30°; a loop candidate is the nearest keyframe at least 30 keyframes older and within 3 m.

Without wheel odometry, publish map → base_link directly:

ros2 launch ros2_lidar_slam dual_lidar_slam.launch.py odom_frame:="''"

Enable use_odom only if that odometry has not already fused the same IMU; fusing it twice makes the filter overconfident.

Save the map:

ros2 service call /lidar_slam_node/save_map std_srvs/srv/Trigger   # ~/maps/slam_<time>.{pgm,yaml,g2o}

The PGM/YAML pair loads into Nav2's map_server; the .g2o file is the optimised pose graph.

docs.title: 6. Check consistency
docs.text:
Record the estimator signals on a representative run:

ros2 bag record /slam/debug

Each message holds the prior, the ICP pose, the innovation and its covariance, NIS, degeneracy eigenvalues, gyro bias and processing time. Then check in /diagnostics:

Value Meaning nis_mean inside nis_bound_low … nis_bound_high the filter is consistent above the upper bound inconsistent: noise underestimated, mount or σ wrong far below the lower bound conservative: the process noise q̃_v (sized for 1 m/s²) can be reduced to the robot's actual accelerations processing_ms must stay well below the 100 ms scan period

For reference, the SIL run on a 52 m corridor loop reached 0.030 m keyframe ATE after eight loop closures, a final error of 0.015 m / 0.18°, and a mean NIS of 1.87, which is conservative, never optimistic.

Degenerate scenes

In a long featureless corridor or a rotationally symmetric room, the scan constrains only some directions. The matcher detects this from the eigenvalues of the information matrix, updates only the constrained subspace, and gives the degenerate direction σ = 10 m. Expect drift along such corridors until a loop closes.

docs.title: 7. Alternative back end
docs.text:
ros2 launch ros2_lidar_slam dual_lidar_slam.launch.py backend:=slam_toolbox

Use slam_toolbox or Nav2 AMCL with the saved map for localisation on an existing map; the built-in back end has no localisation-only mode.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• 2-D only: the floor is assumed flat; a tilted sensor sees the floor.
  • Loop closure runs in the scan callback: 66 ms worst case on x86, expect roughly 2–3× on the Orin's CPU.
  • Hardware-in-the-loop evidence (a recorded bag with NIS inside bounds and bench σ_r) is still required before driving on the map.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• A. Censi, "An ICP variant using a point-to-line metric", ICRA 2008.
  • J. Zhang, M. Kaess, S. Singh, "On degeneracy of optimization-based state estimation problems", ICRA 2016.
  • E. Olson, "Real-time correlative scan matching", ICRA 2009.
  • G. Grisetti et al., "A tutorial on graph-based SLAM", 2010.
  • S. Thrun, W. Burgard, D. Fox, Probabilistic Robotics, 2005.

Full design record: LiDAR SLAM.

docs.title: Calibrate the Stereo Camera
docs.text:
Calibrate the two IMX219 cameras of ros2_stereo, check the result against measurable acceptance criteria, and measure the disparity noise σ_d so that the per-pixel depth uncertainty the node publishes is true for your rig.

Before you start

  • Time: about 1 hour
  • You need: the Jetson with both IMX219 cameras on CSI, a printed chessboard with 9 × 6 inner corners on a flat rigid board, a calliper, a textured flat target
  • You learn: stereo calibration (Zhang + joint refinement), rectification checks, σ_d characterisation, the per-pixel Kalman filter consistency test

Recalibrate after any change

Calibrate once per rig, and again after any change of lens, mount or flip_method. A calibration from another rig produces depth that looks plausible and is wrong.

docs.title: Why the numbers matter
docs.text:
For a rectified pair with focal length f [px], baseline B [m] and disparity d [px] (Hartley & Zisserman §9.3, §12.1):

Z = f·B / (d − d_off)              σ_Z = Z²·σ_d / (f·B)      (first order)

On the Jetbot (f = 339.7 px at 480 px width, B = 0.06 m, so f·B = 20.38 px·m), one pixel of disparity error at 2 m is about 0.2 m of depth. Two things set that error: rectification quality (a row misalignment makes the matcher compare the wrong pixels) and the matcher noise σ_d. This tutorial controls the first and measures the second.

docs.title: 1. Build and start uncalibrated
docs.text:
ROS/build.sh -p ros2_stereo
source install/setup.bash
ros2 launch ros2_stereo jetbot_stereo.launch.py

Without a calibration file the node starts with an explicit warning. Images are being captured, but depth is not to be trusted yet.

docs.title: 2. Capture calibration pairs
docs.text:
Measure one printed square with a calliper; you need its size in metres for step 3.

Hold the board in view of both cameras and capture a pair for each pose:

ros2 service call /stereo/stereo_node/capture_calibration_pair std_srvs/srv/Trigger

Capture 25–40 poses:

  • distance 0.4–1 m;
  • tilt up to ±25° about both axes;
  • board centres spread over the whole image, including the corners.

Cover the corners

With boards only near the centre, lens distortion is extrapolated at the edges. On the synthetic test rig that raised the rectified row error at the image edge from 0.04 px to 0.35 px.

Pairs are written to calibration_capture_dir (default /tmp/stereo_calibration).

docs.title: 3. Run the calibration
docs.text:
ros2 run ros2_stereo stereo_calibrate --images /tmp/stereo_calibration \
    --board 9x6 --square 0.025 --output ~/stereo_calibration.yaml

Replace 0.025 with your measured square size in metres. The tool calibrates each camera (Zhang 2000), then refines both intrinsics and the extrinsics jointly (bundle adjustment). On the synthetic rig with 0.1 px corner noise, keeping the intrinsics fixed gave rectified row errors up to 0.65 px; the joint refinement stayed below 0.09 px over 40 draws (OpenCV 4.6).

docs.title: 4. Accept or reject
docs.text:
Accept the calibration only when all three hold:

Criterion Threshold Why Stereo RMS reprojection error close to √2·σ_c, where the corner noise σ_c is typically 0.1–0.2 px a larger RMS means a bent board, bad detections or a moving camera Rectified row error ≤ 0.5 px; the tool exits with code 3 above it semi-global matching degrades beyond it (Hirschmüller & Gehrig 2009) Outlier views none listed (> 2 × median error) remove the listed images and re-run

Calibrate at the capture size with the same flip_method used at run time. The node rescales the intrinsics to the working resolution exactly (f' = s·f, c' = s·(c + ½) − ½), so no second calibration is needed for another working size.

docs.title: 5. Run with the calibration
docs.text:
ros2 launch ros2_stereo jetbot_stereo.launch.py calibration_file:=$HOME/stereo_calibration.yaml
ros2 run rqt_image_view rqt_image_view /stereo/disparity/color
ros2 topic echo /diagnostics --field status[0].values

Check that straight edges in left/image_rect are straight and that features lie on the same row in both rectified images.

docs.title: 6. Measure σ_d
docs.text:
The node ships with disparity_sigma: 0.3 px, a bound on the 0.278 px measured on a synthetic scene. VPI and SGBM matchers differ, and so does your scene texture, so measure it:

  1. Place a textured plane fronto-parallel at 1.0 m.
  2. Disable the temporal filter (temporal.enable: false in config/stereo_params.yaml, or ros2 param set /stereo/stereo_node temporal.enable false).

  3. Record disparity for 10 s:

    ros2 bag record -o sigma_d_1m /stereo/disparity --max-duration 10

  4. Over the valid pixels of each frame, fit a plane d = a·u + b·v + c and take the robust standard deviation of the residual, σ_d = 1.4826 · MAD. MAD is used because SGM sub-pixel errors are not Gaussian (pixel locking).

  5. Set disparity_sigma to that value.

At 1 m the expected single-frame depth noise is then σ_Z = 1.0² · σ_d / 20.38 m, for example 14.7 mm with σ_d = 0.3 px.

docs.title: 7. Check the estimator consistency
docs.text:
Re-enable the temporal filter and record a static scene. Each pixel runs a scalar Kalman filter on disparity with a χ²₁ gate at γ = 6.635 (1 % rejection). When the noise model is right, the accepted normalised innovation squared averages

E[NIS | NIS ≤ γ] = F₃(γ) / F₁(γ) = 0.925

In /diagnostics, check:

Value Expected temporal NIS mean ≈ 0.925 temporal gated ≈ 1 %

The node goes to WARN when the mean deviates by more than 25 % over at least 10 000 updates. The sampling standard deviation of the mean is about √(2/N) ≤ 1.4 %, so a 25 % deviation is a real model mismatch: re-measure σ_d before touching anything else. q₀ is the only tunable term, for image motion during rotation; set it from a recording and check it with these NIS values.

docs.title: Outputs you can now trust
docs.text:
Topic Content /stereo/depth Z [m], NaN where invalid (REP 118) /stereo/depth/uncertainty σ_Z [m] per pixel /stereo/points point cloud in the left optical frame

Consumers must treat NaN as unknown, never as free space.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Z. Zhang, "A Flexible New Technique for Camera Calibration", IEEE TPAMI 22(11), 2000.
  • R. Hartley, A. Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2nd ed., 2004.
  • H. Hirschmüller, S. Gehrig, "Stereo Matching in the Presence of Sub-Pixel Calibration Errors", CVPR 2009.
  • D. Simon, Optimal State Estimation, Wiley 2006.

Full design record: Stereo.

docs.title: Fly Your First Mission
docs.text:
Write a mission file, have the mission planner check it, and fly it end to end in the full-stack software-in-the-loop (SIL) test, with the real estimator, MPC, flight controller and mission planner nodes closing the loop around a simulated vehicle. No hardware is needed.

Before you start

  • Time: about 30 minutes, most of it building
  • You need: Ubuntu 22.04 with ROS 2 Humble (Installation)
  • You learn: the mission file format, the pre-flight analysis, the mission state machine and in-flight re-tasking

docs.title: What runs
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    MF[("mission file")] --> MP["mission_planner_node"]
    MP -->|"flight/waypoints<br/>flight/nav_command"| FC["flight_controller_node"]
    FC --> MPC["uav_trajectory_controller<br/>(offset-free MPC)"]
    MPC -->|"attitude + thrust"| SIM(("simulated vehicle<br/>uav_stack_sil.py"))
    SIM -->|"IMU 200 Hz, GNSS 10 Hz,<br/>baro 50 Hz, BMS 1 Hz"| EST["uav_state_estimator<br/>(15-state ESKF)"]
    EST -->|"odometry/filtered"| MPC
    EST --> FC
    EST --> MP

The simulated vehicle is deliberately different from what the nodes believe: 10 % heavier, a 3.4 m/s wind that no node knows about, airframe drag and rotor H-force that the MPC does not model, and biased IMU readings. A mission that passes here has been flown against model error, not against a perfect copy of the controller's model.

docs.title: 1. Build
docs.text:
From the repository root:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ROS/build.sh --rosdep -u ros2_mission_planner
source install/setup.bash

-u builds the package and everything it depends on (ros2_flight_controller, ros2_control_system). Run the package tests once to confirm the build:

colcon test --packages-select ros2_mission_planner && colcon test-result --verbose

docs.title: 2. Read the example mission
docs.text:
Source/ROS2_Mission_Planner/config/waypoint_mission.yaml:

mission:
  name: "demo square"
  frame: home            # coordinates relative to the arming position
  end_action: rtl        # return home and land after the last waypoint
  defaults:
    acceptance_radius: 1.5
    hold_time: 0.0
  waypoints:
    - {x:  0.0, y:  0.0, z: 5.0, heading_deg:   0.0, hold_time: 2.0}
    - {x: 10.0, y:  0.0, z: 5.0, heading_deg:   0.0}
    - {x: 10.0, y: 10.0, z: 8.0, heading_deg:  90.0}
    - {x:  0.0, y: 10.0, z: 8.0, heading_deg: 180.0, hold_time: 3.0}
    - {x:  0.0, y:  0.0, z: 5.0, heading_deg: 270.0}
Field Meaning frame home: metres relative to the arming position, z above the take-off point; odom: absolute in the odometry frame end_action rtl, land or hover after the last waypoint acceptance_radius a leg ends only when the FC reports HOVER and the measured position is inside this radius [m] hold_time time to hold at the waypoint [s] heading_deg yaw at the waypoint [deg], counter-clockwise from the +x axis of the mission frame (REP-103)

Speeds are not part of the file. The flight controller's minimum-jerk trajectory limits set them, and the planner reads those limits from the running flight controller at start-up.

docs.title: 3. Fly it in SIL
docs.text:
python3 Source/ROS2_Control_System/tests/sil/uav_stack_sil.py \
  --estimator  install/ros2_control_system/lib/ros2_control_system/uav_state_estimator \
  --controller install/ros2_control_system/lib/ros2_control_system/uav_trajectory_controller \
  --flight     install/ros2_flight_controller/lib/ros2_flight_controller/flight_controller_node \
  --control-params install/ros2_control_system/share/ros2_control_system/config/uav_control.yaml \
  --mission-planner install/ros2_mission_planner/lib/ros2_mission_planner/mission_planner_node \
  --mission-params  install/ros2_mission_planner/share/ros2_mission_planner/config/mission_planner_params.yaml \
  --mission-file    install/ros2_mission_planner/share/ros2_mission_planner/config/waypoint_mission.yaml

The script starts the four nodes, calls /mission/start, and flies the mission to touchdown. It prints a pass/fail line per check and exits non-zero if any check fails. The reference run in the package README gives:

Metric Result Worst waypoint miss 0.09 m Position-control RMS 4.1 cm Touchdown error 4.5 cm Wind estimate (truth 3.0, −1.5 m/s) (2.97, −1.50) ± 0.43 m/s Measured-power ratio (truth ≈ 1.15) 1.13 Duration, checks 71 s, 9/9

Add --trace /tmp/sil_trace.csv to record time, mode, true and estimated position, tilt and thrust for plotting.

Why the wind and power estimates matter

The planner never sees the true wind. It estimates it from the MPC's disturbance estimate d̂ (control/disturbance) and uses the 95 % disc around that estimate, not the point value, when it computes the energy needed to return home. The measured-power ratio corrects the energy model upwards in flight. Both are explained on the Mission Planner page.

docs.title: 4. Watch the mission
docs.text:
While the SIL runs, in a second terminal (source install/setup.bash first):

ros2 topic echo /mission/status      # state, progress, SoC and SoC needed to return, wind
ros2 topic echo /mission/geofence    # signed clearance and the binding constraint
ros2 topic echo /flight/status       # flight-controller mode
ros2 topic echo /mission/preview --once   # planned route (transient local)

/mission/preview is a nav_msgs/Path; add it to RViz with fixed frame odom to see the route, including any detour points.

docs.title: 5. Avoid known obstacles
docs.text:
config/missions/keep_out_example.yaml puts a mast on the first leg and a tree on the straight way home, both taller than the return altitude:

  keep_out:
    - {name: mast, x: 12.0, y: 0.0, radius: 3.0, top: 20.0}
    - {name: tree, x: 12.0, y: 10.0, radius: 3.0, top: 25.0}

Fly it by replacing the --mission-file argument:

  --mission-file install/ros2_mission_planner/share/ros2_mission_planner/config/missions/keep_out_example.yaml

The planner inflates each zone by the safety margin and the trajectory sampling bound, inserts detour points on polygons circumscribed about the inflated circles, verifies the minimum-jerk trajectory through them, and flies the return as waypoints instead of the flight controller's straight RTH. Reference result: two detour points, at least 6.2 m from both zone centres (r = 3 m), 11/11 checks.

docs.title: 6. Change the mission in flight
docs.text:
Add --update-file to upload a second mission while the first one is flying:

  --mission-file install/ros2_mission_planner/share/ros2_mission_planner/config/waypoint_mission.yaml \
  --update-file  install/ros2_mission_planner/share/ros2_mission_planner/config/missions/retask_example.yaml

The planner analyses the new mission from the current position with the current state of charge and wind. If it is feasible, it commands HOVER, waits for the flight controller to hover, and continues with the new plan; home is unchanged. An infeasible upload is rejected and the running mission continues. On a live system the same upload is:

ros2 topic pub --once /mission/upload std_msgs/msg/String "{data: '$(cat retask.yaml)'}"

docs.title: 7. Write your own mission
docs.text:
Copy an example, change the waypoints, and run it through the SIL before it goes anywhere near a vehicle. A mission is refused before arming when:

  • the trajectory, not only the waypoints, leaves the geofence or enters a keep-out zone;
  • the energy to fly it and return, with the wind bound and the reserve, exceeds the battery.

mission/diagnostics and the planner log state which constraint failed.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Mission Planner: survey and orbit patterns, energy model, state machine.
  • Flight Controller: modes, failsafes and the minimum-jerk guidance the planner relies on.
  • Control System: the ESKF and MPC that close the loop.

docs.title: Connect the Flight Controller and Sensors
Connect the Flight Controller and Sensors
docs.text:
Bring up the Ethernet link between the Jetson and the vehicle's microcontrollers, start the micro-ROS agent and jetowl_bridge, and check that every sensor stream arrives at its expected rate with valid timestamps before any controller is allowed to use it.

Before you start

  • Time: about 30 minutes
  • You need: the Jetson; the JetOwl flight controller (STM32N657) on the Jetson's Ethernet port, or no hardware for the simulated sensor link in part B
  • You learn: the vehicle network, the micro-ROS agent, the bridge's links and diagnostics, how to tell a healthy sensor stream from a broken one

docs.title: The links
docs.text:
ros2_jetowl_bridge is the single ROS 2 node between the Jetson and every microcontroller. Each link is switched by a launch argument:

Link Device Transport Default fc JetOwl flight controller, STM32N657 micro-ROS over UDP (agent on port 8888) on vision_mcu JetOwl_Vision camera, STM32N655 + IMX335 micro-ROS over UDP (same agent) off vision OpenMV RT1062 camera JSON lines over TCP or USB CDC off sensor_link hexacopter flight MCU / Gazebo virtual MCU CRC-32 framed UDP off

All links report in one DiagnosticArray on /diagnostics, under jetowl_bridge/<link>.

docs.title: Part A: the JetOwl flight controller
1. Configure the Jetson's Ethernet port
docs.text:
The firmware uses static addressing (lwIP with DHCP off):

Host Address Jetson 192.168.10.1/24 JetOwl FC 192.168.10.2/24 JetOwl_Vision (if fitted, through a switch) 192.168.10.3/24 micro-ROS agent UDP 8888 on the Jetson 
ip link                                   # find the interface name
sudo cp Source/ROS2_JetOwl_Bridge/config/netplan-jetowl.yaml /etc/netplan/60-jetowl.yaml
sudo nano /etc/netplan/60-jetowl.yaml     # replace eth0 with your interface if needed
sudo netplan apply
ping -c 3 192.168.10.2                    # the FC answers once its firmware is running

docs.title: 2. Build and launch
docs.text:
ROS/build.sh -p ros2_jetowl_bridge
source install/setup.bash
ros2 launch ros2_jetowl_bridge jetowl_bridge.launch.py

The launch file also starts the micro-ROS agent. Choose where it comes from with agent:=:

agent:= Agent ros (default) built once from source with micro_ros_setup (create_agent_ws.sh, build_agent.sh) docker the microros/micro-ros-agent:humble container none started elsewhere (Docker Compose service, Kubernetes sidecar)

docs.title: 3. Verify the streams
docs.text:
ros2 topic hz /imu/data              # 200 Hz, frame imu_link, orientation ENU/FLU
ros2 topic hz /jetowl/motor_rpm      # 50 Hz, NaN = unknown (not zero)
ros2 topic hz /baro/pressure         # 25 Hz, variance 1.44 Pa²
ros2 topic echo /jetowl/status       # 2 Hz firmware status, RC link keys
ros2 topic echo /jetowl/link_ok      # true while the FC is alive
ros2 topic echo /diagnostics         # jetowl_bridge/fc: link, rotors, firmware status

The link is declared lost after fc.link_timeout_s = 1.5 s, three status periods.

No /imu/data from the FC?

The firmware IMU path needs I2C1 and EXTI enabled in CubeMX (BOARD_CUBEMX_PERIPHERALS_READY = 1). Until then the FC does not publish /imu/data and refuses to arm. See the CubeMX Setup page.

docs.title: 4. Understand what you must not skip
docs.text:
The bridge contains no control law. The attitude estimate, attitude controller (250 Hz), rate controller with extended state observer (1 kHz), mixer and rotor speed loops run in the firmware; the translational ESKF and MPC run on the Jetson in ros2_control_system. The bridge relays arming from ros2_flight_controller and the firmware only accepts it with:

  • a set-point younger than 0.1 s;
  • a valid attitude estimate;
  • tilt below 20°;
  • a thrust command below 20 % of the maximum thrust.

The MPC idle thrust (thrust_min_n in uav_control.yaml) must therefore be below that 20 % for your airframe, or arming is refused with thrust command too high.

Before the first powered test

Remove the propellers. The FC and vision links have not been run against hardware yet; bench and hardware-in-the-loop evidence is still to be produced (see the JetOwl Bridge limitations).

docs.title: 5. Add the cameras (optional)
docs.text:
ros2 launch ros2_jetowl_bridge jetowl_bridge.launch.py vision_mcu:=true           # + JetOwl_Vision
ros2 launch ros2_jetowl_bridge jetowl_bridge.launch.py vision:=true               # + OpenMV over TCP
ros2 launch ros2_jetowl_bridge jetowl_bridge.launch.py vision:=true connection_type:=usb

docs.title: Part B: the MCU sensor link without hardware
docs.text: The hexacopter's IMU, GNSS and motor encoders reach the Jetson through a CRC-32 framed UDP protocol. In simulation the same frames come from the Gazebo virtual MCU, so the link and every node downstream run identical code in SIL and on the vehicle.

docs.title: 1. Start the simulator and the link
docs.text:
ROS/build.sh --rosdep -u ros2_hexacopter_gazebo -u ros2_jetowl_bridge
source install/setup.bash
ros2 launch ros2_hexacopter_gazebo hexacopter_sim.launch.py gui:=false

hexacopter_sim.launch.py also starts jetowl_bridge with only its sensor link enabled and the sensor_link_sim.yaml overlay. To start the bridge alone against an external virtual MCU:

ros2 launch ros2_jetowl_bridge jetowl_bridge.launch.py fc:=false sensor_link:=true sim:=true

docs.title: 2. Verify
docs.text:
ros2 topic hz /imu/data                 # ≈ 1 kHz
ros2 topic hz /encoders/joint_states    # ≈ 1 kHz, 12 channels
ros2 topic echo /gps/fix --once         # STATUS_FIX with an ENU covariance
ros2 topic echo /diagnostics            # sensor_link: link, clock, imu, gnss, encoders

Observed on the reference run: /imu/data 996 Hz, /encoders/joint_states 998 Hz, /gps/fix with σ_h = 1.27 m, 0.00 % link loss.

docs.title: 3. What makes a stream healthy
docs.text:
Check Where Healthy Rate …: imu / gnss / encoders at the configured rate, watchdog not tripped Loss and errors …: link 0 % loss, no CRC errors, no unexpected MCU reboots Clock …: clock offset and skew converged; σ small against the IMU period Timestamps message headers the measurement instant mapped to ROS time, never the arrival time

On the vehicle, sensor_link.clock.require_sync: true keeps every topic silent until the clock filter has converged. Do not disable it: the ESKF fuses IMU and GNSS by timestamp, and an arrival-time stamp adds the network jitter directly to the estimation error.

docs.title: 4. Bench check without ROS
docs.text:
On the bench, mcu_link_dump listens, synchronises the clock with the MCU and prints a JSON summary:

ros2 run ros2_jetowl_bridge mcu_link_dump --port 9870 --mcu 192.168.1.103:9871 --duration 5

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• JetOwl Bridge: topic contracts, wire format, clock synchronisation and encoder estimator design.
  • Hexacopter Gazebo: the simulator that feeds part B.
  • Fly Your First Mission: use the estimator and controller on top of these streams.

docs.title: Monitor a Running Robot
docs.text:
Find out, from the vehicle's own reports, whether every link, sensor and estimator is healthy; inspect and manage nodes from a terminal; watch the cluster and the Jetson's resources; and record the signals needed to review a controller afterwards.

Before you start

  • Time: about 30 minutes
  • You need: a running stack (native, Docker Compose or the k3s cluster), an interactive terminal
  • You learn: where each package reports its health, the ros2_monitoring node manager, what to record for a flight review

docs.title: 1. Diagnostics first
docs.text:
Every package that touches a sensor or a link publishes diagnostic_msgs/DiagnosticArray on /diagnostics with measured values, not just "OK". Start there:

ros2 topic echo /diagnostics
ros2 run rqt_robot_monitor rqt_robot_monitor        # tree view, if rqt is installed
Status name Package Look at jetowl_bridge/fc: link, …/fc: rotors ros2_jetowl_bridge link age, firmware status, per-rotor RPM rate and valid fraction jetowl_bridge/sensor_link: link / clock / imu / gnss / encoders ros2_jetowl_bridge loss %, CRC errors, MCU reboots, clock offset/skew, per-stream rate jetowl_bridge/vision_mcu: link / image ros2_jetowl_bridge rate, latency, frame gaps stereo node ros2_stereo rate, latency, valid %, temporal NIS mean (≈ 0.925) and gated fraction (≈ 1 %) SLAM node ros2_lidar_slam scan rate, CRC errors, rotation, nis_mean against nis_bound_low/high, processing_ms mission/diagnostics ros2_mission_planner feasibility, wind and power estimates, binding constraint network/diagnostics ros2_network_bridge uplink loss, predicted false-loss rate, B/s, CRC errors, failsafe state

Read the consistency numbers

An estimator whose NIS mean leaves its χ² bounds is telling you its noise model is wrong. Treat that as a fault to investigate, not a number to tune away: re-measure the sensor noise as described in Calibrate the Stereo Camera and Configure and Validate 2-D LiDAR SLAM.

docs.title: 2. The node manager
docs.text:
ros2_monitoring is a curses dashboard with pages for the system, nodes, topics, the graph, Docker and Kubernetes. It publishes and subscribes to nothing and closes no control loop.

ROS/build.sh -p ros2_monitoring && source install/setup.bash
ros2 run ros2_monitoring ros2_monitoring --start-page nodes

ros2 launch gives a node no interactive terminal, so the launch file opens one: ros2 launch ros2_monitoring ros2_monitoring.launch.py page:=nodes terminal:='xterm -e'.

On the NODES page:

Column Meaning LED / STATE alive, inactive, unconfigured, finalized or lost; NEW for 6 s after joining, LOST <age> for 8 s PUB / SUB / SRV endpoint counts per node PID the process hosting the node (* = matched by executable name, — = no match) CPU% / CPU TREND CPU of the process, low-pass filtered with τ = 2 s (100 % = one core) MEM / UP resident memory, time since the node (re)joined Key Action Enter details: overview, publishers, subscribers, services, parameters, lifecycle p load the node's parameters l lifecycle transition (only those the node reports as available) x stop the node's process; the dialog shows the PID, the match rule and every node in that process, and Cancel is the default / · s filter by name · cycle the sort key

What the numbers mean

CPU and memory are per process: nodes sharing a process (components in one container) show the same values. The TOPICS page does not yet measure frequency and bandwidth; use ros2 topic hz and ros2 topic bw.

Other pages: SYS (CPU cores, GPU, memory, disk, sensors, processes), DOCKER and K8S (refreshed every 5 s through kubectl). Disable unavailable back ends with --no-gpu, --no-docker, --no-kubernetes.

docs.title: 3. The cluster
docs.text:
On the two-Jetson deployment, the dashboard runs as the monitoring pod:

kubectl -n jetowl attach -it deploy/jetowl-ros2-jetson-monitoring    # the dashboard
make -C Helm status                                                  # which board runs what
make -C Kubernetes balance                                           # requested CPU/memory per board
kubectl -n jetowl get pods -o wide -w                                # restarts and rescheduling

A pod that keeps restarting is a node that keeps exiting; read its log with kubectl -n jetowl logs deploy/jetowl-ros2-jetson-<node> --previous.

docs.title: 4. The Jetson itself
docs.text:
sudo tegrastats --interval 1000       # CPU and GPU load, EMC, temperatures, rail power
sudo nvpmodel -q                       # active power mode

Watch GPU load and temperature while the perception pipelines run. A thermally throttled GPU lowers the frame rate of every detector and of the stereo matcher, and every downstream estimator then sees a lower sample rate than it was designed for.

docs.title: 5. Record for review
docs.text:
A controller cannot be reviewed without its signals. For a flight or a bench test, record at least the set-point, the measurement, the estimate, the controller outputs before and after saturation, and the diagnostics:

ros2 bag record -o flight_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S) \
  /odometry/filtered /imu/data /gps/fix /baro/pressure \
  /flight/status /flight/waypoints /flight/nav_command \
  /control/attitude_setpoint /control/thrust /control/disturbance \
  /jetowl/status /jetowl/motor_rpm /battery/state \
  /mission/status /mission/geofence /diagnostics

Add /slam/debug for SLAM and /stereo/disparity for stereo characterisation. Check the exact topic names of your launch configuration with ros2 topic list before recording.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Monitoring dashboard: pages, process matching and the maths behind the displayed values.
  • Qt Dashboard: the graphical operator interface.
  • Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Update MCU Firmware Over the Air
Update MCU Firmware Over the Air
docs.text:
Publish a firmware release for the JetOwl flight controller or the JetOwl_Vision camera on the OTA server, download it to the inactive flash slot from ROS 2, apply it, and watch the A/B bootloader confirm the new image or roll it back.

Before you start

  • Time: about 45 minutes
  • You need: the Jetson running jetowl_bridge with the FC link (Connect the Flight Controller and Sensors), Go 1.21+ or Docker for the server, the arm-none-eabi-gcc toolchain to build firmware
  • You learn: the .fw package format, the server endpoints, the A/B boot state machine and its guarantees

Not yet verified on hardware

The OTA layer has been written, compiled, linked and tested on the host, including end to end against the real server over TCP. XSPI flash access, the FSBL jump, the watchdog and a download over a real network have not been run on a board yet. Follow the hardware bring-up order in the OTA design before relying on it, and keep a debugger connected for the first updates.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
build machine                      OTA server (Go, :8080)             STM32N6 (FC or Vision)
 make ota-upload VERSION=1.2.3 ──▶  POST /upload  (header + SHA-256    "ota" task:
   tools/ota_pack.py → .fw           checked, never overwrites)          manifest → download (Range resume)
                                    GET /api/ota/manifest?device= ◀──    → SHA-256 → flash read-back → READY
                                    GET /download?file=           ◀──    ota/apply → pending = other slot → reset
                                    POST /api/ota/report          ◀──    FSBL: verify copy in RAM → trial boot
                                                                         healthy 30 s → confirm, else rollback

OTA never overwrites the running image. Flash holds two slots (A and B, 4 MB each) and a boot record stored twice; every failure — power loss, network loss, corrupted image, hanging image — leads back to a bootable state.

docs.title: 1. Run the OTA server
docs.text:
On the Jetson (or any Linux host on the robot network):

Server_OTA/scripts/build.sh --target linux/arm64      # static binary in Server_OTA/bin
Server_OTA/scripts/run.sh                             # listens on :8080, firmware in data/firmware

Or in a container: docker compose up -d server_ota from Docker/compose. In the two-Jetson cluster, Helm deploys it behind the MetalLB address 192.168.10.200:8080 (Deploy the Stack on a Two-Jetson Cluster).

The address is compiled into the firmware

The MCUs fetch from NET_OTA_SERVER_IP:NET_OTA_SERVER_PORT in Application/Network/Inc/net_config.h, default 192.168.1.101:8080; uploads go to OTA_SERVER in the firmware Makefile, same default. For the cluster deployment, set both to 192.168.10.200:8080. When the server is on another subnet than the MCUs (192.168.10.0/24), the Jetson must forward and masquerade their traffic:

sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 192.168.10.0/24 -o <LAN interface> -j MASQUERADE

docs.title: 2. Publish a release
docs.text:
In JetOwl_FlightControl (or JetOwl_Vision), after a normal build:

make ota-upload VERSION=1.2.3        # → jetowl_fc_v1.2.3.fw, uploaded to OTA_SERVER
make ota VERSION=1.2.3               # package only

The .fw package (JOWL v1) is a 256-byte header followed by up to four segments. The server validates it on upload: header CRC-32, payload SHA-256, the <device>_v<M.m.p>.fw name, and that each segment loads only into the RAM windows permitted for that device. An existing release is never overwritten (409).

curl "http://<server>:8080/api/ota/manifest?device=jetowl_fc"
# device=jetowl_fc  version=1.2.3  file=jetowl_fc_v1.2.3.fw  size=…  sha256=…

Versions are compared numerically (1.10.0 > 1.9.99). A release whose content is corrupted is skipped: an MCU is never offered it.

docs.title: 3. Download to the inactive slot
docs.text:
ros2 service call /jetowl/ota/start std_srvs/srv/Trigger
ros2 topic echo /jetowl/status        # fw_version, ota_state, ota_progress_pct, ota_available, ota_error

ota_state goes idle → checking → up_to_date, or downloading → ready. The SHA-256 is checked four times along the way: the downloaded file against the manifest, the full slot read back from flash, the payload against its header, and finally, in the bootloader, the copy in RAM that will actually run. A dropped connection resumes with an HTTP Range request.

For the camera, use /jetowl_vision/ota/start, /jetowl_vision/ota/apply and /jetowl_vision/status. Both firmwares' ota_* keys also reach /diagnostics through jetowl_bridge.

docs.title: 4. Apply
docs.text:
ros2 service call /jetowl/ota/apply std_srvs/srv/Trigger

The flight controller applies an update only while disarmed. The service marks the new slot as pending, persists the boot record and resets. Then:

FSBL, pending slot S:
    trials < 3 and S valid  → trials++, persist, boot S in trial mode with the watchdog (8.008 s)
    otherwise               → pending = none (rollback), persist, boot the previous image
application in trial, continuously healthy for 30 s → confirm: active = S
Device "Healthy" means FC micro-ROS session alive and the control timer tick running Vision micro-ROS session alive and the camera streaming

trials is incremented and persisted before the jump, so an image that hangs or keeps resetting runs at most three times before the bootloader returns to the previous one.

Power-cycle the FC before flying

The FC refuses to arm for the whole trial-boot session, even after confirmation, because the independent watchdog cannot be stopped until the next reset. Power-cycle once after a confirmed update, then fly.

docs.title: 5. Confirm the result
docs.text:
ros2 topic echo /jetowl/status --once        # fw_version, ota_trial, ota_last_event
curl http://<server>:8080/api/ota/devices    # last reported state per MCU
ota_last_event Meaning staged the new image was set pending and the board reset confirmed the new image stayed healthy for 30 s and is now active rollback_trials three trial boots failed; the previous image runs rollback_invalid the pending image failed verification; the previous image runs fallback the active image was corrupted; the other valid slot was booted

docs.title: Why the boot record cannot be corrupted
docs.text:
The record is written in two copies in two flash sectors. A new copy (sequence number + 1) always goes to the sector that does not hold the newest copy, and the reader takes the CRC-valid copy with the largest sequence number (serial-number arithmetic, RFC 1982). A power cut at any step of a write leaves the other sector intact, so the state read back is either the old one or the new one, never a mixture. The host test cuts power at every flash operation from four different histories and checks exactly this.

Integrity, not authenticity

SHA-256 and CRC-32 detect corruption; they do not stop a forged package from someone who can reach the server. Keep the OTA server on the vehicle network only, until package signing is added (see the limitations of the OTA design).

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• OTA design: flash map, package invariants, watchdog timing proof, verification table.
  • OTA Server API: every endpoint.

docs.title: Deploy the Stack on a Two-Jetson Cluster
Deploy the Stack on a Two-Jetson Cluster
docs.text:
Build one container image per ROS 2 node, bootstrap a k3s cluster on two Jetson Orin Nano Super boards, deploy every node with Helm, and prove that DDS traffic crosses the boards and that the cluster survives the loss of the worker.

Before you start

  • Time: about 3 hours, most of it image builds
  • You need: two Jetson Orin Nano Super boards with JetPack 6.2, an Ethernet switch on the robot, the JetOwl MCUs (optional), the repository cloned with submodules on the master
  • You learn: the image template and runtime contract, k3s settings and where their numbers come from, DDS in Kubernetes, scheduling and failover

One Jetson only?

The same images run with Docker Compose on a single board: see Quick Start, option C.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
Board Role Address (192.168.10.0/24) Runs Jetson #1 master: k3s server + agent .1 API server, image registry :5000, nodes pinned to hardware, floating nodes Jetson #2 worker: k3s agent .4 floating nodes, nodes pinned to worker JetOwl FC / JetOwl Vision MCUs .2 / .3 micro-ROS clients of the agent at .1:8888 MetalLB pool .200–.220 .200 = OTA server

k3s is used because it is a single binary with containerd and a SQLite datastore; a full kubeadm control plane would take a large share of a 6-core, 8 GB board that also runs the robot. There is one server on purpose: an etcd control plane needs a quorum of ⌊n/2⌋ + 1, so two servers tolerate no failure, exactly like one, at twice the load.

docs.title: 1. Network
docs.text:
Both Jetsons and both MCUs go on one switch with static addresses (the MCU firmware has no DHCP):

# master
sudo cp Source/ROS2_JetOwl_Bridge/config/netplan-jetowl.yaml /etc/netplan/60-jetowl.yaml
# worker
sudo cp Kubernetes/cluster/netplan/60-jetowl-worker.yaml /etc/netplan/60-jetowl.yaml
# both: set the interface name first (ip link; enP8p1s0 on the Orin Nano developer kit)
sudo netplan apply

Between the boards, keep open: TCP 6443 (API), 10250 (kubelet), UDP 8472 (flannel VXLAN), TCP 5000 (registry), UDP 7400–7700 (DDS, domain 0) and multicast 239.255.0.1. Wi-Fi stays for the internet and the operator laptop.

docs.title: 2. Bootstrap the cluster
docs.text:
# master: k3s server, registry, nvidia RuntimeClass, kubeconfig; prints the join command
sudo Kubernetes/cluster/install-master.sh
# worker
sudo Kubernetes/cluster/install-worker.sh --token <token printed by the master>
# master: both nodes Ready with their role label
kubectl get nodes -L jetowl.tng-blue.io/role -o wide

The k3s configuration sets values that change failover time and stability:

Setting Value Reason node-status-update-frequency 4 s kubelet status period node-monitor-grace-period 20 s 5 kubelet retries × 4 s; the 40 s default would double failover time system-reserved 500m, 1 GiB JetPack services, Docker, the registry eviction-hard memory.available<300Mi the kubelet evicts before the kernel OOM killer picks a ROS 2 node at random

The resulting allocatable (5.0 CPU / 5.1 GiB on the master, 5.25 CPU / 5.6 GiB on the worker) is the budget the chart's resource requests are checked against.

docs.title: 3. Build the images
docs.text:
The build context is the checkout, so populate the submodules first (the LiDAR AI package needs its NVIDIA sources):

git submodule update --init --recursive

On the master (arm64, native build), push to the cluster registry:

Docker/scripts/build_all.sh --push --tag v0.3.0

From an x86 PC, cross-build with buildx and QEMU instead: Docker/scripts/build_all.sh --platform linux/arm64 --push --tag v0.3.0.

Each image is built from Docker/templates/ros_package.Dockerfile:

  • the build stage builds only the package and the in-repo packages it depends on (colcon build --packages-up-to), with CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=87;
  • the runtime stage keeps install/ and the exec dependencies; the build fails if any installed binary has an unresolved shared library, so a missing <exec_depend> is found at build time, not on the robot.

The entrypoint stays PID 1 and forwards SIGTERM as SIGINT, because ros2 launch in Humble only handles SIGINT. Measured: a clean exit 0 in 0.3 s instead of exit 137 after the grace period.

docs.title: 4. Deploy with Helm
docs.text:
Helm/scripts/deploy.sh --set global.imageTag=v0.3.0     # MetalLB + chart, waits until Ready
make -C Helm status                                     # which Jetson runs what
make -C Helm test                                       # talker on the worker → listener on the master

helm test passes only if a ROS 2 message crosses the Ethernet link between the boards.

Nodes pinned to a device (jetowl-bridge, lidar-slam, stereo, night-vision, the micro-ROS agent and the OTA server) run on the master; the others float and are placed by the scheduler on resource requests, an even pod count and GPU spread. Change a node per robot:

Helm/scripts/deploy.sh --set global.imageTag=v0.3.0 \
    --set nodes.flight-controller.enabled=true \
    --set nodes.mission-planner.enabled=true \
    --set nodes.lidar-ai.placement=worker

The values schema rejects unknown keys and invalid enums before anything is deployed.

docs.title: Why host networking
docs.text: DDS discovery is UDP multicast to 239.255.0.1:7400 + 250·domainId. Flannel's VXLAN does not forward multicast between nodes; the physical switch does. ROS 2 pods therefore use hostNetwork: true, and the Fast DDS profile whitelists the cluster addresses so a participant never announces docker0 (172.17.0.1 on both boards). hostIPC: true and the host /dev/shm are mounted so the shared-memory transport works between pods on the same board; without them, nodes discover each other but never receive data.

docs.title: 5. Operate
docs.text: Task Command Roll out a new tag Docker/scripts/build_all.sh --push --tag v0.3.1 && Helm/scripts/deploy.sh --set global.imageTag=v0.3.1 Roll back helm -n jetowl rollback jetowl Logs kubectl -n jetowl logs deploy/jetowl-ros2-jetson-control-system -f ROS 2 CLI in the cluster kubectl -n jetowl exec -it deploy/jetowl-ros2-jetson-monitoring -- ros2 topic list Resource balance make -C Kubernetes balance Maintenance on the worker make -C Kubernetes drain-worker, later make -C Kubernetes uncordon-worker

docs.title: 6. Test failover
docs.text:
Power off the worker and watch the pods:

watch kubectl -n jetowl get pods -o wide

Expected: the worker becomes unreachable after 20 s + up to 5 s, floating pods tolerate that for 10 s, then are recreated on the master, about 35 s plus container start. The master cannot hold every pod (5.35 CPU / 6.5 GiB requested against 5.0 CPU / 5.1 GiB), so the scheduler preempts by priority: the critical tier and most of the high tier run; normal pods and one GPU perception pod stay Pending until the worker returns.

Losing the master

The worker keeps its pods but nothing is rescheduled, and the MCUs lose their micro-ROS agent (their firmware targets 192.168.10.1). A partition of only the inter-board link can leave both boards running the floating nodes. Design the vehicle's failsafes in the firmware and the flight controller, not in the cluster.
